#3611. 'Vorssaint' Replaced at Least 10 Utility Apps on My Mac

Plenty of Mac apps do one job, and do it quite well. For example, KeyboardCleanTool lets you disable your Mac's keyboard temporarily while you get dust, food particles, and gunk off the keyboard. I love these apps, but if you keep installing utilities, things start to feel crowded; it can be a real problem even trying to remember that you have an app installed for a specific task. This is where Vorssaint comes in: It's the Swiss Army knife of Mac apps, packing over 75 utilities into a single, free resource.

The best thing is that you can choose which of these utilities you wish to enable—if you need only five of Vorssaint's features, you can disable the rest. This prevents the app from becoming a resource hog, which is particularly valuable for those of us with older, base-model MacBooks. Even though Vorssaint has replaced multiple Mac apps on my MacBook, however, it's not always better than the apps it replaces. If you use Vorssaint to set a custom volume level for each Mac app, for example, it doesn't mean Vorssaint can do everything SoundSource does.

Vorssaint is very much a jack of all trades, master of none, and that's perfectly fine for most people. If that sounds like the kind of tool you need, then Vorssaint could be great for you. Here are 10 Vorssaint features that I've used to replace apps on my MacBook:

Unless you're addicted to appearing like you're yelling all the time, you probably don't need the Caps Lock key at all. You can always hold Shift whenever you want to capitalize something, and in my opinion, Caps Lock should be repurposed for something better. Apps such as Raycast allow you to convert Caps Lock into a "hyper key," which means that when you press that button, your computer registers it as a combination of other modifier keys. On my MacBook, pressing Caps Lock equals holding Command-Control-Shift-Alt together, and I've used it to create keyboard shortcuts that don't conflict with those in macOS or third-party apps.

To enable this feature in Vorssaint, open the app, and go to Settings > Features. Go to the "Mouse and keyboard" section, and enable Super key. Vorssaint allows you to map modifier keys to Caps Lock. It also lets you continue using the button for capitalization, switching input sources, or as an alternative way to press the Esc key (useful for keyboards that don't have this button). It works by triggering the "Super key" only when you hold Caps Lock, and toggling the other feature you chose when you press the button once.

Your Mac's Spotlight has a basic clipboard manager, but Vorssaint adds a few more features. The app lets you clean tracking data from URLs, and even adds a "Cut and Paste" feature to your Mac's Finder. The latter is great for people switching from Windows—Finder's cut/paste feature isn't as seamless as the one on Microsoft's platform.

Once you enable these features in Vorssaint, you can cut any file in Finder by pressing Command-X, and paste it elsewhere with Command-V. The URL cleaner is customizable, and it allows you to define parameters to remove. It also allows you to create filters for specific websites, which reduces the chances of breaking URLs when you try this feature. By default, Vorssaint will automatically clean a link the moment you copy one, but you can also manually clean links in the app if you wish to.

The app's clipboard manager has all the basic features you'll need, and it lets you exclude some apps too. This lets you keep Vorssaint from storing clipboard items from sensitive apps. The shortcut to view clipboard history from Vorssaint is Command-Option-Alt-V.

I use Rapidmg, a popular app installer format on the Mac, to auto-mount and install DMG files. After the app is installed, Rapidmg also gets rid of the installer file. Vorssaint has this feature built-in, and you can enable it by going to Vorssaint settings > Features > Disk image installer. It's located under the "Clipboard and files" section.

If you're looking for an app to set a custom volume level for each Mac app, then Vorssaint has a tool for the job. It's good enough to replace basic volume control apps like FineTune, but not nearly as powerful as SoundSource. Vorssaint lets you set a per-app volume level, quickly switch between output devices, and even set priority for audio devices. It doesn't support sending audio to multiple devices at once, tweaking latency levels, boosting volume above the maximum, or sending audio from certain apps only to specific output devices (e.g., Spotify always goes to headphones, VLC always sends audio to speakers, etc.). If you value power-user features, then SoundSource has to be your go-to. For most people, Vorssaint is good enough to get the job done. You can enable volume mixer in the app by going to Vorssaint settings > Features > Volume mixer. It's under the "Sound" section in the app.

There are many good reasons to stop your Mac from going to sleep, such as connecting your MacBook to an external display and using the laptop with its lid closed. Apps such as Amphetamine allow you to keep your Mac from going into sleep mode, and Vorssaint has this feature built-in as well. You can use it by enabling the "Keep awake" feature in the app, which lets you disable sleep mode on your Mac for a custom time interval that ranges from 15 minutes to indefinitely.

If you're missing your iPhone's Dynamic Island on your MacBook, you could install one of several useful notch apps on your Mac. These apps show a now playing widget, brightness or volume levels, calendars, or even have a temporary shelf to help you drag and drop files on your Mac. Vorssaint ships with a notch app, too: Dynamic Island. Once you enable it, Vorssaint's Dynamic Island can show notifications, calendar events, timers, song lyrics, playback queue, etc. Note that this feature is labeled "Experimental" in the app, which means that it's not as stable as most other features. I've also been using it to activate other Vorssaint features such as Keep awake and volume mixer, since Dynamic Island shows toggles to control them.

iStat Menus is one of my favorite Mac apps—it allows me to monitor my MacBook's current load and operating temperatures. Vorssaint also ships with the ability to monitor CPU load, GPU load, RAM usage, network usage, battery temperature, etc. It's not as elegant as iStat Menus, but it'll do the job for those who need a basic system stat monitor. In my tests, though, I observed that Vorssaint incorrectly reports CPU temperature. Two other apps (iStat Menus and TG Pro) reported my Mac's CPU temperature at around 104°F (40°C), but Vorssaint kept showing a number closer to 145°F (63°C). All other temperature readings were nearly identical in the three apps, which indicates that Vorssaint probably has a bug to fix.

Vorssaint can also be a substitute for apps that enhance your Mac's Dock. It allows you to enable features like previewing open windows by hovering over an app's icon in the Dock, quitting apps from the Dock preview, clicking the dock icon to minimize, hide, or cycle between apps' windows, etc. One useful feature allows you to click the green button to maximize any app's window, as opposed to switching to full-screen mode. I don't use it, but I can recommend it to people who switch from Windows and ask me about the maximize button.

macOS doesn't always allow your mouse to work the way you want it to. Third-party "mouse fix" apps add nice features such as smooth scrolling, customizable actions for side buttons, and so on. Vorssaint includes support for smooth scrolling, and a few other features. It lets you map extra mouse buttons to custom keyboard shortcuts, and even has a feature to prevent accidental double-clicks. The latter is good for people who have a mouse with double-click problems. You can enable these features under the "Mouse and keyboard" section in Vorssaint.

Apps like KeyboardCleanTool allow you to temporarily disable your Mac's keyboard for you to give it a good clean, or to allow your cat to sit on the keyboard without disturbing your workflow. Vorssaint supports this, too—you can enable this feature by toggling "Cleaning Mode" under the Tools section in the app. Once you lock the keyboard, you can either click the "Unlock" button or press Esc five times to start typing again.

#3610. Sister Wives’ Christine Details the 'Real' End of Meri and Kody's Relationship

Christine Brown had a heart-to-heart with Meri Brown on Sister Wives about the end of her marriage to Kody Brown.

“I loved my leaving process,” Christine, 54, told Meri, 55, during the Sunday, November 1, episode of the TLC series, referring to her split from Kody, 57, in November 2021, which came less than two years before Meri announced her breakup from Kody in January 2023.

Christine explained that it seemed to be different for Meri, who was Kody’s first of four wives. “I saw that he just drifted you along,” Christine said, suggesting that Meri and Kody’s 2014 legal divorce appeared to be their undoing.

“He did, because was never direct with me and I was willing to figure it out,” Meri confessed, noting that she did a “freaking legal divorce” decades before their actual breakup “thinking things were going to be OK and they were not.”

Meri claimed that Kody “was nice to me for, I don’t know, maybe a month” after that big gesture.

Meri recalled that in 2014, four years after Kody spiritually wed his fourth wife, Robyn Brown, he and Meri got legally divorced “because they were talking about him wanting to adopt Robyn’s kids.”

Meri and Kody legally tied the knot in 1990 before he spiritually wed Janelle Brown, Christine and Robyn, in 1993, 1994 and 2010, respectively. (Like Meri and Christine, Janelle, 57, eventually left Kody as well, confirming her separation in December 2022.)

However, in 2014, Meri agreed to legally separate from their collective spouse and then Kody and Robyn, 48, got legally married, making the adoption of her three children from a prior marriage “easier.”

“Even back then I was like, ‘It’s a mistake. It’s a mistake,’” Christine recalled during Sunday’s episode. “I know that having Kody and Robyn be able to adopt Robyn’s kids was Meri’s goal, and she did it with absolute, pure intentions.”

Christine reflected on seeing that Meri and Kody’s relationship fracture was beyond repair.

“They were struggling before that, for sure, but it was definitely the beginning of the real crumbling between the two of them,” she shared.

During Christine’s discussion with Meri — which marked their first one-on-one conversation since Christine left their plural family — she applauded Meri for being so accommodating with the legal divorce.

“I thought it was for the good of the family,” Meri explained, which Christine totally understood.

However, Christine then confessed that she thought the divorce idea was “kind of planted,” pointing to “a couple of times” when Robyn and Kody both mentioned it in normal conversation.

“Kody’s dad legally divorced his mom to go look for another wife, legally married that wife. So Kody had seen that happen,” Christine told the cameras. “And then in Pinesdale, [Montana], is just another community of our previous church where Robyn mentioned that it happened.”

Christine, who shares six children with Kody, remembered sitting in Meri’s living room in Lehi, Utah, before the family moved and hearing Robyn say it was “beautiful” that this other plural wife “offered to get a legal divorce from her husband so he could legally marry another wife who was coming in with children.”

It was at that moment that Christine said she felt it was part of a bigger plan and that Robyn and Kody were trying to sway Meri into doing the same thing.

“I remember thinking, ‘What are you suggesting here? You think Meri should legally divorce Kody?’ I remember just thinking that and then it happened,” Christine recalled. “And then Meri’s like, ‘This is my idea. I’m coming up with this legal divorce.’ And I’m like, ‘No, you’re not.’”

Janelle agreed with Christine’s account of the situation, saying, “I think there was way more going on whether they were willing to admit it or not. I think so. I think they were wanting to go that direction.”

Meri is still unsure as to how everything went down, telling the cameras, “I don’t know if they had a plan. If it wasn’t a plan, it worked very well in his favor.”

She confessed, “I definitely would have done things different when I divorced him had I been legally married to him. So I think he absolutely benefited. So he can call himself lucky.”

Meri remained in a spiritual union with Kody until January 2023. She was later granted a spiritual divorce from the Wyoming native.

Robyn, meanwhile, is still married to Kody but they are no longer a part of the show.

Sister Wives airs on TLC Sundays at 10 p.m. ET.

#3609. Actor Keith McDermott on Robert Wilson’s Legacy and Ghostwriting His Memoir: “I Saw a Robert Wilson Play and It Changed My Life”

Over the more than 50-year period of his career, Wilson was arguably the most produced American theater director in Europe, if not the world. His aesthetic style has permeated European theater and opera culture to the extent that few directors have remained uninfluenced by what is commonly referred to as the “Wilsonian” use of lighting, set design, and performance style. However, he is not well-known in his own country.

The Robert Wilson productions that have reached the United States are some of the most iconic stage works of the 20th and 21st century: Einstein on the Beach and Lohengrin at the Metropolitan Opera House and at least 10 full productions at Brooklyn Academy of Music. Even in New York, Wilson’s artistic home, and even among artists, a not uncommon response at the mention of his name is “Should I know who that is?”

However, there is another response from New Yorkers of my generation, those of us living here when the city was at the artistic peak of the ’60s and ’70s, when Balanchine oversaw the New York City Ballet, Joe Papp headed the Public Theater, Andy Warhol ran The Factory, and apartments were affordable. That response, my response, is “I saw a Robert Wilson play and it changed my life.”

In 1975, a friend offered me a free ticket to a Broadway play. The title was A Letter for Queen Victoria, and I assumed I was in for a fusty historical drama, but as a young actor pursuing a commercial career, I never passed up an opportunity to see a play, especially if it was free.

Robert Wilson's A Letter for Queen Victoria.

The play began before the houselights went down as a young man and woman in ordinary dress stood in front of the curtain on opposite sides of the stage slowly turning in place. Nothing about their slow, hypnotic movement suggested “performance” until the houselights began to dim. Still turning, they raised their hands from their sides. Their palms, pressed in turmeric, became a blur of orange as their revolutions increased in speed and the curtain rose. The cast included the director’s grandmother as Queen Victoria, and a neurodivergent teenager, Christopher Knowles, whose nonacting presence broke the fourth wall, as he shielded his eyes from the stage lights to gaze into the house.

Audience members left in droves. A woman shouted something about child abuse on her way to the exit. But I sat mesmerized as the play evolved through a series of scenes unconnected by narrative or plot, fantastic in design, exquisitely lit, and often extraordinarily slow. Those of us who stayed until the end leapt to our feet, applauding and cheering for the actors, call after call. I stumbled from the theater into the city night feeling as if I had fallen in love.

My enthusiasm for that play led to both a professional and personal involvement with Bob (as anyone who knows him calls him). As a performer, I have appeared in five Wilson productions in various parts of the world and understudied him in a one‐man show. As a writer, I published an article about his chair collection and a roman à clef in which a character based on Bob pretty much takes over the book. In addition to our working relationship, Bob, a fellow Texan, has been my friend for over 50 years, and early in 2023 he asked me to ghostwrite his memoir.

Our sessions began formally at the Watermill Center, “a laboratory for the arts and humanities” on the South Fork of Long Island, founded by Bob in 1992. He had an apartment there where he stayed when he was in town. Assuming we’d work through his life chronologically, I came armed with questions about his childhood in Waco, Texas, his parents, and his schooling. But later, transcribing our recorded sessions, I cringed at my attempts to get Bob back on topic as he segued into a tale about absentmindedly depositing his airline ticket into a mailbox, then trying to board the plane with the postcards he had meant to mail, or a harrowing memory of six weeks spent in a Greek prison for a bit of hash discovered by airport security. My interruptions only spoiled the spontaneous flow of Bob’s thoughts.

Bob was a storyteller. Everyone who knew and worked with him was familiar with his stories, often told in a regional Texas twang and often more than once – and occasionally with a remarkable addendum. For instance, I knew that in his 20s, while working as a recreational therapist at the Goldwater Memorial Hospital for the terminally ill, Bob had choreographed a “dance” for quadriplegic patients in iron lungs, tying Day-Glo strings to mouth sticks they used to turn book pages that connected to mobiles hung from the ceiling. But in the retelling, I learned that Bob, after attending an Otis Redding concert, had persuaded the singer to come to the ward to accompany his quadriplegic dancers.

Once we gave up the chronological approach and Bob, unburdened by the need to deliver “The Story of My Life,” began to think in terms of “Life Stories,” our process relaxed and stories flowed. In addition to scheduled sessions, I could collect them everywhere, because Bob told them everywhere: at dinner parties, in the car, over the coffee and English muffins I began to deliver early each morning, or on our daily golf cart trips around the Watermill grounds. I always met him armed with my tape recorder.

A story he told frequently, both publicly, in interviews, and privately, was about seeing a policeman about to strike a young boy and intervening. From the sounds the boy made, Bob realized he was deaf. The boy, Raymond Andrews, was diagnosed as ineducable, but Bob realized he simply relied on visual cues not words. At 27 Bob became Raymond’s legal guardian and enrolled him in a school for the deaf. Raymond flourished in the creative community Bob created at his Spring Street loft (in SoHo before it was SoHo). Using Raymond’s drawings and his own observations of the boy, Bob created Deafman Glance, a seven-hour silent opera that signaled his European renown.

Bob told many stories about Jessye Norman, but the one that always brought him and his listeners to tears was of the great singer attempting to get through a Winterreise concert just after 9/11. During the third song, Norman began to cry and had to stop singing. When she regained control, she stood for 10 minutes, motionless, in silence, while the audience wept.

Bob’s vast social network also included socialites and celebrities, and those stories are filled with irresistible gossip: Marlene Dietrich divulged the name of the only contemporary American performer she completely admired (spoiler alert: it was Tina Turner); Diana Vreeland swallowed vials of cod liver oil to act as a buffer for vodka before an evening out; Samuel Beckett claimed that his lead actress in Happy Days was so brilliant because she didn’t understand a word she said.

In June of 2025, Bob went to Lithuania to stage rehearsals of a new production and then to Ljubljana, Slovenia, to direct Tristan and Isolde. When he was away, he sent me emails with story topics for our next session: “Ask me about my boat trip in the Middle East with Helen de Rothschild,” “Ask me about Louis Malle offering me the lead in Pretty Baby.”

When Bob returned to Watermill in July, we were to meet for final interviews, although by that time, I had all the material needed for the book. Shortly before my travels, I received a message that Bob’s health had declined, and he would be unable to see me. He died a week later on July 31 in his Watermill apartment.

Months after Bob’s death, I was still listening to and transcribing our taped conversations. In one conversation, recorded when we were having dinner at an Indian restaurant, Bob was telling me a story about being dressed as Santa Claus and handing out presents in Bali, where he spent every Christmas. Suddenly, he stopped mid-sentence and after a short silence, said, “I love you, Keith.”

I love you too, Bob, you changed my life.

THE SPACE BEHIND THE FACE, a memoir by the visionary theater director and visual artist, Robert Wilson, is published by Penguin Press and arrives on November 3.

#3608. Six Things to Do Between Sets at the Gym

Rest is a crucial part of strength training. Depending on the exercise and your goals, you may find yourself resting 30 seconds, or one minute, or three to five minutes. So what do you actually do during that time? Let’s talk about your options, both in terms of training effectiveness and gym etiquette.

As awkward as it may feel at first, this is the best option for most people, most of the time. Actually rest. Don’t stretch, don’t work a different muscle; just allow your body to recover.

Some gyms will have stools, benches, or folding chairs near the platforms where people are lifting heavy (and thus need the longest rests). I’m mostly thinking of powerlifting and weightlifting gyms, but I’ve been to big-box gyms like Crunch that provide seating as well. And impromptu seats are common in many other places—who hasn’t sat on a plyo box or some other convenient surface?

There are plenty of little actions that you take at the gym (or should take) that are not explicitly exercise. The rest between sets is the perfect time to do these little maintenance tasks. Things like:

Change the weights to what you’ll need for your next set.

Write down what you just lifted in your notebook or lifting app.

If you took a video, watch it to give yourself feedback for the next set.

Trim that video so that you (or your coach, or your friends) don’t have to watch all 20 seconds of you fumbling with the camera and adjusting your belt before you actually lift.

Have a drink of water and, if needed, a snack.

Clean up after yourself! Rack any plates and dumbbells you aren’t using.

During the last few sets of an exercise, it’s time to start thinking about what you’ll do next. This could mean grabbing the equipment you’ll need or changing your shoes, but it's also an excellent opportunity to start warming up—especially if it’s an exercise that can benefit from a little gentle mobility work.

Let’s say you have a few sets of squats left, but after that you’ll do some overhead press. You probably want to warm up your shoulders with some mobility work so that you won’t be so tight when you hit that nice stable overhead position. Or maybe it’s the other way around, and you’re pressing, but next you’ll do squats. It’s a great time to start doing some ankle mobility work so that you’ll be able to comfortably hit a deeper squat.

When the weights are routine, I sit and chill. When they get heavy, I need to pace. (At weightlifting competitions, I not only stake out a warmup platform, I also pick out a walking path that I can pace between attempts.)

Or if you’re more of a cheerful, high-energy person, maybe you just want to dance. You’ll see this most often from people who lift at home, or at a chummy small gym where an impromptu dance party might occur between friends. Alone in my garage gym, I’ve been known to put on some good karaoke songs and sing along, with or without dancing.

The idea is not to get some extra cardio or get your steps in, but just to stay busy and loose and have fun—or, if you’re nervous about a big lift, to keep your head. At a busy commercial gym, make sure not to walk too far away, and consider leaving your water bottle or gym bag on your equipment to let people know it’s still taken.

I promise that it is actually OK to look at your phone between sets. You’re probably doing it anyway. There’s your lifting app, your videos that you took to check your squat form—and, yes, your usual texting and social media stuff.

The risk you’re taking here is that you’ll get distracted and rest too long. Too much rest, say more than 10 minutes, can make you feel both mentally and physically unprepared. Long rests can also lengthen your workout. Sticking to the minimum necessary rest times will get you in and out of the gym a lot faster.

From others’ perspective, a person who sits on a machine for 10 minutes scrolling is committing an unforgivable sin in gym etiquette. Don’t take longer rests than you need, if you’re holding up equipment. (That said, if you’re polite to others who approach, and you accept requests to “work in” (take turns) while you scroll, you’re morally in the clear.)

For your own sake, set a timer when you do anything that might distract you between sets. I like how I can program rest times into a Garmin watch workout, but Hevy also has a timer, and you can always use the regular timer function on your watch or phone.

Another tip: Be mindful about what you’re doing on your phone. Now is not the time to get into an argument on the internet, or check your work email and see what will be waiting for you back at the office. It is a good time to play little games on your phone, or read an ebook, or put together your next great workout playlist.

I’m leaving this option for last because I don’t want it to be your go-to. Just because you can do one exercise while resting for another, doesn’t mean you should.

Why not? If you really want to give squats your full energy, for example, don’t do pull-ups on the squat rack in between. You’ll fatigue yourself more than you realize, and you won’t do your best on those squats.

But supersets can be great if you’re willing to sacrifice a little weight for a lot of time. They’re best for exercises where the exact weight doesn’t matter—you can pair bicep curls with tricep extensions, or pull-ups with dips (so long as you’re a person who can bang out multiple reps of each with ease).

To do a superset, you just do a set of the first exercise, then a set of the second, then rest a short time (if needed at all), and repeat. I have a list of the best superset pairs here—usually you’ll want to do opposing muscles, like a push exercise with a pull exercise.

#3607. Pete Davidson and Ex Elsie Hewitt Reunite for Halloween With Daughter

Pete Davidson and his ex Elsie Hewitt reunited to celebrate their daughter’s first Halloween.

“Smells like Halloween,” Hewitt, 30, captioned a Sunday, November 1, Instagram carousel that included a photo of the former couple with Scottie, 10 months. In the sweet family picture, the model and Davidson, 32, both cooed over their child as she sat in a red wagon dressed as Tony Soprano from HBO’s The Sopranos.

The adorable outfit included a bathrobe-clad Scottie holding onto a plush cigar while a neon “Bada Bing!” sign hung from the corner of her ride in a nod to the late James Gandolfini’s fictional character.

Hewitt and Davidson, who split in May after she gave birth to Scottie in December 2025, both wore dark sunglasses as they bent down and smiled at their daughter in her wheels.

Fans took to the comments section of the post to share their approval of both Scottie’s costume and the couple’s public coparenting move. “I’m sorry, is her hair slicked back? I am LIVING,” wrote one person, while another commented, “We love seeing healthy co-parenting.”

The Sopranos nod held sentimental value for both parents, as their romance involved bonding over Davidson’s adoration for the series, which ran from 1999 to 2007. During an interview with People in December last year, the Saturday Night Live alum recalled how his ex had surprised him by getting members of the Sopranos cast to wish him a happy birthday via a recorded video.

Adding that he had hoped to one day introduce his child to the show “as early as possible,” he told the outlet, “That’s the only thing I really need is, from my soul, is for them [his child] to enjoy The Sopranos the way I do. And then everything else, I just want it to be happy.”

Us confirmed in July that Davidson and Hewitt had reached a “joint agreement pertaining to their child,” according to a source. A statement was also shared with Us via the former couple’s reps.

“We are cooperatively coparenting our daughter whose well-being remains our top priority, and we are fully committed to working together to give her love from both of us,” the joint statement read.

As for what led to their split, an insider claimed at the time that various “stressors” had contributed. “They tried to make it work, but there were different stressors, including having a baby together as two people who didn’t yet know each other that well,” the second source stated. “They are both trying to make it work and have made accommodations in their schedules for the baby.”

#3606. Is Ken Paxton’s Senate Campaign in Texas the Bitter End of Trumpism?

At Coyote Crossing Saloon, a smoke-filled dive bar off Interstate 37, a 64-year-old Texas native named Tracey was showing me his teeth. He’s missing about half of them—a casualty, he said, of toothpicks soaked in horse liniment that serve as a potent stimulant for truckers looking to stay up late on long-haul drives. Tracey is a big fan of President Donald Trump. He voted for him three times and still supports him, even after all the excesses of his second term. But he can’t stomach Ken Paxton.

Dragging on a cigarette, he pointed to the Texas attorney general and Republican Senate candidate’s alleged corruption, his reputed infidelity, and the case of a plea deal his office offered to a Waco man charged with sexually abusing a young boy. “Just because you have all this money, how are you gonna just do as you please and nobody’s gonna say nothing?” Tracey remains a fan of the state’s Republican governor, Greg Abbott. “He’ll win, so I’m happy about that.” But Paxton? “Get him out of there.”

Texas attorney general Ken Paxton embarked on a bus tour of the Lone Star State as his Senate campaign draws to a close.

If Paxton has lost voters like Tracey, Republicans might be in trouble. Texas hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, and this seat could determine who will control Congress for the final two years of Trump’s presidency. Yet the collapse of Trump’s approval across the country has put even red states like Texas in play for Democrats, creating a powerful undercurrent that Paxton’s opponent, James Talarico, has surfed to a narrow but steady lead in the polls. That’s turned Texas into a money pit: $500 million has been blown on advertising already, thanks in part to at least $168 million pumped into the state by Elon Musk, and it’s on track to be the most expensive Senate race in history.

It didn’t have to be this difficult. Since 2002, the seat has been occupied by Senator John Cornyn, who ran for reelection with the backing of the Republican establishment and a sizable war chest. But in the primary, the president backed Paxton, a scandal-plagued culture warrior who went above and beyond Trump’s loyalty tests, while Cornyn drew suspicion that he was fair-weather MAGA. Now Trump has placed a risky bet. These midterms are a referendum on the president, but this race, more than any other, is a gauge of his movement: Can a candidate with many of Trump’s failings but little of his charisma careen into the United States Senate?

Even in the ruby-red counties of West Texas, Trump’s support is slipping. Will Paxton pay for it?

A crowd in Sherman, Texas, settles down into movie theater recliners to watch Paxton speak.

This is the final sprint of the Paxton campaign, a frenetic bus odyssey dubbed the Come and Take It Tour. (There’s a cannon printed on the side of the bus.) The voyage has swept through the border towns of McAllen and Laredo, up through exurbs like Selma—just outside San Antonio—on to Austin and Waco and Dallas, then out through hundreds of miles of high plains to the West Texas towns of Amarillo and Lubbock, and then down to Corpus Christi for a rally with Trump himself.

“The person that is without sin, please cast the first stone,” said Pastor Ruben Mendez in his opening prayer at Paxton’s campaign event in Selma. The room was silent. “I don’t think so. I don’t think there’s anybody that can do that.” Mendez, the pastor of Iglesia Shalom, a small nondenominational church tucked down an alleyway in a suburb nearby, was speaking to a crowd crammed into the Blue Bonnet Palace, a country music venue in a corrugated iron barn just off the highway. A cardboard cutout of Brooks & Dunn hung above the stage alongside a motionless disco ball.

Paxton is locked in a close race with James Talarico, whom Trump has nicknamed “Talafreako.”

The pastor’s reminder that “King David was a flawed man” was met with scattered applause. If the subtext of this homily wasn’t clear enough, a protester soon made it explicit. “Why were you in Dubai?” a young man yelled as Paxton took the stage. He was swiftly bounced by security to chants of “USA!” from the faithful.

The protester was referencing the latest chapter of the biblical Paxton oppo file. The Wall Street Journal reported that Paxton spent New Year’s Eve 2024 partying in Dubai with Tracy Duhon, his rumored mistress, as well as two men who were then fugitives from US justice, one of whom had donated to Paxton. This indiscretion joins a long list of scandals that supporters of Paxton are willing to overlook to back the candidate (and, perhaps more importantly, keep Texas red). On the tour, they often invoked faith to make their case.

House Republican Darrell Issa, who served as chairman of the House Oversight Committee and worked with Paxton when he was a crusading state attorney general, stumped for the candidate on his swing from San Antonio to Georgetown. When I asked why he felt compelled to campaign for Paxton given the baggage, Issa echoed Pastor Mendez.

The line was lengthy to get into the rally in Corpus Christi.

“Is President Trump a man without flaws? No. But neither was Andy Jackson, neither was Bill Clinton, neither was Abraham Lincoln,” the congressman said. “So you judge somebody in elected office based on the honor that they bring to the office, the energy they bring, and the initiatives that they’re involved in, and that’s where [Paxton] excels. So am I going to say that this is somebody that, like our savior, was without sin? No. But I’m not somebody without sin, and neither are any of the voters.”

Some would argue that Paxton’s sins are more exotic than those of your ordinary Texan. He was charged with two counts of felony securities fraud by Texas prosecutors and in 2024 reached a deal to avoid trial that involved paying nearly $300,000 in restitution. Separately, the Texas House impeached him in 2023 on charges of bribery, corruption, and abusing his office. (Paxton has denied the allegations that led to his impeachment.) With state legislators under intense pressure from Trump, he was acquitted by the Senate. “Yes, it is true that my intervention through TRUTH SOCIAL saved Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton from going down,” Trump boasted afterward.

There’s also Paxton’s reputation for jet-setting: In his 11 years as attorney general, an Associated Press investigation found, Paxton spent an extraordinary amount of time traveling to plush locales including “California wine country, Caribbean resorts, and European tourism hot spots.” It cost the taxpayers at least $1.9 million to cover the expenses of his security detail. And then there was, of course, the 2013 surveillance video that caught Paxton pocketing a man’s $1,000 Montblanc pen. (His campaign called the incident a “mix-up,” and Paxton returned the pen after he was contacted by a sheriff’s deputy.)

Even some of the ads supporting him carry a bit of a shrug. Angela Paxton, who is suing her husband for divorce on “biblical grounds,” which is King James for “cheating,” appears in a spot urging Texans to vote Republican down the ticket. “Let’s talk about the elephant in the room,” she says at the start of the ad, which ends without any further mention of the elephant.

For many in the Republican establishment, these indiscretions have pushed Paxton beyond the pale, but that’s of little concern to the nominee’s supporters. “He may not have his life together,” said Janet, a Paxton backer from Corpus Christi, “but he’s better than the alternative.”

There was strong turnout for a Trump rally to support Paxton in Corpus Christi.

Kevin, a 62-year-old from the San Antonio suburbs, brought his wife to see Paxton speak in Selma. “I believe in this country there is a battle between good and evil,” he said. “I try to judge characters in a biblical sense.” Where does that leave Paxton, a man accused of violating quite a few of the commandments? “I’m okay with Ken Paxton,” Kevin said, waving a hand as I ran down the list of transgressions. “I believe Trump is the best president we’ve ever had. And we got to have people in there to support him.”

Jason Norton, 50, a bearded and tattooed pastor at King’s Trail Cowboy Church who delivered the prayer at Paxton’s stop north of Dallas, had a similarly permissive view of his alleged infidelity. “Christian does not mean perfect. Nobody would approve of that. And I’m sure he probably regrets it. But what he did hurt himself and his family. What Talarico’s doing will hurt the entire state.”

In a quaint historic town north of Fort Worth, I met Steve Bannon at the Texas headquarters of his War Room podcast. A longtime Paxton backer, Bannon has spent much of this campaign season in the state, broadcasting to the Trump base while helping to advise the Republican’s campaign. “We have not seen the data yet that shows part of our coalition actually coming out and voting against Trump,” Bannon told me. “I think most of them are staying home. That’s a huge win for us. If they come out and vote against us, we’re fucked.”

After Musk dumped $168 million into the race, Republican super PACs pumped out ads casting Talarico as too extreme for Texas. The Democrat’s disposition as a love-thy-trans-neighbor seminarian is a cover for something far more sinister, the argument goes. “Even the Bible says the devil comes as an angel of light,” Pastor Norton told me. “Just because somebody’s sweet doesn’t mean they’re right.”

It doesn’t help the Democrat that, like many in the party, he dabbled in the kind of heady progressive rhetoric trendy in the early 2020s, something anathema to red-state voters. Among the hits, of which Texans are regularly reminded in Paxton’s speeches, Trump’s posts, and endless campaign ads: Talarico’s remark in 2021 that “God is nonbinary”; his comment in the same year that there are “six really common biological sexes” and his description of himself as “a Christian who hates Christianity”; his 2022 run for reelection to the Texas House, which he said would be a vegan campaign, reasoning that reducing meat consumption was “necessary to fight climate change”; and his comment that the American flag is a “complicated symbol.”

Talarico has since walked back some of these lines, calling them “cringey” and “provocative.” But Musk’s money cannon ensures Texas voters are relentlessly confronted by them, and the race appears to have tightened in the final stretch of the campaign. For voters susceptible to these kinds of criticisms of Talarico, a Paxton rally provides a potent narrative. The notes from his stump speech that draw the loudest applause can drive the neutral observer to mild psychosis. We’re going to stop Sharia law from coming to Texas, goes one. The Pfizer vaccine was less than 1% effective, offers another. And of course: James Talarico wants to trans your kids.

Paxton was greeted by a sea of red hats as he arrived onstage.

That last bit is one of Paxton’s favorites, and it hit hard in some of the more incandescent-red counties we passed through. “I mean, this guy is really obsessed with transitions,” Paxton mused into the mic, winding up for the big delivery. “He wants to transition our kids, he wants to transition Texas off of the oil and gas industry.” (Wry pause.) “How about we transition him and his crazy ideas right out of Texas!” (Applause, cheers, hoots, and hollers as Paxton stepped back from the podium and smirked, almost bashfully, eyes darting back and forth as he soaked up the response.)

Some of the attacks on Talarico are more extreme. Paxton and a number of his campaign surrogates warned that the Democrat would help usher Sharia law into Texas. When I met with Bannon, he introduced me to Patriot Mobile cofounder Glenn Story, who’s active in Texas politics and counts Paxton as a friend. “I’m the one who told him to start talking about Sharia law,” Story said. “You go up to the Costco near me? Towelheads everywhere,” he said, using a slur for Muslims. “Come with me, I’ll show you.” Reluctant to spend my afternoon driving around looking for people who might appear Muslim, I declined.

At a stop in Sanger, a small town in a ruby-red county north of Dallas, the star of the warm-up acts was Brandon Gill, a young House Republican who has emerged as a favorite among the party’s hard-line base. He walked out to a roaring welcome, and one man shouted, “Brandon for president!” The heckle was deftly parried by Gill: “Let’s say Ken Paxton for Senate first.” As Gill ran through the list of well-worn criticisms of Talarico’s liberalism, Stacey, a woman in the crowd, shouted: “It’s demonic!”

“That’s right,” Gill replied. “It is demonic.”

Outside the venue, I spoke with Stacey and her friend Claire, two Paxton superfans from nearby who called themselves “MAHA moms.”

“He seems like a nice man,” Stacey said of Talarico. “He’s just misguided. If he was my neighbor, I’d vote for him to be on my HOA board. But not for the Senate.” They were confident that Paxton would keep the seat red. But Claire was concerned that her parents, both Republicans, had written in names in protest of Paxton’s candidacy.

On a good day, Ken Paxton is not a gifted orator. This was a bad day. It was Sunday night, the last stop of the weekend, and the candidate walked onto a stage at Schulman’s Movie Bowl Grille in Sherman, a highway town 60 miles north of Dallas, to speak to a few dozen supporters picking at tacos while leaning back in big pleather recliners.

By this point I had seen Paxton deliver his stump speech, a 15-minute case for his Senate candidacy, some half a dozen times. At Schulman’s Movie Bowl Grille, his delivery was pained. He seemed tired. He stumbled over his jokes, stopping and returning to the top after realizing he forgot the punch line. He struggled through a section meant to serve as a blistering indictment of his opponent, and he eventually spent several minutes looking down at the podium and listing Talarico’s crimes against Texas off a piece of paper as the crowd sat in silence.

At one point an elderly man with a walker had had enough.

“More enthusiasm!” he shouted from the audience.

Paxton looked up from his papers and out into the crowd. “What?”

“More enthusiasm!” the man shouted again.

“Yes,” Paxton said meekly. “We all need a little more enthusiasm to go to the polls.”

Trump never hesitates to remind voters at his rallies that Paxton “may not dress right, he may not talk perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen.” The candidate has a lazy eye, a casualty of a childhood accident in which a berry was thrown at his face, requiring multiple surgeries, and a subsequent college basketball injury. He presents as meek, almost sheepish, and speaks in a monotone that belies his reputation as a bare-knuckle radical. He slurs his words and stumbles over his lines.

Trump rallied the faithful for Paxton in Corpus Christi.

“Darrell,” he said at one stop, addressing Issa, “California arreddy has tt—you already have two senators, you d—we don’t need a third.” He’s less the guy you want to get a beer with, per the old campaign cliché, and more the guy you feel a bit sorry for when it’s his turn to address the room at a regional sales conference. At a Trump rally for Paxton in Lubbock, the president told the crowd that his praise of Jon Husted’s “very powerful ass” boosted the senator’s election campaign in Ohio. “Maybe I should do that with Ken Paxton,” he mused, “but I’m not sure your body is going to qualify.”

For Talarico and the Texas Democrats, who haven’t won a seat in the United States Senate since 1988, the Paxton campaign presents an extraordinary opportunity. “Billy Begala says: For the last 30 years, all you had to do to win in Texas is win the Republican primary and then go on vacation,” said veteran Democratic strategist Paul Begala, whose son Billy works in Texas politics. Paxton may have taken that truism a little too far. After announcing his candidacy for the Republican nomination in an appearance on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show, he “cleared his calendar and booked a hotel in Augusta, Georgia, during the storied Masters golf tournament,” according to the Associated Press, “a trip that cost Texas taxpayers at least $25,000.” Over July Fourth weekend, while Talarico hit the trail, Paxton was in Europe, sightseeing in London and Iceland with his rumored mistress. As Talarico raised tens of millions of dollars from small-dollar donations throughout the summer, Paxton struggled to keep up. A week before the general election, Talarico had raised $158 million to Paxton’s $39 million.

“Ken is a different type of candidate in modern times,” Bannon said. “He has a hardcore grassroots base, but he’s not a good fundraiser.” In the primary against Cornyn, Paxton “didn’t raise any serious money. This was primarily a grassroots-driven thing.”

Paxton, Bannon added, is “a populist fire-breather who is not particularly charismatic.”

The last-ditch operation to save the populist fire-breather who is not particularly charismatic came this week in the form of two Trump rallies. They may end up as the last major events of the campaign. On Thursday, the Paxton campaign announced it was canceling a rally in El Paso scheduled for Sunday, just two days before the election.

At the first of Trump’s appearances, in Corpus Christi, I watched from the press pen as Border Patrol union chief Paul Perez revved up the crowd with a question. “Is Texas Trump country?” he bellowed. A sea of bright red hats, bobbing in chaotic unison in a portside hangar, went ballistic. They had braved the rain and the dour mood spreading across the country to see a president in whom they very much still believed. But across Texas, the cracks in Trump’s support are deepening. Just two years after he beat Kamala Harris in the state by more than 1.5 million votes, The Economist’s poll tracker finds Trump’s approval in Texas is underwater by 18 points. This has fueled fears among the state’s Republicans that many of those who broke for Trump in 2024 could stay home this year or, God forbid, vote for the Democrat who thinks God is nonbinary.

Many rallygoers were decked out in full American flag regalia.

Another’s shirt echoed the Paxton campaign bus.

“Clearly, it has been a challenge for Ken to run during difficult personal times, but one of the reasons we admire him is that he is resilient,” said Matt Schlapp, the chairman of the Conservative Political Action Conference, who held a fundraiser for Paxton at his Virginia home last month. “He will win this race, but, like last time, there will be some fear and trembling along the way.”

Others in the coalition aren’t so sure. “Paxton is in deep shit,” Rich Baris, a pro-Trump pollster, said in a podcast appearance this week.

Trump may rally the base, but it’s hard to see how a historically unpopular president making the race about him helps with the broader electorate. After the president commanded Republicans to host a “Trumpapalooza” midterm convention that served more as a celebration of his presidency than as a typical party congress, Paxton privately told donors the event hurt his campaign. “When we did that convention—it dropped our numbers,” Paxton said, according to audio of his comments obtained by The New York Times. “Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.”

At the rally in Corpus Christi, Trump spoke for more than an hour. He extolled the glories of his presidency and made little mention of Paxton. After airing a supercut video of Talarico’s cringiest comments, Trump turned to the crowd. “The only man standing between Texas and this raging lunatic is a man named President Donald J. Trump, thank you!” he said. As the crowd went wild, Trump added: “And I need the help of Paxton.”

On the Come and Take It bus tour, Paxton was less a glimpse of Trumpism’s future than a showcase of what might be left behind when Trump is gone. The familiar accommodations were still required: overlook the scandals, forgive the personal failings, keep faith with the fighter standing between you and the forces of darkness. But there was none of the showmanship that made those demands easier to accept in Trump. The Paxton cocktail is the controversy without the charisma—and a test of whether a record of pure allegiance to Trump is enough for a Republican to win Texas. Defeat may well announce the bitter end of pure Trumpism, or at least prove that Trump alone is the movement. When he leaves the White House in 2029, what will remain of it?

Paxton is not known for his oratory—or his skills as a fundraiser.

Rosario Dawson and Hayden Christensen know exactly how to get Star Wars fans worked up. Put them together, add a little Anakin-and-Ahsoka nostalgia, and people are already paying attention. Wrap both actors in sheer blue fabric so they look suspiciously like Force ghosts, and suddenly everyone starts wondering whether Dave Filoni is trying to tell us something about an upcoming movie release or another new Star Wars project. That is exactly what happened after Dawson shared a photo with Christensen that put a very funny spin on their Ahsoka connection.

In an Instagram post, the two Star Wars mainstays are not actually dressed as Ahsoka Tano and Anakin Skywalker. Christensen appears to be wearing regular clothes under a layer of translucent blue layer, while Dawson wears what looks more like a medieval or fantasy costume. If anything, the dress gives off a little Princess Fiona energy. See for yourself in her post below:

A post shared by rosariodawson (@rosariodawson)

Dawson made the joke even more obvious with her caption: “MAY THE FORCE GHOSTS BE WITH YOU 👻👻.”

The costumes are goofy, simple and immediately recognizable. Christensen looking like a Force ghost is also perfectly reasonable within Star Wars movie canon. Dawson getting the same treatment, however, is where fans started getting nervous. Because, uh… Why is Rosario Dawson a Force ghost?

To be clear, nobody at Lucasfilm announced the death of Ahsoka Tano's death through an Instagram costume photo. Dawson is not dressed as Ahsoka here, and there is no reason to think she casually spoiled one of the biggest possible developments in Ahsoka Season 2. That didn't stop fans from noticing the implication and asking a ton of questions.

Comments under the Clerks 2 actress's post quickly filled with people who remembered that becoming a Force ghost usually requires a fairly serious prerequisite. Fans wrote:

I understand the reaction. Ahsoka has survived Order 66, Darth Vader, the World Between Worlds and enough lightsaber fights to make most Jedi reconsider the profession entirely. She has also spent years bouncing between animated and live-action Star Wars, becoming one of the franchise's most durable characters in the process.

Christensen as a Jedi specter has precedent. Anakin appeared as a Force ghost at the end of Ahsoka Season 1, and the original trilogy was later reworked to insert the actor into the old footage. Christensen is also returning for Season 2, with Anakin expected to remain part of Tano's story.

Dawson's Ahsoka, meanwhile, is still very much alive when Season 2 begins. She and Sabine Wren remain stranded beyond the known galaxy while Grand Admiral Thrawn has returned home and prepares for whatever comes next. So when the actress playing her suddenly appears next to Anakin's actor, both covered in ghostly blue fabric, fans will read into it.

For now, though, I am choosing the much less stressful explanation. They found some blue fabric, put it over their heads, and somebody took a photo. Nobody is dying. Probably.

Season 2 of Ahsoka hits the streaming calendar on January 20, 2027, for everyone with a Disney+ subscription. Fans can also stream all of the Star Wars movies -- including the prequels featuring Hayden Christensen -- using that same membership.

#3604. You Can Now Lock Your Private ChatGPT Conversations With a PIN

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you have personal conversations with ChatGPT that you don't want others to see, you can now add an extra layer of security for those specific chats. The new Locked Chats feature allows you to hide sensitive conversations behind a four-digit account PIN (or biometric authentication on mobile), meaning others with access to your device or screen can't read them.

Locked chats are retained in your chat history—unlike temporary chats, which are private conversations that aren't saved by default—so you can return to or continue them at any point. However, once locked, they are hidden from your regular chat history, pinned chats, and regular conversation search. To access them, you have to go to Projects > Locked chats and enter your PIN or device unlock method (such as Face ID or Touch ID).

To start a locked chat for the first time, open an existing conversation that you want to keep private and open the options menu. Select Lock chat > Lock chat and create or enter your account PIN. This moves the conversation to your locked chats project. You can repeat this with any existing conversation or start a locked chat from scratch under Projects > Locked Chats by entering your PIN or authentication method and typing a message to launch the chat. When you're done, select Lock now to end access to locked chats and hide them from the sidebar.

Note that if you don't already have an account PIN set up, you should be prompted to do so the first time you attempt to lock a chat. Select Create a PIN, enter your four-digit code, and enter it again to confirm. You can also enable biometric authentication in Account PIN settings. If you reset your account PIN at any point, all locked chats are permanently deleted and cannot be recovered.

Locked chats are available on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans on both mobile and desktop apps. The feature is not available for ChatGPT for Healthcare. There are other limitations, too: For example, temporary, archived, and group chats can't be locked, nor can those with shared links, scheduled and background tasks, or meeting recordings. OpenAI says locked chats are rolling out gradually, so they may not be available to all users yet.

Brittany Mahomes is calling out NFL officials after the Kansas City Chiefs suffered their second consecutive loss.

“You can’t tell me you call that on a game winning TD [touchdown], oh wait yeah I can cause it’s us,” Brittany, the wife of quarterback Patrick Mahomes, wrote via her Instagram Stories before adding a smiling face emoji following the Sunday, November 1, Chiefs game against the Denver Broncos. The Chiefs were defeated 28-24.

Brittany, 31, continued in white text over a black background, “That was the weakest call I have ever seen, you can’t tell me otherwise.”

The post was later screenshot and shared via X by NFL insider Ari Meirov, whose followers disagreed with Brittany’s take on the fallout. “No way Brittany Mahomes is complaining about refs bruh,” one fan wrote with crying face emojis, while another wrote, “Chiefs fans crying about the refs is amazing to me.”

Brittany is a dedicated public supporter of her husband, 31, who played a strong personal game on Sunday, passing for 321 yards and three touchdowns. She’s a fixture at most Chiefs games, often bringing the couple’s three children, Sterling, 5, Bronze, 3, and Golden, 21 months, along with her.

She’s also been vocal about on-field action, recently throwing subtle shade at Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak following his team’s October 4 loss to the Chiefs. “We’re winning. We’re gonna win the game.’ 🤭,” Brittany posted via Instagram, seemingly referencing a halftime interview Kubiak, 39, gave to CBS, during which he guaranteed the Raiders would win. She often extends the colors through to her kids’ wardrobes, recently taking to her Instagram grid to share a carousel of shots that captured Stirling wearing a “Red Kingdom” shirt and Chiefs hair bows, Bronze rocking a personalized Chiefs shirt of his own while sucking on a red lollipop, and Golden in a pair of hand-stitched overalls that featured her dad’s #15 across the front.

“The best times🥹❤️,” Brittany captioned the adorable post, to which Patrick responded with three red heart emojis, and Patrick’s mom, Randi Mahomes, commented, “Love this too much.”

#3601. The Mamdanis Take Manhattan!

Billionaire Michael Bloomberg attended plenty of museum galas when he was mayor of New York City. Bill de Blasio didn’t—not even the Brooklyn Artists Ball at the Brooklyn Museum, a quick 30-minute walk up Prospect Park West from his beloved neighborhood of Park Slope. Eric Adams couldn’t wait to get his own tickets to art shindigs; in 2022, a few months into his one-and-only term as mayor, he arrived at the Met Gala red carpet wearing a long leather jacket emblazoned with the words “End Gun Violence.”

“I walk around with swagger in my pocket,” Adams told ABC News from the red carpet.

The city’s current head of government, Zohran Mamdani, is perhaps the most culturally literate mayor since Ed Koch. Or maybe ever—he instructed the city to invest over $320 million in the Department of Cultural Affairs, the largest amount in New York history. And he pays attention to the smaller sums too. When the department announced that city-funded grants for artists would double from $5,000 to $10,000, Mamdani filmed a video of himself, brush in hand, behind an easel, trying his best to paint dollar signs à la Warhol.

“Not everyone’s an artist!” he says, flashing that Mamdani grin. “But a lot of New Yorkers are.”

But when would he show up in a tux to one of the primo arts institution fundraisers that dot the social calendar, particularly as the fall season starts humming?

And now he has. Mamdani has officially attended his first art gala as mayor: the Studio Museum Gala, held at The Glasshouse this past Monday evening. Celebrating the museum’s first year in its new building, it raised over $4 million for the institution. While mingling among guests at the cocktail hour, Mamdani, who did indeed put on a tux for the occasion, posed for photos with First Lady Rama Duwaji and luminaries, such as collector Bernard Lumpkin and the artist Rashid Johnson.

The event was honoring longtime board chair Ray McGuire, the Lazard president and mega art collector who’s served as chair of the Studio Museum’s board for 23 years—and, in case you forgot, ran his own quixotic campaign for mayor in 2021. Through all the toasts, Mayor Mamdani and the first lady sat next to Studio Museum director Thelma Golden.

Mamdani has a bit of a history with the Studio Museum—it’s where he spent his most recent birthday, checking out work by Taylor Simmons, the Atlanta native currently in the museum’s residency program.

Rama Duwaji, Thelma Golden, Zohran Mamdani, Kathryn Chenault, Rashid Johnson, and Lake Bell

As it turns out, the world’s most famous mayor has had a hell of a week museum-going. On Monday, he also released a video filmed at The Met—it featured Mamdani standing in the Rockefeller Wing and wandering through the Great Hall. In it, he informs us that The Met is not just a place to check out pre-Columbian masterworks: It’s also a place to cast your vote.

“Only in New York City can you vote in places like the Metropolitan Museum of Art,” he says.

The Met and the Studio Museum are both part of the Cultural Institutions Group, a subset of New York cultural mainstays that receive funding from the city. Other institutions on that list include El Museo Del Barrio, the Brooklyn Museum and the Bronx Museum of the Arts. Cherished institutions such as, say, the Whitney Museum of American Art don’t receive city money, though that hasn’t stopped Mamdani from extending his support to them. A few weeks into his mayoralty, he alighted to the Whitney’s Renzo Piano–designed building in the Meatpacking District to announce a few mayoral appointments and a ban on junk fees on hotel bookings. He also gave the museum’s programming a shout-out.

“One of the last times I was here I saw the wonderful exhibition of Alvin Ailey,” he said, referring to “Edges of Ailey,” which was up at the Whitney in late 2024.

Later in the year, Duwaji stopped by one of the museum’s fundraisers, the Whitney Art Party—though the mayor did not attend with her. That evening, January 27, Mamdani instead made a surprise appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon.

I’ve been tracking Mamdani’s interest in New York’s gallery scene since at least February 2025, when I was invited to a “Party for Zohran” at the Avenue A music venue Night Club 101. The event was co-hosted by Tribeca gallery Theta and Greene Naftali’s Carol Greene, as well as artists such as Martine Syms, Ser Serpas, and Aria Dean. “The art world is coalescing around a mayoral candidate,” the publicist Kaitlin Phillips, who was brought in to do PR for Mamdani early in his primary campaign, texted me in mid-February 2025, back when his campaign still seemed like a major long shot.

On March 2, I went to the party. After taking in some performances and live podcasts, Mamdani and I stepped outside to chat on Avenue A, talking about the art scene, which he was still getting fully acquainted with. He did, however, understand what it’s like to be an artistically minded person in New York.

“I think for me... Look, I’m the son of a filmmaker. I’m a failed artist myself,” he told me, though I still think the track kinda bangs. “I think that ultimately politics and art, there’s a commonality in the act of storytelling.”

I asked him about his platform for the arts in New York City.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

“At the core is a belief that art is something that every New Yorker deserves in their life,” Mamdani said back then. “And that that is not something that can simply be restricted to the museums or a Museum Mile, but it is something that also is committed to the community organizations and neighborhoods in the outer boroughs that are, for many New Yorkers, the only conduit to having that.”

Since taking office, Mamdani has named Diya Vij, an arts-organizations veteran, to lead the Department of Cultural Affairs, and assembled a slew of heavyweights to serve on his Committee on Arts and Culture. He’s also started picking board members for various museums. His campaign deputy Elana Leopold sits on the MoMA board, while Battery Park City CEO Raju Mann sits on the board of MoMA PS1.

As far as we know, though, no word has surfaced on who will be the mayor’s rep on The Met board—the most powerful perch of them all. Adams picked Scott Sartiano as his rep early in his term, and his fellow board members have indicated to me that Sartiano was an active board member who was pivotal and energizing for the team. (I wrote a whole profile on Sartiano, pegged to the rise of Zero Bond, back in 2024.)

But I’m sure it’ll be a thoughtful pick. Even through his meteoric rise, the mayor’s platform for artists in New York hasn’t really changed since that night we chatted on Avenue A.

“Artists have brought imagination and honesty to every corner of our city—from our sidewalks and subways to our museums, parks, and theaters. For generations, they have come to New York to explore, create, and challenge convention, shaping our city’s identity and drawing people from around the world,” Mayor Mamdani told me in a statement. “My administration is committed to supporting them and ensuring every New Yorker can experience the arts. We doubled city-funded grants for artists for the first time in nearly 20 years, and we’re partnering with organizations like TDF, The Met, and cultural institutions across the city to expand access to free and low-cost Broadway and opera tickets, as well as free admission to more than 20 cultural institutions. Because the arts are essential to who we are as a city, and every New Yorker should have the opportunity to experience them.”

#3600. Jessica Alba Deletes Halloween Pics After Nancy Kerrigan Costume Is Criticized

Jessica Alba’s 2026 Halloween costume didn’t land with everyone.

“Happy Halloween from Tonya … and Nancy,” Alba, 45, captioned a since-deleted Sunday, November 1, Instagram carousel that showed her dressed as former competitive figure skater Nancy Kerrigan with a faux bloodied bandage around her knee. Standing beside Alba was a friend dressed as Kerrigan’s former skating rival Tonya Harding, who held a baseball bat.

The combined costumes referenced the infamous 1994 attack on Kerrigan, 57, who was struck at the knee with a police baton by a man who was involved in a plan hatched by the ex-husband of Harding, 55. Harding eventually admitted to overhearing her ex’s plan but was never criminally convicted of any involvement. She was issued a lifetime ban from the U.S. Figure Skating Association as a result.

“Immature. We expect better, Jessica,” wrote one person in Alba’s post’s comments section, while another person wrote, “Why would you want to revisit this traumatic moment that ended people’s careers?”

Us has reached out to representatives for Alba for comment.

Other social media users noted that they didn’t see the harm in Alba’s costume, sharing praise for her and her friend’s creativity. “Brilliant costumes,” wrote one person, while another left clapping-hand emojis and a third shared a crying-laughing emoji.

Alba wore the costume to Vas J Morgan and Michael Braun’s “Hockey Horror” celebrity-studded Halloween party in Los Angeles on Saturday, October 31. Photos shared by Deuxmoi via Instagram on Sunday included a snap of the Honest Company cofounder posing for photos on the ice amid a string of stars who joined in the celebrations.

Paul Wesley attended with wife Natalie Kuckenburg, wearing a Jason Voorhees costume in a nod to the Friday the 13th franchise, while Brooks Nadar went as a seductive “fembot” from the Austin Powers film series. Other celebrities included Paris Hilton, Machine Gun Kelly, Salma Hayek and Natasha Lyonne.

Alba’s portrayal of Harding comes after the former athlete prepares to return to figure skating. One day prior to the Halloween party, she said in an interview with KOIN 6, an Oregon CBS affiliate, that she can’t “walk away” from the sport despite her ban.

On Saturday, December 12, she is scheduled to take part in “Tonya and Friends” in Vancouver, Washington, where she will skate for the public at Mountain View Ice Arena.

Per reporting on her interview by People on Saturday, Harding told KOIN 6, “I just want people to come out and have fun and be able to enjoy a real skating show.”

The TrueBlack Glossy coating is better at reducing glare than a matte screen while delivering a clearer picture (though some reviews claim it’s still not bright enough to mitigate intense glare if bright light hits the screen directly).

A native 4K, 280 Hz refresh rate allows for high-detail gaming and multimedia use, while its Frame Rate Boost mode offers versatility for playing different kinds of games. For example, FHD at 330 Hz also makes it a solid choice for competitive shooting games and high-FPS play. The monitor has an overall 0.03 ms response time, which is best-in-class, and minimizes motion blur. Other notable features include NVIDIA G-SYNC and AMD FreeSync support, and reduced burn-in risk due to OLED Care Pro and the Neo Proximity Sensor.

If you’re looking for a gaming monitor with dual-mode features, nearly instantaneous response time across a range of refresh rates, low input lag, and inky blacks, the 27-inch ASUS ROG Strix OLED XG27AQWMG monitor for gamers is a great choice.
