Earlier this week, I was doomscrolling on Reddit — as one does — when a post on r/espresso caught my eye. I'm often seen lurking on r/espressocirclejerk, but I don't need to frequent the source, r/espresso, for a few reasons. So if I do dip my toe into the main Subreddit, it must be for a special occasion.

And then I saw this post: "My controversial take is that some of you dont[sic] enjoy espresso, you just enjoy buying expensive equipment". Thank you, Reddit user mindlesspointer. Thank you.

I don't think this should be a controversial take. I think this is entirely the truth. Don't let the Internet tell you to spend thousands on gear to prove you like espresso. I'm an ex-professional barista — one independent specialty coffee shop and two chains — and now a professional coffee machine tester and director of The Coffee Lab, so I feel uniquely positioned to comment on this.

The Reddit room was split. Half of the commenters agreed, while half disagreed. Some users defended their commitment to progression and the journey: "People like the feeling of progression in a hobby. Same way in a video game people like building out their character, finding fancier guns, etc.," wrote user Noah_Joseph.

Others pointed out that their "basic" espresso machines did the trick. PlsNoOlives (love that name, even though olives are one of my favorite foods) added: "The day I realized making a yummy latte for myself and a friend was my peak satisfaction and now I just want to pour a swan on top. I don't even dial in new beans anymore, I eyeball it. Breville Bambino Plus, we ride for life. (Please don't break.)".

As a fellow Breville Bambino Plus owner, I have to say this comment spoke to me. Not once have I felt the urge to upgrade from my Bambino Plus

And no, I'm not saying you can't spend an ungodly amount of money on gear. Do whatever you want — it's your money. Maybe I'm just bitter because I don't have enough money to buy anything over $500 (and even that's a Black Friday, saved-up-all-year purchase). Who knows!

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

But I know I'm in the majority here. Most people can't afford a Lelit Bianca ($2,999), Rocket Espresso R Nine One ($6,990), or La Marzocco Linea Mini($4,980). Would I buy one if I had the money? I don't know. Depends on how much money we're talking. Do I have $10k spare? Sure, I'd grab a cheeky Linea Mini and then go on a cruise.

However, that's not my reality, and I'm 99.9% sure it's not yours. Please, please listen when I say this: You can get excellent, barista-quality coffee at home for a fraction of the cost. My entire dream espresso setup is just $650 — Breville Bambino Plus, Comandante C40 MK4, and the Wacaco Exagram Pro scale.

I've tested well over fifty coffee makers at this point. Some manuals, such as the AeroPress; some drip machines, such as the Moccamaster KBGV Select; some espresso machines, such as the Lelit MaraX3; some automated pour-overs, such as the Ratio Four. If it exists, I've got my caffeine-jittery mitts on it.

The flat white in this article's main image? Made it on the $349 Casabrews Marenza. I mean, I probably wouldn't recommend this machine for espresso enthusiasts for other reasons, but it's proof you don't need to spend $$$$($) on an espresso machine to get truly impressive results.

You know what the most important variable is? You. You are the barista. You are the Don of that kitchen. Show the espresso machine who's boss. You will get a perfect espresso. You will achieve flawless microfoam. Your latte art will be worthy of the Louvre. Let's manifest.

Let's do a little game. Take a look at these espresso shots. Can you guess which were made on a cheap machine and which came from a prosumer model?

The answers are thus: cheap, cheap, expensive, cheap, cheap, cheap, expensive, cheap (lever!), cheap, cheap.

I feel like that scene in The Simpsons Movie where the EPA guy is saying "tough, soft, tough, tough, tough, soft".

Anyway, back to coffee. Did you get them all right? Sure, I admit some look cheap, but some could go either way. Taste-wise, if you're using high-quality beans and a high-quality grinder (that does not need to be over $300), you can get $2,000+-beating espresso. Number 8 (and the espresso I'm holding in the main image) was made on the Flair 49 Pro — no electricity involved at all!

This year, I've run two blind taste tests: one between the $299 Baratza Encore ESP Pro vs the $1,500 Mazzer Philos, and one between the $299 Breville Bambino vs the $1,999 Lelit MaraX3.

You know which product won? The cheaper one. Both times.

I've linked the articles so you can read them, but the TL;DR is this: I made two lattes with coffee ground on a cheap and expensive grinder and asked people to choose their favorite. Then, I made Americanos and flat whites made on a cheap and expensive espresso machine and asked people to choose their favorite. The cheap machines won both taste tests.

Naturally, this didn't take things like longevity, quality of materials, and machine appearance into account. This was purely taste-based.

Again, I'm not poo-pooing those who have money to spend on premium, prosumer gear. I'm saying that you don't need to spend thousands to prove you like espresso. Do not let people on the Internet trick you into thinking otherwise.

If you see someone with a $10,000+ setup and you're wondering if your espresso will always taste inferior because you can't afford the same gear, please stop wondering. They just have loads of money (or irresponsible spending habits). It doesn't automatically mean they care more about coffee as a hobby than you.

You are the most important variable. With practice, good beans, and passion, you can make prosumer-level coffee without spending a fortune.

Trust me. I've tested enough espresso machines, grinders, and beans to know. Fellow Tom's Guide readers are on your side — I asked my readers their favorite espresso machine, and the Bambino Plus won by a huge margin.

We've got this, fellow poor espresso enthusiast.

#3575. Heidi Klum Shocks In Severed Hand Halloween Costume

Heidi Klum has done it again. The Project Runway host exceeded all our Halloween expectations by transforming herself into a giant, severed human hand nearly two meters tall for the latest edition of her annual party, held Saturday night in New York City. The costume, which required hours of work by her makeup and prop team, left no detail to chance: hyper-realistic veins modeled after her own anatomy, wrinkles, red-painted nails, and an exxagerated version of the rings she typically wears.

“Mike [Marino, from the special effects team ProRenFX] has all of these scans of my body, so he was able to use those to create an exact replica of my hand,” Klum explained to Vogue. “We wanted everything to be as realistic as possible—the anatomy, the veins, the muscles, all the little details that make a hand look like a real hand.”

The costume’s structure used the model's legs to form two of the fingers, while her right arm provided mobility for the thumb. Only her eyes and mouth were visible amid the bloody wounds on her palm, from which—to top off the gruesomeness of it all—Heidi Klum would occasionally spit out the fake blood that a team of assistants injected into her mouth. The most macabre part was at the wrist, where a horrific gash exposed a jumble of blood, bones, and torn flesh.

Heidi Klum (L) recieves an injection of fake blood to augment her 2026 Halloween costume.

Other guests at Klum's party included Kyle MacLachlan, who arrived dressed as his character from The Flintstones; Neil Patrick Harris and his husband David Burtka, dressed as the girls from The Shining; and Heidi Klum and Flavio Briatore's daughter, Leni Klum.

Before making her grand entrance, the host had built up anticipation on social media by posting clues about this year’s costume, such as a photo of her real hand that showed her wedding ring alongside the small tattoo of husband Tom Kaulitz's name. It, too, was part of her Halloween costume. “Nothing was overlooked! I love that Mike pays attention to things that most people might not even notice at first. The details make these costumes so special. It’s not just any giant hand: It’s my giant hand!” Klum said.

Heidi Klum 2026 Halloween costume, as seen from the back.

This is the 25th annual Halloween party thrown by the former Victoria’s Secret Angel: The event began in 2000, and has only continued to expand in scope. “ “Can you believe it? Twenty-five years of Halloween, costumes, incredible transformations, and so many amazing memories,” she said.

Last night’s “amputated hand” joins Klum's collection of Halloween costumes that ranges from last year’s mythological Medusa (with a petrified Kaulitz by her side) to E.T., to Shrek’s Fiona, to a disgusting giant worm inside which she feared she might suffocate. We're already looking forward to what she comes up with for next year.

Zendaya, Timothée Chalamet and Florence Pugh have spent enough time promoting the Dune franchise together that you would think they have the group-photo routine down by now. Apparently, all it takes is one camera, one slightly cramped set, and Zendaya trying to maneuver everybody into position to throw that theory out the window. The entire Dune Part 3 cast reunited to celebrate Denis Villeneuve's first two Dune movies heading back to theaters, and the resulting video is wonderfully awkward.

In the video, posted by the official Dune movie Instagram account, Zendaya directly addresses a social media user's question about the first two installments possibly heading back to theaters. In the process, the actres nearly loses control of the whole operation, backs straight into Pugh and somehow leaves Chalamet looking like the guy who accidentally wandered into someone else's photo. Seriously, check out the post below, because you barely get a glimpse of the lead actor's eye, let alone his whole face:

The clip -- which also features Robert Pattinson, Jason Momoa and Anya Taylor-Joy -- starts simply enough, with Zendaya trying to pull everyone together for the shot. Then she backs up, bumps into Pugh, and has to readjust while laughing through it all. Meanwhile, Chalamet is practically being edited out of his own franchise reunion. It's incredibly silly, especially given how serious these three usually look in the movies.

Of course, the timing makes sense, though. Dune and Dune: Part Two return to IMAX this month ahead of Dune: Part Three's release. IMAX has formally announced that fans can catch both movies as a double feature on November 13, followed by individual screenings from November 14 through November 18. That's already a pretty good excuse to spend nearly six hours back on Arrakis. So Warner Bros. is sweetening the deal considerably.

Every screening will include exclusive footage from Dune: Part Three, which hits the 2026 movie calendar on December 18. That makes the re-release considerably more interesting for fans who have already seen the first two movies. And, if that footage is just nearly as impressive as what's been screened thus far, fans will have more incentive to grab their tickets and sandworm popcorn buckets for the threequel.

Villeneuve's latest film is a book-to-screen adaptation of the second novel in Frank Herbert's series, Dune Messiah, and brings Chalamet, Zendaya, and Pugh back as Paul Atreides, Chani, and Princess Irulan. The cast also includes the aforementioned Momoa, Pattinson and Taylor-Joy along with Rebecca Ferguson, Javier Bardem and franchise newcomer Robert Pattinson.

So Much For Zendaya Taking A Break After Dune 3

We've already gotten some tantalizing information about the movie, including Chalamet saying he approached playing Paul differently this time around. The actor previously explained that while filming his final Dune movie, he dug deeper into tiny details of Paul's world than in the previous installments.

There are also plenty of reasons to keep an eye on Chani and Irulan. Zendaya became much more central to the story in Dune: Part Two, while Pugh's Princess Irulan should have considerably more to do as the story moves into Messiah. The third entry is set to be the final movie in Denis Villeneuve's critically acclaimed sci-fi trilogy, so we can probably expect one heck of an ending. Let's hope the film concludes a lot less awkwardly than this Instagram video.

But, before we get to the finale, audiences get another chance to see the first two movies in IMAX, plus a preview of what's coming next. While we wait, you can also revisit the first two Dune movies at home with an HBO Max subscription.

#3573. Everything You Should See Along With ‘You Can See Everything’

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

You Can See Everything, the new documentary about Theranos founder (and accomplished con artist) Elizabeth Holmes from filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, is breaking records (and brains). Not only is it raking it in at the box office in a way that few documentaries can manage, it’s also dominating the pop culture chat right now thanks to genre-defying techniques; a huge, rule-breaking twist (that I won't spoil); and its unrepentant and inexplicably mesmerizing subject.

While some might argue that you should head into this incredible film experience fresh, if you’re unfamiliar with any of the three major figures involved, you will benefit from a little prep work before you head in—and if you've already seen it, you're no doubt eager to dive even deeper into this truly remarkable (in every sense of the word) story. Here’s what you should watch, read, and listen to before or after You Can See Everything.

To put it simply: There’s a lot going on here. To ensure you can appreciate the film, you should make sure you know at least the basics about three things: Elizabeth Holmes (and why she’s infamous), and the work of both Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Here’s the crash course.

The 2019 podcast The Dropout is one of the most efficient ways to get the background on Holmes and Theranos. In the style of a true crime podcast, this show from ABC and journalist Rebecca Jarvis offers a deep dive into Holmes and her crimes that will give you all the background you’ll need.

John Carreyrou is the journalist who broke the Holmes story wide open, and his award-winning book Bad Blood offers a more journalistic and less sensational investigation than other accounts, providing a close-up look at Holmes in her CEO persona—an alternately terrifying and charismatic person who comes across as a “character” Holmes is playing. The book will inform your viewing of the documentary in important ways.

While Nathan Fielder is getting most of the attention for You Can See Everything, co-director Lance Oppenheim brings his signature technique to the film—it wouldn’t be nearly as interesting without his visual sensibility and framing.

Oppenheim has helmed several notable films, as he’s made a name for himself as a brilliant documentarian over the last few years, but to get ready for You Can See Everything, check out Spermworld, his 2024 exploration of unregulated sperm donations (you read that right). The doc deals with people who are as reality-challenged, manipulative, and possibly delusional as Holmes, and it will prep you for his visual style of extreme close-ups and excessive coverage that seems almost impossible in a normal documentary setting. You can stream Spermworld on Hulu.

If you’re unfamiliar with Nathan Fielder’s work, you need to strap in, because he’s unlike any other comedian or documentarian you’ve ever encountered.

To get a sense of his style, start with Nathan for You, a comedy-documentary-reality TV hybrid in which Fielder—as a version of himself—tries to use his business experience to help struggling people and small businesses. Presented as totally sincere, Fielder’s ideas are nevertheless increasingly elaborate and, in a word, unhinged. This show will familiarize you with Fielder’s persona and approach, but if you only have time to cram one episode, check out the series finale, “Finding Frances.” It follows Fielder’s attempts to reunite one of his earlier clients with his long-lost love, and it is a nearly perfect encapsulation of his style and approach. You can stream Nathan for You on HBO Max, Hoopla or Paramount Plus, or rent it episode-by-episode on Prime Video.

You should also watch at least some of Fielder’s other series, The Rehearsal. Here, Fielder (again, portraying a version of himself) attempts to help people prepare for difficult conversations utilizing increasingly outlandish techniques and scenarios that spiral into comedic insanity, including building sets, hiring actors, and immersing himself and his subjects in an alternate reality of sorts—an approach that will prepare you for some of You Can See Everything’s swerves. If you don’t have time to watch the whole thing, just check out the first episode, “Orange Juice, No Pulp.” It’s a self-contained chapter and will give you the basics. You can stream The Rehearsal on Apple TV or HBO Max, or rent episodes on Prime Video.

Have more bandwidth before watching You Can See Everything, or want a deeper dive after the documentary has melted your brain? Here’s what else you can check out.

The companion podcast to Carreyrou’s book, Bad Blood: The Final Chapter, is well worth a listen. Hearing the journalist’s perspective about his investigation and work during and after Holmes’ trial offers additional insight into her personality and methods that will really resonate after watching her in Fielder and Oppenheim’s doc.

Once you’ve noodled on You Can See Everything for a moment, there are two more movies you should check out.

For more on Holmes’s specific grift and how she pulled it off, Alex Gibney’s excellent The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley is the way to go, especially if you didn’t follow the Theranos story closely at the time and your main visual guide to Holmes is the new documentary. Gibney’s film is more traditional, but offers a wealth of insight into Holmes and her bubble. You can stream The Inventor on HBO Max or rent it on Prime VIdeo.

If you more from co-director Lance Oppenheim, watch Some Kind of Heaven, his 2020 breakout documentary about The Villages retirement community in Florida. It’s the film that put Oppenheim on the map, and offers hints of the same detached observational style that makes You Can See Everything so arresting. You can stream Some Kind of Heaven on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Speaking of which, if you loved the visual style and “enhanced” reality of You Can See Everything and want to see more of that, catch the Robert Pattinson-starring Primetime, still in theaters. It’s Oppenheim's narrative film directorial debut, and combines his hyperstyled visual flair with thriller pacing and a narrative based on a true story.

The Curse, Fielder’s 2023 TV series, is his first work of fiction, and it offers some fascinating insights. It follows a newly married couple (played by Fielder and Emma Stone) who struggle to get an HGTV-style show off the ground as things get excruciatingly awkward (and, eventually, kind of surreal). After watching You Can See Everything, it will be interesting to see how Fielder views the power of editing, the ethics of reality TV, and working with a name actor to get the results that he wants. Plus, similarly to the film, The Curse swerves into a final act that will melt your brain. You can stream The Curse on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

You should also definitely watch The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu series starring Amanda Seyfried. It’s a well-made film, and Seyfried’s performance was rightly praised for capturing the weirdness of Holmes' public persona. You can stream The Dropout on Hulu.

#3572. Heat Director Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself at LA Gun Range

Michael Mann was rushed to the hospital Saturday, after the director of films such as Collateral, The Insider, and Ferrari accidentally shot himself at a Los Angeles gun range. According to People, the bullet from Mann's gun struck his leg while the 83-year-old artist was returning the firearm to its holster.

“On Saturday, at a gun range, a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered, resulting in a superficial injury to film director Michael Mann. He was treated and is being released,” a spokesperson for Mann said in a statement to media.

In a separate statement that did not name Mann, the Los Angeles Police Department confirmed the incident, which TMZ reports occurred at The Range LA, a members-only shooting club on the Westside region of Los Angeles.

Robert DeNiro, Al Pacino, and Michael Mann at the world premiere of Heat.

“Yesterday at around 4 p.m., officers responded to the 11000 block of Missouri Avenue for a radio call for shots fired at that location," the LAPD statement reads. "Responding units’ investigation determined the shooting to be accidental. The subject was transported to a local hospital in stable condition. An injury report was completed.”

According to Deadline, the incident is not expected to delay work on Heat 2, which is scheduled to begin production in January, 2027. The director, who has been nominated for four Academy Awards and is the winner of two Emmys and a BAFTA, is also responsible for films including Hunter (1986) and The Last of the Mohicans (1992); he is also known for creating the acclaimed television series Miami Vice.

Michael Mann's latest film, the sequel to 1995 crime classic Heat, will explore the origins of the characters played by Al Pacino and Robert De Niro in the original film. Its cast reportedly includes Leonardo DiCaprio, Christian Bale, and Adolescence creator Stephen Graham.

#3571. 23 Years Later, Gandalf’s Greatest Lord of the Rings Line Is Still the Wisest Quote in Fantasy History

Gandalf’s wisdom strikes a chord even years later

Peter Jackson’s epic adaptation of J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings trilogy features a massive cast, with many characters delivering at least one incredibly poetic line across the films. Honestly, is there any line more heartbreaking than Boromir’s anguished “I would have followed you, my brother, my captain, my king”?

However, it's Gandalf (played phenomenally by the formidable Ian McKellen) who best uses his words throughout the films to demonstrate his tremendous wisdom and depth. With so many banger one-liners in his arsenal, narrowing down Gandalf’s best quote is a tough task.

Thankfully, we're confident we’ve done just that. Better yet, we’d argue this famous line perfectly captures what makes Tolkien’s story about Frodo and the Fellowship a timeless classic more than two decades after the film's original release.

Gandalf’s quotes range from incredibly snarky — “Fool of a Took! Throw yourself in next time, and rid us of your stupidity!” — to full of authenticity and wisdom — “Many that live deserve death. Some that die deserve life” — and are bound to resonate with anyone. But while these are all plenty memorable, neither resonates as being his best.

However, one line does, and, interestingly enough, it comes from a scene in 2003’s The Return of the King featuring the same character with whom Gandalf had a contentious relationship at the very start of the Fellowship. We’re talking about Pippin Took, who, over the course of the three films, has evolved from an annoying halfling into someone Gandalf is fond of.

During the Siege of Minas Tirith, Pippin, convinced that he and the combatants of Gondor are doomed to die at the hands of Mordor’s armies, sadly remarks that he never imagined that the Fellowship’s adventure would "end like this."

Gandalf turns to the hobbit and with a shake of his head, delivers this beautiful quote:

"End? No, the journey doesn't end here. Death is just another path, one that we all must take. The grey rain-curtain of this world rolls back, and all turns to silver glass, and then you see it: white shores, and beyond, a far green country, under a swift sunrise.”

While this may look like an average quote about the meaning of death, Gandalf’s words to Pippin here show just how far everyone in the Fellowship has come since the beginning of The Lord of the Rings trilogy.

Throughout Jackson’s trilogy, we watched major and minor characters alike give their lives to help Frodo carry the One Ring from the Shire to Mordor and destroy it in the fires of Mount Doom. Boromir and even Gandalf lay down their lives to give Middle-earth a chance at a peaceful future.

Although many sacrifices ended in death, Gandalf’s quote offers pivotal clarity on why losing a life doesn’t necessarily mean the journey is over. It’s a deeply spiritual perspective, which is fitting given that The Lord of the Rings is the epitome of the fantasy genre.

By describing death as “just another path, one that we all must take,” Gandalf tries to reassure Pippin. He presents death as a natural part of life, suggesting that although Pippin is right to fear it, it need not feel insurmountable since everyone will die one day.

Gandalf's words also carry a measure of hope by rejecting the idea that, once dead, a person’s life suddenly ceases to exist. In saying “The grey rain-curtain of this world rolls back,” the wizard describes death as crossing a threshold into something new and unexplored — making death feel less like something to fear and more like another adventure a person can look forward to when they pass.

Though the afterlife takes many forms in fantasy, Gandalf’s description of it as “white shores, and beyond, a far green country, under a swift sunrise” is especially comforting to Pippin. Before joining the Fellowship, Pippin had spent his whole life surrounded by the Shire’s green, rolling hills. The idea that life after death could resemble a place that feels like home is comforting.

Ultimately, Gandalf’s best quote may not be particularly snappy or as funny as his trash talk, but it’s still easily one of the hardest-hitting lines in The Lord of the Rings because it comes at a time when great courage is needed — and Gandalf, using kindness and empathy, is eager to provide it.

Witney Carson just blew viewers away by competing on this season of Dancing with the Stars during her second trimester of pregnancy. But that didn’t stop her from showing up for this year’s family Halloween costume. The category was Avengers, and she was electrifying as “Fat Thor”.

The beauty of Halloween is it’s a day where a person can be anyone or anything. For this year's holiday, Witney Carson’s two boys dressed up as Spider-Man and Captain America, and the DWTS pro opted for the Avengers: Endgame iteration of Chris Hemsworth's God of Thunder, who's best known as “Fat Thor” by fans. Check out the amazing costume reveal:

A post shared by Witney Carson McAllister (@witneycarson)

This is so good! In general, it's also so funny and clever for her to channel the version Thor who has let himself go and lost his abs following defeat at the hands of Thanos. I mean, she essentially found the perfect hack for walking around her neighborhood with her kids while in PJs and a robe while six months pregnant, and matching with them. And, by the looks of it, fans are loving it. Just check out these comments:

It seems that as a pregnancy costume, “Fat Thor” has been quite popular as of late, and I love to see it. #3569. The Best Apple Watch for Most People Is Over $100 Off

The Apple Watch Series 10 was released in September 2024, and it's one of the best ways to get into the Apple Watch in 2026 without breaking the bank. Right now, the titanium 46 mm case model with cellular capabilities is $112 off, bringing the price down to $637 (originally $749). That's the lowest price after Apple raised prices this summer due to the RAM shortage, according to price-tracking tools. The same model in gold titanium is also over $100 off, reaching $679 (originally $799), saving you the same amount compared to the latest Series 12 going for $799.

The Apple Watch Series 10 was considered the best Apple Watch for most people last fall and is a great replacement if you're still wearing the more budget SE. There are also some key upgrades from the Apple Watch 9, although they're less noticeable than previous Apple Watch upgrades. If you're curious to know how it compares to other flagship smartwatches from its time, you can check out our head-to-head comparison.

Some of the first things you'll notice on the Series 10 are a thin case and a big OLED screen (either 1.6 inches or 1.8 inches, depending on which model you get). The Series 10 has audio playback, meaning you can listen to podcasts, take calls, or listen to Spotify on its speakers. The sleep features allow notifications for signs of sleep apnea. What you're giving up by saving on this version over the latest Series 12 is a faster S11 chip, a newer Health Sensing System and the Readiness app (tracks daily insights, vitals, and other metrics), a longer battery life (from 18 to 24 hours), 5G RedCap support (it helps save on battery life and has better network coverage compared to 5G), and audio intelligence features like Live Rewind, Siri Recap, and Sound Recognition.

If those extra features don't matter to you, the Series 10 is a great Apple Watch to get in 2026 at a discount, when many are still suffering from their price hikes.

#3567. 15 Best Western Movies Of The 2020s (So Far)

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The Western may be the prototypical American film genre, but it's long past its glory days. While Hollywood's Golden Age saw Westerns produced at an exponential rate compared to other genres, it has been on the defensive since the old studio system's collapse and the arrival of New Hollywood auteurs in the '70s. America was ready to move on from the old-fashioned forms of mythology it had been fed for decades.

However, the Western has never truly died. Every decade since then has seen attempts to spin the genre anew, many of which stand out as essential modern entries. We already have a list of the 15 best Western movies of the 21st century, but we want to take a look at our current decade so far. The year 2020 has, admittedly, been a light stretch for the genre, but we still have a worthy list of movies that embrace Hollywood's most established genre conventions or, more often than not, subvert them to communicate something new.

Here are the 15 best Western movies of the 2020s (so far).

As the /Film team writes, "Butcher's Crossing" is a bleak, brutal, abstract Western well-suited to an actor like Nicolas Cage, who's spent most of his career proving he'll take on almost any project. Gabe Polsky's adaptation of John Williams' 1960 novel lets him play a haunted frontier obsessive who finds himself in bleak circumstances. He plays Miller, a buffalo hunter in 1970s Kansas who convinces Will Andrews (Fred Hechinger), a Harvard dropout hungry for real-world experience, to bankroll a trip to a hidden Colorado valley where thousands of animals graze undisturbed. It's a get-rich-quick scheme, but two men's hubris against nature soon leads to self-destruction.

Polsky strips the Western of its mythic romance and ties the frontier's bounty to a body count. Though you may expect a Cage freakout in the isolation of the Western wilderness, he keeps things relatively restrained, evoking his true movie-star days when he could tell worlds of stories with just a look on his face. It's worth checking out for getting to see him in the zone alone.

We can get this out of the way: "Cry Macho" is not Clint Eastwood's best Western. Of his directorial efforts in the genre, it almost certainly sits at the bottom. That it flopped in theaters isn't surprising, though its release in the wake of the COVID pandemic had something to do with that as well. But there's something disarming about a 91-year-old icon directing himself in a movie that so directly interrogates his own mythology and screen image. Eastwood plays Mike Milo, a washed-up rodeo star in 1979 who's hired by his old boss (Dwight Yoakam) to retrieve the man's teenage son, Rafo (Eduardo Minett), from his mother in Mexico. The kid, who comes with a pet rooster named Macho, doesn't want to be saved, and the whole situation sets up a slow, low-stakes tale about late-life redemption.

Based on N. Richard Nash's novel, which Hollywood tried to adapt for decades, Eastwood becomes one of his downbeat, late-career larks: a handout movie about unlearning manhood's toxic institutions. Mike spends most of the movie learning the facets of humility that bring him closer to himself and others. All the way to the end, Eastwood has been making movies about the ability to change, no matter the age.

Viggo Mortensen already had an overlooked Western in his repertoire with 2004's "Hildago." Now, this melancholic entry into the genre, which he wrote, directed, starred in, and scored, joins its ranks. It's an admirable display of one-man ambition from a star whose career has always been off the beaten path since "The Lord of the Rings." He turns "The Dead Don't Hurt" into a muted, poignant frontier love story. Vicky Krieps plays Vivienne Le Coudy, a fiercely independent French-Canadian woman who falls for Holger Olsen (Mortensen), a gentle Danish carpenter, in 1860s San Francisco. She follows him to a Nevada town, where he leaves to fight in the Civil War.

Mortensen shuffles the timeline, letting the film drift through memory, grief, and the small tragedies of separation by war. It's a magnificent role for Krieps, who gives Vivienne a sharp, self-possessed spark that keeps the movie from drifting into the weepie malaise of a woman simply waiting for her lover's return. It's a patient, humane Western that examines the consequences of violence.

If most Westerns champion or interrogate the foundational institutions of how the country came to be, "Eddington" ruthlessly grills us as we are now, or more specifically, how we were in the year 2020. The titular New Mexico town is a pressure cooker of mask mandates, Black Lives Matter protests, and conspiracy-brained doomscrolling. At the center is Joaquin Phoenix's flailing sheriff, Joe Cross, whose lawman bluster masks his inability to reconcile with the world around him. Nevertheless, he decides to run for mayor against the sly incumbent (Pedro Pascal) as Eddington unravels all around him.

It's all dressed up in Western iconography: the sheriff's hat, the dusty main street, the standoff. And yet its savage satirical swings in the face of every facet of the political spectrum, and how it contributes to a greater sense of an unmoored and neglected social contract, are unique for the genre. The film captures how it felt to live inside the fraying American mind during the pandemic, when everyone was convinced of their own dogmas. "Eddington" is divisive, provocative, and infuriating, and in the process, it captures something true about the contemporary American spirit.

Reichardt is a magician at capturing a kind of anti-mythic restraint; she did it to an effect of dread in "Meek's Cutoff," and here she affords it an enchanting sense of sadness. The tenderness between the two outcasts at the center gives their quiet friendship such richness, moving and breathing in long, hushed stretches that act as meditations. It's a kind movie that recognizes the world's harsh conditions and yearns for a peaceful respite amid the animosity.

"The Harder They Fall" makes its cheeky sensibility clear from the jump: It opens with a title card stating, "While the events of this story are fictional, these people existed," then throws a Black Western all-star team into a flashy revenge tale. Jonathan Majors' Nat Love hunts down Rufus Buck (Idris Elba), the outlaw who killed his parents, setting off a showdown that pulls in Zazie Beetz's Stagecoach Mary, Lakeith Stanfield's Cherokee Bill, Regina King's Trudy Smith, and Delroy Lindo's Bass Reeves. These were all real people, and there's a glee in smashing them together like action figures.

Jeymes Samuel directs with the heightened style of someone who grew up watching spaghetti Westerns and music videos in equal measure, and the soundtrack he co-produced with Jay-Z contributes to the film's personality. The story is thin, and the violence is more stylish than weighty, but Samuel's intention is to make a pop action movie that corrects the Western's whitewashed history by giving long-ignored figures the pulpy, gun-slinging spectacle they've long been denied. Like many movies on this list, it's been somewhat forgotten, but it deserves another look.

The title of this one feels like a bit of a cruel joke, since it's up in the air whether we'll see any more of "Horizon" beyond "Chapter 1." (Though "Chapter 2" screened at a couple of film festivals, no one has heard anything about it since.) Whether it's crueler for the audience or for Kevin Costner is up in the air, since the legendary actor reportedly bet his own money, a good chunk of his fortune, on this multi-part epic. This first chapter plays like what it is: a monster-sized passion project that indulges in all the minutiae of the sprawl it sets up.

"Chapter 1" is honestly quite good, as Costner has proven himself perfectly adept at depicting the dusty texture and varied characterizations of the Western frontier, starring as a mysterious drifter who finds himself in the crosshairs of multiple intersecting plot lines. It has a patient, widescreen love of the genre that becomes infectious, and the filmmaking has a classical sense of sweep you don't see much anymore. Whether the full saga ever comes to fruition is unclear, but it would be genuinely regrettable if we didn't get to see more. Maybe Costner needs to learn not to blindly back huge projects in the future, though: This isn't even the first Western he's bankrolled that bombed.

Martin Scorsese's late-career turn to the Western offers no gunslinging or high-noon showdowns, just a relentless, brutal reckoning with the generational racial violence built into the capitalist systems on which America is built. His 3+ hour epic is harrowing, depicting one of our nation's darkest chapters. Based on David Grann's 2017 nonfiction bestseller, it is, unfortunately, very accurate to the real story. It concerns the 1920s Osage murders in Oklahoma, where white settlers systematically killed members of the oil-rich Osage nation to take their wealth. Leonardo DiCaprio's Ernest Burkhart, a weak-willed World War I veteran, marries Mollie (Lily Gladstone) at his uncle's urging, the sinister "King" Hale (Robert De Niro).

Whereas Grann's book relayed the story as an FBI procedural and mystery, Scorsese bares the terrible reality of the killings from the jump, affording the film its specific, terrible power that separates it from its source material. The banality of evil, the polite smiles, and the slow poison arrive with a grim, chilling inevitability. With its sweeping cinematography and Robbie Robertson's final score, this Western interrogates the mythology of American enterprise and uncovers the dark secrets behind generational wealth.

Kevin Costner appears yet again on this list as the man who seems determined to keep the Western alive (he's been consistently dedicated throughout his career, and we have a ranked list of all his Westerns). He and Diane Lane reunite as on-screen spouses after "Man of Steel," and their chemistry is the soul of this slow-burning 1963 Montana neo-Western. They play retired sheriff George and his wife, Margaret Blackledge, who lose their son in a riding accident and then watch their daughter-in-law (Kayli Carter) remarry and vanish with their grandson into the clutches of the menacing Weboy family. Determined to bring the boy back, the couple heads to North Dakota, where they find a clan far more dangerous than they bargained for.

Thomas Bezucha's adaptation of Larry Watson's 2013 novel is quiet and elegiac for most of the runtime, then it erupts into a brutal, tense final act. Lesley Manville stands out as the Weboy matriarch, weaponizing false hospitality and unafraid to exploit other characters' emotional triggers. As a Western about grief, family, and the lengths people go to hold on to what's left, it carries surprising poignancy, while the filmmaking delivers unforgiving suspense.

Though known for shaky-cam thrillers like "United 93" and the "Bourne" franchise, Paul Greengrass proved he could do something tender and unhurried in this 2020 adaptation of Paulette Jiles' novel. It helps that it's anchored by one of our great movie stars, Tom Hanks, always reliable, as our ranked list of his 15 greatest movies proves. He plays Captain Jefferson Kyle Kidd, a Civil War veteran who travels through post-war Texas, reading newspapers aloud to weary crowds, offering them a brief respite from their troubles. Then he's asked to deliver Johanna (Helena Zengel in a remarkable turn), a girl raised by the Kiowa after her parents were killed, to relatives hundreds of miles away.

That sets up a familiar odd-couple road-trip dynamic, but Hanks' reassuring tenor and Greengrass' patience with the material add a pleasant warmth. Dariusz Wolski amplifies the world's lived-in qualities with gorgeous, dusty cinematography, earning the film an Oscar nomination. The story's argument that truth and compassion are the real tools on the world's frontier rings true. It feels old-school in all the right ways.

The streaming shelf life is kind to some movies, and this old-fashioned Western starring Tim Blake Nelson has quietly come around to dominate Netflix. Potsy Ponciroli's lean 2021 gem is distilled genre worship, where commitment to the form's tenets transcends pastiche and becomes the real thing. Nelson is Henry, a widowed Oklahoma Territory farmer in 1906 trying to raise his restless teenage son, Wyatt (Gavin Lewis), in peace. That peace evaporates when Henry finds a wounded stranger and a satchel of cash in the dirt, and a smooth-talking Stephen Dorff arrives with a posse claiming to be the law.

Ponciroli works with a small canvas: one farmhouse, a few acres, and just a handful of actors, yet wrings every ounce of tension from it, building to a siege that nods to "Shane" and "Unforgiven." It's indebted to the greats but carves out its own lane, and it still feels refreshing in a decade that's been somewhat slight for the genre. In that context, something this low-key and sharp still stands out.

Jane Campion waited 12 years between features, and her break paid off with "The Power of the Dog." That's largely thanks to Benedict Cumberbatch, who delivers a career-best performance, as our review notes. Adapted from Thomas Savage's 1967 novel, the film unfolds on a 1925 Montana ranch, where Cumberbatch plays Phil Burbank, a magnetic, merciless cowboy who rules the land and his men with a lethal mix of charm and contempt. When his gentle brother George (Jesse Plemons) marries widow Rose (Kirsten Dunst) and brings her and her fragile son Peter (Kodi Smit-McPhee) onto the property, Phil sets out to destroy them through cunning, subtle Machiavellian manipulation.

In a genre that orbits the tenets of machismo, this film dismantles manhood from the inside. Campion peels away the armor Burbank wears as he mythologizes himself as the unflappable Western cowboy. Ari Wegner's beautiful cinematography and Jonny Greenwood's typically singular score help depict this. The film earned 12 Oscar nominations and won Campion Best Director, a win that was more than earned for this poignant and effective deconstruction.

Felipe Gálvez Haberle's debut feature may have flown under the radar, but it resonates with those who see it — it's got a 94% Rotten Tomatoes score and is likely to leave you speechless. Set in early 1900s Tierra del Fuego, at the windswept bottom of South America, it follows three riders hired by sheep baron José Menéndez (Alfredo Castro), a real-life tycoon, to clear a path through his vast holdings: a sadistic British lieutenant, MacLennan (Mark Stanley); an American mercenary, Bill (Benjamin Westfall); and a mixed-race Chilean tracker, Segundo (Camilo Arancibia).

That clearing means the genocide of the Indigenous Selk'nam people, and Gálvez keeps the violence matter-of-fact, with his tight, boxy frame making the gray, gorgeous landscapes feel suffocating. His final verdict is an apt examination of how nations launder their founding atrocities into official history, just as the stories of the American West have been romanticized into our stories of gunfighters, lawmen, and good vs. evil. It's a hard watch but essential because, like the best deconstructive Westerns, it exposes the genre's myths.

Denis Johnson's 2011 novella barely exceeds a hundred pages, so Clint Bentley's adaptation covers most of a life in under two hours, luxuriating in the small moments and quietude the story demands. Joel Edgerton plays Robert Grainier, an orphaned logger and railroad laborer in the early 20th-century Pacific Northwest who watches the forests he fells and the world he knows get swallowed by progress. He marries Gladys (Felicity Jones), builds a cabin in a river valley, and learns how quickly a wildfire can erase everything, leaving him to live out his decades alone with his grief.

Bentley and co-writer Greg Kewdar lean into Terrence Malick-style lyricism, with Adolpho Veloso's cinematography finding wonder in every shaft of light and Will Patton's gravelly narration carrying the story along like a true American folk tale. It follows the Western tradition of impending anxiety: how a frontier man is meant to integrate into regular society when his way of life inevitably disappears — the world of the Western never lasts forever. It's a standout Netflix production, even if the streamer's algorithm frustratingly hampered its potential for breakout success.

Director Mona Fastvold's 2020 drama reimagines Western tropes as an aching love story, told in the hushed, formal language of a true 19th century period piece. Based on Jim Shepard's short story, it unfolds in upstate New York in 1856, where farm wife Abigail (Katherine Waterston) is numbed by the death of her young daughter and records her days in careful, poetic prose. Her husband, Dyer (Casey Affleck), is a decent, stoic man lost in his own grief, so the arrival of new neighbors Tallie (Vanessa Kirby) and her controlling husband, Finney (Christopher Abbott), jolts her awake.

That, of course, leads to a slow-burning affair between the two women, which blooms in stolen glances and small, camouflaged gestures. Waterston and Kirby are electric and heartrending together, and their bruised dynamic conveys a love story that understands the courage it takes to embrace a feeling the world wants to deny. "The World to Come" arrived alongside "Ammonite" and "Portrait of a Lady on Fire" in a wave of period queer romances, and it earns its place among the crop.

#3565. Patrick Stewart Had A Surprising Love For This Classic MTV Animated Series

The late, great Sir Patrick Stewart had a silly streak you might not know about. Case in point: He was a big, big fan of Mike Judge's MTV animated series "Beavis and Butt-Head," the perennial Gen-X text about two snickering teenage wastoids who do little other than make butt jokes. In a 2020 interview with National Post, Stewart called the series "brilliant."

The actor landed in the population's mass consciousness when he began playing the stern authority figure of Captain Jean-Luc Picard on "Star Trek: The Next Generation" in 1987. Film fans might also have recognized him from earlier films like John Boorman's "Excalibur," David Lynch's "Dune," or Tobe Hooper's "Lifeforce," and he played very serious characters in those films as well. Stewart was an authoritative, stalwart presence in most of his roles.

It wasn't until after becoming famous on "Star Trek" that Stewart began to embrace his silly side. You might have seen Stewart's performance of "'A' You're Adorable" from the set of "Next Generation," or his spirited humor on his 1994 episode of "Saturday Night Live." He was King Richard the Lionheart in Mel Brooks' spoof "Robin Hood: Men in Tights," and, in 2013, Stewart wore a lobster costume for Halloween. He had a regular role on the animated comedy series "American Dad!," and turned up on episodes of "The Simpsons" and "Futurama." Stewart established his actorly reputation with po-faced and classical roles, but eventually embraced comedy as well.

And, as he himself confessed, he was a longtime lover of the lowbrow "Beavis and Butt-Head." Indeed, according to the interviewer, Stewart was very good at imitating Beavis' gravelly laugh.

Patrick Stewart wasn't wholly articulate about his love for "Beavis and Butt-Head," a phenomenon many of the show's fans might have encountered themselves. Sometimes it's just hard to describe why something connects with you. Stewart said:

"I love that show. I'm so sorry that it's gone. [...] I don't know why it appealed to me, but it did. It was brilliant, that's why. Incredible characters. Heh heh heh heh."

When the interviewer suggested that a lowbrow cartoon might provide a balance to Stewart's notoriously highbrow tastes — he spent many years in the Royal Shakespeare company, after all — Stewart bristled at the implication. "I would call 'Beavis and Butt-Head' extremely highbrow," he said, "Not lowbrow at all." One can certainly argue that "Beavis and Butt-Head" was a dumb show made by smart people. It can even be seen as a sociological study of the modern teen experience in the mid-1990s, a portrait of two young males who have been expertly trained by television to remain dumb and seek out only the basest of creature pleasures.

Stewart noted that he was always a fan of slapstick comedy, going back to his childhood:

"I grew up loving Laurel and Hardy. In fact, my grandmother babysat Stan Laurel when he was a few months old — she ran a boarding house in the northeast of England. I worshipped them. And of course I loved Chaplin, and when I was a little older I fell in love with Danny Kaye."

Just because Stewart had a talent for playing serious characters didn't mean he liked serious entertainment all the time.

Patrick Stewart even admitted that he always assumed his career would eventually provide him more opportunities to play comedic roles. Sadly, when establishing himself, Stewart recognized that he was seen as a non-comedic figure. In his words:

"I always thought, when I became a professional, that I would just move into comedy. [...] But it never happened. I became this sort of, ugh, somber, dreary, kind of pompous figure."

Of course, as it so happens, Stewart did eventually move into comedy. Not exclusively, of course, but after "Star Trek: The Next Generation," Stewart certainly began appearing in more comedic roles. We've already mentioned his role on "American Dad!," which proved Stewart was an undersung comedy genius, and the actor was involved in several other collaborations with that show's creator, Seth MacFarlane. Stewart appeared on multiple episodes of MacFarlane's "Family Guy," and narrated his films "Ted" and "Ted 2."

One might also happily recall Stewart's expert comedic turn on the TV series "Extras." (This scene is a work of genius.) He also did a lot of whimsical voice work, and notoriously played the voice of the Poop Emoji in "The Emoji Movie." He was certainly being goofy while gleefully chanting, "We're number two!" In light of his whimsy, then, it's easy to understand why Patrick Stewart might enjoy the idiotic antics of "Beavis and Butt-Head."

In 2020, Stewart lamented that "Beavis and Butt-Head" had gone away. One can only imagine his delight when Mike Judge brought his characters into the modern era in 2022. His beloved cackling teen wastoids lived on.

The sudden news of Patrick Stewart's death sparked a litany of tributes to the actor. And, as part of that, celebrities have been sharing personal stories about working with Stewart. Admittedly, I wasn't expecting Jeremy Clarkson to enter the fold and share an anecdote about Stewart. However, this Star Trek fan completely forgot Stewart was on Top Gear and didn't know the behind-the-scenes story about him reporting to set.

Stewart was a guest on the second season of the Top Gear reboot, and as Clarkson said on X, the Captain Picard actor was pretty excited to be a part of the show. He also showed up with so little fanfare that the show's crew mistook him as a common worker there to deliver a package. But, as Clarkson explained, Stewart did something to make his status known:

Patrick Stewart turned up so early and so unobtrusively to be a star in the reasonably priced car, we mistook him for a delivery driver and asked him to go round the back. Took his hat off and said, 'But I’m the captain of the Enterprise'. Fucking nice guy.

Fortunately, Stewart's line landed him on the stage, and he was able to participate in the episode. He ended up driving a Suzuki Liana around the test track and ultimately beat the late Sir Michael Gambon's lap time. Stewart took a lot of pride in that, despite mentioning he had a good deal of respect for Gambon.

After Patrick Stewart’s Death, Anthony Mackie’s Take On Working With Him On Doomsday Hit Me Hard

With this BTS info in mind, I took the time to rewatch Patrick Stewart's interview on Top Gear and learned where his obsession with cars began. His family was poor growing up, and as such, they didn't have a car of their own. There was one family on his street that owned a Jaguar, and the X-Men icon actually ended up dating their daughter.

The Shakespearean actor had a grand time on Top Gear, which made it surprising that he never found the time to pop up on the show again. Granted, Stewart kept pretty busy over the years, so maybe just never had the chance to between all the acting roles he was taking on?

Circling back to Clarkson's story about Patrick Stewart's arrival, though, I'm not the least bit surprised by it. Most stories I've heard from actors and actresses as of late point to Stewart being a very polite and low-key kind of guy, but he did have occasional and humorous outbursts. He also liked to occasionally wrestle on the set of Star Trek: The Next Generation (which I would pay to see footage of).

As for Top Gear, the show isn't currently in production at The BBC, though the network does have plans to revive it. The show's spiritual successor, The Grand Tour, is available to stream on Prime Video and worth a watch for those who enjoy the format. I enjoy watching it every now and then, even if I prefer watching Star Trek if given the choice between the two.

CinemaBlend continues to offer condolences to the family and friends of Sir Patrick Stewart as he's laid to rest. It's my hope that like Jeremy Clarkson, fans continue to celebrate Stewart's life and share fun stories about him.

He graduated from the University of Southern Indiana with a degree in Journalism and a minor in Radio and Television. He's great at hosting panels and appearing on podcasts if given the chance as well.

#3563. BioWare Fan Creates a Graveyard of Shut Down Studios at EA Offices

In memoriam of all the studios and IPs that were lost over the years

The gaming community has become increasingly disgruntled with EA over the past few years. Shutting down BioWare, the beloved development studio behind Mass Effect, was the straw that broke the camel's back, causing an uproar on social media platforms and leading some fans to take action in the real world.

Gamers feared for the future of several development studios following EA's buyout involving Saudi Arabia's private investment fund, Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners, and private equity firm Silver Lake. A former EA manager foresaw the closure, but players were still appalled when it became official in October. Despite recent failures, BioWare was the studio that developed some of EA's most iconic video games, such as the Mass Effect trilogy, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and the Dragon Age series.

It was painful to see BioWare being shut down, especially knowing that the studio had been working on Mass Effect Universe, the next installment in the series, for over half a decade. As more news about the canceled game surfaced, fans' discontent only grew. Each new detail that came out seemed to fuel their fire, leading to petitions and protests, both offline and online.

For Halloween, a displeased fan decided to set up a graveyard outside the EA offices in their town. The graveyard wasn't created only to honor BioWare, the last to be affected; it was created in memory of the several development studios shut down by Electronic Arts. There were tombstones for Bullfrog, Pandemic, Visceral, Westwood, Origin, and Maxis (heavily restructured), as the creator said they ran out of time to make more. These studios were behind beloved games, such as Destroy All Humans!, Star Wars: Battlefront, Dungeon Keeper, Ultima, SimCity, Theme Park, Spore, and many more.

Each tombstone featured the studio's logo, establishment and closure dates, a meaningful quote, and "RIP" at the top in large print. The quote for BioWare is: "It had to be Me. Someone else might have gotten it wrong." This is an iconic quote from character Mordin Solus in Mass Effect 3, but it also represents the legacy of the studio that helped define what modern RPGs are.

This is just one of the many examples of fans trying to make their voices heard. In Madrid, someone spray-painted "Save Mass Effect" right outside of the EA office building — no doubt a player who prefers Renegade runs.

While in New York City, fans chose the Paragon route and bought a "save Mass Effect" billboard in Times Square. The reach of fan outcries is more expansive than many would've thought. However, even if EA has noticed the protests and pleas, it remains silent. EA sees Star Wars as a more reliable franchise for a sci-fi action game, so it's unlikely that it will go back on its decision. Nevertheless, it is beautiful to see the gaming community come together and fight for what they believe in.

#3562. One Of The Best Neo-Western Shows Is Streaming On Prime Video

When it comes to neo-Western TV shows, it might seem as though Taylor Sheridan holds a monopoly. But not only has "Yellowstone" spawned many a clone since its 2018 debut, there are also plenty of pre-Sheridan neo-Western series well worth checking out. "Longmire" is one of them. Thankfully, you can now watch this oft-overlooked series on Prime Video, and those looking for shows in the vein of "Justified" should definitely pay attention.

The neo-Western crime drama series started out on the A&E network back in 2013, but switched to Netflix halfway through its six-season run. The show is based on the Walt Longmire Mystery novels by Craig Johnson, in which the titular sheriff of northern Wyoming's fictional Absaroka county investigates numerous suspicious deaths. The books have been published since 2004, with Johnson since having written 22 novels, three novellas, and numerous short stories.

In 2010, A&E ordered a pilot based on Johnson's fictional universe, with John Coveny and Hunt Baldwin developing the show for television. The network then ordered it to series in 2011, with Australian actor Robert Taylor, whose previous credits included "The Matrix" and whose more recent work includes "The Meg," in the lead role of Walt Longmire. Interestingly enough, Coveny would go on to co-executive produce and write several episodes of "Yellowstone." But before he gave Sheridan a hand, he and Baldwin had six seasons worth of neo-Western crime drama to oversee.

In "Longmire," Robert Taylor's Walt Longmire is a dedicated sheriff who oversees his northern Wyoming county with the help of his deputies, an indefatigable drive for justice, and a wry sense of humor. But his unflappable nature hides a deep pain. The sheriff lost his wife prior to the events of Season 1 and when we first meet him, he's about ready to give up on his re-election bid and let challenger, Branch Connally (Bailey Chase), take over. But his daughter Cady Longmire (Cassidy Freeman) and new deputy, Victoria Moretti (Katee Sackhoff), convince him to push forward.

Over six seasons, we see Walt and his team solve many murder cases, often with the help of Walt's best friend Henry Standing Bear (Lou Diamond Phillips), a member of the Cheyenne people. Yes, like Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton on "Marshals," this Western lawman has a Native American confidant who often helps with cases. Unlike "Marshals" and it's struggle to figure out what it's actually about, however, "Longmire" actually garnered impressive reviews and was well-received by audiences.

In fact, "Longmire" became a major hit for A&E. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the Season 1 premiere drew 4.1 million total viewers, making it A&E's most-watched scripted series debut ever. The show also became the highest-rated new cable scripted hour-long drama of the year among the 25-54 demographic. Naturally, it was renewed for a second and third season, after which A&E canceled the show, ostensibly because its audience skewed too old (though financial considerations were almost certainly a factor). Thankfully, "Longmire" became one of many shows saved from cancellation by Netflix, with the streamer picking the show up for a fourth, fifth, and sixth season. Now, you can see all of them on Prime Video.

Though it was set in Wyoming, "Longmire" was filmed in various locations around New Mexico. Not that it mattered too much. The show was full of impressive landscapes and sweeping vistas which made it feel very much like the kind of show that, in the age of AI and streaming movie blandness, is slowly slipping away. That was part of the reason critics liked it so much, with Nancy DeWolf Smith of The Wall Street Journal highlighting in her Season 1 review the "glorious setting under the big sky of Wyoming," adding, "If it weren't for a few modern conveniences, like cellphones and trucks, it might as well be 1875, so rugged and unspoiled does the scenery look."

DeWolf wasn't the only one impressed, either. On Rotten Tomatoes, the show has a very respectable average critic score of 88%, with Season 4 even managing to push the Tomatometer all the way to 100% (though that is based on just seven reviews). Otherwise, Season 1 garnered a "certified fresh" rating and an 85% critic score, which is pretty darn good for a show that few outside of its dedicated fanbase have heard of.

Unfortunately, in 2017, Netflix canceled "Longmire" following what was, according to author Craig Johnson, a dispute over the rights whereby the streamer wanted to buy the show outright from production company Warner Horizon Television. Considering the wealth of source material, the show could have gone on for much longer than it did. Alas, Walt and co. were told to pack it up after their sixth season. Thankfully, we can now enjoy all six seasons on Prime Video.

It's been a big year for the iPhone, thanks to the launch of the all-new iPhone Duo. It's Apple's first foldable, and arguably the most exciting new iPhone for the past several years. By comparison the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the best traditional iPhone to date. But which one is the better iPhone?

The iPhone Duo has a lot going for it, including the large foldable display, but it makes some compromises that we'd really like to see fixed. Meanwhile the iPhone 18 Pro Max has improved just about every aspect of what makes an iPhone an iPhone — but at the expense of its "wow" factor. Thankfully we have put both phones through the ringer in the Tom's Guide labs, testing everything that makes them tick.

Here's what we learned about iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro Max, and which of the two is actually the best iPhone.

iPhone 18 Pro Max: up to $1,000 off w/ trade-in + unlimited @ T-MobileT-Mobile is taking up to $1,000 off the iPhone 18 Pro Max when you trade-in an old device and sign up for an eligible unlimited data plan. In our iPhone 18 Pro Max review, we said the A20 Pro chip raises the bar for performance in a smartphone. It features a 6.9-inch OLED 120Hz display (2868 x 1320), A20 Pro chipset, and 256GB of storage. You also get a 48MP main, 48MP ultrawide, and 48MP telephoto lens w/ 4x zoom. The front camera is 18MP.

Save up to $1,200 on the iPhone Duo at T-Mobile. All you need to do is trade in an eligible device and sign up for an eligible plan. Or, if you want to keep your old device, you simply need to sign up for a new line and port your old number from an eligible carrier for the same discount.

117.8 x 84.1 x 11.3mm ( 3.31 x 4.64 x 0.44 inches) (Closed) / 117.8 x 164.6 x 5.2mm (6.48 x 4.64 x 0.21 inches) (Open)

163.4 x 78 x 8.8 mm (6.43 x 3.07 x 0.35 in)

The iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 / £1,299 / AU$2,299, which gets you a model with 256GB of storage space. Additional storage is available for an extra fee, with 512GB costing $1,499 / £1,499 / AU$2,699, 1TB costing $1,899 / £1,899 / $3,499 and 2TB setting you back $2,499 / £2,499 / $4,699. The Pro Max has been on sale for several weeks, and currently has delivery wait times of two to three weeks.

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$3,499 for a model with 256GB of storage. Higher storage options include 512GB at $2,199 / £2,199 / AU$3,899, 1TB at $2,599 / £2,599 / AU$4,699 and 2TB at $3,199 / £3,199 / AU$5,899.

The iPhone Duo is technically on sale, but online retailers and carriers have delivery wait times pushing back towards the end of the year — and into 2027. It's possible some brick & mortar locations may have physical stock, but you'll need to check your local establishments to find out for sure.

The most obvious difference between the iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo is the overall shape and look of the devices. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a traditional looking iPhone with the same 6.9-inch display as the iPhone 17 Pro Max. This screen is covered in Ceramic Shield 2 glass, and has an anti-reflective coating to minimize glare.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Meanwhile the iPhone Duo has a foldable design, with a wider 5.4-inch display, and a larger 7.6-inch display that unfolds as you open the phone. This larger screen has a similar aspect ratio to the 4:3 design utilized in Apple's iPads.

The outer display has the same Ceramic Shield 2 glass and anti-reflective coating. The inner display has a nano-texture matte display that minimizes glare, but also mutes some of the colors in a way a lot of people aren't used to.

According to our testing the iPhone Duo is slightly brighter, with a maximum brightness of 2,558 nits. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is slightly dimmer with a maximum brightness of 2,326 nits.

The iPhone Duo's folding nature means it is both thinner and thicker than the iPhone 18 Pro Max. When folded the phone has a thickness of 11.3mm / 0.44 inches, which is reduced to 5.2 mm / 0.20 inches when unfolded. The iPhone Duo, by contrast, is 8.8mm / 0.35 inches thick.

The Pro Max is slightly lighter, with an overall weight of 249 grams / 8.78 ounces compared to the iPhone Duo's 154 grams / 8.96 ounces. That makes the Duo the heaviest iPhone has ever made.

Both phones have IP68 water and dust resistance, and can handle being submerged in up to six meters of water for up to 30 minutes. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is an eSIM-only model in North America, but physical SIM cards are available in other regions. The Duo is only available with eSIM, regardless of where you buy one.

One advantage the iPhone 18 Pro Max has is the inclusion of Face ID, though this does mean you lose a little bit of screen space to the Dynamic Island cutout. The iPhone Duo has a hole-punch camera on the outer display and a hidden under-display camera on the inner display.

The other crucial difference between the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the Duo is the fact the Duo only has two cameras. Both phones feature 48MP main and ultrawide-angle lenses, though only the Pro Max model features the 48MP telephoto lens (with 4x optical zoom).

It's also worth pointing out that, despite the similar resolution, the two have different camera lenses and hardware specs. This includes the lack of variable aperture which, at the moment, is exclusive to the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

But hardware is one thing, how do these cameras actually compare? We put both through a 10-round camera face-off to find out — and here's a quick rundown.

In terms of the main camera, there isn't a whole lot of difference, The two phones manage to capture pretty similar photos, with the same lighting and colors in most places. However the iPhone 18 Pro Max has stronger contrast and captures shadowy areas a little better.

The same is true of the ultrawide cameras. Unless you're looking extremely closely, more than the casual observer ever will, there's nothing to really differentiate the shots from both phones.

Again, selfies aren't that dissimilar, even though the Duo has a lower resolution 12MP camera — compared to the Pro Max's 18MP Center Stage lens. Both manage to capture a realistic image, and pick up the finer details pretty well.

At 2x magnification the loss of the telephoto lens doesn't make a huge difference to the quality of the iPhone Duo's zoomed-in photos. No doubt thanks to Apple's 2x "optical quality" feature, which simply crops down a higher resolution image to simulate magnification.

Increase the magnification to 10x and you can see a much bigger difference. The iPhone 18 Pro Max performs so well that you wouldn't really suspect that this has been zoomed in quite so far. However, the iPhone Duo produces a shot that is blurry, pixelated, and missing many of the finer details that the Pro Max's camera had no issues with.

We're back to even footing with the low-light shots, and despite the Pro Max having a slightly wider aperture, the photos from both phones came out pretty well. Both cameras preserved the details, and lit up the display with minimal noise and loss of quality.

Overall, the cameras on iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo are fairly evenly matched in every way except for zoomed-in shots. All the digital tricks in the world can't seem to make up for the fact that the telephoto lens is missing on the Duo. So, if you can't live without taking higher-quality zoomed-in shots, then the Duo is not for you.

There's very little difference in performance power, on account of the iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo sharing the same A20 Pro chipset. However, in terms of raw benchmarking scores, the iPhone 18 Pro Max has a slight advantage in all three major categories: computing, graphics and AI.

As you can see the iPhone 18 Pro Max managed a single-core score of 4,025 in the Geekbench 7 test, compared to the iPhone Duo's 4,007. That's not a huge difference, though the gap grows a little larger when you look at the multi-core results: The iPhone 18 Pro Max scored 11,525 while the Duo came in with 11,363.

3DMark's Solar Bay Unlimited graphics test saw the 18 Pro Max record a score of 17,850 and an average frame rate of 67.9fps. Meanwhile the Duo was quite a bit lower with a score of 16,496 and an average frame rate of 62.3 fps. AI processing also had a rather large gap, with the 18 Pro Max scoring 71,974 in the Geekbench AI 1.7 benchmark. The Duo recorded a score of 69,438.

It's worth mentioning that the iPhone Duo actually scored better than the smaller iPhone 18 Pro in the graphics and AI testing. This is worth bearing in mind if you want maximum performance, but were worried the Pro Max might be a little too big for your tastes.

Both iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo run iOS 27, and have the same basic selection of software and AI features. The main feature of this is Siri AI, which is the upgraded assistant capable of more AI-heavy tasks than the Siri of old. This includes better understanding of your requests, and the ability to understand personal context that helps you specifically.

iOS 27 also includes features like expressive voices for Siri, the adjustable Liquid Glass interface, Siri Mode on the camera, smart tab optimization in Safari, alongside AI powered editing features like Reframe, Extend and CleanUp. In other words, if the iPhone 18 Pro Max can do it, so can the iPhone Duo.

The real difference in software is that the Duo has a new UI, designed to take advantage of the new screen sizes. This includes the ability to multitask with split-view apps, the first and only iPhone to do so, while also offering a taskbar on the right side of the screen. However a lot of work still needs doing to optimize the apps for those screens, which is not something Pro Max owners have to know about.

The iPhone Duo also features some exclusive features, including the Smart Take camera mode that follows a single subject with the aid of AI. The recent iOS 27.2 update added stylus support from the Apple Pencil USB-C, which is another thing that isn't possible on any other iPhones.

Still, for the most part, the software experience is similar enough that it doesn't make that much difference. Certainly not when it comes to deciding between those two price tags.

It's unsurprising that the iPhone Duo does not have as strong a battery life as the iPhone 18 Pro Max. For starters the battery is much smaller, with 4,883 mAh to the Pro Max's 5,567 mAh. The foldable also has to contend with the fact that it has a much larger screen to power, which is going to drain the battery much faster when in use.

Our battery life testing found that the iPhone Duo lasted 13 hours and 20 minutes, which is over four hours less than the iPhone 18 Pro Max's 17 hours and 31 minutes.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max also managed to recharge slightly faster, despite the fact both phones support up to 60W charging speeds. The Pro Max regained 44% of its battery in the first 15 minutes, which rose to 77% after half an hour. The Duo, on the other hand, reached 42% after 15 minutes and 66% after 30 minutes — despite the fact it has a smaller battery.

In other words, if you value battery life above all else, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the phone to go for. It has the larger, longer lasting battery, and manages to restore any lost charge much faster than its folding sibling.

Overall, there isn't a whole lot of difference between the iPhone Duo and the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It's true, the design of the two phones couldn't be more different, and the experience of using a foldable is completely different to that of a traditional phone. That said, from a user perspective, you're getting a lot of the same qualities and results from both phones.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max does have better battery life and the all-important telephoto lens. Combined with the noticeably lower price tag, that's enough to sway people in that particular direction. More so when you remember that they're a lot easier to get hold of at the moment.

The iPhone Duo has the benefit of being something new and exciting, alongside the fact the larger screen offers a lot more utility. It's a device that offers the same productivity benefits as a tablet, with stylus support and split-view apps. But the downside is that you have to pay a premium and make some sacrifices in the process — particularly the long wait to get your hands on one.

#3559. Remember Patrick Stewart With His Star Trek Co-Star Brent Spiner's Hilarious Impressions

When you do seven seasons of television, four movies, and a three-season encore with someone, you can't help but develop a familial relationship with them. It might run the gamut from warm to dysfunctional, and there may be a full-scale falling out, but you can't choose your TV family. The casting director can, but as long as there's an audience, you're stuck with them.

When Walter Koenig died earlier this week, we were reminded that he had a somewhat chilly relationship with his "Star Trek" cast mate William Shatner. So it was nice that Shatner wrote a touching remembrance, because, y'know, life is too damn short. Fortunately, life is long enough that we got to see Brent Spiner lightly roast Patrick Stewart over and over again with a dead-on impression of his co-star. Spiner could scarcely make a convention appearance or do an interview without being asked to trot out his impersonation of Stewart's sonorous baritone. It wasn't broad in a Rich Little sense. It was nuanced, elegant and deeply affectionate. Stewart didn't love it, but it was a tool Spiner and Jonathan Frakes used to get their Shakespearian-trained co-star to loosen up.

Just listen to Spiner bust out his Stewart at the 2016 San Diego Comic Con (and watch Shatner howl with approval).

Spiner knew these requests were coming, so he made the audience beg for it. Here's a fun instance of this:

There's a deep, deep rabbit hole of Spiner goofing on Stewart, and I encourage you to tumble down it because we need the laughs nowadays, but here are a few more highlights.

Impersonations are tough. They might sound great in your head, but you'll know straight away if you're hitting the mark via the reaction from your audience. It's a rare talent, one that has been mastered by comedy gods like Eddie Murphy, Dana Carvey, and Bill Hader. The difference with Spiner's Stewart is that a) he knew it irked his friend just enough, and b) torturing your friends is a part of the bond. Spiner explains as much here:

This one's a little shaky, but I don't think Spiner has ever been in better voice as Stewart. This is a scream.

And here, you get a long run-up to an impression that arrives at the 3:45 mark, but you should watch it all. Spiner so clearly adored Stewart, which meant getting a kick out of his innocuous egotism. You could puncture Stewart's star bubble, and he'd (grudgingly) roll with the punches. He loved performing. He loved performers. He learned to love making an fool out of himself (with the help of Ricky Gervais). He was a joy to behold.
