#3558. Tatiana Maslany's Cult Sci-Fi Series On HBO Max Is Worth Revisiting

Even as ads become more and more common on streaming platforms, taking away the few remaining reasons we had to transition from traditional cable in the first place, it's quite rare to get an ad for older titles. It makes sense that a streaming platform would want viewers to know about upcoming movies and shows, not 13-year-old cult TV series.

And yet, that's exactly what HBO Max is doing with its latest addition — and with good reason. HBO Max and Peacock are now the co-exclusive home of the BBC Studios sci-fi series "Orphan Black," which starred Tatiana Maslany, Tatiana Maslany, Tatiana Maslany, and also Tatiana Maslany, alongside many other Tatiana Maslanys.

You see, "Orphan Black" focuses on Sarah Manning (Maslany) who happens to be one of several human clones, all genetically identical. The show follows Sarah as she witnesses the suicide of one of the other clones, and quickly uncovers a vast conspiracy involving her origin and plans to have her and her "sisters" killed.

"Orphan Black" remains one of the best sci-fi shows of all time. It's a character-driven story that's mostly a showcase of Tatiana Maslany's incredible acting talents, but with plenty of plot twists that keep you hooked. Across five seasons, it developed a strong cult following that's kept "Orphan Black" alive all this time.

Nearly a decade since the show ended, it's never a bad time to revisit this wacky, dark, always-fun sci-fi thriller.

The main reason to watch "Orphan Black" is to witness Tatiana Maslany deliver a once-in-a-generation performance as every single clone featured in the show. Each clone has their own personality, accent, and mannerisms. It's truly a testament to Maslany's Emmy-winning performance that it becomes easy to forget there's actually just one actor in scenes with multiple clones interacting. Each character feels like a completely different person.

Without Maslany, the show falls apart, but it's the writing and plotting, in addition to her performance, that makes this such a memorable show. "Orphan Black" starts out with a compelling mystery before evolving into a proper thriller, with the stakes rising every season and more dangers being introduced to the plot. It is a perfect show for fans of the twisty "Manifest."

Still, underneath the many, many twists and turns, "Orphan Black" is above all else a compelling exploration of a group of women coming together when they realize their whole world was based on a lie, and the question of nature versus nurture. The show also features a very diverse cast of people of color and also queer characters, as the story explores bodily agency and integrity, and ethics in science. And the show was a dream come true for board game fans, constantly featuring some of the biggest games of the 2010s prominently for both set dressing and as a way to convey the many plot elements and mysteries.

"Orphan Black" lasted for five seasons, with BBC America canceling the show after its fifth season back in 2017. Still, that wasn't the ending of the show.

Though the series ended on a rather definitive note, a spin-off series titled "Orphan Black: Echoes" premiered in 2023. Curiously, the show took a whole year to reach the U.S., where it debuted on BBC America and AMC. The spin-off took place 37 years after the ending of the original, following a now-adult Kira (daughter of the protagonist of the original series), and starring Krysten Ritter as a woman with amnesia. The spin-off was met with mixed reviews, who praised it for being more than just a clone of "Orphan Black," but noted that it failed to really make an impact like its predecessor. It lasted one season.

There was also a 10-episode audio series titled "Orphan Black: The Next Chapter," which actually continued the story of the main series and starred Tatiana Maslany as all the clones, while also bringing back other original cast members. Lastly, there was even a Japanese remake of the show, titled "Orphan Black – 7 Genes" which aired back in 2017 on Fuji TV.

It's a testament to the enduring popularity of the "Orphan Black" world that it continues to inspire new stories, and that its fans continue to show up even after so many years. If you've never had the pleasure of meeting all the clone sisters, the addition of "Orphan Black" to the HBO Max library is the perfect opportunity to do so.

Anytime a member of the Dutton family gets brought up on Marshals or Dutton Ranch, my ears perk up. So, this year, my gears really got going when there was a conversation in Marshals about Kayce’s brother and sister. That’s because, as that show continues its run on the 2026 TV schedule and we wait for Season 2 of Dutton Ranch, Kayce’s comments about Jamie and Beth got me thinking about how these Yellowstone sequel series could cross over.

As the marshals were dealing with the McCoy family and a very dangerous threat in Episode 5 of Season 2, Kayce specifically spends time with Will, who is injured. They discuss Will’s family and his issues with them. That causes Kayce to open up just a bit about his. Here’s how that conversation went:

Now, while no names were named, it’s pretty obvious who Kayce is talking about here. Jamie is his middle brother, and he did become estranged from the Duttons. Meanwhile, Beth is his older sister, and really is tougher and meaner than all her brothers. As Kayce said, she’s very capable of eating just about anybody for lunch...and, you know, she killed Jamie.

It was interesting to hear him talk about his siblings in such a way, while also totally avoiding the elephant in the room when Will asked what happened to Jamie. It was that avoidance that gave me a theory about how Marshals and Dutton Ranch could cross over.

At this point, the question about a crossover for these shows is more a when than an if. Both Luke Grimes and Kelly Reilly have said they’re down, and Cole Hauser said he’d love to go back to Montana too. This week’s episode of Marshals made me realize just that can happen if they dive into the mystery surrounding Jamie’s death.

There have been plenty of Yellowstone references in Marshals that made me think diving into the death of Jamie could be a possibility. I mean, it is an unsolved case, and Kayce is a law enforcement officer in Montana. The drama is too good not to explore. Then, on Dutton Ranch, Jamie’s death proved to be a point of conflict between Beth and Beulah. So, I feel like everyone has to come together to deal with this at some point.

They could do just that in a crossover event. In it, an investigation into Jamie’s death could be opened on Marshals, and it could bring Beth and Rip back up to Montana. Kayce could also go to Texas to warn them. Either way, Yellowstone’s ending coming back around in both shows would be so juicy it’d be worthy of a two-episode event, and it would be both a meaningful and logical way to bring the Dutton siblings and these two shows together.

So, if anyone from either show is reading this, I’d love for a crossover to happen this way. In the meantime, I’ll keep watching both shows on Paramount+.

The CurvX earns that higher price by doing more than simply vacuuming an open stretch of floor—its 22,000 pascals of suction can handle pet hair, crumbs, and debris caught in carpet, while the DuoDivide main brush guides hair toward the center to reduce tangles. The Roborock app gives you further control, allowing you to clean specific rooms, create schedules, set virtual barriers, and mark areas the robot should avoid, while SmartPlan 2.0 adapts the routine to different rooms and floor types.

#3555. Project Hail Mary: How Julia Roberts Solved A Major Acting Problem For Ryan Gosling

In a new interview with IndieWire, Ryan Gosling admitted that acting in his 2026 sci-fi film "Project Hail Mary" was lonely work. Luckily, a visit with, of all people, Julia Roberts gave Gosling an idea of how not to be so lonely. It seems Roberts was partially responsible for Gosling's inspiration for creating Moppy Ringwald, a makeshift scene partner that Gosling required to stay sane.

As those who have seen "Project Hail Mary" can attest, Gosling's character — Dr. Ryland Grace — spends a huge portion of the movie alone, the only human onboard a space vessel sent to investigate a faraway sun. Grace was meant to be part of a three-person crew, but his companions died during the long journey. After waking up light-years from home, Grace, sporting a long caveman-like beard, struggles to regain his memories all alone in the cosmos.

Eventually Grace does gain some companionship in the form of Rocky (James Ortiz), an intelligent alien rock spider. But for a long time Gosling was the only actor on set, and he began to experience the same painful isolation that Dr. Grace was going through. Eventually, the crew made him a companion: a mop with a face and a dress attached. They nicknamed their creation Moppy Ringwald.

As he recalls in the IndieWire interview, Gosling made the request for Moppy Ringwald's construction after a chance meeting with Julia Roberts.

Ryan Gosling told IndieWire that he got to a point where was "tired of acting alone" on "Project Hail Mary." When he left the set for a breath of fresh air, he just so happened to run into Julia Roberts filming "After the Hunt," which was also an Amazon MGM Studios production. The two had never spoken before, but they struck up a conversation. Gosling said:

"I'd never met her, and she sat down and talked to me. [...] She was talking about how much fun she was having on her set with Luca Guadagnino on 'After the Hunt.' She said, 'You should come over,' and I needed human interaction. So I went down to the set, and they were shooting a party scene, and they were all drinking and having fun, and they seemed like they were having a great time."

"After the Hunt" is a terse drama about allegations of sexual assault and the dark secrets lurking in the past of a high-profile Yale philosophy professor. It's a pretty good movie – /Film accurately gave it a 6.5 out of 10 – but it's definitely not a feel-good movie. Calling it "a great time" might seem incongruous, but Gosling was clearly relieved to be on a set where a party scene was being shot, just grateful to be around people.

It was the experience of visiting the set of "After the Hunt" that let Gosling acknowledge just how much he missed working with other actors. Of course, the story of "Project Hail Mary" demanded that Gosling's character be the only human around, so he and the film's directors, Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, came up with Moppy Ringwald.

Yes, the solution to Ryan Gosling's on-set loneliness was a little strange, but luckily Phil Lord and Christopher Miller were not only game but also a little whimsical. Gosling recalls the inception of Moppy Ringwald thus:

"I said, 'I want a friend, I want someone to act with,' [...] They were like, 'okay, but what do we do?' And I said, 'I want to get a mop, and I want to make it into a person and talk to it.' And they stopped everything on our fancy, expensive day, and crawled around the sets looking for tape and glasses, and a dress. And they helped me build this mop lady for me to do scenes with, who we called Moppy Ringwald."

The set, Gosling said, was a high-tech marvel full of working LED screens. It was, however, a mop with sunglasses that ultimately saved shooting. And Gosling said he learned a very important lesson that day, and it's one we can all take to heart. "If you're having a problem and you can't solve it," he said, "talk to Julia Roberts. That's the big lesson here. She'll solve it for you." So be sure to have Ms. Roberts on speed-dial at all times, dear readers. She'll be there for you.

Moppy Ringwald actually does have a blink-and-you'll-miss-it cameo in "Project Hail Mary," and is featured even more in the deleted scenes, but it's nice just to know that Gosling really bonded with his "co-star." Knowing that Moppy was on set, often just of-camera, serving as Gosling's ersatz "scene partner," makes rewatching "Project Hail Mary" just that much more rewarding. And we have Julia Roberts to thank.

#3554. I drove the Volvo EX60 for a week and it’s an all-electric SUV I’d buy with my own money — here’s why

The 2027 Volvo EX60 sets a new benchmark for mid-size electric SUVs by pairing punchy dual-motor performance and soothing Scandinavian design with staggering real-world efficiency. While its $68,745 as-tested price tag remains a serious financial commitment, it overdelivers on every front.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

​The mid-size SUV segment is one of the most crowded spaces in the automotive world, largely because these vehicles must carefully balance family hauling with everyday utility. The 2027 Volvo EX60 checks every box, made even more compelling by the fact that it’s an all-electric model offering up to 330 miles of range.

​After driving the 2027 Volvo EX60 P10 AWD for a week, I’m convinced it sets the benchmark for luxury electric SUVs. With an as-tested price of $68,745, it undercuts two of my favorite alternatives: the Audi Q6 e-tron and Rivian R2.

Inheriting much of the charm and punchy performance of the smaller EX30 — which happens to be one of the best electric cars I’ve tested all year — the EX60 easily proves it’s worth the price of admission. Here’s why.

Dual Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motors (AWD)

​I drove a total of 189.4 miles during my week’s worth of testing the 2027 Volvo EX60 P10 AWD, achieving an outstanding average efficiency of 4.1 mi/kWh. That doesn’t just make it one of the most efficient luxury EVs on the road — it easily outperforms similarly sized rivals like the Subaru Trailseeker, as well as three-row haulers like the Kia EV9 and Hyundai Ioniq 9. In fact, its energy consumption rivals much smaller crossovers like the Subaru Solterra and Toyota bZ.

​Where the EX60 truly shines is in low-speed, stop-and-go suburban driving. I recorded a peak short-distance efficiency of 5.43 mi/kWh, while highway cruising settled at an impressive 3.85 mi/kWh over long distances. Put simply: you'ill stretch your battery pack significantly farther between charges than in almost any competing mid-size luxury EV.

When it comes to charging, the EX60 features Tesla's NACS port for straightforward Level 3 DC fast charging at Tesla Superchargers. At home, plugging into a standard 120V Level 1 wall outlet yielded a charging rate of 5.34 miles per hour — the fastest Level 1 recovery speed I’ve tested to date. In practice, that meant adding roughly 50 miles of range back into the pack in just under 9.5 hours of overnight charging.

​I can’t overstate the EX60’s outstanding efficiency, largely because being frugal isn't what this segment is about. Most mid-size electric crossovers struggle to reach the 3 mi/kWh baseline I consider average, but the EX60 goes the distance by surging past 4 mi/kWh. That puts it in the same efficiency territory as aerodynamic sedans and smaller crossovers like the Lucid Air and Kia EV6.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

​In the luxury EV space, dual-motor all-wheel-drive haulers are power hungry — and previously I've tested like the Audi Q6 e-tron and BMW iX xDrive45 prove how difficult that barrier is to break. Yet, the EX60 shatters expectations by achieving those figures despite packing a 503-horsepower dual-motor powertrain. Volvo just proved that compromise is no longer mandatory for a mid-size SUV.

​Volvo employs a distinctive design language that I find fascinating, standing in stark contrast to the over-the-top visual excess often found in Mercedes-Benz and BMW cabins. The Scandinavian-inspired design language Volvo carries over from its other EVs delivers what I call "silent luxury."

​Borrowing heavily from the playbook of the smaller EX30, the EX60 strips away dashboard clutter in favor of an open, airy aesthetic anchored by a crisp 15-inch curved OLED center display. Thoughtful packaging touches — such as a sliding center console that extends to reveal dual cupholders, paired with rich woven textile surfaces — further elevate the understated tone that gives the cabin a calming look and feel.

Few things frustrate me more in modern EVs than dealing with outdated, sluggish software. Volvo’s infotainment system continues to make major strides, delivering a polished interface that feels contemporary.

From a home screen that logically positions Google Maps and core media functions as the primary focal points, to clean-looking icons and fluid animations that respond to every tap, the software experience is every bit as impressive as the minimalist cabin surrounding it.

Navigating tight parking spots is a breeze thanks to sharp exterior cameras that provide comprehensive 360-degree coverage. Beyond the impressive daytime clarity and wide dynamic range in high-contrast lighting, the real highlight is how Volvo arranges the feeds on screen. Instead of forcing you to rely on a single perspective or cycle through menus, the system splits into a simultaneous three-camera view that gives you real-time visibility out front, directly behind, and from an overhead bird's-eye angle all at once.

​Moving up to a mid-size SUV, I was worried that the EX60 might lose the pep and responsiveness that made the smaller EX30 so thrilling to drive. Luckily, it delivers driving dynamics that are just as engaging, making this mid-size crossover surprisingly fun to manuver. The EX60 P10 AWD serves up almost that exact same punchy sensation, courtesy of dual permanent-magnet synchronous motors that produce 503 horsepower and 524 lb-ft of torque.

​Not only does it leap forward instantly whenever I stomp on the accelerator, but it's also remarkably agile during quick highway overtakes. There's zero hesitation from this zippy crossover. Thanks to its low center of gravity and planted stance, it gives off genuine sports car vibes in how eagerly it handles corners and responds to my acceleration.

As with the previous XC40, EX40, and XC90 models I’ve tested, I’ve always appreciated Volvo’s signature "Thor’s Hammer" headlights. However, the EX60 brings a major functional upgrade by shifting to fully adaptive dynamic matrix LEDs. It's easily one of the smartest lighting setups on the road, functioning very much like the adaptive matrix headlights found on Rivian’s R1T, R1S, and R2.

Rather than simply toggling high beams on and off, the system actively shapes the light beam around oncoming traffic and lead vehicles. Watching it adapt in real time at night looks almost surreal: the matrix array carves out precise dark cutouts around other cars while keeping the shoulders, signs, and open lanes ahead brilliantly illuminated.

Highway driving is an absolute breeze in this EV because Volvo’s latest iteration of Pilot Assist with adaptive cruise control naturally adapts to changing traffic flow. Not only does it keep the crossover centered and smoothly applies braking and acceleration when needed, but thoughtful details throughout the system highlight just how refined it truly is.

The EX60 excels at reading the road ahead through its high-resolution camera and radar suite, gently letting off the pedal and applying a gentle brake when another car cuts into my lane. Additional safety touches enhance the experience further, including extra-bright blind-spot warning LEDs integrated into each side mirror and clear visual notifications in the digital driver's display that render nearby adjacent vehicles in real time.

The EX60 delivers the fastest Level 1 charging rate I’ve recorded from any EV to date. Replenishing at a rate of 5.34 miles per hour, nothing else I've tested on standard household power comes close — especially when most competitors struggle to reach 4 miles per hour. For drivers who haven’t yet installed a dedicated Level 2 charger at home, the EX60 can recover a practical amount of daily driving range from an ordinary 120V wall outlet.

When you need to charge on the road, the EX60 features a native NACS (North American Charging Standard) port, providing seamless access to Tesla’s extensive Supercharger network. You can also equip the vehicle with optional adapters, ensuring you still get access to standard CCS DC fast chargers and older public stations.

While the 2027 Volvo EX60 undercuts many of its luxury rivals, namely BMW, Audi, and Mercedes-Benz, it’s far from a budget EV. Starting under $60,000 for a base trim — and climbing to $68,745 for the P10 AWD I tested — it remains a stretch for some households when cheaper options exist. That becomes even more pronounced when stacked against incoming competition like the Rivian R2, which enters the market starting under $60,000 for a top-of-the-line trim.

It’s not often I say this, but the 2027 Volvo EX60 stands out as one of the most satisfying EVs I have tested all year. There’s no denying that its $68,745 as-tested price remains a serious financial commitment for many households, but unlike many luxury crossovers that demand major trade-offs, the EX60 overdelivers across the board.

Not only does it preserve the punchy driving dynamics that made the smaller EX30 so enjoyable, but it also scales up into a practical mid-size footprint with generous passenger room and clever storage. Coupled with Volvo's signature "silent luxury" interior aesthetic, what truly steals the show is its staggering real-world efficiency of 4.1 mi/kWh — alongside a class-leading recovery rate of 5.34 miles per hour on simple Level 1 home charging.

If you have the budget for a premium crossover, the EX60 doesn't just meet expectations, it sets a new standard for the class.

#3553. Star Wars Zero Company’s Cast Talks About That Huge Order 66 Moment

Bit Reactor wanted a memorable Order 66 scene from the outset

What series is stuffed with more iconic moments than Star Wars? From Qui-Gon Jin’s defeat to Luke blowing up the Death Star, Star Wars is full of classic scenes ranging from tragic to triumphant. One of the prequel trilogy’s most memorable sequences is when Emperor Palpatine orders the clone army to “execute Order 66” in Star Wars: Episode III — Revenge of the Sith. A montage then plays out showing clone commanders and their troops murdering several Jedi.

Order 66 and the Great Jedi Purge have been depicted in various Star Wars media, like Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order and Star Wars: The Bad Batch. Bit Reactor’s beloved strategy game Star Wars Zero Company has its own huge Order 66 moment.

Polygon recently spoke with several Zero Company cast members — Jonathan Freeman (male Hawks), Dee Bradley Baker (Trick), and Vic Michaelis (Runa) — about their reactions to that Order 66 moment. We also chatted with creative director Greg Foertsch about how Bit Reactor brought Order 66 to life.

“A lot happens across the galaxy in a snap,” Baker said. “It's a dramatically really interesting moment in Star Wars.”

[Ed. note: Spoilers follow for Star Wars Zero Company.]

Just when you think your team of misfits is ready to undertake their final mission, Palpatine issues Order 66, leading clone trooper Trick to turn on his allies, including a Jedi Padawan, Tel-Rea. Republic intelligence officer Bennic also tries to arrest Zero Company, further adding to the betrayal. Fans have experienced Order 66 and the Great Jedi Purge across various mediums and Star Wars stories, but Zero Company does something different. Players are forced to control Trick in actually carrying out the attack. Star Wars Zero Company is an excellent game, and it’s surprising and innovative moments like this that could propel it into the end-of-year awards conversations.

From the outset, Bit Reactor wanted to “straddle” Order 66 with the game’s setting, according to Foertsch, because Zero Company takes place during The Clone Wars and into the early days of the Empire. Still, it presented a challenge, as the developers needed to ensure players cared about Trick prior to his forced betrayal. By the time the mission comes around, Trick (one of your strongest companions) has likely become an integral part of your squad, seeing as how he’s been there since the beginning. That reliability was intentionally baked into canon between him and the main character too.

“By tying Trick to Hawks prior to the game, that [ensures] they have a connection that extends beyond the current version of Zero Company that the player is experiencing,” Foertsch said.

The player will also care for the Padawan Tel-Rea (if she’s still alive), and will be made to attack her as Trick. Baker called Order 66 “the heartbreak of the clones,” and nothing is more heartbreaking than the player being forced into a position where they have to harm a squadmate.

“We felt it was a really unique moment, and something very special to Zero Company,” Foertsch added.

Order 66 first happened in 2005’s Revenge of the Sith, but it’s no less relevant to today’s world. “Everything flips, and tyranny takes over,” Baker said. “In some ways, maybe it's the most important moment in Star Wars, to show how democracy falls and how diabolical authoritarian [rule] can be. That's an important and relevant moment in our world right now.”

To Freeman, the Order 66 moment encapsulated Zero Company “in a nutshell.” While so much of Star Wars focuses on the grand machinations of the movers and shakers throughout the galaxy, Zero Company, ahem, zeroes in on a wily bunch of outcasts on their own side adventure during the Clone Wars. “It's just so cool to take the huge, epic, iconic story [of Star Wars] and pinpoint this very specific important moment and show it happening in real time to people off to the side,” Freeman said.

He enjoyed how Zero Company’s Order 66 moment involved random, regular people being perplexed by this sudden hologram of their new emperor showing up, a scene that surely took place throughout every city and major hub of the new Galactic Empire. “I think that's what makes this story special,” he said.

Getting perspectives on Order 66 from characters who aren’t Jedi or clones was a shared goal among Bit Reactor’s team, according to Foertsch. “We wanted to show that event from a different lens, and a very different perspective than fans had ever seen before,” he said.

The Order 66 turn is especially impactful on Freeman’s Hawks. He and Bennic had been bonding throughout the game, but suddenly they’re placed at a crossroads. Hawks picks the path of sticking with Zero Company, while Bennic continues working for what has now become the Galactic Empire.

“The relationships in this script are just so good,” Freeman said, calling them a “vital” part of the game and its story. He was glad Hawks and Bennic reconciled at the end, but, unlike players, he knew they’d be friends again from the very beginning. Freeman tipped his hat to developer Bit Reactor, saying, “[to] have time for these moments, for the relationships to stand out and to have such consequence and heart, is pretty impressive.”

For Michaelis, Order 66 in Zero Company “feels very Star Wars-ian.” Their character, Runa, isn’t at the hangar with Hawks, Trick, and the others when Order 66 goes down. Instead, she’s at the holotable, where she spends most of the game. “I was learning about [Order 66] in real time with a lot of people,” Michaelis said.

Like Freeman, they’re new to Star Wars, but have been a lifelong fan of the series. They said that there are some roles “where it's a job and you're saying stuff,” but working on Star Wars is different. “Watching the game come together, with the Star Wars music piped in underneath, it really is like, ‘Oh my God, we are in Star Wars. We're in Star Wars right now,’” they said. “It is very surreal, and [Order 66] was one of those moments too.”

Star Wars Zero Company may have been the first time Michaelis experienced Order 66 as part of the Star Wars grand apparatus, but the same can’t be said for Baker. Having voiced the clones for nearly two decades now, Baker has experienced the clones’ betrayal time and again. He noted that The Bad Batch even opened with it in a “shocking” moment.

Baker recently told Polygon in an interview that he can’t remember all the different clones he’s voiced in the same way that the fans do. For Order 66, he similarly can’t keep track of every time he’s been a part of The Clone Wars’ climactic moment. “Once again, the fans know better than me how many times I've been through Order 66, I would imagine.”

#3552. This 2000s War Movie With A Pricey Budget Was Dead On Arrival At The Box Office

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Hollywood has had major success adapting real-life feats of wartime heroism. Clint Eastwood might wish that more people saw his underrated World War II movie "Letters from Iwo Jima," but the reviews were absolutely stellar. More recently, Sam Mendes' used his grandfather's stories about his World War I service to make the excellent "1917," and even Sam Elliott's most difficult production, the war movie "We Were Soldiers," debuted to solid reviews. But not every war film based on true events has fared quite as well. Take 2005's "The Great Raid," which told the story of how the lives of 500 American prisoners of war were saved while boring critics something fierce. It also lost a heck of a lot of money in the process.

Director John Dahl is best known for his cult 1990s hits "Red Rock West" and "The Last Seduction." He's since gone on to enjoy a prolific TV directing career. But before pivoting to the small screen, he oversaw his first war movie with "The Great Raid." The film chronicles the real-life efforts of a group of Army Rangers to rescue American soldiers from a Japanese POW camp in early 1945. It remains one of the most effective rescue attempts in U.S. military history. Unfortunately, Dahl's film wasn't quite as successful, making back a fraction of its budget and earning mixed reviews (if we're being charitable). That said, one of the soldiers featured prominently in the film, Captain Robert Prince, gave "The Great Raid" his seal of approval. So, if the man who led the real-life operation was pleased with Dahl's interpretation, what did audiences and critics have against the movie?

"The Great Raid" is based on the books "The Great Raid on Cabanatuan: Rescuing the Doomed Ghosts of Bataan and Corregidor" by William B. Breuer and "Ghost Soldiers: The Forgotten Epic Story of World War II's Most Dramatic Mission" by Hampton Sides. Both focus on the Raid at Cabanatuan, which took place in early 1945 and saw 110 Army Rangers (with assistance from Filipino guerrillas) set out to rescue a group of 500 American soldiers who were being held in a Japanese POW camp on the island of Luzon, Philippines.

"The Great Raid" showcases how Lieutenant Colonel Henry Mucci (Benjamin Bratt) enlists Captain Robert Prince (James Franco) to lead the 6th Ranger Battalion on this daring mission. With Prince leading the charge, the rangers must go 30 miles behind enemy lines to save their fellow soldiers, who've been held captive for three years and face execution at the hands of the Japanese. Joseph Fiennes plays Major Daniel Gibson, the captives' malaria-stricken senior officer whose partner, Nurse Margaret Utinsky (Connie Nielsen), is trying to help by smuggling medicine into the camp. But Utinsky's efforts are discovered, and she's imprisoned just as the rangers formulate their plan and prepare to pull off one of the most dangerous missions of World War II.

As thrilling as that sounds, "The Great Raid" was, in the estimation of many a critic, a drag of a war movie that could nonetheless conceivably be given another chance in the age of the dreaded streaming movie. One thing it can't do, however, is make back its budget. The film only managed to gross $10.8 million at the box office against a budget as high as $80 million, making it a major financial failure.

"The Great Raid" isn't as bad as, say, the John Wayne-led disaster that is "The Green Berets" (a film that Roger Ebert once described as "cruel and dishonest"). But so far as war movies based on true stories go, it's hardly a triumph.

At the time of writing, the film has a 39% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes based on 119 reviews. Marc Savlov of the Austin Chronicle blamed "enough chatty exposition to sink the Bismarck" for undermining a movie that otherwise had "the makings of a fine, moving, epic war film." Other reviewers similarly lamented the movie's plodding pace and uncanny ability to make a thrilling rescue mission feel underwhelming.

That said, while The Washington Post's Stephen Hunter admitted that "one might have wished for a better movie," he also found the film to be "a riveting, even inspirational account of an American feat of arms about which few know but about which many more should." What's more, Robert Prince, the man who led the rescue operation, was — according to Seattle PI — pleased with the film. According to the outlet, Prince thought "The Great Raid" captured the spirit and significance of his mission. It might have helped that he wisely pushed back against John Dahl's attempts to, as Seattle PI put it, "turn him into a John Wayne." As the former Ranger told the outlet, "Let's set something straight. We all worked together. I had no bigger impact than Colonel Mucci."

At least, then, Dahl can rest assured that the man who was actually there at the real-life raid liked his film well enough. Otherwise, "The Great Raid" has been mostly forgotten, although it's available to rent from the usual digital platforms.

I know that sometimes taking a hard stance against a beloved movie like One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest is always risky, but this is one that I've held for a long time, and I’m comfortable if the comments about this take aim at me. I simply don’t like the movie. Weirdly, I don’t have a problem with the Oscars it won (and it won a lot in one of the best Oscar races ever), and I don’t dislike anything about the production of the movie. The Cuckoo’s Nest cast and their performances are fantastic, the directing from Miloš Forman is top-notch, and the dialogue is spot on. There is a fundamental flaw with this book-to-screen adaptation, and that is the reduction of the most important character in the book, Chief Bromden, into something way less than he should have been.

I love the novel One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest by Ken Kesey. When people ask me what my favorite book ever is, I usually answer with the 1962 novel that helped define a generation. I’ve read the book four times over the years, and every time I read it, I get something new out of it. When I first read it, sometime in high school in the early ‘90s, I focused on what the movie focuses on: R.P. McMurphy (Jack Nicholson in the movie, in one of his best roles) and his exploits in the ward of the mental hospital.

I was taken by McMurphy. His anti-authoritarian posturing was perfect for an anxious wanna-be rebellious teenager. He is loud and brash, and lives life his own way. It’s basically any 15-year-old’s dream. Minus the getting locked up part, obviously. I also loved the stories of the other guys in the ward, like Billy, Martini, and Harding. They all get their own glory in the movie. However, in each of my subsequent readings, it’s always been about Bromden. The story is told through his eyes, and it’s his thoughts that continue to stick with me.

Here’s the problem with the movie: Bromden is more or less irrelevant to the story. Sure, he gets his big moment at the end, just as in the book, but it feels so much less deserved in the movie. He’s basically a tall Native American that McMurphy needs for his basketball team in the movie. Gone from the movie are his thoughts on the ward and society as a whole. His backstory–his father being cheated by the United States and Bromden’s retreat into himself, landing him on the ward–is erased from the character.

He’s a side character who befriends McMurphy because McMurphy treats him like a regular guy. He’s not the center of the story, as he is in the book, he’s barely a character at all. Some may disagree with me, but I don’t like that Bromden has his revelation at the end of the movie and decides to smother McMurphy after the latter is lobotomized, basically because McMurphy gave him a piece of Juicy Fruit. His motivations in the book are far bigger.

In the book, Bromden tells the story of McMurphy’s battle against Nurse Ratched on the ward of the hospital. He’s not an unreliable narrator, though. He’s telling the reader what he’s observing on the ward. He’s mixing that in with memories of his childhood and of his father, and weaving that into a larger narrative about “The Combine.” The Combine is society, trying to get everyone to follow the rules, and breaking down those who refuse to play ball.

Nurse Ratched (Louise Fletcher in the movie) represents the Combine in Bromden’s small world in the hospital. She is at war with McMurphy, who is refusing to play by the rules of the ward, goading everyone else to join him in his defiance. To Bromden, McMurphy is a hero, fighting societal norms and yearning to break free of The Combine. Indeed, to destroy the whole machine itself. None of that is part of the movie, at least not in any real way. Yeah, McMurphy is a rebel, but he’s just a criminal. He’s not representative of anything bigger, as he’s meant to be in the book. Even by the filmmakers’ account, they were just looking to cast an Indian who was tall and big. He was really seen as nothing more than a side character at best.

That really irks me when I watch the movie, as I did just recently for the first time in a couple of decades. It didn’t change my opinion, overall. The story is about mental illness, yes, but it’s about so much more.

The author of Cuckoo’s Nest, Ken Kesey, agreed with his assessment. Though he loved the play that was adapted from the book a decade before the movie (as do I), he didn’t like the movie for the same reasons I don’t. Ratched isn’t the villain in the book, as Kesey has pointed out. The villain is the Combine, and Big Nurse was only a cog in the machine. She is representative of the Combine, but the machine is way bigger than her. In a documentary called Completely Cuckoo, which is an extra on the digital download I bought with my Apple subscription, Kesey says:

There's something in the American soul. We're going to take this monster with a tail and throw it over its back and whip it. This is the Combine, and this is the Murphy.  The villain in Cuckoo’s Nest is the Combine. It's not the nurse. When you drop it down to being the nurse, you're back into melodrama.

Kesey claimed in later interviews that he’d never seen the movie, and never intended to. While he was initially hired by the producers (which included Michael Douglas) to write a screenplay, they rejected it because he wanted the film to be more like the book, trippy and psychedelic, with a bigger concept than what he called a Hogan’s Heroes-style melodrama. The screenplay, which won an Oscar, is great, but it’s not the Cuckoo’s Nest I love, and that is a flaw I’ll never be able to get over.

November is Native American Heritage Month, which is what inspired me to revisit the movie. After watching the movie again and realizing that I’m never going to see it as the book’s equal, I really can’t wait to read it again.

#3549. 5 Best Western Movies Where The Main Character Dies

A common description for a happy ending, that being a hero "riding off into the sunset," comes from Western films. The sunset both bathes the hero in an angelic light and signals a conclusion without being melancholy. Just as the sun will rise again before long, it also suggests the hero will go on to have further adventures and/or a long and happy life, even if the movie never actually receives a sequel.

But not all Westerns end like that, especially more modern ones that aim to revise the Western film formula that Old Hollywood perfected. Many of those revisionist Westerns look to explore the consequences of the genre's inherent violence. There's easy romanticism to be found in gunslinging outlaws, who have been idolized as freedom seekers refusing to let unfair laws dictate their lives. But many other Western movies make a point that lives spent on crime and killing almost never come with happy, sunset-lit endings. Even for Westerns about heroic lawmen, sacrificial deaths are not out of the question. And of the Western films across the decades that end with their hero (or antihero) lead perishing, these are the very best.

Named for its gunslinging hero played by Alan Ladd, the 1953 film "Shane" is often ranked as one of the greatest Westerns of all time. It's a mature and solemn Western movie from an era before we started getting harsher deconstructionist Westerns, and it helped set the blueprint for those later films.

"Shane" is set in 1880s Wyoming and inspired by the history of the Johnson County War. Ladd's Shane is a cowboy drifter who settles on a small farm owned by the Starrett family. Young Joey Starrett (Brandon deWilde) looks up to Shane, who tries to steer him away from violence until the very end. The movie ends with Shane taking up his gun again and killing a ruthless land baron and his hired killers. A wounded Shane then rides out of the valley. The final shots, concealed in darkness, show Shane perfectly still, almost slumped over on his horse, as he rides through a graveyard.

Now, Shane's fate is deliberately uncertain, but ever since I first saw the movie, I interpreted those last shots as symbolizing death. Why else have Shane ride through a graveyard of all things? Note even how it mirrors that typical "hero rides off into the sunset" ending mentioned previously. Except, in this film, Shane's final ride is into the dark of night.

"Shane" has become the model for similarly ambiguous Western endings. Compare Spike Spiegel falling over unconscious, maybe dead, in the untidy ending of the anime space Western "Cowboy Bebop." The 2017 superhero film "Logan" also takes a lot from "Shane," down to featuring characters watching the movie and having Laura (Dafne Keen) recite Shane's last words over Logan's (Hugh Jackman) grave.

Sergio Corbucci's Spaghetti Western "The Great Silence" is one of the darkest Western films ever made, a reputation cemented by its brutal ending. Set in late 1898 Utah during a huge blizzard, "The Great Silence" follows a nonspeaking gunslinger, known only as "Silence" (Jean-Louis Trintignant). He's hired to kill a sadistic bounty hunter, Loco (Klaus Kinski), by a woman who Loco widowed, Pauline (Vonetta McGee).

This set-up sounds like typical Western storytelling, right? But the snowbound setting is not the only thing that sets "The Great Silence" apart from your typical Western. Like in many other Westerns, the film comes down to a gunslinging duel between the hero and the "black hat," with the hero always pulling off the lucky shot that brings the bad guy down. Not there, though: Loco wins the gunfight, killing Silence. Pauline then tries grabbing Silence's gun to avenge him only to be killed herself, followed by a whole saloon of people.

"The Great Silence" is a prophetic title because it's hard to have any other stunned reaction after seeing an ending like that. The bad guys, particularly a bad guy as ruthless as Loco, getting such a clean victory doesn't subvert storytelling convention as much as riddle it with bullets.

"The Great Silence" was an influence on Quentin Tarantino's 2015 Western claustrophobia-thriller "The Hateful Eight." Both films are set in a blizzard-afflicted mountain range and end with a cabin full of dead bodies.

No two actors have ever had better chemistry than Paul Newman and Robert Redford in "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid," starring the two as the eponymous outlaws of Old West legend. But history says that duo likely met their end in November 1908 during a shootout with the Bolivian army. That's how the movie ends: Butch and Sundance are wounded and are only two men against an entire army, but they rush out to face their fate. The film notably ends on a freeze frame of the duo running side-by-side, guns in hand, as the sound of gunfire plays over the still image.

The original ending for "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" actually showed them dying, but it thankfully wasn't used. The freeze frame is a perfect conclusion. We've just spent two hours seeing these guys trick their way out of trouble, and there's just enough plausible deniability that maybe they escaped this time, too.

Plus, "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" is a fairly lighthearted film overall. The ending preserves that: We don't get a mood-spoiling ending of our charismatic gunslinger heroes being gunned down, à la "Bonnie and Clyde." Instead, we get a reminder this final shot wasn't the end of their story, for they ascended into immortal legends. After all, you just watched a movie called "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid," didn't you?

Some people would argue that Sam Peckinpah's "The Wild Bunch" killed the Western itself, at least for a time. That's almost by design, because it's very much about the end of the Wild West. (Note the movie is set in 1913, much later than most other Westerns.)

The titular bunch are four survivors of an outlaw gang led by over-the-hill Pike Bishop (William Holden). The others are Dutch Engstrom (Ernest Borgnine), the Gorch brothers Lyle and Tector (Warren Oates and Ben Johnson), and Angel (Jaime Sánchez). Chased by bounty hunters and confronted with vanishing opportunities, they head to Mexico and sell their services to General Mapache (Emilio Fernández). A former member of the gang, Deke Thornton (Robert Ryan), accompanies hired agents of the railroad in tracking them so as to commute his own prison sentence.

When Angel incurs Mapache's wrath, the other four forsake their reward to rescue him. There's a wide shot of them marching in lockstep together, and that's purposefully the only time in the film they look heroic. But despite the noble sentiment, the entire Wild Bunch meet bloody ends in a climactic shoot-out. Said sequence features a turreted, bullet-spraying machine gun, the kind of weapon that creates gore on an industrial level unseen in Westerns where the only guns are simple revolvers and rifles.

The one survivor is Deke, who arrives to find Pike and everyone else already dead. Another film might lambast him as a traitor, but "The Wild Bunch" concludes by showing his loneliness and suggesting he'll throw himself back into a new struggle (the Mexican Revolution) because violence is what he's best at doing.

Andrew Dominik's 2007 Western "The Assassination of Jesse James by The Coward Robert Ford" has a mouthful of a title, but it invites you to consider: Which of the two named characters is the movie's lead? Legendary outlaw Jesse James (Brad Pitt)? Or the naive Robert Ford (Casey Affleck), who indeed ended James' life with a rather cowardly shot in the back of the head?

The film runs almost three hours long (and Dominik claims there's an even better and longer "Assassination of Jesse James" cut), so there's plenty of focus on both men. Robert is the POV character from the beginning, but in the first stretch of the movie, Jesse naturally swallows up your attention. He's also a surly, violent criminal, hardly the kind deserving of a fabled heroic reputation. You're not heartbroken when Robert betrays and kills him, but then the film continues into essentially an extended epilogue, where Robert lives in shame rather than with the "applause" he expected.

There's a pivotal scene of Robert, standing in a bar, hearing a folk singer playing "The Ballad of Jesse James," a song that survives to this day. (I first heard it covered by the English rock band The Pogues on their 1985 album "Rum Sodomy & the Lash.") The ballad portrays Jesse as a hero, someone who stole to feed the poor like Robin Hood did, and it lambasts Robert Ford as a "dirty little coward that shot Mr. Howard" (referring to James' alias of Thomas Howard).

Robert himself is murdered at the movie's end by another fame seeker, Edward O'Kelley (Michael Copeman). It's a fitting, cynical, and broadly true to history closing note that underlines how the legends of the Wild West became remembered as those legends.

Both The Big Bang Theory and Young Sheldon welcomed various guest stars over the course of their respective runs. And, in some cases, they managed to get some seriously high-profile individuals. One such person who holds the distinction of having been on both shows is Elon Musk. Now, as the heavily reviewed Musk documentary continues its run in theaters, EP Steve Holland is speaking about the experience of working with the Tesla head honcho.

While Musk appeared in both of the aforementioned sitcoms, his TBBT appearance in "The Platonic Permutation" involved multiple lines of dialogue. Holland recalled the filming day in Jessica Radloff's Young Sheldon: The (Juicier-Than-Meemaw's-Brisket) Inside Story of the Hit Comedy (via USA Today). Essentially, Holland's first thoughts on the performance set the tone for how filming went:

Readers can watch the episode with an HBO Max subscription, and I doubt they'll disagree. Elon Musk's scene with Howard Wolowitz at a soup kitchen is fairly lengthy and longer than many other Big Bang Theory cameos I've seen in the past. Apparently, Holland and crew learned their lesson when the businessman was brought on for Young Sheldon two years later, as that cameo featured far fewer speaking lines.

Holland continued talking about working with Musk and recalled the SpaceX founder having trouble reciting his lines. Eventually, he did get it, however, and when he got a response, that turned things around:

There was a moment where he said words out of order and we said, 'Actually, this is the line,' and when he said it in the right order and it got a laugh, he said, 'Oh, so it matters what order you say them in.' You could see it sort of click.

Musk has made a handful of appearances in movies and TV over the years, but this is one of the rare times I've heard about the experience of working with him. It doesn't sound too different than what any non-actor would do on the set of a show, which isn't necessarily a bad thing!

I don't think Musk has ever claimed to be an accomplished actor or worthy of his own starring role in a blockbuster on the 2026 movie schedule. For what it's worth, Steve Holland finished by stating that he found Elon Musk easy to work with, and that he had a good sense of humor:

It was a small interaction and he was perfectly easy to work with and was game to make fun of himself. Maybe less surprisingly now than then, but he liked being on camera.

Not to get too political, but I'm not so sure Elon Musk would appear on Georgie & Mandy's First Marriage these days, what with TBBT co-creator Chuck Lorre feuding with the Trump administration. That drama aside, it also feels as though Musk's acting days are over, as he hasn't had any major TV or movie gigs since he hosted Saturday Night Live in 2021. I also don't imagine he'd accept an invite to host that show again, but I could always be wrong.

For now, it seems like Musk is content promoting Tesla's flying Roadster, and other scientific developments involving space. That's fine by me, because I'm not sure how he'd fit into the '90s setting of Georgie & Mandy as well as Jay Leno did.

#3547. Author Andy Weir Will Write A Project Hail Mary Sequel Under One Condition [Exclusive]

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Is author Andy Weir ever going to write a sequel to "Project Hail Mary?" That remains to be seen, but he's not opposed to it. Weir just has one very important condition to make it a reality.

With Ryan Gosling in the lead role, the film adaptation of "Project Hail Mary" made enough money at the box office to justify a sequel, pulling in $684 million worldwide. It's also undoubtedly going to be in the awards season conversation. Both Weir's publishing agents and the folks at Amazon MGM Studios would probably love to pull the trigger on a follow-up.

Speaking recently with /Film's Jeremy Mathai, Weir addressed the possibility of a sequel to his 2021 novel, which went on to inspire this year's blockbuster movie. For Weir, it all comes down to having an idea worthy enough. Anything less and he's content to just leave it alone. Here's what he had to say about it:

"I would be happy to do a sequel for 'Project Hail Mary' if I got a good idea for one, and I feel like I've had some okay ideas, but not a real good one. I'd rather do no sequel at all than have one that's middling. I'm not going to try to force it, either. I'm not going to go, like, 'I've got to get a sequel idea because in a few years, maybe Ryan won't want to do another movie like this. I've got to get on it.' No. If I come up with a cool idea for a sequel, then I'll workshop it. I'll write it. I'll do all that."

The ending of "Project Hail May" reveals what happens to Grace and Rocky. It's a complete ending, one that doesn't necessitate a sequel. That's where the idea of a follow-up gets tricky.

Both the book and movie focus on Ryland Grace, a science teacher, who wakes up in space having no recollection how he got there. He comes to discover that he must solve a complex problem that is causing the Earth's sun to die out. If he fails, humanity perishes. "Project Hail Mary" makes some changes from the original book, but it's largely very faithful.

That said, a sequel is a difficult prospect because the "Project Hail Mary" movie changes the books' perfect ending (in a good way). As the man behind the book, Andy Weir would surely stay loyal to his text rather than the movie. So, if he were to write a sequel and Amazon decides they want to adapt it, they would have to contend with Weir jumping off from his ending rather than the movie's ending. But that's a relatively small issue that could surely be worked out.

For the time being, it doesn't seem like this is something anyone needs to worry about anytime soon. Weir further confirmed to /Film that, "Right now, the book I'm working on now is another standalone novel, not a sequel to anything." Weir's next book may tackle the hot button topic of artificial intelligence, but that has yet to be confirmed. For the most part, what he's working on is a great mystery.

You can grab "Project Hail Mary" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

If you use Google Chrome, you can turn on a new safety feature that will warn you if you navigate to a suspicious website that looks like others already known for malicious behavior. The alerts are part of Enhanced Protection mode in Chrome's Safe Browsing, which checks your activity against potentially harmful sites and warns you if you're at risk of encountering malware, phishing, intrusive ads, or social engineering attacks.

Most internet users are familiar with the full-page alerts that appear if you navigate to a site that's known to be malicious. These red "dangerous site" warnings indicate a high risk of harm to the user and can't really be ignored since they take up the entire screen and urge you to go back to safety.

The new "suspicious site" alerts indicate possible risk of harm based on patterns consistent with other known malicious sites. This means that Google isn't as confident that the website is actually dangerous, but it looks a lot like others that are spreading malware or running phishing scams. These suspicious site warnings are smaller pop-ups with the text "This site doesn't seem right" and two button options: Mark as safe or Back to safety. The different colors, text, and formatting make it easy for users to distinguish between what Google deems dangerous versus suspicious.

Safe Browsing in Chrome has three options: standard protection, enhanced protection, and no protection at all (which isn't recommended). Standard protection checks your browsing activity, extensions, and downloads against Google's list of unsafe sites, which is updated periodically. By contrast, enhanced protection works in real time and uses AI analysis. Note that enhanced protection does require you to share more information about your activity to Google, and the data are linked to your Google Account.

#3545. The Batman Part 2's Mystery Villains May Have Just Been Confirmed in Major Leak

Several newcomers were confirmed for The Batman Part 2's cast over the summer, including Sebastian Stan, Scarlett Johansson, Brian Tyree Henry, and Charles Dance. Their roles in the DC film haven't been confirmed yet, though that hasn't stopped the speculation. Rumors pointed to Stan playing the serial killer Victor Zsasz while Stan himself seemingly confirmed he'd be playing Harvey Dent in an interview with the French outlet Le Journal du Dimanche. (That article has since been updated, and the mention of Harvey Dent removed from it.) Now, it seems like Heidi Klum's Halloween costume team has confirmed Stan and Henry's roles in The Batman Part 2.

Klum dressed up as a severed hand for Halloween (gross). Prosthetic makeup designer Prosthetic Renaissance made that hand, and the company previously worked on 2022's The Batman. Now, an image is circulating online showing Prosthetic Renaissance making Klum's severed hand, and in the background are what look to be prosthetic molds for The Batman Part 2 characters.

In the picture, you can spot a mold for what looks Brian Tyree Henry. The lower-left part of his face looks to be wounded in some way, indicating that he's Harvey Dent and will begin a transformation into Two-Face in the sequel. Up top is a mold with "Zsasz" written on it, aligning with the rumors that Stan would play the serial killer. There's also a mold that looks like it could be for Charles Dance.

Most interesting perhaps is the mold with "Owl 3" written on it. The Court of Owls, a secret society of wealthy Gothamites influencing the city from the shadows, has long been rumored to play a part in The Batman Part 2, and this seems to confirm it. "Owl 3" could be for a mask for one of its members, or perhaps the costume of one of the Court's assassins, named Talons. Reeves has previously said the sequel's villain has "never really been done in a movie before."

Steven Soderbergh is taking over in the director's chair to finish filming The Batman Part 2 after Matt Reeves stepped down to address a family matter. After being previously slated for an October 2025, release, The Batman Part 2 is now scheduled to be released in theaters on Feb. 18, 2028.

#3544. Leonard Nimoy's 5 Best Cameo Appearances, Ranked

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Leonard Nimoy accrued his first screen credit in 1951, playing a small part in one of the vignettes in Arthur Lubin's "Queen for a Day." He then landed a leading role in the 1952 film noir "Kid Monk Beroni" (playing the title character) and appeared in the Republic serial "Zombies from the Stratosphere." It was on TV, though, that his early career really thrived, and he turned up in many, many hit shows of the day, including several Westerns. Few, for instance, remember the time Nimoy was on "Tombstone Territory." He similarly guest-starred on the forgotten "The Man from Sheanadoah" and even popped up at one point opposite Clint Eastwood on "Rawhide."

The point being: Nimoy may be best known for playing the half-Vulcan character Spock in the "Star Trek" franchise, but he also had a long and prolific career otherwise. For example, he directed "Three Men and a Baby," one of the highest-grossing movies of 1987. On top of that, Nimoy published books of photography and continued to act in various roles up until his death in 2015 at the age of 83.

Indeed, be it his association with the "Transformers" property, his role on the "Mission: Impossible" TV show, or his tenure on the sci-fi series "Fringe," Nimoy had plenty of notable, smaller parts under his belt. Here are our picks for the best ones.

A "howcatchem" rather than a "whodunnit," episodes of the show "Columbo" would reveal their killers right away. Once they committed their murder, Columbo (Peter Falk) would show up, and everyone would underestimate him for his slovenly demeanor. Of course, Columbo was sharp as a tack, often solving the mystery without the perpetrator initially realizing it.

In the 1973 episode "A Stitch in Crime," it was Leonard Nimoy's turn to play the suspect-of-the-week. Nimoy portrays Dr. Barry Mayfield, who kills his science partner, Dr. Edmund Heideman (Will Geer), so he can steal their research, claim it's 100% his, and get all the credit. The murder involves surgery and the implantation of a faulty suture. Only people looking very closely would be able to tell. When a nurse (Anne Francis) becomes suspicious, Dr. Mayfield thwacks her with a tire iron as well. But on "Columbo," there is no such thing as a perfect crime, so it's only a matter of time before the title detective begins sniffing around, finding mistakes in Mayfield's evil deeds.

This is a personal story, but I recall watching this episode of "Columbo" as a child, long after I was already familiar with Nimoy's Spock, so it was a shock to see Spock doing such villainous things. Nimoy could certainly play a cold-blooded character, but to see him portray a spiteful murderer in a one-off appearance on "Columbo" was downright shocking. It was "Columbo" that made me realize that Nimoy is a skilled actor and not just a "Star Trek" guy.

In the "Big Bang Theory" episode "The Transporter Malfunction," both Leonard (Johnny Galecki) and Sheldon (Jim Parsons) get vintage, mint-in-box "Star Trek" transporter toys. Sheldon doesn't intend to open his, but he receives advice in a dream from his own Spock action figure ... who speaks with the voice of Leonard Nimoy. Spock notes that a toy is meant to be played with. Unfortunately, Sheldon breaks his toy. But rather than lament his transporter, he swaps it with Leonard's. He figures that Leonard, who also intends to keep the toy in the box, will never know.

Thereafter, the action figure of Spock behaves as Sheldon's conscience, admonishing him for doing something so devious. Sheldon argues that there is nothing wrong with the arrangement, but Spock, through small plastic eyes, scolds him. He is not happy. Naturally, by the end of the episode, Sheldon confesses to his wrongdoing.

"The Big Bang Theory" attempted to pay homage to geek culture throughout its crackerjack 12-season run and frequently made references to comic books, "Star Wars," and "Star Trek," even including many actors and luminaries from those realms. Nimoy doesn't appear on camera, but it's certainly fitting that a Spock collectible would serve as the conscience for a morally struggling nerd like Sheldon. The episode gave Nimoy a great chance to recite some very funny lines as well. When Sheldon points out that Vulcans don't have emotions where he comes from, Spock points out that he, an action figure, came from a factory in Taiwan.

Leonard Nimoy appeared on two episodes of "The Simpsons," including the much-celebrated "Marge vs. the Monoral." In the episode, Mr. Burns (Harry Shearer) is busted for illegal nuclear dumping and forced to pay a $3 million fine. Springfield, with a new influx of cash, thus has a town meeting to debate its usage. But just as Marge (Julie Kavner) convinces her peers to use the money to repair the deeply damaged Main Street, a con man named Lyle Lanley (Phil Hartman) gets them to spend their cash on his monorail system instead by deploying a "Music Man"-style musical number.

Naturally, the monorail is built with the cheapest materials, and Lyle intends to abscond with the remaining funds. To give the launch of the monorail a good face, its maiden voyage is granted a celebrity guest in the form of Nimoy. During the launch ceremony, Nimoy cracks about the vessel being able to go warp 5. Mayor Quimby (Dan Castellaneta) doesn't recognize Nimoy, thinking he was one of the Little Rascals. Later, on the monorail, Nimoy observes an eclipse and makes a poetic comment about the continuation of the universe's cosmic ballet. The man sitting next to Nimoy asks to change seats.

The funniest part of Nimoy's performance comes at the end of the episode when he remarks, "My work is done here. When Barney (Castellaneta) points out that he didn't actually do anything, Nimoy chuckles and retorts, "Didn't I?" He then dematerializes, as if being beamed up. The joke is marvelously absurd.

"I, Robot," one of the most famous episodes of the anthology sci-fi series "The Outer Limits," adapts a story by Eando Binder and has nothing to do with the famous Isaac Asimov work of the same name. In the episode, a humanoid android named Adam Link (Read Morgan, voice by John Caper, Jr.) is put on trial for the murder of his creator. Adam is defended in court by the old-school lawyer Thurman Cutler (Howard Da Silva), and it becomes clear that the robot is like a child that doesn't understand its own strength. There's a lot of prejudice on display, as "I, Robot" is all about humankind's tendency to wield technology in an irresponsible way.

Leonard Nimoy, meanwhile, plays Judson Ellis, a reporter who observes this case from the outside, and he gets to deliver the episode's chilling coda. Upon being found guilty during the trial, Adam runs out of the courthouse to save a child from being hit by a truck and is destroyed in the process. As Ellis puts it, this display of heroism means that the story here is only beginning.

Nimoy's "The Outer Limits" role further cements his already strong association with the sci-fi genre in general. What's more, this particular episode was remade when "The Outer Limits" was revived in the 1990s. However, in the remake, Nimoy plays Da Silva, defending the offending android in court. Adam Nimoy, Leonard Nimoy's son, directed that episode.

The "Futurama" episode "Where No Fan Has Gone Before" reveals a dark wrinkle about Earth in the 31st Century. It seems that Trekkies, taking hold of their zealotry, have become religious crusaders. To solve the issue, humanity kills all the Trekkies (pushing them into a volcano) and jettisons the various episodes of "Star Trek: The Original Series" into space. The "Star Trek" cast, now reduced to being just living heads in jars, then flee the planet in a rocket.

As might happen in a real "Star Trek" episode, though, the show's episodes are recovered by Melllvar (Maurice LaMarche), an all-powerful cloud alien who, naturally, becomes obsessed with them. Thus, he uses his powers to gather up and resurrect the "Star Trek" cast, giving them bodies again. Leonard Nimoy initially stays behind on Earth (he had just signed a six-month lease on his apartment), but he's eventually reunited with his co-stars on Melllvar's world by Fry (Billy West) and his friends.

"Where No Fan Has Gone Before" relentlessly mocks "Star Trek" and Trekkies, but the episode does so with affection and a good deal of knowledge, making it clear that the creatives behind "Futurama" are Trekkies themselves. As a result, Nimoy gets to banter with William Shatner, Walter Koenig, George Takei, and Nichelle Nichols. DeForest Kelley appears on-screen as well, but since the actor had died in 1999, he has no lines. As for James Doohan, he's replaced by "Welshie," a character voiced by David Herman.

Nimoy clearly had a sense of humor about himself, and "Futurama" is proof, allowing him to say some very silly things. Keep an ear out for Nimoy talking about his photography career.

While I don’t expect Inde Navarrette to stop talking about her breakout role in Obsession anytime soon, one role is starting to become a big topic for her. Navarrette has been cast as Rogue in the upcoming X-Men reboot, and naturally, a lot of people want to know what’s going on with that high-profile film. Obviously, the actress can't answer a lot of what people want to know right now. On that note, I can’t give over how she decided to get out of a question about playing the famed mutant by going full Nikki!

The next X-Men movie is one of the biggest titles on the schedule of upcoming Marvel movies and is set to hit theaters in May 2028. And that means that it won’t be long before Navarrette is shooting the movie alongside her castmates like Adam Driver, Sadie Sink, Samara Weaving, Christopher Abbott and Kit Connor. For now, though check out what happened when someone asked about the status of her prep:

Oh my goodness, the way I was just transported back to my first viewing of Obsession! Navarrette perfectly recreated her Nikki scene, which has made her into a meme. During the interview with Entertainment Weekly, she was asked if X-Men training had begun. She went right into the “No, no, no, don’t do that” moment from the horror hit before saying she “thought we were having a nice interview!” in between playful laughter.

During the moment, she was paired with Obsession writer/director Curry Barker, and therefore clearly trying to continue to promote her breakout hit as they start their awards season campaigning. I especially like how quoting her own character from the movie led her to geek out over her love of Nikki directly after.

Later, she did, however, end up sharing some thoughts on her Marvel Cinematic Universe debut, but she kept things super vague. In her words:

No, I’m really excited to tackle [it]... I want to play people authentically and real, and no matter the world or finding belief in terms of, I mean we have magic in [Obsession], yet, it’s a person, right? So, I’m really excited to kind of tackle that. And, there’s a lot, I’m excited.

It sounds like we can expect Navarrette to pay attention to Rogue’s inner workings above all else, which is honestly the most important thing, anyways. She also brought up a “transformation” in regards to her portrayal, and it definitely has me curious. Oh, and when she hosted SNL over the weekend, she mentioned hitting the gym more. But that was also specifically said as a shot at Shane Gillis’ controversial comments, which he made on the sketch show a few weeks ago.

Obviously, now that she’s on the Marvel team, Navarrette is sworn to secrecy on all things X-Men, and I expect her to remain pretty tight-lipped. In recent months, however, she has talked a bit about Rogue’s iconic accent. The 25-year-old said she does want to “go there” in regards to doing justice to the character’s Mississippi roots.

Of course, Inde Navarrette and Marvel Studios want to keep us surprised with all the fine details, and she's doing a good job of keeping things under wraps. And, hey, now we know she can expertly dodge questions by simply channeling Nikki!

#3542. Josh Hartnett's Twisty Neo-Noir Thriller With Bruce Willis Is Streaming For Free

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Josh Hartnett once starred in a darkly comedic neo-noir thriller, and you can stream it for free at this very moment. Co-starring the action legend Bruce Willis as part of an impressive ensemble, "Lucky Number Slevin" didn't get its flowers back in 2006, but it's since garnered a loyal following. /Film editor Ben Pearson even counts it among his favorite movies of all time.

Streaming now on Tubi and Pluto TV, "Lucky Number Slevin" was directed by Paul McGuigan, whom Hartnett had previously worked with on 2004's "Wicker Park." The movie focuses on a case of mistaken identity, which puts a man named Slevin (Hartnett) in the middle of a war between two rival New York crime lords. Under the watchful eyes of Detective Brikowski (Stanley Tucci) and an assassin named Goodkat (Willis), Slevin must devise a plan to save his skin as these forces converge around him.

The movie only made $56 million at the box office against a budget of $27 million, making it, at best, a modest success at the time. Many critics hated "Lucky Number Slevin," but fans have learned to love it, which has helped it endure over the last two decades. It was no doubt aided by the peak DVD era, as well as being in rotation on cable TV for a number of years. That has, in turn, made it a continuing discovery for many viewers in the streaming era. It's why we're talking about it now.

This is a very fine example of the box office not being the end all, be all when it comes to sealing a movie's fate. Though, it is a little harder for a film like this to keep its head above the water in the endless sea of choices across dozens of streaming services these days.

A big part of what has helped "Lucky Number Slevin" is the fact that it has a downright unbelievable cast. Aside from Josh Hartnett and Bruce Willis, its ensemble includes the likes of Lucy Liu ("Charlie's Angels"), Morgan Freeman ("The Shawshank Redemption"), Ben Kingsley ("Sexy Beast"), Stanley Tucci ("The Devil Wears Prada"), and the late, great Robert Forster ("Jackie Brown").

Hartnett made his acting debut in a long-running horror movie franchise as part of 1998's "Halloween H20." From there, thanks to his roles in the likes of "The Faculty" and "Pearl Harbor," he rapidly moved up Hollywood's A-list. The early 2000s also saw Harnett working on high-profile projects such as "Black Hawk Down" and "Sin City." In more recent years, he's made something of a resurgence, appearing in everything from M. Night Shyamalan's thriller "Trap" to Christopher Nolan's Best Picture Oscar winning "Oppenheimer."

In an interview with with GQ, Hartnett spoke very fondly of "Lucky Number Slevin," calling it one of the best times on set during the course of his career to date:

"It all came together in the course of like, two weeks. And then yeah, we were allowed to go make this movie. It was just a bunch of friends again, a bunch of young people going up to make this film. It was one of the best experiences I ever had on set."

Most recently, Netflix added Hartnett's miniseries about a town terrorized by a sea monster, "Below." In addition, the actor only just starred in Amazon MGM Studios' steamy thriller "Verity," which was a big hit.

You can grab "Lucky Number Slevin" on Blu-ray or DVD from Amazon.
