#3541. What to Wear When Exercising Outdoors, Based on How Cold It Is

I fell in love with cold weather running while I was training for a spring marathon. It wasn’t a choice at first: Some weeks, the weather was bad for days on end, and if I stayed home, I would fall behind in my training. Everybody else in my training group was braving the elements, so I did too—with no regrets.

I got to run on quiet mornings while snow was softly falling. I signed up for a winter race that herded finishers into a heated barn for hot chocolate and soup. I set a personal record at a spring race, during which I pushed myself hard without breaking a sweat. I now find it sad when somebody tells me they’re afraid of running in the cold, or that they would run in the winter but don’t know what to wear.

No, cold weather doesn’t have to stop you from running, but getting dressed can be a puzzle: How do you keep from freezing your butt off at first and avoid overheating once you start to sweat? Fortunately, it isn’t as tough as it looks. With the right gear, your fingers and ears can stay toasty while you jog through a winter wonderland. Below, I’ll give you a temperature-by-temperature running cheat sheet, and then dive into the specifics on how to buy the best socks, shirts, and more.

When I get dressed to run in winter, I take a look at the “feels like” temperature, not the actual high or low. I also make sure to check the weather for the time I’ll go running, not for the whole day. It doesn’t matter how warm it will be at 2 p.m. if my run will be happening at 6 a.m., before the sun is up. I use the Carrot Weather app, but any app that gives you hourly feels-like temps will work just fine.

Next, use the 20-degree rule. Imagine that the temperature is 20 degrees (Fahrenheit) warmer than it really is. What would you wear then? Here's an example: if it’s 50 degrees out, you should dress as if it were 70: in a T-shirt and shorts, most likely. If it’s 30 degrees, you’d dress as if it were 50: long pants and maybe a light jacket. Get the idea?

Everybody has their own preferences. Some people wear shorts even when it’s snowing, while others will pop a beanie on as soon as there’s a detectable chill in the air. I’m a pretty middle-of-the-road runner when it comes to keeping warm, so here’s what I wear at each “feels like” temperature, starting with warmer weather and working our way colder. I'll give a guide to each type of garment or accessory at the end.

At 50+ degrees Fahrenheit, I’m wearing basically the same things I would for a summer run.

Head and hands: Nothing special. No gloves and no hat, unless it’s a baseball cap to shade my eyes from the sun.

We’re starting to feel the first bit of a chill. This is where I may start bringing gloves, although they’ll probably get stuffed into a pocket by the end of the run. Remember, with the 20-degree rule, it will feel like 60 degrees by the time you're warmed up.

Bottoms: Leggings, lightweight long pants, or shorts.

Top: Something with long sleeves, but ideally made of thin material (think long-sleeved T-shirt, not a full-on sweatshirt or jacket). If you wore a sun shirt in the summer, that's a good layering option for these cool temps. I like my REI Sahara Shade hoodie here, but any long sleeve will do. If you run fall and winter races, you'll probably be handed a free long-sleeved version at some point.

Hands: I usually just pull my shirt's sleeves over my hands, but you could wear knit gloves if you want. Consider something like Flipmits for an intermediate option (they can be folded down into a wrist cuff when your hands warm up).

Head: A headband if you need protection for your ears.

You may see a few snowflakes drifting down, but don’t bundle up in a snowsuit. Once you’re warmed up, it will only feel like 50 degrees—so go for something in “light jacket” territory.

Bottoms: Leggings or running tights. The fleece-lined kind can be nice. (I have these.)

Top: You’ll want some kind of jacket or sweatshirt. A lightweight, reflective rain jacket is great here, or just throw on a regular hoodie over your T-shirt. (I go with cotton sweats in dry weather or light snow, but I'd go for synthetics or wool if there's rain or sleet.)

Hands: Definitely wear gloves. The cheap knit ones are usually good enough, but consider treating yourself to a nice pair of running gloves.

Head: Your choice of hat or headband; I’d stick with the headband.

Feet: This is around the temperature you may start to want warmer socks. That goes double if snow is in play: snow that falls onto your shoes will work its way through the mesh, melt, and make your feet wet. Wool is a good material here, so consider something like these from Smartwool.

This is where I’ll officially say it’s “cold.” Whatever warm-weather gear you were getting away with at warmer temps, you’ll probably have to swap it out now. Shorts people will break out their long pants. Headband people will wear a real hat.

Bottoms: Leggings and shorts. I don’t care if you think it looks goofy to wear both; this is an A+ hack. Or try a puffer skirt.

Top: It’s definitely jacket weather. Rather than getting a warmer jacket, I like to wear the same light jacket as I did at 30 degrees, but this time with a long-sleeved fleece or wool base layer underneath.

Hands: Real gloves, please. You can keep wearing your little knit gloves if you’re able to tuck your hands inside your jacket sleeves, or if you have a pair of mittens to wear over top; otherwise, get windproof gloves.

Head: A hat, and maybe also a buff for your nose and mouth. (If you have any cloth masks still hanging around from the early COVID days, they’re perfect for cold weather runs.)

Feet: Warm socks for sure. If you’ll be doing a lot of running in these temperatures, you may want shoes that are specialized for the elements. Look for ones with Gore-Tex uppers, like the Brooks Ghost GTX.

This is where I tap out. If a run is just barely in the teens, I’ll make do with the 20-degree items I mentioned above, adding an extra layer wherever needed. But if that isn't enough, I opt for the treadmill. You certainly can run in this weather if you are determined. You’ll want windproof everything, some kind of face covering, and you may need eye protection such as goggles.

Whenever the weather gets to your own personal “too cold” temperature, remember that you still have options. The early afternoon is often the warmest part of the day, so a run may be tolerable then. There’s also no shame in using a treadmill (even if you have to join a cheap gym for this reason alone).

Everybody has different preferences, and with practice you’ll figure out if you’re the kind of person who wears three shirts before it hits freezing or the type to run through the snow in shorts. But this should give you a starting point when you head out for your first (or next) cold weather run.

As you continue on your cold-weather running journey, you may need to buy some new gear or repurpose things from elsewhere in your closet. And yes, the first few minutes of your run will feel chilly. But if you’re wearing the right shoes and clothes (and planning routes with a few extra factors in mind, which I’ll discuss below), winter running is not just feasible; it’s actually fun. So here are the items you may want to consider.

Your feet need to be warm and, if possible, dry. Warm socks go without saying, but there are some extra considerations when you’re picking socks to run in. Wool socks are ideal because they keep your feet warm even when they get wet. You may not think of winter as a wet time, but any snow that meets up with your body heat will turn into water. If you don’t have wool socks, synthetic wicking fabrics are a good second choice. Cotton is a no-no

First, the socks have to be able to fit into your shoes. If you’ve been running in super thin cotton or synthetic socks all summer, thick socks may not fit. Smartwool run socks are available in a thin version that can fit no problem—but in colder weather you’ll want some thickness for extra warmth. That thickness, in turn, may mean that your winter running shoes need to be roomier than the shoes you wear in summer. If you’re buying a new pair, make sure to try them on with the type of socks you intend to run in.

If your warm socks fit, you can make do with the same shoes you wore in the summer. Your feet will stay dry if the weather is dry and you stay out of puddles. If you encounter snow and slush, though, your feet will have to endure warm-but-wet conditions for the rest of your run. That can be okay for short runs, but for serious winter running, consider upgrading your shoes.

Some running shoes are available with water-resistant uppers. This level of water resistance will keep stray snowflakes out of your socks, but it isn’t reliable if you’ll be stepping in slush puddles. In that case, you’ll want something more waterproof, like Gore-Tex shoes, many of which are made for running trails.

If you expect to run on a lot of ice or packed snow, especially on trails, spikes can give you a little extra grip.

Yaktrax makes a rubber harness that stretches to fit your shoe, with steel coils and small spikes, for about $40.

Microspikes are a notch up from there, costing around $90 for what look like a miniature version of the chains you’d put on car tires.

And if you’re really dedicated—and are seeking a purpose-built pair of snow shoes—you can attach individual spikes: either these traction spikes from IceSpike, or via a DIY approach using sheet metal screws. (There’s a tutorial here.)

The versions that include rubber, like Yaktrax, can wear out quickly on pavement, so it’s best to save these for runs on trails or on unplowed paths. You’ll also want to be careful about the fit. I tried a pair that were similar to Yaktrax, but they were a tad too big. Shortly into my run, I found that the rubber stretched enough to pull the front set of spikes up over the top of my shoe. I've since gotten better-fitting ones, and they work great.

Spikes and specialized shoes help you go more places, in worse weather—but remember that they’re not required to just head out on a chilly day. Regular shoes are fine if the weather is cold but dry, or if you’re willing to put up with a little moisture.

I actually love when the weather gets cold enough that I need a jacket, because then I get to wear something that gives me extra pockets! Stick with thin jackets that have some room inside. By the time temps dip into the 20s or below, you’ll be doing some serious layering: for example, an undershirt, a long-sleeved warm layer, and a jacket. A great option for that warm layer is a wool base layer like this one. (Don’t worry, it’s not itchy.) If you can’t wear wool, a synthetic fleece is a good alternative.

Before you run out to buy all new clothes, experiment with what’s in your closet. Try repurposing a thin sweater, for example. Some people would never wear cotton for running (it can be cold when wet), but I wear it as my undershirt layer and have lived to tell the tale. Just make sure to shower or change after your run, so you aren't sitting around in cold, wet clothes.

The jacket is the most important layer. You can grab a sweatshirt in a pinch, but to be really well-equipped for nasty weather, you’ll want a jacket that is windproof and water-resistant. Jackets made for running are lightweight, for layering. Consider ones that are visible at night, with bright colors and reflective areas, and that come with zippered pockets.

Once it’s too cold for shorts, you’ll want to start layering your bottoms, too. Loose pants let cold air in, which is why leggings or “running tights” like these are standard winter wear for all genders. Running tights come in different thicknesses; go for something fleece-lined for your coldest runs, or layer two pairs.

You need to keep your ears warm, but don’t reach for a winter hat right away: an ear warmer or headband can cover your ears while still letting heat escape from the top of your head. And if anything is falling from the sky (say, snow), a baseball cap will keep it out of your eyes.

Fleece or knit hats are great for cold enough days, of course. The dividing line between earwarmer weather and hat weather is a personal one, and depends on whether you’re overheating. If you’re wearing a hat but sweating into your base layers, the hat is probably overkill.

Gloves, however, are essential. I keep a pair of cheap knit gloves in my jacket pockets, but windy or very cold days call for something stronger. You can layer gloves; I find gloves under mittens work well. You can also get windproof insulated gloves, which are warmer than any number of layers of holey knit gloves.

Your face will freeze on windy or very cold days, so this is where your old stash of pandemic face masks really shines. Consider a balaclava or even a fleece-lined bandana. A neck gaiter stays on better than a scarf if your neck is cold. At this point, every inch of you is covered but your eyes. Sunglasses can take care of that.

HBO’s Harry Potter show is truly becoming one of the most anticipated titles on the 2026 TV schedule. Not only will fans be transported back to The Wizarding World, but we’ve been promised a more accurate adaptation of the J.K. Rowling book series. Oliver and James Phelps, who portrayed Weasley twins Fred and George in the movies, are among those who may be tuning in. With that, the pair give their two cents on one moment they’d like to see in the show that didn’t make it in the films.

Fred and George Weasley had a lot of memorable moments in the movies. From attempting to do magic that went horribly wrong when tampering with the Goblet of Fire to really coming through for Harry when he was locked in the Dursleys’ home, they did quite a bit. While many great Weasley Twins moments from the books made it to the movies, Oliver Phelps -- while being interviewed with his brother by Jonatan Blomberg of Moviezine -- shared one funny moment from the books that he wants in the show, and I hope we get it:

I think one thing I always laughed at was in the second film when they’re de-gnoming the garden. And I just remember reading that and thinking that was hilarious. So that would be quite cool to see as well. Because you see them also — they’re using magical stuff, what they do in the Wizarding World but, also, I suppose in Fred and George’s way of doing it as well. So that would be quite cool to see.

The scene that Oliver Phelps is talking about involves Mrs. Weasley making Fred, George, and Ron spin and throw gnomes over the garden wall as punishment for rescuing Harry from the Dursleys using their dad's car. That would have been funny to see in the movies, and I would've even taken it as a deleted scene. Sadly, that funny moment was never filmed for the flicks, but given the show's producers are aiming for a thorough adaptation, I think there's hope for it to be in the TV show.

Interestingly, another moment Jonatan Blomberg talked about wanting to see in the show was a devastating scene that wasn’t shown in the movies — Fred Weasley's death. In Deathly Hallows - Part 2, fans only see the aftermath, with the Weasleys crying around Fred’s body in the Great Hall. I’ve got to agree with the host because, as sad as that scene was in the books, audiences would truly be able to feel the tragedy from The Battle of Hogwarts if they actually see the character die.

In terms of the upcoming HBO series adaptation, Oliver and James Phelps have spoken about wanting to help the other actors taking over their iconic Harry Potter roles if they needed them. The best advice the Phelps Brothers had to give their successors, Tristan and Gabriel Harland, is to enjoy themselves since they’ll be playing the “fun guys.”

The Phelps Twins have a point, as the Weasley Twins bring so much humor and lightheartedness to the series to, in their words, “diffuse the tension.” This makes me all the more excited about how the Harland Twins will be able to accomplish that in the TV show.

Let’s cross our fingers that we’ll get to see some de-gnoming from the Weasley brothers in Season 2 of Potter, which is currently filming. With each 10-episode season covering each book, there are a lot of possibilities for fans to see both big and small moments not featured in the films!

Be sure to check out the long-awaited Harry Potter TV series when it hits HBO on Christmas Day and becomes streamable with a HBO Max subscription. You can also catch Oliver and James Phelps’ performances in the film series by streaming all eight installments on the previously mentioned platform.

#3539. Buffy The Vampire Slayer's Controversial Thanksgiving Episode Is Worth Revisiting

"Buffy the Vampire Slayer" never shirked away from a good holiday episode. Probably the most famous one is Season 2's "Halloween," a particularly creepy "Buffy" episode where a warlock's spell makes the people of Sunnydale actually become the costumes they're wearing. "Buffy" Season 4 then revisited Halloween in the episode "Fear, Itself" before moving onto the next holiday, Thanksgiving, in Season 4, Episode 8, "Pangs."

Season 4 is a transition point for "Buffy," and the season's quality — as well as later "Buffy" season rankings — typically reflect those growing pains. This season moved the show's characters out of high school and into college. Co-leads Angel (David Boreanaz) and Cordelia Chase (Charisma Carpenter) left the show for the spin-off "Angel," and charming vampire Spike (James Marsters) went from villain to unwilling ally. All the changes swirling around Buffy are what drives her during "Pangs," where she decides to organize a Thanksgiving for her closest friends: Willow (Alyson Hannigan), Xander (Nicholas Brendon), and Giles (Anthony Head). Xander brings his girlfriend Anya (Emma Caulfield), and Spike (James Marsters) crashes the party in his first episode as a semi-official member of the Scooby gang.

While this was before the term "Friendsgiving" became popular, that's exactly what Buffy puts together in "Pangs." But the event is complicated by the villain of the week: Hus (Tod Thawley), a vengeful Native American spirit. One of the Chumash people, Hus wants revenge on the descendants of the settlers who oppressed his tribe. As a result, Buffy and the Scoobies find themselves in an awkward place with a "monster" who has legitimate grievances.

Some rank "Pangs" as one of the best Thanksgiving TV episodes ever, while others contend it bites off a bit more than it can chew (vampire and Thanksgiving meal puns both intended).

"Pangs" aired in time for Thanksgiving 1999, and watching it now is like a time capsule that preserves what the attitudes were around Native American restitution and Thanksgiving myths back then. Willow mentioning that her mom doesn't celebrate Columbus Day is treated as something unusual, whereas now that sort of backlash is more accepted.

By 1999, the term "Indian" was still in the process of being replaced by "Native American," which plays out in "Pangs," as Buffy checks Giles' use of the former term. Across "Pangs," the white characters also discuss how the founding myths of Thanksgiving (that pilgrims and the Natives shared food and culture peacefully) were pretty bogus. Yet, "Pangs" treats settled history as, well, history. Buffy feels guilty as a white person snuffing out a Native person's revenge, but the lives Hus is threatening now need protecting.

Hus' vengeance quest kicks off when it turns out the construction site of UC Sunnydale's new anthropology building sits on top of an old Christian mission site where the souls of Chumash warriors rest. That's a potent image: a building promoting diversity built over a colonial mission and Native American bones. Hus even infects Xander with a magical disease, like how white settlers brought diseases that decimated Indigenous populations.

Now, it's important to remember what the characters say isn't necessarily what the episode believes. Willow says they should help Hus "bring atrocities to light," while Giles counters: "If the history books are full of them, I'd say they already are." Willow's a young bleeding heart, Giles is an older, stuffy British man, and those lines reflect who they are. The character who most memorably wields the soapbox is Spike, who tells the Scoobies to get over themselves.

Hus barely speaks, which hurts the episode's framing that he's a wronged human and not a monster, but the episode almost preempts that with another Spike line. When Willow says they can talk Hus out of wanting revenge, Spike replies, "You exterminated his race, what could you possibly say that'd make him feel better?"

Again, "Pangs" tends to split "Buffy" viewers. Some praise the episode's humor and characterization, but others highlight the political themes as poorly-aged. But others, even Native American writers, have praised "Pangs" in spite of itself. Writer Jane Espenson is still proud of it, too, calling it one of her best "Buffy" episodes.

Speaking to Yahoo TV in 2016, Espenson revealed how "Pangs" first came about:

"Joss [Whedon] had mentioned a few times that he always wanted to do a Thanksgiving episode in which the characters had to eat their dinner with a dead Native American on the table as a reminder of the losses built into the holiday."

That about sums the episode up: Progressive intentions to spotlight historical atrocity while still centering white people and using a Native person as a prop. That's not to say Espenson wrote the episode carelessly. The Chumash tribe was chosen because its members lived in the area of Southern California where Sunnydale is meant to be.

"Pangs" also unlocked Spike's role as the new sarcastic comic relief. The "Buffy" writers sometimes struggled with finding Spike's proper role, eventually turning him from a villain into a reluctant hero. He spends "Pangs" tied to a chair, throwing barbs at Buffy and co., and getting shot full of arrows by Hus' ghostly warriors.

Like the holiday it celebrates, "Pangs" has some inextricable flaws, yet there's still fun to be had with it.

Few movie franchises have had the cultural impact of the James Bond movies. Generations grew up watching 007 on the big screen (with the movies currently streaming with an Amazon Prime subscription), and all eyes are on what Denis Villeneuve will do with the developing 26th film. Specifically, who will play James. There are a number of names being tossed around online, and someone recently asked Jack Lowden about taking up the martini and pistol as the beloved MI6 agent.

No Time To Die's tragic ending brought an end to Daniel Craig's Bond movies, opening the door for someone else to take the mantle. Folks have been taking bets on who might play Bond next, and Lowden is just one such choice. In an interview with GQ he was asked about the online discourse, saying:

On this… It’s all very flattering. It’s nice to be mentioned – for any role – and I’m just not really going to add to the noise.

While he's not adding his own commentary to the situation, it sounds like Lowden has seen Gary Oldman's comments that he's on the shortlist to play 007. He seems to appreciate anyone considering him for a major role, yet alone something as big as James Bond. We'll just have to see who ends up playing that iconic character next, and whether or not it's the Slow Horses star.

Later in the same interview, Jack Lowden spoke more about his career, and aging in the entertainment industry. The actor, who is now 36 years old, spoke about his age changes the way people perceive him. When asked by the journalist about reaching the era when "You either become a leading man or you don't," Lowden said this:

I count myself lucky, in that I’ve had a relatively gradual build. So I’ve been allowed to develop as a man, as a person, outside the spotlight. It’s funny – you go from being ‘a bright young thing’ to just ‘a thing’.

Luckily that process has opened him up to new roles, and now he's a popular choice online to replace Daniel Craig as 007. Whether or not he actually get passed the baton remains to be seen, but the fact that he's allegedly on the short list is a testament to his talent and starpower.

As a reminder, Oldman's comments about Lowden came from an appearance on Global TV’s The Morning Show . He gushed about his Slow Horses co-star possibly getting the role saying:

It’s been rumored that [Jack] is on the shortlist. We’re going to find out pretty soon, aren’t we? Because they have picked him. They have made their choice, but they have not announced it yet. So my fingers are crossed for Jack.

Clearly Lowden has Oldman's endorsement. Now that I think of it, it's surprising that the Oppenheimer actor never actually appeared in a Bond movie. I feel like he would have been a great antagonist for 007, especially considering his villainous roles in projects like Lost in Space and (especially) Air Force One. My FOMO is through the roof.

While we wait for Bond 26 casting news, folks can watch Slow Horses on Apple TV as part of the 2026 TV schedule. We'll just have to see if Oldman gets his wish and his co-star gets to land the career-changing role.

#3537. Legendary Sci-Fi Writer Harlan Ellison Wrote An Underrated Daredevil Story For Marvel

Harlan Ellison is one of the defining science fiction writers of the 20th Century, and one of the lights on the fuse of his imagination was the comic books he read as a child. He never outgrew them, either, maintaining a huge archive of his comic collection well into adulthood that he called the "living beating heart of [his] house." He praised Jack Kirby, co-creator of the Fantastic Four, the X-Men, and the Avengers, as a "master of the form" for his series, "The Forever People," at DC.

Ellison's bibliography is scattered with comic book credits, including and beyond Marvel and DC superheroes. Alongside artist Bernie Wrightson, he devised the story for 1971's "Batman" #237, a Halloween issue titled "Night of the Reaper." He also helped author the 1985 Marvel one-shot "Heroes for Hope," an "exquisite corpse" issue featuring the X-Men with contributed pages from many other writers, including Stephen King and George R.R. Martin, along with Alan Moore (who wrote a chilling three pages X-Men story about Magneto).

Some of the Marvel comics bearing Ellison's name include two issues of "Daredevil," No. 208 and 209, that form a loose two-parter. (For reference, #208 is credited to both Ellison and a co-writer, Arthur Byron Cover. #209 only credits Cover for scripting but includes a "From an idea by Harlan Ellison" credit.) The issues were both drawn by another legend in David Mazzucchelli, one of the many artists who has worked on both Daredevil and Batman and made the two characters so similar.

Now, Ellison's "Daredevil" story came after Frank Miller overhauled "Daredevil" in the style of film noir. However, the comic still reads a bit more like Stan Lee. The story even starts with a robot dressed like a little girl calling for help.

In "Daredevil" #208 (titled "The Deadliest Night of My Life!"), Daredevil is lured into a trap by the aforementioned robot little girl. Locked inside an underground bunker that seems to stretch across the whole city, Daredevil has no choice but to keep moving through rooms designed to kill him. It's largely an extended action sequence issue that doubles as a great showcase of Daredevil's acrobatic skills.

While falling onto a spiked floor, Daredevil uses his radar sense to map the floor and contorts his body just right to avoid any of the spikes. He later climbs between two walls lined with literal knives, too.

The comic's narration doesn't do much besides keeping you locked inside Matt's head as he dodges death, but a few flourishes show Harlan Ellison's influence on the script. When Daredevil is locked in a room and gassed to weaken him, he muses, "This is how they broke Winston Smith in '1984.'" (There's an internal homage on this page, too, when Matt remembers Bullseye killing Elektra back in "Daredevil" #181.)

The villain of "Daredevil" #208 turns out to be Elizabeth Dawes Sterling, old money and mother of the super-villain Death-Stalker/Phillip Wallace Sterling, killed back in "Daredevil" #158. Now dying herself, Mrs. Sterling used her fortune to convert her house into an automated death trap for her son's supposed killer. Another sign of Ellison's erudition and background in science fiction prose writing is that the comic name-drops MIT computer scientist Marvin Minsky's theory of "telepresence" to explain how the house and its traps run remotely.

"Daredevil" #208 could well read like a standalone issue. There's a nice button of an ending where Matt, who was heading home hoping to get some sleep before a day in court on the opening page, shows up to that court appointment with less than an hour of sleep. But the very last panel of the comic shows two of the little girl robots from the beginning of the issue.

No. 209 follows on from that. It turns out the robots are all rigged to explode, and the issue follows Matt trying to find and neutralize them all before they can do more damage. Within that narrative lies a more human heart to the story in the form of Johnny Squarejohn, a low-level criminal and a former childhood friend of Matt Murdock. The issue's title, "Blast from the Past," is a nifty pun on both sides of the story.

Johnny eventually pieces together that Matt is Daredevil, and, after following him to find the last robot, sacrifices himself to save Matt when it explodes. It's a familiar but effective story for a one-shot character: The former scoundrel who realizes his mistakes and redeems himself with one sacrificial act. "Daredevil" is the most Catholic superhero, and so stories of redemption — especially for the low-level criminals who've just made some bad decisions — are always a strong fit.

This two-parter may not be the peak of "Daredevil" as a comic or of Harlan Ellison's writing career. But it's a well-crafted adventure that melds two seemingly different stories together with the skill of a greater writer.

#3536. Anker’s New Soundcore Space 2 Headphones Are Already 18% Off

Anker released the noise-cancelling Soundcore Space One headphones a few years ago, and while they were a more budget-friendly alternative to premium models from Bose and Sony, their performance and fit still fell short in several areas. The brand’s updated Soundcore Space 2 headphones are a major upgrade across the board: They’re comfier, have better ANC, and are currently 18% off at $106.49 (originally $129.99), a rare price cut for a still-new release from a popular brand.

Battery life is one of the Soundcore Space 2’s most attractive features: They last up to 50 hours with ANC on and 70 hours with ANC off, and a five-minute charge gives you up to four extra hours. The noise cancellation is strong for the price, blocking out lower-frequency sounds well. Comfort is also a major upgrade from its sparser predecessor, with roomier, more plush memory foam earcups and a padded headband. They’re also travel-friendly, as the earcups rotate and fold.

The Soundcore app allows you to customize EQ and sound presets, giving you added flexibility if you don’t like the default tuning. Instead of touch-sensitive panels, these headphones use conventional buttons, which help prevent accidental commands while adjusting the earcups and are easy to operate. Along with supporting Bluetooth 6.1, they also have a wired-cable option, which isn’t always the case with modern wireless headphones. That said, they don’t support USB-C audio.

If you want over-ear noise-canceling headphones that perform well but don’t have $200 to shell out for a more expensive model, the Anker Soundcore Space 2 headphones are a comfortable, effective, and long-lasting alternative that hover around $100 at the current discounted price.

#3535. Brandon Sanderson Officially Teases Speedy Release of Remaining Stormlight Archive Books

The prolific fantasy writer is eager to return to the series soon

It's only been two years since Brandon Sanderson released Wind and Truth, wrapping up the first half of The Stormlight Archive. While the author is plenty busy with several more books and multiple live-action adaptations of his work, Sanderson is already thinking about getting started on the second half of the beloved series. Talking on a Halloween stream (in a pretty great Shrek costume), the fantasy author revealed he's already got a loose release schedule for the next five Stormlight Archive books.

When asked during the stream if The Stormlight Archive would release the last five entries every three years starting in 2031, Sanderson said that timeline is "pretty realistic." Almost immediately, however, the author laid out an even quicker schedule he sees as a possibility. He teased that when the series returns, readers will likely get two or three books released consecutively, each two years apart. The last two would follow "a little after." Sanderson added that he's feeling the urge to get back to writing the series soon, and once he starts he thinks he'll "rip through the first few of them pretty quickly." That's no surprise, considering Sanderson is seemingly always writing and releasing new novels in a number of series within his wider Cosmere universe.

The Stormlight Archive began with The Way of Kings in 2010 and is planned as a ten-book series. The first five books are in their own arc, with the remaining five acting as a sequel to the first half. It has also been confirmed that a big time skip will occur between books five and six. It may seem wild that Sanderson is already planning for The Stormlight Archive to be completed in over a decade, but it makes a lot of sense when you know just how many projects the author is juggling at all times.

On Dec. 8, Sanderson will release The Fires of December's print edition, a standalone story in the Cosmere universe under the Hoid's Travails banner. He is then set to start the third era of the Mistborn series with Ghostbloods, which is currently scheduled for release in December 2028. The next two books in the series will then be released in 2029 and 2030 if Sanderson's tentative plan is accurate.

Outside the realm of books, Sanderson is also handling a number of adaptations of his work at Apple TV Plus. The author made an unprecedented deal with the company earlier this year that gives him unmatched creative control on projects, including final approval. First up in that deal will be a film adaptation of the first Mistborn trilogy. Sanderson is writing the script for the films. There is also a television adaptation of The Stormlight Archive in the works.

It’s hard to believe now there was a time when Steve Carell was not a veteran in this industry. He really kicked things off with The Daily Show during Jon Stewart’s run and was on a long list of big names who came through The Daily Show in its heyday on Comedy Central. This includes some heavy hitters like John Oliver, Samantha Bee, Hasan Minhaj, Ed Helms, and more. It was Carell though who spoke out about his time on The Daily Show and how some Star Trek fans and Stephen Colbert helped him find his footing on TV.

Apparently, whilst working together it was Colbert who gave Steve Carell some prime (and frankly fascinating) advice. It was in the late nineties that both Hollywood personalities joined Jon Stewart on The Daily Show, but Colbert had a couple of years on Carell when he signed on – though Carell previously said on The Late Show it was also Colbert who got him hired by Comedy Central.

From what the actor told Amy Poehler, he was having a little trouble figuring out how to make the gig work when Colbert gave him the key to opening up the world of news satire.

I know Colbert, Stephen, gave me great advice, which was, ‘Come up with a character, and that will make it that much more palatable.’ My character was someone who didn’t quite understand, didn’t quite get it, but was super serious about everything he was asking.

If you ever saw The Colbert Report, you should know this is the approach Stephen Colbert himself took, but I didn’t realize it was advice he was cultivating in a little petri dish and then decimating out into the Comedy Central world when newbies needed it.

This is where Star Trek comes in. As someone who works with quite a few Trek fans, I’m aware of how passionate and positive they can be, and how much they like to fill up convention Halls at places like San Diego Comic-Con. Apparently, Carell at the time was not. The actor told Amy Poehler on her “Good Hang” podcast that he realized how helpful being able to turn the joke on himself could be during none other than a Star Trek fan convention.

It was while talking to people at a Klingon speakers convention and realizing making fun of these people who were so passionate about the franchise they boldly went where few other fans had gone and learned the language, was not the way to move forward. Carell likened the hobby to “woodworking” or “photography” and when he got to the convention he realized The Daily Show shouldn’t be mocking these fans.

I remember doing one field piece which were, it was a Klingon speakers convention. You know, you go and obviously the idea is ‘Let’s make fun of people who meet and learn how to speak Klingon.’ And they were the nicest, gentlest, I really liked these people a lot. … And I thought, ‘No, it has to be about what an idiot I am.’

Steve Carell would later leave The Daily Show to take the lead in The Office. He’s had both a movie and TV career in the decades that followed, and he's among the more recognizable names in Hollywood these days. Regardless, it’s easy to see another path that could have been taken: one where he took the easy route and mocked the Star Trek fans, one where he didn’t create “a character” that later resonated with audiences. One that may never have led the man to bigger and better things. I don’t know if Carell’s ever thanked Stephen Colbert for that little nugget of wisdom, but it was certainly helpful advice.

#3533. Patrick Stewart Played One Of The Scariest Villains In Modern Movie History

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Patrick Stewart was an icon of the stage and screen. He passed away at the age of 86 recently, and though it's hard to say someone who lived a good, long life is gone too soon, he's one of those people who was never going to be here long enough. While he'll forever be known as Jean-Luc Picard from "Star Trek" and Charles Xavier from "X-Men," he once played one of the best movie villains in recent memory. As hard as that may be to believe for those who haven't seen the movie in question, it's no less true.

That movie is 2015's "Green Room." Helmed by Jeremy Saulnier, before the director's action thriller "Rebel Ridge" with a 95% on Rotten Tomatoes topped Netflix's charts, it's a real punch-in-the-gut, no-holds-barred, slow burn thriller with Stewart at the center of it all as the head honcho of a band of neo-Nazis. It may be incredibly difficult for certain people to even imagine the actor behind Professor X doing such a thing, but boy did he do it. And he didn't hold back one bit.

"He's known popularly as a couple of these characters in science fiction franchises. He was excited about doing something different," Saulnier told /Film in an interview for "Green Room" in 2016, noting that Stewart wanted to get away from the characters he was known best as. Speaking further, the director explained that he didn't choose Stewart. Rather, Stewart chose this movie:

"The thing about someone like Patrick Stewart is...when you're doing an independent, punk rock genre flick, Patrick Stewart has to choose you. [Laughs.] He got involved because he was looking for something fun, something adventurous, to shake things up a bit."

Shake things up he did, indeed. "Green Room" sees Patrick Stewart and some skinheads face off with a punk band (including the late Anton Yelchin) who wind up in a terrible situation. The down-on-their-luck group is simply trying to get enough money to make it home in the midst of a failed tour when they get the chance for a solid payday. The catch? They have to play at a seedy club for some seedy sorts. But desperate times call for desperate measures.

While I won't spoil it for those who haven't seen it, something goes terribly wrong after the show, and the band winds up trapped in the green room, with a bunch of skinheads outside hoping they can cover some tracks and avoid trouble. Stewart plays Darcy, the leader of these neo-Nazis, and when he finally makes his entrance into the movie, he makes one hell of an impression.

The man we all know as Patrick Stewart totally disappears behind the character that is Darcy. Yes, he resembles Stewart physically, but this is a cold, unfeeling, humorless, awful person who would rather see a whole group of (relatively) innocent musicians die than see his skinhead cohorts on the wrong side of the law. The things he commands his loyal followers to do in an attempt to clean up this mess are unforgivable. The feelingless manner in which he executes these plans is straight-up chilling.

In the way that Stewart was the heart of David Lynch's "Dune," he was the evil core of Jeremy Saulnier's "Green Room." Even if Darcy isn't the one personally getting his hands dirty, the things he's sanctioning with no regard for the people on the other side of these violent acts are more than unforgivable. They're downright vile.

It takes a certain level of confidence as an actor to be so despicable. Darcy is the kind of role that might scare a lesser actor for fear that they might be associated in real life with the character. Not Patrick Stewart. He seemed to relish the opportunity to play someone so plainly contemptible. This is a killer with beliefs that are indefensible, doing indefensible things without a second thought.

It's not as hard, in some ways, to be a villain like Darth Vader who is so far removed from reality. Yes, he's one of the best movie villains of all time, but it's easy to like a villain like that. The same goes for Hans Gruber in "Die Hard," who is the kind of baddie we love to hate. What makes Stewart's turn as Darcy in "Green Room" so remarkable is that he's very human, one with no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's a performance worth marveling at, yet a character that makes the viewer sick with hatred. He's reprehensible.

"Green Room" was, unfortunately, a flop from A24 that deserved better. It didn't get the audience it deserved at the time of its release, but it has become something of a cult favorite in the years since. That has more than a little to do with Stewart's Oscar-worthy performance as this movie's legendarily great villain. Not a likable one, but the relatively rare, purely evil sort that makes one question what humans are capable of.

To take it one step further? In a career filled with outstanding roles, this may well be one of Stewart's very best moments. Not as a hero, but as a straight-up villain. A scary f***ing villain.

You can rent or buy "Green Room" on Amazon Prime Video.

#3532. 10 Shows Like 'A Different World' You Should Watch Next

You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

The original A Different World was a groundbreaking sitcom in its era, spending six seasons highlighting Black academic drive among a cast of characters so indelible that we're now checking in on them decades later. Spearheaded by Queen Sugar's Felicia Pride, the update has been a critical and ratings hit for Netflix, earning the rarest prize of all in streaming television: a quick second season renewal. While you're waiting for season two, here are some other smart coming-of-age shows that blend heart and humor with realistic drama.

An easy pairing with A Different World, this show follows Black-ish's Zoey Johnson (Yara Shahidi) as she leaves home to attend a (fictional) California liberal arts college (the last couple of post-graduation seasons shift the focus to her brother Andre, played by Marcus Scribner). The emphasis is on driven young people who are capable of making big mistakes on the path to adulthood. A true comedy-drama, Grown-ish feels real(-ish) in a way that few other college shows have managed. Stream Grown-ish on Hulu.

Adapted from and expanding upon the 2014 movie, this show takes us to a (fictional) Ivy League school for a comedy-drama that tackles campus life and politics from a rather different perspective than that of Rooster. Logan Browning leads the ensemble cast as Sam White, who kind of inadvertently starts the titular radio show following a racially charged incident on campus. Far from the racial screed that some bad-faith YouTubers seem to find it, it's never shy about confronting the complicated and occasionally silly contradictions of campus activism, with each episode approaching life at Winchester University from a different character's perspective. Stream Dear White People on Netflix.

Kimberly (Pauline Chalamet) is an endlessly naïve scholarship student; Bela (Amrit Kaur) is an aspiring comedy writer on the make for the hottest guys; Whitney (Alyah Chanelle Scott) is an overachieving athlete and senator’s daughter; and Leighton (Reneé Rapp) is a closeted sorority girl. They're all randomly assigned to room together as freshmen at the fictional Essex College in Vermont. Created by Mindy Kaling and Justin Noble, this comedy-drama isn't nearly as salacious as its title suggests. There's sex for sure, but mostly it's a funny, queer-friendly show that's a little less about one overarching romance than it is about growing up, and the value of female friendship. Stream The Sex Lives of College Girls on HBO Max.

Even though we're backing up a couple of years to follow teens in their high school years, this British import's setting is a decent match, finding its students living away from home and family for the first time in their lives. At the fictional prestigious boarding school St. Gilbert’s, five Black teens are newly attending on scholarships, but their integration into the existing cliques is less than smooth—especially given that they're there largely as a PR stunt. Boarders blends teen romance, coming-of-age drama, and a delightful willingness to take the piss when it comes to the whole "rich private school" thing. Stream Boarders on Tubi.

Another modern take on a beloved '80s/'90s sitcom, this one's a bit different, serving as a total reimagining with no narrative connection to the original. And while A Different World is a comedy with dramatic heft, this one's more of a straight drama. It’s jarring for fans of the beloved original to tune in to find a serious show with the same premise as the Will Smith original—one that often leans into heavy realism. Jabari Banks plays, er, Will Smith, a 16-year-old from West Philadelphia who moves in with his auntie and uncle in Bel-Air following a gun charge and a run-in with a Philly drug lord. Banks is charismatic and believable, bringing a ton of personality to a show that occasionally veers down dark alleys. Stream Bel-Air on Peacock.

Comedian Benito Skinner plays himself, kinda, in this buzzy comedy that sees a former high school jock facing his freshman year in college while desperately trying to convince himself and everyone else that he's as straight as they come (relatable, except for the jock part). Much of the appeal is in its deft blending of tones: It's both a frequently raunchy college comedy and a sweet coming-of-age story about accepting yourself without worrying about what everyone else thinks. The cast includes Adam DiMarco (The White Lotus) and Rish Shah (Ms. Marvel), and, though it's more a story of one young man's coming of age, there's a strong ensemble backing him up. Stream Overcompensating on Prime Video.

The heart of All American (for most of its run) is Spencer James (Daniel Ezra), based on real-life NFL linebacker Spencer Paysinger. A star player for his high school team in Crenshaw, he's recruited by the coach (Taye Diggs) of a team in Beverly Hills to come and play for them, forcing Spencer to navigate two very different worlds while trying to build a life and potential career. Stream All American on Netflix.

Following a family tragedy, the already awkward 15-year-old Devi Vishwakumar (Maitreyi Ramakrishnan) has a pretty terrible freshman year of high school, and decides that she’s going to turn things around the following year, hoping that a nearly academic study of sex will get her the boyfriend(s) her raging hormones have begun to demand. It works, to a point—but getting a surprise yes to sex from her crush leads her to question what she’s really ready for. More about burgeoning sexuality than sex specifically, this Mindy Kaling-produced series is both honest and charming. Stream Never Have I Ever on Netflix.

For realism in a show about the college experience, you could do a lot worse than this docuseries following several students at Gallaudet University, a school for deaf and hard-of-hearing young adults. In one sense, it's a specific setting where perspectives on deafness vary wildly, even in Gallaudet's self-contained world (aside from being a show about academically driven and horny college students, this is also a great primer for hearing people about some of the issues). But even for all of that, the challenges in building a life and future away from home are pretty universally relatable. Stream Deaf U on Netflix.

There's a reason A Different World has returned in 2026, and a lot of that has to do with the fact that there was nothing else on TV quite like it back in the late '80s and early '90s. For all of its sitcom sensibilities, the show tried hard (especially after multi-hyphenate creator Debbie Allen arrived to rework things after its first season) to paint a realistic picture of college life and an HBCU. Of the few shows on TV with largely Black casts, almost none would go so far as to highlight achievement and excellence; A Different World managed to do so while building a cast of characters so memorable that we're more than willing to catch up with them nearly forty years later. Stream A Different World on Netflix.

Calling something “super” doesn’t make it so; we should expect evidence before accepting the upgrade

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new CNBC report describes how the language at the top of the industry is shifting. On their third-quarter earnings calls, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Tesla and SpaceX’s Elon Musk traded “AI” for “super intelligence,” roughly a month after President Trump ordered federal agencies to replace the term artificial intelligence with super intelligence.

According to the report, The CEOs of Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet stuck with “AI.” Whatever the motivation behind the swap — alignment with the White House, marketing, or genuine conviction — the word "superintelligence" deserves scrutiny, because it carries a promise that the people using it have every incentive to make sound inevitable.

Companies are free to pursue superintelligence, to spend heavily researching it and to explain why they think it’s within reach. But describing an ambition and demonstrating that you’ve reached it are different things, and readers deserve language that makes clear which one is on the table.

Superintelligence generally describes AI that substantially exceeds human intellectual capabilities across a broad range of activities. That’s an enormous claim, far beyond being able to generate an essay quickly or outperform someone on a particular test.

The breadth is the point. A calculator can beat me at arithmetic without being more intelligent than a person in any meaningful sense, and an AI system that excels in one domain hasn’t thereby shown it can apply the same judgment everywhere else.

Before accepting the label, we should be asking what was measured, who evaluated the system and whether the results hold up outside the conditions chosen to demonstrate it. For that reason, it's understandable why some tech executives haven't started using the term.

I have a responsibility here, too. If an executive says their company is working toward superintelligence, my headline needs to make clear that it’s still a goal. A prediction about what AI might eventually do shouldn’t become a claim about what you can use today. Readers should be able to trust us to make that clear.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

For someone deciding whether to rely on a chatbot, “superintelligence” can carry a consequential suggestion, that the system knows better than they do.

That could affect how carefully a person checks an answer, how much authority they give its advice or how willing they are to let it act on their behalf. The language encourages expectations that the technology then has to meet.

Useful AI doesn’t require that kind of promise; in other words, we know that it can make mistakes. In fact, there are clear labels on most chatbots now indicating that AI does, in fact, make mistakes. An assistant can help someone organize research or understand an unfamiliar document without being presented as intellectually superior to humanity.

Consumers need specific information about how well a product works, where it makes mistakes and what requires human review. “Superintelligence” supplies none of that on its own.

If anything, a grander claim should invite closer examination. A company asking us to believe it is approaching intelligence beyond human abilities should be prepared to explain how it would recognize that achievement — and how anyone outside the company could verify it.

It's more important than ever to look at AI with extra scrutiny. And we can acknowledge progress without accepting every label.

Skepticism about the word doesn’t require dismissing the technology. AI can improve, become more useful and change the way people work while companies’ descriptions of it still deserve challenge.

We also shouldn’t treat the possibility of future superintelligence as proof of its arrival. Executives are entitled to make forecasts., but for readers paying for these products, the useful tests are concrete and unchanged — whether the tool does what you need, whether you can check its work, and whether it gives you enough control over what it does on your behalf. Calling it “super” answers none of those questions, and the company still has to show its work.

#3529. The Batman 2 Spoilers Leak: BTS Photo Teases Two-Face, Victor Zsasz And Court Of Owls

"The Batman Part II" is currently shooting, with filmmaker Steven Soderbergh filling in as on-set director while Matt Reeves reportedly deals with a family crisis. The movie's story remains shrouded in mystery — it hasn't even been confirmed which characters new cast members Sebastian Stan, Scarlett Johansson, Brian Tyree Henry, and Charles Dance are playing. But naturally, rumors have swirled, and new leaks may have confirmed some.

For a long while, the going assumption was that Sebastian Stan would play Harvey Dent/Two-Face, with Johansson presumed to be playing his wife Gilda Dent and Dance playing his abusive father Christopher Dent. But in June this year, scooper Jeff Sneider reported that Henry was playing Dent, and that Stan would instead play Victor Zsasz. (A rich kid turned serial killer, with a kink for carving a tally of his victims into his flesh, Zsasz is the kind of bad guy who'd fit right into the dark world Reeves established in "The Batman.")

Sneider's report is looking likely thanks to a leak from ... Heidi Klum's makeup department. Let me explain. The supermodel is well known for her elaborate Halloween costumes. This year, she went as a severed hand. Mike Marino, the makeup artist who designs Klum's costumes, was also the makeup artist on "The Batman" and is returning for "Part II." In some detective work worthy of Batman himself, fans have spotted what appear to be props from "The Batman Part II" in a video showcasing the making of Klum's 2026 costume.

The props include what looks a lot like a cast of Brian Tyree Henry's face with a disfigured lip, i.e. Two-Face. There's also a box labeled "Zsasz" and, most intriguingly, a box labeled "Owl 3," which likely suggests the Court of Owls, an evil secret society in Gotham City.

If this leak is true, fans who were preparing for Sebastian Stan as Harvey Dent should buckle up for disappointment. But at the same time, Zsasz is the kind of role that will let him stretch his acting legs. Brian Tyree Henry as Two-Face is also promising because the man knows how to play a good guy turned villain — check out his incredible voiceover performance as Megatron in the animated prequel film "Transformers One."

But what about the Owls? Created in 2011 by Scott Snyder and Greg Capullo, the Owls have manipulated Gotham from the shadows for hundreds of years. They're distinguished by their owl-themed masks and employ similarly-themed, near immortal assassins called Talons. (The creative, out-of-universe reason for the owl theming is that owls eat bats.) They're commonly dismissed as a myth in Gotham, to the point that they're even the subject of their own nursery rhyme:

"Beware The Court of Owls, that watches all the time, ruling Gotham from a shadowed perch, behind granite and lime. They watch you at your hearth, they watch you in your bed, speak not a whispered word of them, or they'll send the Talon for your head."

The original "Court of Owls" storyline is widely considered a modern classic. Many Bat-fans, not to mention Robert Pattinson, have long put the Court forth as ideal villains for a sequel to "The Batman." That movie was about Bruce Wayne investigating the institutional corruption of Gotham City. That makes the Court of Owls a thematically consistent villain for "Part II" — what if Batman keeps peeling back those layers and discovers the rot goes even deeper and is centuries old?

"The Batman Part II" is currently scheduled for a theatrical release on February 18, 2028.

#3528. Google Quietly Linked Your Phone Number Across Your Accounts, but You Can Stop It

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In recent weeks, Google has been automatically connecting Android users' phone numbers to every Google account they are signed into on their devices—without requesting consent to do so. This means that if you are logged into personal, work, and disposable accounts on your Android phone, Google may have silently verified and linked your number with all of them even if you've deliberately kept them separate. If you that's not something you want, there's a way to fix it.

As Android Authority reports, some Android users have recently received confirmation emails from an official Google address stating that their phone number has been verified. Google has required occasional phone number re-verification but appears to have updated its support documentation about a year ago to make this feature opt-out by default. As part of this process, Google also adds your phone number to all Google Accounts that are signed in on the device, including current accounts and phone numbers and any that are added or updated in the future.

Updating this setting does not disconnect phone numbers and Google accounts that have already been linked. You can find out which are which via your Google Account Personal Info page. Select your profile picture in the upper-right corner to go through each signed-in account and open the Phone section to select and delete any numbers you don't want associated.

Finally, Malwarebytes advises scrolling down to the Usage section on the Phone page to view which services are listed as well as reviewing your Security & sign-in settings. If you added your phone number for two-step verification or to a separate app like Google Pay, deleting it from the Phone page won't remove it entirely from your account, and you'll need to update those settings separately. Automatic phone verification shouldn't be the culprit here, but it's useful to audit what your number is being used for and on which accounts if you want to keep things separate.

#3527. Clayface Concept Art Shows Disturbing Alternate Designs For DC Universe Villain

The DC Universe has delivered its first properly scary film. Though a bit shapeless, "Clayface" is an effective and very gory body horror movie. Drawing from a script by Mike Flanagan and Hossein Amini (and borrowing a whole lot from Sam Raimi's "Darkman" along the way), director James Watkins re-imagines the titular Batman villain as a tragic but still very horrific movie monster here.

Indeed, Tom Rhys Harries's Matt Hagen goes through quite a transformation in the film, and it's heavily reliant on implication (much like the special effects in James Cameron's "The Terminator"). A creepy eye here, a spiky hand there — it's really comic book-y until the final act finally reveals the mud-like Clayface fans know from DC's comics. Now, concept artist Carlos Huante has now taken to Instagram to share some of his early design work on "Clayface" before the film was properly greenlit by Warner Bros. Pictures.

"I did some work on it before it was green lit," Huante wrote. "It wasn't clear what they were going to do with it at first but, it was an origin story and after this image it was clearer it was going to be a horror movie rather the Batman supervillain.. which is cool by me.. but i still wanted to go for it with full Clayface creature.. but i was only hired for a week and even that seemed to be a stretch for their budget.. weird times.."

Again, for most of "Clayface," the Matt Hagen characters look fairly ordinary. With his asymmetric skull and one of his arms fused to his torso, he comes across as a man who's simply unable to hold a consistent physical form in this artwork.

Notable, "Clayface" originated with Mike Flanagan, who pitched the project to DC Studios in the first place. That said, the final version of the film belongs to James Watkins, which is why the director has said that DC Comics fans should blame him if they don't like it. Still, we can't help but wonder about the iteration of the movie where the Clayface character's body morphs in unnerving ways (as opposed to him merely copying others).

#3526. Anthropic Is Officially Stepping In to Stop Claude from Cloning Games

Anthropic tries to limit AI replicas of existing games

AI games have taken over digital storefronts this year. Steam Next Fest, a demo showcase event, was a disaster, as AI games flooded the platform, making it harder for fans to filter the results and find hidden indie gems. According to itch.io, the number of game pages being created has doubled in the past two months, likely related to the popularity of "vibe coding" and AI tools such as Claude. It's not just "original" AI games that are a big concern; AI-generated remakes and copycats have become a growing issue in the gaming industry.

On Oct. 30, an X user spotted an update to Claude Code's rules that reads as follows:

"Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets. Don't build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original."

On Oct. 30, an Anthropic spokesperson confirmed to Game Developer that the update is real. Anthropic member of technical staff Addy Osmani also posted on X an explanation: "We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance."

The rule is worded to prevent users from using dialogue to bypass it. This way, Claude will only generate AI games based on designs and assets made by the user. The specific guidelines that the artificial intelligence tool uses to distinguish original materials from copied assets are unknown, but if the user believes they're being wrongfully accused of not using their own assets, they must contact a staff member in order to clear things up and continue their work.

It's great to see Anthropic take action, and hopefully, it will deter users from employing non-original materials. This matter is particularly problematic for independent developers, who are afraid that their games could be stolen by "vibe-coders." Several small developers have canceled public playtests and opted for private testing in a controlled environment to prevent AI clones from surfacing. With 25,000 wishlists on Steam, thousands of fans were looking forward to trying the Drunken Goddess Reflux demo during the Steam Next Fest in October. Unfortunately, devs Alliance Arts and Who You chose to pull out of the event to stop dishonest players from copying their game. Similarly, Digital Sun canceled the public playtest of ReVamp and opted for a controlled playtest on Discord instead.

While the Claude update sounds like good news for developers, this kind of safety limit on LLMs can still be circumvented by users. Alternatively, vibe-coders can simply turn to so-called "open-weight" models that are free to use and whose safety guardrails are easy to remove.

#3525. The One Problem With Star Wars, According To Project Hail Mary Author Andy Weir [Exclusive]

You know what they say about opinions: Everyone has one, and that goes double when it comes to "Star Wars." It's not exactly a state secret that the galaxy far, far away has gone through something of a rough patch in recent years. The divisive sequel trilogy and the overall Skywalker Saga ended on the sourest note imaginable with "The Rise of Skywalker" in 2019, which then led to a prolonged hiatus on the big screen only broken by the tepidly-received "The Mandalorian and Grogu" earlier this year. Now, Simon Kinberg's reported trilogy of movies appears to be the next major gambit following the Ryan Gosling-starring "Starfighter" next year ... but, clearly, that's not stopping any of us from debating the best way for "Star Wars" to move forward.

You can count "The Martian" and "Project Hail Mary" author Andy Weir among those with some thoughts on the matter. The novelist has already enjoyed a big 2026 to this point, beginning with Phil Lord and Chris Miller's blockbuster adaptation of "Project Hail Mary." As he's gearing up to release another passion project of his, the upcoming Audible original sci-fi series "Exoplanet" that he's executive producing, I had the opportunity to speak with Weir over Zoom. During our extended conversation, the topic of "Star Wars" came up and, unsurprisingly, Weir had plenty to say.

When asked what he'd personally do if in charge of the franchise, the author pinpointed one specific concern that certain fans will likely agree with:

"'Star Wars' is more about massive upheaval. One problem that happens is, if you're going to have a story about a monumental war, then when it's over and the good guys win, you want it to stay that way. So it's very unsatisfying if you roll into a new monumental war."

Sound familiar? That's probably because that line of criticism was a concern many had with J.J. Abrams' "The Force Awakens" in 2015. Although it remains the highest grossing and one of the most well-received movies in the entire series, there was certainly some trepidation over taking the original heroes' hard-fought victory and rendering it moot — this time, by replacing the Empire and the Rebellion with the vaguely different (but not really) factions of the First Order vs. the Resistance.

Andy Weir went on to diagnose the best direction to take "Star Wars" in the future, as he sees it. This time, his suggestion is to go back to a strategy that Lucasfilm actually established nearly a decade ago with "Rogue One." As he explained, "I feel like the best way, in my opinion, to do another 'Star Wars' movie — and I'm not George Lucas and this might be a terrible idea — but would be to have the story of other people during the Galactic Civil War."

Of course, Weir acknowledges that Luke Skywalker, Leia Organa, and Han Solo were the "movers and shakers" during the events of "A New Hope" and beyond. But he thinks there's room to tell smaller, "tangential" stories alongside their own ... and points to one particularly relevant historical example:

"Think of it like this: We know what happened in World War II, but there are some really good fictional stories that take place during World War II. So if you treat the Galactic Civil War as, 'Okay, that's established canon, those are the things that happened,' but there's still a lot of stories to tell about other people living through those wars. So that's what I would do."

This should also feel reminiscent of arguably one of the best and most critically-acclaimed additions of all — "Andor." The Disney+ prequel series doesn't quite fit the contours of Andy Weir's ideas for where to take the franchise in film, but that doesn't mean he fails to appreciate everything it brought to the "Star Wars" universe on streaming TV. Quite the opposite, in fact. When I bring it up, Weir is quick to share his enthusiasm for the Tony Gilroy production and its unique advantages as a show. But he wouldn't necessarily use this as an example of what future films could do:

"'Andor' was amazing and really good, and it was a series and [that was the correct choice]. You're going to do a movie, you've got to tell your whole story in like two hours. So it needs to have a lot more — 'Andor' was very intellectual, extremely clever, extraordinarily well-written, very well- — I mean, I loved everything about it. But it's not something that you could make into a movie."

That's extremely high praise, especially from such a successful sci-fi author, but Weir is right to note that "Andor" couldn't have had the same impact were it reimagined as a movie. So where can this franchise possibly go next on the big screen? For "Star Wars" to thrive in its next iteration following the sequel trilogy, Lucasfilm is betting that looking ahead in the timeline is the way to go. What Weir presupposes, however, is that looking back at "Rogue One" may hold the answers. Failing that, well, maybe they can make Weir's wacky "Star Wars"/"Star Trek" crossover happen instead.

#3524. These Shokz Bone Conduction Headphones Are $70 Off Right Now

Bone conduction headphones are ideal for activities where it is vital to be able to hear your surroundings. That's because they use a technology that sends audio vibrations through to the inner ear while leaving your ear canals open. Shokz is one of, if not the best brand making bone conduction headphones right now. At the high end of Shokz's offerings sit the OpenRun Pro 2s, which impressed me when I tested them out for review, but they are a bit pricey at $180. But right now, the older but still capable OpenRun Pros are discounted to $109.95 (originally $179.99), the second-lowest price they've reached according to price-tracking tools.

If you've never used bone conduction headphones, they're worth a try, and the Shokz OpenPro are a great introduction to the technology. Previously, bone conduction headsets tended to suffer from poor bass compared to in-ear models. The OpenRun Pros are designed to compensate for some of that—you won't get the same thumpy bass you'd get from regular headphones, but it'll be the best you can get from any other bone conduction headphones.

As the name implies, these are meant to be used on outdoor runs. You can use them as everyday headphones too; they can take calls, but you'll need to be mindful of the fact that they don't block any competing sound. #3523. How Young Sheldon Star Annie Potts Really Feels About The Georgie And Mandy Spin-Off

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Often, when a sitcom is spun off from a hit series, the show to which it owes its existence is still on the air. For instance, in the 1970s, Norman Lear's "All in the Family" ran concurrently with its spinoffs "Maude," "The Jeffersons" and, technically, "Good Times" (which was spun off from "Maude"). Then there are spinoffs that arrive immediately after the final season of a hugely popular show. Sometimes, the creators hit the jackpot, like with "Frasier." And sometimes you get "AfterMASH."

Chuck Lorre and Steve Molaro have taken a unique approach with their post-"The Big Bang Theory" sitcoms. They devised a prequel series for Sheldon Cooper (Jim Parsons) with "Young Sheldon," and then stayed in that timeline with "Georgie & Mandy's First Marriage." There have been some regrets regarding the transition from "Young Sheldon" to "Georgie & Mandy's First Marriage" (Lorre in particular wishes they hadn't killed off George Sr.), and genuine anger in the case of Annie Potts, whose beloved Connie "Meemaw" Tucker didn't make the main cast for the new series.

Potts and other cast members like Raegan Revord and Lance Barber were particularly upset about the secrecy. "We were totally ambushed by this," said Potts. "I was, anyway." Though Potts, Revord, and even Barber have made appearances on "Georgie & Mandy's First Marriage," it seems like there's still a bit of resentment over how it all went down, according to Jessica Radloff's dishy behind-the-scenes book "Young Sheldon: The (Juicier-Than-Meemaw's-Brisket) Inside Story of the Hit Series." Potts certainly isn't holding back.

In Radloff's book, Potts says, "I think if they had been able to say, 'We're going to be spinning off, and these are the characters we'll be spinning off... it doesn't mean we don't love you all, but this is where we want to go creatively next.'" Potts was also concerned about losing a lucrative gig at the age of 73 because, sadly, Hollywood sexism and ageism is alive and well in the 21st century.

Potts felt that the writers' decision to have Meemaw bring Georgie into the gambling room, and have Mandy live with her, made her a natural for the main cast of the spinoff. That's why getting passed over stunned her:

"I felt devalued. It's like [they were saying], 'It was fun to have you in this, but we don't really need you in that because you don't bring all that much to the party.' So, being entirely honest, I will confess to having those sinking feelings of, like, just not feeling that worthwhile."

When the "Georgie & Mandy's First Marriage" writers told her Meemaw would make guest appearances, she didn't feel it was the "generous invitation" Lorre and company thought it was. This is no way to treat the actor who gave us such memorable characters as Janine Melnitz ("Ghostbusters"), Iona ("Pretty in Pink"), and the voice of Bo Peep in the "Toy Story" movies. Fortunately, she recently landed a main cast role in Fox's well-received medical comedy "Best Medicine."

#3521. South Park Season 29 Just Found The Funniest Replacement For Kenny

The following contains spoilers for episode 4 of "South Park" Season 29, "Guinea Pig on a Stick."

Season 29 of "South Park" has been a hilarious experiment. After three decades, the adult animated comedy has officially changed its name to "South America," mirroring the titular town changing its name in reference to the sitting President of the United States renaming the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario. After Season 28 took on some shockingly big targets, mostly involving AI and the Trump administration, the current season has taken on billionaires, data centers, the e-bike craze, "looksmaxxing" and "aura farming," and even the beef crisis in the U.S.

Back in the season premiere, "South Park" even brought back Mike Judge as the unmuffled voice of Kenny McCormick — only to kill him yet again in that same episode. We haven't seen Kenny since then, and it appears the show will not bring him back this season. Still, the show must go on, and it seems "South Park" has found the funniest replacement possible.

It's none other than Randy Marsh, father of Stan Marsh. Yes, the adult man with a mustache and a drinking problem is now a main member of the South Park gang, and it works surprisingly well. That's because Randy is now the size and look of a 10-year-old (though still with a mustache) thanks to an overuse of anti-aging creams from Sephora in Episode 3 of the new season. It's ridiculous, it's very funny, and it's pure "South Park America."

One of the biggest issues with "South Park" the last 10 years or so has been the increased focus on Randy Marsh. This alone isn't inherently an issue, as Randy is the focus of some of the all-time best "South Park" episodes, like "The Losing Edge" (an episode that gets referenced in last week's episode of the current season). But a problem arose when writers decided to stick Randy up in his weed farm and separate him from the rest of the town. It was funny for the first couple of episodes, but season after season it quickly lost steam.

So, when Randy finally sold the farm and moved the family back to South Park/South America, things finally were on the right track. Last week, Randy got into looksmaxxing and transformed into a 4th grader, which was funny, but not a big part of the plot. That changed this week, when it became obvious that Randy was going to remain a 4th grader for a while longer. He's even referred to throughout the episode as Little Randy, and is an integral part of the story of the episode alongside Stan, Kyle, and Cartman. This results in some hilarious scenes of Stan being angry at his dad for trying too hard to act cool (like when he shows off his Italian brainrot on Roblox) or for being drunk at school.

Little Randy feels like a uniquely "South Park" way of doing something like "Pickle Rick" from "Rick and Morty," both a dumb one-off gimmick and one of that show's deepest episodes. Little Randy could have been a one-off silly gag about how childish Randy is, but instead the show turns him into an essential part of the story and of the kids' dynamic.

This is important, because one common criticism of "South Park" is how disconnected the adult and kids' storylines feel. Having Little Randy, however, bridges the two. It allows Randy to still be involved in the adult stories because he knows that world, such as in this week's episode when he is the one that suggests the boys try going to a farm to investigate the lack of beef in South America. Plus, seeing Randy be his beer-chugging self at middle school is inherently funny, and adds a new dynamic to the nearly 30-year-old show by placing him with the other 4th graders, especially now that Stan has to be constantly embarrassed by his father hanging around.

The fact that Little Randy is older also allows "South Park" to humorously explore current slang and references in an organic way. There's a lot of potential to mine with Randy being both a kid and an adult for the remainder of the season. If Kenny is gone, at least we have Little Randy.
