#3520. You Should Update Your Garmin Watch's Heart Rate Zones

Zone 2 training is still having a moment—even if no one can agree on what it actually means. Legend has it that your easy, conversational-pace cardio—aka your Zone 2 heart rate—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine, to faster race times, and even to a longer life.

Whether Zone 2 deserves quite this much hype is debatable, but still, there are plenty of good reasons to master heart rate training more broadly. To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you your desired workout. Even if you believe every word of the Zone 2 gospel, it's completely pointless if your watch has the wrong idea of what your Zone 2 is. If you train with a Garmin watch, here’s how—and why—you should reset your heart rate zones now (and periodically).

When you first set up your Garmin, it asked for your age, weight, and a few other details. From there it generated heart rate zones, often using a default formula based on a maximum heart rate estimated from your age (typically some version of 220 minus your age). But these formulas are often wrong, since they give a single number for everybody at the same age, while real maximum heart rates vary from person to person.

Plus, there isn’t one universally agreed-upon heart rate zone system. So if your watch assumed a max of 180 and yours is actually 195, every zone it gave you is shifted. Your "Zone 2" might really, for you, be Zone 1 (AKA a pace so easy it barely feels like a workout). Or your "Zone 2" might actually be a moderate-to-hard effort that's digging you into a hole, while you think you're taking it easy. At every step of the way, there’s a different formula and definition that determines what heart rate zone shows up on your watchface.

To complicate things further, Garmin gives multiple options to set up your zones:

Percent of max heart rate. This is the simplest approach. You enter (or let the watch estimate) your max, and each zone is a slice of that number. It's only as good as your max heart rate figure, which, as noted above, is often a guess.

Percent of heart rate reserve (HRR). This method factors in both your max and your resting heart rate, so zones are based on the range your heart works across rather than just the top of it. It tends to produce more personalized zones, but it means your resting heart rate needs to be current, too.

Percent of lactate threshold heart rate (LTHR). Here, your zones are anchored to the effort level where your body starts producing lactate faster than it can clear it, a point that's closely tied to how you actually perform. Many coaches consider this the most meaningful anchor, because it reflects your real physiology rather than a formula.

That third option raises its own question: Where does your lactate threshold number come from?

In the past, getting a lactate threshold estimate from a Garmin meant wearing a compatible chest strap and doing a guided test, which involved a structured, hard run on your part. On newer models, however, that's no longer the case. Garmin has been rolling out an updated lactate threshold detection that works from the wrist's optical heart rate sensor, with no chest strap and no dedicated test. Instead, the watch estimates your threshold automatically from regular outdoor runs. This feature is typically on by default and generally requires a baseline VO2 max estimate and a run or trail run recorded with heart rate. If you'd rather not leave it up to the algorithm, you can turn auto-detection off and enter your own lactate threshold heart rate manually in the heart rate zone settings. Which watches have this varies by model, so check your specific device.

Even if you set your zones carefully once, they don't stay accurate forever. Several things change over time:

Your fitness changes. As you get fitter, your resting heart rate often drops, and your lactate threshold heart rate can shift. Zones based on where you were a year or two ago may not reflect where you are now.

You age. Your maximum heart rate tends to decline gradually over the years.

You change sports. Running, cycling, and swimming each have different heart rate behavior, and Garmin lets you set sport-specific zones for exactly this reason. If you've never touched them, you may be using running-based numbers on the bike, or vice versa.

You switched watches or imported old data. Zones can carry over from a previous device or a profile you set up years ago.

Your resting heart rate has changed. An outdated resting number could be throwing things off.

None of these have dramatic consequences, but if you’re focused on heart rate training, it’s worth trying to be as accurate and up-to-date as possible. If your zones are set too high, you may not be getting the aerobic stimulus you think you are. You'll also underestimate how hard your harder sessions really are, and your training load and recovery metrics can end up skewed.

On the flip side, if your zones are set too low, your "easy" runs could actually become the classic trap of training in the gray zone: too hard to recover from well, too easy to drive big gains. And because Garmin's training status, recovery time, and load features lean on your heart rate data, bad zones can quietly nudge those numbers off as well.

The good news is that fixing all this should take less than 10 minutes. First, decide whether you want zones based on max heart rate, heart rate reserve, or lactate threshold. There’s a good chance you can trust the lactate threshold your watch gives you, or you can find your actual max heart rate.

The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded. If you want a more deliberate test, a coach or a structured max-effort protocol can help, but only attempt hard testing if you're healthy and your doctor is comfortable with it. Also keep in mind that reading from a wrist-based sensor can also spike unreliably, so a chest strap gives more trustworthy numbers when accuracy matters.

Next, check your recent average resting heart rate in Garmin Connect and make sure the number your zones are using is current.

In your watch's user profile or in Garmin Connect, find the heart rate zone settings. From there you can adjust your max, change how zones are calculated, and set different zones for different sports.

Finally, put these new zones to the test. Go for an easy run or ride at what your watch calls Zone 2. Can you hold a conversation, breathing comfortably in full sentences? Does it feel sustainable for a long time? If it feels either laughably easy or surprisingly taxing, your zones probably need another look.

Maybe Zone 2 is the cornerstone of your training, or maybe you think it's completely overrated. Either way, the principle is the same: You should be able to train by feel, and your watch can only help you do that if the numbers behind it are right.

Garmin gives you more ways to set your zones than most brands do. Spend 10 minutes figuring out which method your zones are using, confirming the number behind it is current, and updating it in your settings. It’ll make every easy run, hard interval, and recovery metric on your wrist more useful.

"The Man with the Bag" sees Arnie play Santa Claus himself, who, after his sack of presents is stolen by an elf, enlists the help of a criminal called Vince (Ritchson) to retrieve it. The pairing of Ritchson and Schwarzenegger makes a lot of sense. Both are major action stars who've demonstrated their comedic chops in several projects, Ritchson's most recent example being the Prime Video action comedy "Playdate." In that sense, the "Reacher" star is vying to become the modern-day Arnie and is surely hoping "The Man with the Bag" comes to represent an unofficial passing of the action-comedy torch.

Thus far, it's been tough to know what to make of "The Man with the Bag." In 2024 we learned Schwarzenegger and Ritchson were making a Christmas comedy with an unbelievable premise. Amazon then delivered a teaser trailer in September 2026, which provided a tease of Arnie and his co-star's rapport. Now, we have our first good look at the movie, and it certainly looks to be an enjoyable watch even if it's not necessarily destined to become a holiday classic.

Prime Video has plenty of great Christmas movies already, and now the streamer is hoping to add another to its catalog with "The Man with the Bag." The latest trailer for the Adam Shankman-directed film reveals a lot more about the plot, opening with a scene in which Alan Ritchson's career criminal Vince is seen sitting alongside his daughter, Emma (Berkeley James). It seems he's been away for four years, likely serving a prison sentence, and now that he's out he's back to his old tricks.

His latest client, Kris, is revealed to be Santa himself, who's hired Vince to help retrieve his sack of gifts ahead of Christmas. A "disgruntled elf" who became "obsessed with shiny things" and who calls herself Nadia Nice (Awkwafina) has taken the bag and checked into a fancy hotel. It's here that Santa and his new criminal cohort attempt a heist to retrieve the bag and save Christmas.

It looks as though we'll be getting plenty of amusing back-and-forths between the two leads along the way, with Santa reinstilling some magic into Vince's life and helping him bond with his daughter. We knew the movie was shot on-location in New York (via Ritchson's Instagram) but it's nice to see from the trailer that many of the scenes actually look like it rather than most of the footage looking like it was shot in a streaming-age green screen hellscape.

"The Man with the Bag" is set to hit Prime Video on December 2, 2026, when it will hopefully manage to remind us of the infinite joys of the Christmas action movie.

#3518. Netflix’s ‘Cliff Booth’ Won’t Play on Cinemark or Regal’s IMAX Screens

Netflix‘s theatrical play was bound to have a few hiccups as it works through the kinks of putting movies in theaters for extended runs. One of its big upcoming releases, David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-adventures of Cliff Booth” starring Brad Pitt, won’t be playing at some major theater chains when it opens this Thanksgiving.

Regal and Cinemark have declined to play “Cliff Booth” on their IMAX screens as part of the film‘s IMAX-exclusive theatrical run beginning November 25, IndieWire has learned. For now, the film will play only on AMC’s IMAX screens worldwide, plus a few other smaller circuits with IMAX screens, bringing its worldwide screen total to about 550. AMC has about 200 IMAX screens in the U.S., which is the majority, while Regal has about 100 and Cinemark has closer to 20. Related Stories Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place Producer Titles Can Be Bought, but Real Creative Producers Take Them for Themselves

Those theaters will likely hold “Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” for a second weekend rather than play a Netflix movie that will be available to stream sooner (it drops on Netflix on December 23, in time for Christmas). Normally, IMAX dictates what titles will play on its screens, and theaters don’t have much of a choice, but in this case, because IMAX came aboard as a partner late in the game, IMAX allowed theater chains to opt out of “Cliff Booth” if they chose and would rather stick with “Hunger Games,” which it looks like they’ll do.

“Regal’s premium screens are among our most valuable assets, and one of the factors we consider in how we allocate them is the level of commitment distributors make to the theatrical marketplace,” said Brooks LeBoeuf, SVP of US Content for Regal Global Entertainment in a statement to IndieWire. “Shortened theatrical windows have a direct impact on those decisions, as they limit the opportunity for audiences to experience films on the big screen. We will continue to prioritize releases that recognize the value of theatrical exclusivity, including ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,’ which will have our full support in IMAX.”

It’s a small letdown for Netflix, but there’s always a fight for premium IMAX screens, and moving “Cliff Booth” to Thanksgiving so it could have this IMAX-exclusive window was a big part of the thinking. Netflix had originally slated Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia” movie there, but it moved into February so that it could have a longer run in theaters and a clearer window at IMAX screens.

This isn’t even the only kerfuffle around screens and streamers that took place this week, as Puck, which originally reported the “Cliff Booth” news, added that Regal, Alamo Drafthouse, and also AMC are all among chains that are opting to not play Amazon’s “Ali G: Who Iz I?” as part of an “extended release” Amazon is planning for the film. That movie opened in just 150 select theaters last weekend as part of a brief theatrical stunt, and it’s dropping on streaming even sooner; though it never reported box office data for it, the Sacha Baron Cohen comedy is intending to continue its run, though the major chains are now opting not to hold it. Amazon did not respond to a request about how many screens the film will play on this weekend.

Netflix just added 30 movies and shows to kick off November 2026. Like many of the best streaming services, Netflix reliably kicks off a new month with a huge drop of movies and TV shows, and the world's biggest streamer isn't bucking that trend this month.

A major library refresh is always welcome, but it can lead to decision paralysis. After all, with so many options to consider, it would be easy to fall into the trap of spending more time scrolling than streaming.

That’s why I’ve put in the hard work for you and sorted through everything added to Netflix in November 2026, and picked out five movies and shows worthy of your watchlist.

My selections include the hilarious 2010s comedy "Bridesmaids," two movies released just a week apart, the intense war thriller "Fury," and the captivating psychological drama "Whiplash." And for those feeling nostalgia, I've got you; be sure to stream the '80s classic "Stand By Me."

Binge-watchers, I haven't forgotten about you either. "Rectify" seasons 1-4 have just found a new home on Netflix, and this slow-burn drama was critically acclaimed across its whole run for good reason.

Want to know more about my top picks? Let’s jump into the five Netflix movies and shows you need to watch to start your November right.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

What's it about? When the underachieving, thirtysomething Annie Walker (Kristen Wiig) is asked to be maid of honor for her lifelong best friend, Lillian (Maya Rudolph), she struggles with her own messy love life while also wrangling an eccentric group of bridesmaids, which includes Helen (Rose Byrne), who wants the maid of honor gig herself.

Why you should watch it: For starters, “Bridesmaids” is absolutely hilarious, but it was also a trailblazer. Released in the early 2010s, a period when male-led raunchy comedies were particularly popular, this Paul Feig flick proved that women can be just as funny, and also equally inappropriate (I'll warn you, there's potty humor aplenty). Melissa McCarthy even nabbed an Oscar nomination for her supporting role.

What's it about? In 1945, during the Allies' invasion of Germany, Don “Wardaddy” Collier (Brad Pitt) commands a Sherman tank nicknamed Fury. Alongside his crew of five fellow soldiers, they face overwhelming odds against enemies that are better-equipped as they head into Nazi territory and attempt to strike a decisive blow to turn the tide of war.

Why you should watch it: “Fury” is an intense war movie that really brings you into the heat of battle. Its tank-centric action scenes are exhilarating and well crafted. However, it’s the camaraderie and close brotherhood of its cast that stands out the most. This is a great movie to watch on Netflix if you’re a fan of HBO’s acclaimed “Band of Brothers.”

What's it about? Andrew Neiman (Miles Teller) is a student at a prestigious music conservatory, drafted into the institution's top ensemble, conducted by the exacting Terence Fletcher (J.K. Simmons). Under Fletcher’s ruthless direction, Andrew is tormented and reaches a breaking point as his skills are pushed to their absolute limit.

Why you should watch it: Inspired by writer/director Damien Chazelle’s own experience in a competitive high school jazz band, “Whiplash” is a modern masterpiece. It’s an incredibly intense ride that builds to a genuinely note-perfect finale. J.K. Simmons steals every single scene with a memorizing performance that won the Oscar, SAG, Globe, BAFTA and Critics' Choice awards.

What's it about? Daniel Holden (Aden Young) has spent the last 19 years on death row for the murder of his girlfriend. When new evidence sees his conviction overturned, he returns to his hometown in Georgia and attempts to reintegrate into society. But that’s not so easy when there are ghosts around every corner, and many locals remain convinced of his guilt.

Why you should watch it: Critically acclaimed throughout its run, “Rectify” arrives in full on Netflix on November 1. You can binge-watch all four seasons; 30 episodes total. Critics praised the show for its performances, writing, and authentic portrayal of Southern culture. It’s very much a slow-burn drama, but stick with it, and you’ll be richly rewarded.

Stream "Rectify" seasons 1-4 on Netflix now

What's it about? Based on Stephen King’s novella “The Body,” this small-town drama follows a day in the life of four adolescents living in (the fictional) Castle Rock, Oregon. Looking for something to do on a hot summer’s day, they head off into the woods to locate the dead body of a missing boy. This adventure proves to be life-defining for them all.

Why you should watch it: “Stand By Me” is a certified classic from the late, great Rob Reiner, and one of the most beloved coming-of-age movies of all time. With an all-star young cast — Wil Wheaton, River Phoenix, Corey Feldman and Kiefer Sutherland — it’s charming and relatable. And if you were wondering, yes, it does feature the iconic Ben E. King song.

#3514. Pokémon Fans, Mark Your Calendars For November 30

Pokémon has had a big 2026 thanks to its 30th anniversary. The festivities have seen the release of a 30th Celebration set for the Pokémon TCG, FireRed and LeafGreen coming to Switch and Switch 2, and a nearly endless number of merchandise collabs. From Adidas sneakers and Santa Cruz skateboard decks to McDonald's Happy Meals and a Stern pinball machine, there have been a lot of products to enjoy this year. Now, however, it looks like Pokémon has at least one final and major announcement in store.

The news comes thanks to the official X account for Pokémon in Japan, which seems to be mysteriously counting down to something. Serebii's Joe Merrick, via BlueSky, posted about the mysterious countdown last week: "They just tweeted this with 843. On October 18th they posted this with 1025. There was precisely 182 hours between the tweets. 1025-182 = 843."

"Assuming an hourly countdown," Merrick continued, "this ends November 30th at 14:00 UTC." You can see the full post from BlueSky below:

Shortly after this post, the Japanese Pokémon account once again posted, this time with an image of Teddiursa with the 30th anniversary logo, along with the numbers 676. Once again, the math comes out to something being revealed on November 30, 2026. Fans have translated the words beneath the images, which comes out to "Continue with Pokémon."

Understandably, this mystery only continues to grow, and it's an admittedly strange piece of marketing. The posts mostly went unnoticed for a while. After all, the numbers under the Pokémon in the original posts weren't their corresponding Pokédex numbers, and combined with the 30th anniversary logo, it just seemed like the usual, random social media marketing to remind folks that, yes, this beloved franchise has turned the big 3-0 this year.

Now, the real guessing game begins. A new trailer or reveal for Pokémon Winds and Waves would make the most sense. The leaked release window for Pokémon Winds and Waves is November 2027, so this would be exactly a year before those games come out. Since the starters and a short trailer were unveiled in February, The Pokémon Company and GameFreak have been silent on the Gen 10 games, and many insiders said no new information would be given until February of next year.

Of course, this could also just be a publicity stunt with very little payoff. It wouldn't be the first time a Nintendo property has created hype online, only to reveal something underwhelming. Even Pokémon might just be counting down to a new music collaboration, card collection, or merchandise release that has nothing to do with Gen 10 and everything to do with milking the 30th anniversary for all it's worth.

We also have to consider that it's just the Japanese account that's counting down right now. If it were a trailer or reveal for Winds and Waves, it seems likely the English social media accounts would be involved as well. Pokémon has global popularity, and many releases launch worldwide, even if they appear in Japan first, so the odds are good at least that, no matter what is shown off, English-speaking fans will have a chance to get it too.

For now, we'll all just have to wait and see. Pokémon, at least in Japan, is certainly counting down to something. If the suspense is killling you, you thankfully don't have to wait too long. November 30 is just a few weeks away.

Pokémon is a Japanese multimedia franchise created by Satoshi Tajiri and Ken Sugimori, launched by Nintendo, Game Freak, and Creatures in 1996. Centered on fictional creatures called Pokémon, the series spans video games, trading cards, animation, films, merchandise, and competitive events. Players assume the role of Trainers who capture, battle, and trade Pokémon. It is one of the highest-grossing entertainment franchises in history.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. A travel router sounds unnecessary until you run into unreliable hotel wifi, device limits, or a public network you’d rather not use. The TP-Link Roam 6 is built for exactly those situations, and its AX3000 variant is currently down to $69.99 from $79.98 on Amazon, while the cheaper AX1500 is $44.99, down from $59.99, with price trackers showing both at their lowest prices so far.

The AX3000 is the one I would look at if you travel with several devices, work remotely, or simply want more headroom. It can deliver up to 2,402Mbps on the 5GHz band and 574Mbps on 2.4GHz, compared with 1,201 Mbps and 300 Mbps, respectively, on the AX1500, and it can handle up to 80 connected devices instead of 60. You also get a 2.5Gbps WAN port for faster wired internet, plus USB 3.0 for things like phone tethering, a USB modem, or file sharing. None of those upgrades will fix bad hotel internet, but they make the AX3000 better suited to heavier use once you are on a decent connection.

The AX1500, meanwhile, still gives you Wi-Fi 6, Gigabit Ethernet, USB tethering, and the core travel-router features, making it the easier pick if you mostly travel solo or just want a simple way to get a laptop, phone, and a few other devices online.

#3511. ‘Who Killed Alex Odeh?’ Review: A Scattered but Searing Documentary Examines America’s Tacit Acceptance of Anti-Arab Discrimination

Times change, the arc of the moral universe bends towards justice, and yet one thing that has remained true for as long as I’ve been alive is that prejudice, bigotry, and explicit displays of racism have always been openly permissible in America — so long as they’ve been targeted at Arabs and/or Muslims. That sad and immutable fact was on full display throughout Zohran Mamdani’s mayoral campaign last year, and the say the quiet part out loud reaction to Abdul El-Sayed’s current senate race has somehow managed to be even worse on both sides of the aisle (Democrats lament that he “doesn’t share our values,” while Republicans straight up just call the guy a jihadist). But anyone old enough to remember 9/11 knows that it didn’t start with the likes of Vicky Paladino, just as I assume that anyone old enough to remember the assassination of Alex Odeh knows that it didn’t start with 9/11. Related Stories Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place Producer Titles Can Be Bought, but Real Creative Producers Take Them for Themselves

The sole fatality of a bomb that had been planted at the California office where he served as the West Coast Regional Director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC), Alexander Michel Odeh was murdered on the morning of October 11, 1985, leaving behind his wife Norma and their three young daughters Helena, Samya, and Susan. To this day, his slaughter remains “unsolved.” And yet, as Jason Osder and William Youmans’ scattered but vital documentary “Who Killed Alex Odeh?” makes clear soon after it begins, there’s little doubt as to who was behind the killing.

Indeed, the film establishes that the case was effectively solved within days of the attack, and that all three of the primary suspects — all members of a right-wing terrorist group known as the Jewish Defense League — were only allowed to flee to Israel because powerful forces within the American political system preferred for them to get away with it. And to get away with it. And to get away with it. More than 40 years later, no efforts have been made to prosecute or extradite the presumptive murderers. One of them has even moved back to the United States.

And so, despite affecting the aesthetic and tropes of the true-crime format, “Who Killed Alex Odeh?” directly contradicts the expectations of its supposed genre. Instead of establishing a vast mystery for their movie to explore, Osder and Youmans — one of them Jewish, the other a Palestinian-American — give shape to the galling absence of one. Stunted and searching by design, their film unpacks the sociopolitical context of Odeh’s killing in order to illustrate how the easily Google-able question posed by its title could possibly remain “unanswered” for so long, and even partakes in some light subterfuge as part of an effort to pin down the culprits on camera.

What the documentary finds, or at least calls new attention towards, is alternately eye-opening, obvious, and eye-opening for its obviousness. First and foremost, Osder and Youmans use Odeh’s murder as a lens through which to examine the militarization of Jewish extremism at home and abroad (with an emphasis on the emergence of ultra-nationalist JDL founder Meir Kahane). Propelled by archival footage, the film has little room for personal reflection, but implicit in its focus is the willfully short-sighted extent to which “terrorism” has long been framed as an exclusively Muslim practice; Osder suggests in the press notes, but not the documentary itself, that American Jews are seldom taught about the more violent expressions of Zionism, an implication supported by my own memories of going to Hebrew School at a conservative New England synagogue.

“Who Killed Alex Odeh?” also examines how the tacit permission of such violence is what also allows it to ferment. That Israel welcomed Odeh’s alleged killers back to the holy land, and that President Reagan refused to recognize the severity of the hate crime they had committed against a fellow American on American soil (he never so much as sent a letter of condolence to Odeh’s widow), sent a clear and enduring message that the world’s most powerful governments were okay with the spilling of Palestinian blood. It’s since been alleged that Mossad and the U.S. State Department combined to shut down the murder investigation.

In the most harrowing sequence of a film that has little use for suspense, Israeli investigative journalist David Sheen disguises himself as an ultra-Orthodox Jew and meets one of the alleged killers while wearing a hidden camera — Baruch Ben-Yosef’s outspoken prejudices seem inextricable from his comfortable position as a pillar of his community. Later, when Osder lures him into a sit-down interview under false pretenses, Ben-Yosef excuses himself from the conversation when Odeh’s name is mentioned, his irritation softened (and made even more upsetting) by the “this again?” attitude of someone who seems to believe that no one could possibly still give a shit about the 1985 murder of a single Palestinian expat.

Somewhat diminished in the film’s erratic attempts to contextualize this ever-metastasizing sickness is Odeh himself. Born in Palestine but displaced to Egypt as a child because of the 1967 Arab-Israeli War, the righteous but mild-mannered Odeh dedicated his adult life to combating discrimination against his people in America. Home video footage and old clips from his television panel appearances paint Odeh as more of an egghead than a firebrand. He worked to make in-roads with the local Jewish community, and didn’t have much of a public profile aside from an occasional appearance on “Newsline.” During his final appearance on the show, he debated a member of the JDL.

Osder and Youmans also interview members of Odeh’s immediate family, whose “what is there to say besides the obvious?” has already been internalized by the rest of the documentary. A different and possibly more rewarding film might have done more to investigate the pain of living in a country that has all but signed off on the hate-based murder of your husband or father, but “Who Killed Alex Odeh?” has little patience for investigations. The only thing more obvious than the identity of Odeh’s murderers is the continued lack of political will to hold them accountable. And a country that lacks the political will to address the slaughter of one Palestinian is a country that lacks the political will to address the slaughter of Palestine itself.

“Who Killed Alex Odeh?” is now playing in theaters.

#3510. The 10 Greatest Epic War Movies of the Last 100 Years, Ranked

War is one of those horrific things that should never have to occur in reality but which makes for undeniably compelling films — put it right up there with serial killers and the apocalypse. There's no denying that the violence and destructive nature of war can make for visceral and technically impressive viewing, whether the films want to grapple with the psychological and political implications of it or not. War is hell, but war movies are monuments of filmmaking.

War movies can come in many different forms. Some can be tense thrillers set in the clandestine world that underlies international conflict, and others are intimate dramas that examine the emotional toll that war takes on soldiers and their loved ones. Then there are the epics, the grandiose films that try to capture the true immensity of armed conflict and combat through massive set pieces or large-scale storytelling. There's nothing on the level of a war epic, and they've been an integral part of film history for at least the last 100 years. These are the greatest epic war movies of the last century.

Ridley Scott knows scope and spectacle. His career is littered with epics like the sword-and-sandal Oscar-winner Gladiator, gritty war dramas like Black Hawk Down, and medieval thrillers like The Last Duel. For better and worse, the director has tackled many different eras of history and the conflicts that defined them. In his greatest war epic, Kingdom of Heaven, Scott took on the Crusades with an astounding scale, if not anything approaching historical accuracy. It's big bloody epic entertainment that few directors still working are capable of accomplishing.

Set in the time of the Third Crusade, the film follows Balian of Ebelin (Orlando Bloom), who goes from a disillusioned blacksmith struggling with his faith to the defender of the Kingdom of Jerusalem during its three-day siege. The film covers a lot of ground both geographically and historically, but Scott approaches it more like mythology and entertainment than as a factual representation, and contextualizes it through a more modern political lens. Although notoriously released in a heavily edited version that critics and audiences detested, the much more acclaimed director's cut is an essential war epic.

Scott is also one of several filmmakers to tackle the notorious Napoleon Bonaparte on film, but his rendition of the character pales in comparison to the totemic silent film Napoléon directed by Abel Gance. An influential epic that used a variety of cinematic techniques in its visuals and editing when most of its contemporaries were far more static affairs, what Gance accomplished with Napoleon is still breathtaking to behold. An early widescreen technique called Polyvision was also developed solely for the film, predating similar techniques like Cinerama by decades, but which was lost for years until the film received a proper restoration.

Chronicling the early years of Napoleon's life and his rise in the military, various edits of the film have been shown over the years, with the shortest running just under two hours and the longest over nine. It's a staggering and overwhelming war epic to consume, and even if some of its performances and dramatic elements are crude by today's standards, they are outweighed by its technical achievements and the cinematic experience of it.

While John Woo will always be best known to Western audiences for his modern bullet-riddled action movies, from his Hong Kong Heroic Bloodshed efforts like Hard Boiled to his Hollywood blockbusters like Face/Off, he staged a major cinematic comeback with his epic historical war film Red Cliff. Based on the historical battle that occurred near the end of the Han dynasty in 3rd-century China, the film was Woo's triumphant return to Asian cinema after years of diminishing returns in Hollywood. It reinvigorated him as a filmmaker and reaffirmed to audiences his unparalleled skill at directing action.

In the waning years of the Han dynasty, the warlord Cao Cao (Zhang Fengyi) declares war through the Emperor on the southern lords in order to consolidate and maintain power. Bloody battles ensue, with the film focused through the perspectives of strategist Zhuge Liang (Takeshi Kaneshiro) and general Zhou Yu (Tony Leung). Historically speaking, the events aren't important, since Woo's emphasis is on the spectacle and the human drama, taking inspiration from the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

Leo Tolstoy's totemic epic novel War and Peace has inspired several adaptations on film and television, including the notorious Hollywood version directed by King Vidor and starring Henry Fonda and Audrey Hepburn. While that film may be technically impressive in many respects, its scale and fidelity to Tolstoy's novel are both eclipsed by Sergei Bondarchuk's staggering Soviet epic. Produced in four parts and released over two years, Bondarchuk's film is the definitive adaptation and so monumental that it seems impossible to ever repeat or improve upon in terms of sheer size.

Set during the Napoleonic Wars, the film dramatizes Tolstoy's fictional narrative of the intersecting relationships of several Russian families amid the political turmoil and devastating conflict. Sweeping, romantic, and utterly epic in every way, Bondarchuk's film has been held up as the ideal of Soviet cinema, and was embraced and acclaimed worldwide. It became one of the longest films to ever win an Academy Award. War and Peace is everything and more in an epic fashion.

In terms of pure filmmaking spectacle, it's hard to beat Steven Spielberg. The director is a showman of the highest order. That doesn't mean he can't use his filmmaking powers to craft something with deeper substance beyond wonder and sentimentality. Some of his greatest are those that examine the darker side of human nature, like Munich and Schindler's List. His war epic, Saving Private Ryan, is perhaps the perfect synthesis of his sensibilities, offering a moving portrait of heroism and duty that's more effective because of the harrowing violence of its combat sequences.

Following a squad of soldiers sent on a special mission to save one man whose brothers were all killed in combat, the movie began development as a WWII adventure story in the vein of Where Eagles Dare before Spielberg turned it into a more honest depiction of the violence. War films had been gritty and violent long before Saving Private Ryan, but Spielberg completely redefined how combat should be captured on camera. Almost every modern war film made since owes a debt to this epic.

For the last decade and a half, director Christopher Nolan has exclusively worked on epics. Superhero epics, sci-fi epics, Greek epics. His greatest epic in that time is his intense war film Dunkirk. Like Saving Private Ryan, Nolan wanted to put an emphasis on the experience of war and to immerse the audience in it. That's accomplished in the film with minimal dialogue, an emphasis on practical effects, tightly constructed editing, and percussive sound design. Dunkirk is one of the most technically precise and impressive war movies ever made.

As its title suggests, the film dramatizes the Dunkirk evacuation of over 300,000 Allied soldiers during WWII. While the film features several recognizable stars, such as Tom Hardy, Kenneth Branagh and Harry Styles, they all serve as part of the larger ensemble to focus on the collective efforts it took to pull off what was hailed as a miracle. For all his faults as a filmmaker, Nolan has always known how to deliver spectacle on the largest scale possible, and in Dunkirk he delivers it in service of astounding history. It's what makes it the greatest war epic of the 21st century.

Like Spielberg and Nolan, Wolfgang Petersen was no stranger to large-scale films. His tenure in Hollywood was marked by disaster films like The Perfect Storm, action blockbusters like Air Force One and mythological epics like Troy. His name on a film almost guaranteed a certain level of spectacle, but his greatest epic is also, ironically, his most contained. Das Boot is a sprawling war drama following the crew of a German U-boat during WWII that combines tense action sequences with intimate character dynamics.

Based on the autobiographical novel of the same name by Lothar-Günther Buchheim, the film depicts the experiences of the men on the submarine U-96 as they head into service. The crew is a nuanced group, representing many different men of varying ideologies who are bonded only by their loyalty to each other and their cynical Captain (Jürgen Prochnow). Das Boot minutely details not only the thrill and danger of combat, but also the tedium of life onboard the boat. It's the ultimate submarine movie and a masterpiece of German cinema.

For all the spectacle and intensity crafted by filmmakers like Spielberg, Nolan, and Petersen, the war film that truly communicates the utter dehumanizing brutality of war is Elem Klimov's Soviet masterpiece Come and See. It's a surreal, nightmarish vision of the horrors of war through the eyes of an innocent, and it leaves a deep impression. It was Klimov's final film as a director after he lost interest in it and felt there was nothing else left for him to explore.

Flyora (Aleksei Kravchenko) is a Belarusian teen boy who is conscripted into the Soviet resistance and witnesses unspeakable atrocities committed by the occupying Nazis. The film wallows in the ugliness of war as a plea for peace, and it's hard not to be moved by its violence and startling imagery. Come and See is neither exciting, thrilling, nor inspiring; it's a corrosive film where war is the ultimate hell, certainly leaving nothing of the darkest corners of humanity.

From one of the ugliest war epics to one of the most objectively beautiful. Akira Kurosawa's Ran was released the same year as Come and See and was the legendary director's final epic. Inspired equally by Japanese legends and William Shakespeare's King Lear, the film was a massive production that is often considered the director's last true masterpiece. Most notable is the film's vivid and bold use of color, which is used to delineate characters and evoke emotions. Kurosawa painted the storyboards for the film himself, and Ran is easily the most visually arresting war movie ever made.

Hidetora (Tatsuya Nakadai) is an aging warlord who decides to cede his power to his three sons, which results in violent betrayal and war between them all, leaving Hidetora to wander the countryside as his mind begins to fail him. Ran is Kurosawa's ultimate epic; the culmination of one of the most impressive filmmaking careers of all time. It's a singular war epic of an unparalleled beauty that belies its dark narrative of greed, hubris, and retribution and the chaos they wreak.

As a director, David Lean has been one of the most major influences on modern cinema, and while his epics occupy but a small section of his total filmography, their impact has been massive. The Bridge on the River Kwai and Doctor Zhivago alone would qualify Lean as a quintessential director of epics, but Lawrence of Arabia places him at the apex. The World War I drama, which was based on the life and memoirs of T.E. Lawrence, is the epitome of the epic genre.

Following Lawrence (Peter O'Toole) during his time in the British Army, where he served as part of the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire, the film charts his rise through battles and alliances and fall into psychological torment and disillusionment. Beautifully composed on Super Panavision by cinematographer Freddie Young, Lawrence of Arabia is an epic meant to be experienced on the largest scale possible, a paragon of epic filmmaking, the greatest epic war film of the last 100 years, and likely the next 100 as well.

#3508. Jenna Ortega’s New Sci-Fi Movie Crashes So Hard Studio Hides New Box Office Numbers

Klara and the Sun is being hidden in the shadows.

The new movie, which was directed and co-written by Taika Waititi, is an adaptation of the Kazuo Ishiguro sci-fi novel of the same name that follows an android named Klara (Jenna Ortega) who is sold as an Artificial Companion to a rural family in a dystopian future. 2026's Klara and the Sun, which also stars Amy Adams, Natasha Lyonne, Mia Tharia, and Steve Buscemi, debuted on October 23 and eventually earned a 3-day domestic gross of $701,000, falling short of expectations. So far it has earned less than $2 million worldwide against a reported budget of at least $20 million.

Variety now reports that Sony Pictures Releasing, the studio that is distributing Klara and the Sun (which was produced by a number of production companies, including Columbia Pictures, Spyglass Media Group, HarperCollins Publishers, and 3000 Pictures), is no longer reporting the movie's domestic box office results. ScreenRant has reached out to Sony for comment. This news, which comes in the wake of a report that Klara and the Sun's impending theatrical release in Spain was cancelled, has led to some confusion as to the movie's domestic performance during its sophomore frame.

While various outlets agree that the movie continued to play in 880 domestic theaters over Halloween weekend, just as it did during its opening weekend, the exact reported gross varies widely. Box Office Mojo's reporting suggests that the movie earned $45,000, which sees the movie experiencing a week-on-week drop of 93.6%, which would give it the second-worst sophomore drop of all time, behind 2026's Stray Kids: The Dominate Experience (-94.9%).

However, The Numbers reports that it earned a superior $145,000, dropping 79% (which would place it among the Top 100 sophomore drops of all time, but outside the Top 50). Several other outlets have not reported numbers for the Taika Waititi movie whatsoever.

Per The Numbers, Klara and the Sun's cumulative global total after 10 days in theaters is $1.84 million.

Variety's report also suggests that the movie was given a smaller-scale release than planned in the first place (to compare, Taika Waititi's previous non-Marvel movie, 2023's Next Goal Wins, opened in 2,240 domestic theaters) because Klara and the Sun reviews eviscerated it, earning it a disappointing 24% score on Rotten Tomatoes. However, audiences have been kinder to the movie on the same platform, giving it a Popcornmeter score of 74% with an average rating of 4 out of 5.

Regardless, this has not prevented the movie from experiencing a substantial drop, even if the exact scale of the drop remains unknown.

#3507. Watch the ‘Rehearsals for a Revolution’ Director and Editor Explain How Memories Can Help Fight Authoritarianism

Pegah Ahangurani’s “Rehearsals for a Revolution” is one of the year’s most powerful films, combining half a century of Iranian history with the director’s own personal story of being exiled to London. It all forms one powerful tapestry that begins with a single word: “Yad.”

The Persian word for memory and remembrance ties the entire film together, allowing Ahangurani and editor Arash Ashtiani to weave timelines together under the idea that memory is its own form of revolution. At our Art of the Doc event in Los Angeles, the duo sat down with IndieWire editor-in-chief Brent Lang for a wide-ranging conversation that began with the film’s opening word. Related Stories Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place Producer Titles Can Be Bought, but Real Creative Producers Take Them for Themselves

“I wanted to emphasize the act of remembering, because the central idea of my film is about remembering,” Ahangurani said. “I grew up in Iran and I’ve lived there my whole life, and I know very well that the authoritarians, including the one in Iran, they don’t only censor people. They also try to erase our memories, erase our past, and replace it with their own version of history. They try to rewrite it, and we shouldn’t let them steal our memories. I think remembering is one of the few things we have. We should remember our past, we should remember our victims, we should mourn them. Only after that can we start to heal.”

#3506. Why the Holidays Are Actually the Best Time of Year to Start Working Out

If you have even the tiniest inkling that you might want to get in shape in the new year—or anytime really—don’t wait until January. This isn't a "winter arc" self-improvement pitch; it's just facts. The best time to start a gym habit is before the holiday season. Heck, in December, you’ll even have the place mostly to yourself.

Sure, technically “right now” is always the best time to start exercising, but the holiday season is special. If you wait until January, gyms will be packed. The first two weeks of the year, everybody thinks they’re at the start of an amazing new fitness habit...and by February, most of them have forgotten all about it. Don’t make life harder for yourself by starting during the big rush. Classes will fill up, you’ll have to fight people for the squat rack, and it will be hard to have any real fun. So start now.

In October and November, gyms and classes are at more or less their normal capacities. This is a good time to feel out the vibe of a new place. But it gets better: Once December rolls around, the fair-weather gymgoers will be off shopping for gifts after work and attending holiday parties on the weekends. They won’t feel like getting out of their warm beds in the morning, either. When you arrive, the squat rack will be free. You’ll have your choice of treadmills. The gym will be your oyster.

If you start now, you'll have about two months to get up to speed before the rush starts in January. And that is a perfect little time frame to set a small goal and keep it. Vow to hit the gym three times a week, and you’ll be able to get in 24 workouts before Christmas, even if you take a few days off for festivities. You can get a lot stronger in 24 workouts. Or run, if that's the fitness journey you're most excited about. If you start a couch-to-5k running plan now, you’ll be routinely running 30 minutes at a stretch by the time we get to January.

Yes, the holiday season can be busy and stressful, but remember that working out tends to help our brains manage stress. Mark workouts on your calendar, and keep those appointments with yourself.

Don’t worry about missing out on deals. Any gym or studio that offers a January special probably offers sales year-round anyway. And ultimately, if you get into the habit of actually using the gym, you're getting a lot more value for your money than somebody who joins in January and quickly stops showing up.

Whether they're potted or in the ground, there's still hope for your mums

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you're struggling with your pots and plants heading into fall, or, specifically, you keep finding yourself staring at your once-gorgeous chrysanthemum and wondering where its luscious blooms went, I can help.

Mums are wonderful fall flowers, giving us one last burst of color before the grays of winter set in. As with any plant, mums require some care, and there are steps that you can take right now to help your plant before it's too late.

Here’s three things you can do to salvage what you have left of this gorgeous autumnal plant.

Yes, I'm talking about wilted stems, dried-out ones, and even browning blooms. They all need chopping off! Grab some pruning shears and trim to the point where you can see a green stem — if it’s not salvageable, then chop as close to the root as possible.

As always, you want to do this with sharp pruning shears for the best chop. This promotes strong roots, ready for the next blooming season, and obviously, it helps make your plant look lovely and tidy.

Next, give it a good drink. If your plant is potted, then it’d be smart to fill either a bucket or your sink (if the plant is easy to carry inside) with water and place the plant in it. This way, you’re properly watering the roots, which will probably be very dry.

Leave your plant to sit in this water for around 30-45 minutes. The soil should be damp but never wet, as this will encourage mold.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The next step is to repot it. This is important for encouraging growth, so you need to find a new vessel, one that's around 1-2 inches larger than its old home. You need a well-draining, standard potting mix, much like what you used the first time around.

The ideal soil for your plant, this is Amazon's Choice and it will provide natural fertilizer for up to 2 months for your plant. At an affordable price for the amount, it's even made using responsibly sourced peat.

Think about your plant's positionOnce repotted, you may be tempted to pop it back in its usual spot. But it's worth switching things up — clearly, this wasn't working before. It needs direct sunlight for around 6 hours a day to encourage new buds to bloom. So a sunny windowsill works great if you’re keeping it inside.

If inside, keep this plant away from heat sources. You don't want to dry it out or warm up the soil. Saying that, though, these plants do like cool fall afternoon temperatures.

Going outside? You still need to put it in a sunny spot, ideally where the sun hits first thing in the morning. A plant stand or wooden deck is the best home for an outdoor mum plant, rather than concrete.

Make sure to avoid high-wind spots, and don’t assume that hiding your plant underneath shelter is doing it good — it's actually preventing it from soaking in the sunlight that it desperately needs. Positioning is arguably one of the most important factors in growing a healthy chrysanthemum.

If your mum plant is potted in the ground, then the rules are slightly different: you do need to water it, but this can be done using just your hose. Turn it on and run it over the soil bed for around 10-15 minutes for a good drink.

You still need to prune it back, as you would if it were potted, but it might also help to prune back any nearby plants to avoid overcrowding. This will also ensure your mum plant gets all the sunlight, instead of being hidden in the shadows of other stems.

Another step that might help is adding mulch to the mix. You only need a layer around 1 inch tall, but mulch keeps the roots cool in the fall and protects them from frost in the winter. Better yet, it can help retain moisture, so you won't need to water as often.

On sale today, this mulch can be used for lots of gardening jobs, indoors and out, especially at this time of year. Apart from adding an attractive look to your beds, it can help to suppress weeds and keep in moisture.

#3503. 10 Best George R.R. Martin Books of All Time, Ranked According to Goodreads

George R.R. Martin is perhaps the preeminent titan of contemporary fantasy. His A Song of Ice and Fire books captured the world's imagination like nothing since the heyday of Harry Potter. Despite the lackluster conclusion to the Game of Thrones show, House of the Dragon is still very popular, and HBO is currently developing a host of spinoffs. People can't get enough of Martin's grittier, bloodier, more morally gray take on the genre's beloved tropes.

He's certainly earned this success. Martin is a terrific writer, with a talent for sprawling fantasy worlds, vivid characters, political intrigue, and snappy dialogue. This extends beyond ASOIAF to the many other novels, novellas, and short stories he has published since he got started in the early '70s. This means there's a wealth of Martin goodness for fans to dive into. Here are his ten strongest works, according to the users of the book review site Goodreads.

"Sometimes I think the humanity of him is all hollow, a mask..." Fevre Dream is Martin's take on a vampire story but with his own distinctive twist. For example, all the action takes place on a steamboat chugging along the Mississippi River. The book has been memorably described as Bram Stoker meets Mark Twain. The story follows Abner Marsh, a struggling steamboat captain, who is offered a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to command the most magnificent steamboat ever built, the Fevre Dream.

However, his mysterious benefactor, Joshua York, is later revealed to be an immortal bloodsucker. This is an inherently tense premise, with Marsh trapped on the ship with the vampires. It makes for an enjoyable book, if a rather slight one, lacking the depth of the Game of Thrones books. On the plus side, York is at least a far more complex vampire than the genre usually serves up. His motives are mostly altruistic, and he's far from a stock villain.

"Thrones are won with swords, not quills." Many fans were disappointed when it was announced that Martin's latest book in the ASOIAF universe would be a fictional history rather than the long-awaited Winds of Water, but there's no denying Fire and Blood's impressive scope. It delves deep into the rich history of House Targaryen, spanning from the arrival of Aegon the Conqueror to the early days of King Aegon III's reign. It clocks in at almost 1000 pages.

The book is very meta and is presented as if it were written by a scholar from the Citadel in Oldtown. The fact that it's meant to be a historical text rather than a novel means it's obviously a lot drier and less absorbing than the Game of Thrones novels. This means it's sure to delight GoT superfans, though it may be a little inaccessible to more casual readers. On the bright side, the book does at least contain source material for many more HBO spinoff shows.

"A broken oath tarnishes a knight's honor forever." Game of Thrones fans who have read every book in the main series and are craving more should definitely check out the Tales of Dunk and Egg series, following the knight Ser Duncan the Tall and his young squire, Egg, who is secretly Aegon Targaryen. Set nearly a century before the events of A Game of Thrones, the plot of this novella centers on Dunk's service to Ser Eustace Osgrey during a drought in the Reach.

All of the Dunk and Egg stories are enjoyable. The plots are smaller in scope and more political, like the early seasons of GoT, and that's also their charm. However, the characters do cross paths with a few important historical figures, like Bloodraven and Daemon Blackfyre.

"Silence is a prince's friend." The fourth ASOIAF book shifts its focus to the aftermath of the War of the Five Kings. With the death of King Joffrey and the crowning of Tommen, the power struggles within King's Landing intensify. Cersei Lannister grapples with her newfound authority, facing threats from within and outside the capital. Meanwhile, Brienne of Tarth embarks on a perilous quest to find Sansa Stark, who is hiding in the Vale under Littlefinger's protection.

A Feast for Crows is notable for not featuring primary viewpoint GoT characters like Jon Snow, Daenerys, and Tyrion. Instead, the main characters here are Cersei, Brienne, Sam, and Jaime, while Sansa and Arya each receive three chapters. This is both the book's blessing and curse. The absence of Jon and Tyrion is keenly felt, but it's also fascinating to spend more time seeing things from the perspective of Cersei, Brienne, and Sam. For this reason, A Feast for Crows is sure to remain one of Martin's most divisive books.

"I detest cute animals." This sci-fi novella tells the eerie tale of Simon Kress, a wealthy and callous collector of exotic pets. Kress acquires a terrarium filled with sandkings, insect-like creatures with a hive mentality that build elaborate castles and engage in war. Fascinated by their behavior, Kress begins to manipulate the sandkings, pitting them against each other in increasingly cruel experiments. When he loses control of the critters, all hell breaks loose.

This is Gremlins on steroids. Sandkings is dark, gory, and gruesome; Martin at his most unrestrained. Readers who appreciate this aspect of his work are likely to enjoy it. The highlight is the fascinating description of the sandkings. Each colony consists of hordes of 'mobiles' along with a single queen, or 'maw', which cannot move but controls the others through telepathy. They're also capable of evolving and adapting to their environment, gaining in intelligence and ability. They're like mini versions of StarCraft's Zerg.

Your answers point to the great house whose words, values, and way of surviving in Westeros match your own. Bend the knee — or don't. That's very much up to you.

Winter is Coming — and you have always known it. You prepare not out of fear but out of duty, because the people who depend on you deserve someone who takes the long view.

You understand the game — its rules, its exceptions, and exactly when the rules become the exception. You play it without illusions and without apology.

You carry a sense of destiny that is difficult to explain and impossible to ignore — the feeling that you are not simply participating in the world but meant to reshape it.

You are a force — direct, powerful, and difficult to ignore when you enter a room or a conflict. You do not negotiate with challenges. You meet them.

You understand that power does not always announce itself — that sometimes it arrives with flowers, good wine, and a smile that doesn't quite reach the eyes.

"Other knights serve the lords who keep them [...], but we serve where we will, for men whose causes we believe in." The Hedge Knight is the first entry in the Dunk and Egg series. The story begins with Dunk's journey to Ashford Meadow, where he hopes to prove his worth in a tournament. As Dunk competes in the tournament, he becomes embroiled in a conflict between noble houses. Along the way, he also encounters Egg, who becomes his squire.

The Dunk and Egg novellas are light and lean; this one is just 160 pages long. The characters are likable, and the writing is clear and engaging throughout. The plot is simple but hooks the reader's interest, proving that Martin's books don't need White Walkers or epic quests to save humanity to be compelling. It builds up to a satisfying conclusion, while also planting the seeds of future adventures. Indeed, Martin is said to be planning more installments in the series.

"Kill the boy and let the man be born." A Dance with Dragons picks up where A Storm of Swords ended and runs concurrently with A Feast for Crows. However, it focuses on the major characters, like Jon, Daenerys, and Tyrion. In the North, Jon struggles with his role as Lord Commander of the Night's Watch. Across the Narrow Sea, Daenerys grapples with ruling Meereen. Finally, Tyrion Lannister, on the run after murdering his father, navigates the treacherous political landscape of Essos.

The book is great, loaded with tense scenes and significant plot developments, including several that were cut from the show. However, A Dance with Dragons is also a little frustrating in that it builds up so well and leaves the reader wanting more. All these storylines are meant to continue in The Winds of Winter, but it's unclear when that book will materialize. Martin has admitted to "struggling" with the sprawling text, something that must only be exacerbated by the high expectations fans have for it.

"The brightest flame casts the darkest shadow." A Clash of Kings, the second ASOIAF book, plunges readers into the chaos that follows the death of King Robert Baratheon. With the Iron Throne up for grabs, multiple factions vie for power. In King's Landing, young King Joffrey's reign is threatened by his uncles, Stannis and Renly Baratheon, who each claim the throne. In the North, Robb Stark is declared king and seeks vengeance. Daenerys, likewise, plots her return to Westeros from across the Narrow Sea.

A Clash of Kings impressively avoids the sophomore slump, if anything, raising the stakes established in the preceding book. Martin also greatly expands the canvas of his fantasy world: there are more characters, more locations, and more mysteries, from the rising White Walkers to the shadow magic of Melisandre. In terms of viewpoint characters, this book also introduces fan favorites Theon Greyjoy and Ser Davos Seaworth.

"If you would take a man's life, you owe it to him to look into his eyes and hear his final words." Martin's magnum opus begins simply enough, with Ned Stark, Lord of Winterfell, being summoned to King's Landing to serve as Hand of the King to his old friend, King Robert Baratheon. From there, it quickly expands in scope and ambition, adding in Shakespearean levels of noble drama and shocking plot twists. The infamous beheading of hero Ned remains one of the most hard-hitting moments in the entire series.

The book is just so finely constructed. The dialogue is great, the scheming is addictive, and the battle scenes are intense. A Game of Thrones is also dark and harsh from the get-go, with characters meeting grisly fates like being covered in semi-molten gold. Practically every chapter ends on a cliffhanger, propelling the reader onward and making its 700-odd pages fly by.

"Fear cuts deeper than swords." Martin's highest-rated book on Goodreads is the third entry in ASOIAF. In this one, the War of the Five Kings rages on, with Robb, Joffrey, Stannis, Balon Greyjoy, and Renly all vying for the throne. Betrayal and treachery abound, leading to shocking and pivotal moments such as the infamous Red Wedding and Joffrey's assassination. Jon and Daenerys also have monumental storylines: the former goes beyond the Wall, while the latter amasses an army in Essos.

A Storm of Swords is a whopper of a novel, almost 1000 pages long, but it never drags or feels like a slog. It's the perfect blend of fantasy thrills — dragons, knights, magic, battles, mysterious beasts — and rich characterization, with figures like Daenerys and Jaime revealing themselves to be complex and often contradictory. This may be the central strength of the series: that it avoids simplistic binaries and instead looks at everything in shades of gray.

#3502. I Tested ChatGPT's New 'Slides' Tool, and Here's How It Compares to Gemini

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

ChatGPT's capabilities continue to expand apace, and the latest feature is a fully capable slideshow creator. Announced a few weeks ago, ChatGPT Slides lets you create PowerPoint-style decks from inside your conversations, and it's now appearing for those on the Pro tier and above (meaning right now, you need to spend at least $100 a month to get it).

If you're on the free ChatGPT plan or the $20-a-month Plus tier, you can still get ChatGPT to generate downloadable PowerPoint files from the content of your conversations. However, they'll be more basic than those made in the full version of ChatGPT Slides, and there are no collaboration or native edit options.

ChatGPT Slides is part of OpenAI's push to give users a complete office suite inside the ChatGPT apps. Pages (the word processor) is already available for Pro tiers and above, while a spreadsheet app is on the way—the idea being that you will soon be able to get all your work done without any help from Google or Microsoft.

While Chatgpt Slides is only available on pricey plans right now, it's likely to come to lower subscription tiers in the future. But for now, how does the tool compare to what's available in the free and Plus tiers, not to mention what you can do with Gemini inside Google Slides? I've taken a detailed look.

When it comes to testing out AI tools, it helps to focus on something you're already knowledgeable about so you can spot any mistakes. To test this, I decided to see what ChatGPT could hoover up from the web about the new iPhone Duo. If you're on the free or Plus plans, you can start a conversation, then ask for a slideshow or PowerPoint about it.

Plus accounts also have access to a specific Presentations add-on, available via the + (plus) menu in the prompt box, though I get the impression this feature is in a state of flux since ChatGPT Slides arrived. In any case, you can begin asking about the iPhone Duo specs and early online reactions, and then say "build me a slideshow on the key features and reviews so far".

What I got back on the $20 Plus account was a fairly competent slideshow on Apple's foldable, with accurate information as far as I could see, and a simple series of layouts. It looked like something you might whip up from a template if you were in a rush and didn't have time to properly align all the bullet points or be very selective about which details you included and which you left out. One neat touch is that ChatGPT was able to drop in an official photo of the iPhone Duo at the start of the slideshow, but I had to specifically ask for one.

You can go back and make specific edits to the slideshow, but you have to describe them in the general prompt box—you can't select individual slide elements and make more precise changes. Still, if all you want to do is occasionally convert your ChatGPT conversations into a rough and ready slideshow, there's no real need to upgrade from the free or Plus accounts for now.

Switching to a Pro account, I gave a similar task to ChatGPT Slides hoping for something more comprehensive. To begin with, Slides gets its own dedicated area in the app, so you can start up a blank presentation from scratch—there are some basic image and text features, but the idea is to use prompts to build your slide deck. It's like a really basic Google Slides, with a prompt box.

Creating a slideshow this way feels rather tedious: Typing out what you want to say and then waiting for ChatGPT to do it isn't as intuitive as just throwing in some graphics and text yourself, as you might do in PowerPoint. It also seems to be a bit buggy, at least during the time I spent testing it, with some requests not properly completing.

Starting a standard conversation with ChatGPT and then turning all the information into a deck is much more useful from my perspective. My iPhone Duo slideshow was longer, laid out better, and more informative than the one I created on the Plus plan—there were even charts of battery life and official photos this time.

However, whether I used the free, Plus, or Pro tools, my presentations didn't come across as particularly well thought through. They don't really flow smoothly, either across individual slides or the slideshow as a whole—it feels very much like an algorithm, rather than a person, has decided what information to include and where on the slides to stick it.

Whether you create presentations in chats or through the ChatGPT Slides space, you're able to click on individual elements and do some basic manual resizing and repositioning. You can also request edits via prompts: "Drop in an image of a cat", "make this pop more", "center all of this information", or whatever it is.

ChatGPT Slides does offer collaborative tools, which I wasn't able to test, and I can see that being useful for teams heavily invested in ChatGPT's ecosystem. I can also imagine ChatGPT Slides coming in handy when you've got a lot of information you need to quickly dump into a slideshow that looks vaguely presentable.

In general though, I think I'd much rather stick to the traditional way of making slideshows for now. These old methods are more precise and more manageable, and give you full control over what's shown and where—even if they do take a bit longer. What's more, modern-day presentation tools come with so many templates and other layout aids that it's not difficult to put together something that's easy on the eyes while including all of the information you think is most critical.

Google is, of course, also all the way in on AI (and then some), and if you pay for Google AI Pro ($19.99 a month) or above, you can have Gemini pop up right inside Google Slides to give you some assistance with your presentation-making. To compare the tools, I gave it the same task as I did ChatGPT, asking for a slide deck on the new iPhone Duo.

Gemini actually asked some questions along the way: about wht visual style to use, the audience to aim the slideshow at, and the details to highlight. Though it's always possible to put this sort of information manually into a prompt, this would be a helpful additional to ChatGPT Slides.

What Gemini and Google Slides produced was impressive in terms of the layout and overall vibe of the presentation: It felt much more like a human being had put together the slide deck compared to what ChatGPT had produced, in terms of the information chosen, the way the slides were laid out, and the color picks.

However, Google's result had its faults too: The presentation got the facts on the maximum brightness of the iPhone Duo screen wrong, and produced an "iPhone Duo" graphic that looked like two iPhones from around 2021 stuck together. ChatGPT Slides at least managed to pull official imagery from the Apple website.

You can't attach individual edit prompts to specific parts of your presentation in Google Slides as you can in ChatGPT Slides—you have to mention them in the general prompt box. That said, Google Slides is obviously a much more mature and established slideshow tool compared to the OpenAI equivalent, in terms of its features and layout options (it has been around for a decade, after all).

Given that extra software structure and the lower cost of entry, Gemini and Google Slides is the better option for AI-assisted slideshow making at the moment—though I wouldn't bet against OpenAI catching up. For now, ChatGPT Slides is something that's good to have available if you're already paying a lot for ChatGPT every month, but not a feature that makes it worth your while to swap your AI allegiance.

#3501. New Power Rangers Image Brings Back 90s Zords With Jaw-Dropping Redesign

The Zords from the original Mighty Morphin Power Rangers series are about to return, as Power Rangers reimagines them in a bizarre new form.

Debuting in 1993, the original Dinozords instantly captured the imagination of every 90s kid, equipping each of the Rangers with a towering mech packed with sci-fi weaponry. Famously, the Dinozord footage was reused from Japanese show Kyōryū Sentai Zyuranger, limiting what Power Rangers could do with them.

Now, thanks to a massive audience and a change in medium, Power Rangers has far more latitude in reimagining these iconic machines. And what Power Rangers is doing with them is truly weird, even as the franchise has earned its fans' benefit of the doubt...

Upcoming issues of BOOM! Studios' Mighty Morphin Power Rangers will seemingly transform each Power Ranger into the biological animal that inspired their Zord. The transformation can be seen in connecting covers by Phillip Sevy, showing each Ranger alongside their new animal form.

Previously, it seemed that the Zords might simply be granted life, but a newly shared summary for issue 7 has revealed this unique twist, strongly implying it's the Rangers themselves who will become dinosaurs, prehistoric beasts and dragons.

In the second half of this monstrous two-parter, the Power Rangers are trapped in their Zord forms!

Unable to turn back into humans, the team is left helpless as Rita’s latest monster goes on a rampage... the Trauma Dumpster releases its humiliating truth bombs that make you tell your darkest secrets!

But Tommy has an idea why the Rangers are stuck in these forms... and even better, how to switch back! Can he reach them in time to defeat Rita and her Trauma Dumpster before everything becomes a tyrannosaurus wreck?

The issue, coming from Marguerite Bennett and Phillip Sevy, will continue the new series' exploration of psychological issues, depicting the original Rangers as adults, grappling with monsters who represent their regrets and traumas. That will become very literal as Rita Repulsa unleashes the "Trauma Dumpster."

While issue 6 will depict Jason worrying that's no longer the right leader for the team, the latest villain will seemingly transform the Rangers in the meantime, perhaps via the monster's weaponized "Truth Bombs."

Introduced in the first series of the 90s show, the Zords were the Power Rangers' ultimate weapons - gigantic mechs which they could directly pilot, unleashing slashing claws, electrical blasts and explosive hidden cannons.

Yelling "We Need Dinozord Power, Now!" the Ranger would trigger a lengthy, frequently reused sequence where the Zords emerged from various hidden locales, running to their owners' aid. When the Zords weren't enough, they could be combined into the bipedal Dino Megazord, piloted by the combined efforts of the team.

Later series upgraded (and eventually destroyed) the Dinozords, but no Zords since have quite captured the iconic status of the originals.

The iconic nature of the original Zords has seen them reimagined in a variety of ways, most recently in Pallie Paul Allor and Gustaffo Vargas' Power Rangers Green. The series follows an older Tommy Olvier in exile and retirement, with the shattered Dragonzord acting as his home, now named "the Dragon's Grave."

Now, Mighty Morphin Power Rangers is going even further, trapping the show's 90s heroes in the forms of their classic Zords - bring on dragon Tommy Oliver!

Mighty Morphin Power Rangers #6 is coming November 25, followed by #7 December 30.
