#3500. Artisans Break Down the Tricks and Treats of Designing a Trojan Horse at SCAD Savannah Film Festival

As part of the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking team presents “Behind Their Lens,” a series of panel discussions with some of the most exciting artisans, directors, and producers of 2026. On the artisans panel, “The Odyssey” production designer Ruth de Jong, “Paper Tiger” and “I Play Rocky” costume designer Amy Roth, and “Disclosure Day” editor Sarah Broshar spoke to students and guests about their process and approaches towards each of their particular corners of the giant puzzle that is putting a film together.

But there was one thing that united all of them, across their different creative disciplines, and that was the importance of (sometimes quite literally) climbing hilltops to create a sense of authentic surprise. Related Stories Ruth Madeley Never Thought Acting Was an Option — Now, She’s Playing a Disability Rights Legend in ‘Being Heumann’ Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place

If a costume designer can delight a director without being asked for something specific, then the movie is alive. If the editor’s intuitive sense of rhythm is working in harmony with the footage that’s been shot, then in a lot of respects the film is showing the post team what it wants to be. And if a production designer can build a Trojan Horse to the right scale and it falls down? Well, don’t panic. It can look even more weathered and accurate to the initial plan when it’s picked back up again.

“Obviously the scale [of the horse] came from me needing to fill it physically with the actors and the IMAX camera and [cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema] and Chris. So that’s how we proportionally worked out and built several of them, then built a separate body of the horse to physically shoot that scene, lowered it into a tank, and shot that on a set near our city of Troy,” De Jong said.

But in addition to needing to half-drown Odysseus (Matt Damon) and his companions, an IMAX camera, cinematographer, and acclaimed director, some of the aspects that make the Trojan Horse truly look like it’s been in the wars came about organically.

“[For the opening], we mounted the horse to a massive trench plate and got a dredger. We dredged up really deep into the sand. We did a few tests a couple of days before. We put the horse in the waves. It took a beating. It fell. We had to rebuild it overnight to then shoot the next day. So the horse you are seeing in the film went through a lot before it got shot. It was very physical,” De Jong said. “Water always wins.”

But according to De Jong, the work of production design, even on projects without the grand scope of “The Odyssey,” is always the same. “ I feel deeply that if my sets are too obvious, I’ve failed because they should fade to the back and the actors should just be immersed in their worlds, and the audience should be lost in that world,” De Jong said.

This is as much the case for good contemporary costume design, where the clothes should just help us make judgments about the characters and feel the shifts in the story, something Amy Roth talked about doing almost invisibly in both “I Play Rocky” and “Paper Tiger.” With the former, Roth took a lot of cues not just from the existing material around “Rocky” and Sylvester Stallone, but about how the character of ‘Mike’ would feel about his body as he worked himself up into becoming Sly.

“He really was like three people,” Roth said. “Dressing him early on was taking hints from a future Sly and putting them in the way he dresses so that we can see the impetus of how ‘Rocky’ came to be. He was big into working out and he was very body conscious. So that silhouette was important to me and I was literally, like, layering clothing onto Anthony so that he couldn’t bulk up,” Roth said.

Meanwhile on “Paper Tiger,” Roth worked in a silent partnership with the sets in order to give the characters caught up in a mob scheme more or less agency. “The house was very beige, so I put the actors just so that the mother was in focus. And then in the end she starts to fade. She starts sort of matching the walls; the mother and father sort of fade into the background.  And that’s just me doing my thing. I don’t think I even discussed that with James [Grey, the director], but he would’ve liked it.”

What the director likes and how the director is responding gets very important in the edit, which is where Broshar’s developed a great read on Steven Spielberg over the course of their many collaborations.

“When you’re spending hours and weeks and months and years sitting in a room with somebody, you get shorthands. You don’t have to say words as much. You can just kind of feel a twitch. If I make a little twitch, Steven will look at me, like, ‘What? What are you thinking?’ You can tell,” Broshar said. “I think you’re just always trying to sit down and watch the movie or watch the scene like you’ve never seen it before. I always watch myself watching something, and I try to see if I’m feeling tense or if I am getting distracted or thinking about what’s for lunch — and that is a real red flag.”

One of the ways in which Broshar can help surprise herself and the other folks watching a cut is with sound, especially on a delightfully bonkers action sequence like “Disclosure Day” has in its train chase. “Like anything, it just takes patience and imagination, and you keep an eye on the timing of things — where and how do you want to see the train, how far away is it, when do we hear the train, how loud is it?” Broshar said. “ I have great assistants who do really good sound work, and I just kept asking them for more. They’d say, ‘We spent three days on this.’ And I’m like, ‘Great. Now spend three more.’ And let’s just keep [going] more, more, more, more. And then, you know, it all gets polished out as soon as great Gary Rydstrom and Bryan Chomier and their team come in with sound.”

Whether it’s sound, color, or the elements of nature themselves, it’s the surprises and flourishes that artisans build into their work that help each filmmaking department feel alive.

We put the new Fitbit head-to-head with Apple’s best smartwatch

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earlier this week, my colleague Dan walked 6,000 steps with the new Fitbit Edge and the Apple Watch Series 12 to test which was more accurate when it comes to one of the most basic smartwatch requirements: step counting. Dan found that the $179 Fitbit Edge came out on top of the $399 Apple Watch Series 12. Keen to find out more, I strapped both to my wrist and repeated the test.

Sure, both of these trackers will do a lot more than just count your steps. The Apple Watch Series 12 is like having an extension of your iPhone on your wrist, and is the best smartwatch on the market for most people. The Fitbit Edge seems to toe the line between the $99 screenless Fitbit Air and the Google Pixel Watch 5 — a bright screen, built-in GPS, and a continuous heart rate monitor.

Like all these walk tests, I strapped one watch to each wrist and used a $5 clicker tool from Amazon to count my steps as I walked manually. Both trackers count steps using an internal accelerometer, which measures the swing of your arms. Each swing counts for two steps, and it doesn’t matter whether you wear your watch on your dominant or non-dominant hand. It doesn’t matter if you walk with your hands in your pockets or holding a cup of coffee; the accelerometer should still measure your body’s movement.

Read on to find out which came out on top. You can also read our Apple Watch Series 12 review and our Fitbit Edge review here on Tom’s Guide.

As with all of the best Apple Watches, the Apple Watch Series 12 still doesn’t tell you the number of steps you’ve taken during a specific workout; instead, you see an overall number of steps throughout the day, which you can now pin to your home screen. This is probably because steps aren’t actually that useful a metric beyond a certain point, but annoying for me when writing these articles. For this comparison, I downloaded a third-party Pedometer+ app onto my Apple Watch.

I split this walk up into three different walks, manually clicking each time I took a step. When I got home, I downloaded my data.

As you can see from the results, this one is incredibly close. The Apple Watch Series 12 overcounted by 23 steps; the Fitbit Edge missed 71 steps. With only 50 steps between them, it’s a tough one to call, but unlike Dan, I can say the Apple Watch Series 12 was slightly ahead here.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

It’s worth noting that 50-70 steps is pretty much spot on. The average person takes 2,000 steps a mile, so an extra 23 steps is nothing.

To really compare these two watches head-to-head, you’d need to look at more than just how well they count steps. Both are designed to be worn 24/7 and help you track more than just walking workouts.

However, there are some big differences: as mentioned above, the Apple Watch Series 12 is designed to be an extension of your iPhone on your wrist, with plenty of apps at your disposal. The Fitbit Edge, on the other hand, is definitely more of a basic fitness tracker than a smartwatch.

We’ll continue to test and compare the two watches, but which would you buy?

#3498. This New Garmin Feature Is Draining Battery Life, but There's a Quick Fix

Garmin users are taking to the company's support forums with a common grievance: The newly introduced "OK Garmin" hands-free voice feature appears to be eating through battery life. The feature arrived through Garmin’s September software updates, bringing hands-free voice activation to the Fenix 8, Forerunner 570 and 970, Venu 4, and several other models. Here's how to make sure Garmin's new updates aren't slashing your watch's battery life.

Last month's updates for select watches also brought all-day fall detection, a set of new Quick Workouts and Garmin Run Coach plans, as well as that "OK Garmin" hands-free voice command feature. It's exactly what it sounds like: Instead of pressing a button, users can simply say “OK Garmin” to activate voice commands. However, it looks like "OK Garmin" in particular is what causes some watch's projected runtimes to drastically drop, allegedly by roughly 35% to 50% in some cases.

Garmin does acknowledge that enabling these settings shortens battery life, though it doesn't say by how much. The tradeoff makes sense, since the watch has to listen constantly for its wake phrase. Even so, giving up several days of runtime is a steep price for a feature that many people may seldom use. Luckily, the fix is simple: Turning off "OK Garmin" should restore your battery life estimates right away.

If your watch has been draining faster since the update, go to Settings > System > Voice and disable "OK Garmin." If needed, you can also switch off the Phone Assistant wake word from the same area. The good news is that turning this feature off won't even take voice commands away—you can still trigger them manually using the watch's physical controls.

Keep in mind that these numbers are battery estimates rather than independently tested, real-world runtimes. Some of the battery complaints that surfaced after the update may also stem from unrelated issues. Still, trading away as much as half your battery life just to avoid pressing a button is a difficult bargain to defend.

#3497. The Arcane Knowledge Directors Wish They Could Summon

As part of the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking team presents “Behind Their Lens,” a series of panel discussions with some of the most exciting artisans, directors, and producers of 2026.

On the directors panel, “Blue Heron” writer/director Sophy Romvari, “Josephine” writer/director Beth de Araújo, “Custom of the Country” director Josie Rourke, “The Good Daughter” director Steph Green, and “Toy Story 5” co-director Kenna Harris spoke about their different paths into directing — a fair amount of team sports — and how they approach everything from thinking about locations to communicating their vision clearly with different members of their crews. Related Stories Ruth Madeley Never Thought Acting Was an Option — Now, She’s Playing a Disability Rights Legend in ‘Being Heumann’ Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place

But the panel also spoke about the ways in which film as a medium is constantly changing and skills they would like to be able to bring to future projects, and that all directors might want to be aware of.

Rourke, whose first feature film had the challenge of creating a sweeping historical scope for “Mary Queen of Scots,” has been thinking about how directors and visual effects artists can work better together since she had to drop some (digital) castles into some Scottish hillsides.

“I just knew it wasn’t working, but I couldn’t figure it out. And in the end, I called a friend of mine who’s a really good architect and said, ‘Listen, just pop into the edit,’ [to look at the castle assets], and he looked and went, ‘Yeah, that wouldn’t stand up,’” Rourke said. “It was really interesting because my body had a visceral fear of wanting to use that structure. It’s just an imaginary castle but [I knew] it was dangerous.”

Rourke’s instinctive awareness is something she’s since worked on trying to better communicate with VFX teams, but there’s even more nuance to how those discussions are had. “Some of the smoke and mirrors about [VFX choices] is about cost. So I don’t even know how to look at this and go, ‘Here’s how I would achieve that more economically,’” Rourke said. “I know how to cut costume or cut set or cut script or cut the schedule, but I don’t know how to be in dialogue that is sensibly and creatively managing the budget for visual effects.”

Harris, who has been embedded in the world of digital animation for years as a story artist before fusing into a hivemind with their fellow co-director Andrew Stanton to tackle “Toy Story 5,” still has things about the process they want to learn, too.

“I wish I understood simulation a little bit better because I want to learn how to talk about in a way that feels more collaborative. And the reason I say that is because there are certain things that even today in a really fancy studio like Pixar that are still hard to crack, visually,” Harris said.

One of those things is folds in clothing — the ability to create the sense of clothing moving along a character’s body naturally or bunching up around the elbow in a believable way, the seemingly simple but actually quite complicated to craft illusion of a hood lying against someone’s shoulders.

“If I was gonna say, ‘Hey, I really care about sleeve folds,’ I’m sure my producer, Lindsey Collins, would be like, ‘What? Why? Why, why would you care about that?’” Harris joked. “But artistically, I’m fascinated by it. We’re still relying on these physics-based engines for things like that, and when I look at a lot of 2D art, there are people who can design the hell out of just making clothing [work], it’s beautiful the way that cloth works on our bodies, and it’s just so hard to do on a feature scale. And so, I think it would be awesome if I understood simulation more technically because then maybe I would get closer to having a conversation of finally getting to see the sexy clothes folds that I’ve wanted my whole life.”

Clothing is something that’s both important and underrated in live-action, too. For as much and as proudly as “Blue Heron” is an indie film, it was the first time that Romvari had worked with a costume designer and saw the power of what having a creative collaborator in that department could do.

“It’s often seen as this very frivolous and just clothing and, you know, often is treated as just like a woman’s department and who really, you know, just put something on them. But I’ve learned so, so much through working with my costume designer, Maria [Katarina], how integral it is for continuity, aesthetically, but also for actors’ safety and comfort,” Romvari said.

Costume does a lot of silent work in “Blue Heron” since it is a period piece set in the late ‘90s (horrid thought) with sections taking place in a more contemporary timeline as well. The shift in clothing, and how characters feel about themselves through how comfortable they are in their clothes, articulates things that they themselves can’t quite say.

“Just so often costume designers are asked, ‘Can you just throw something on them?’ And now I understand the inner turmoil that they go through when they’re like, ‘Do you know how much time I spent dying that shirt and then using this artificial scrub to make it look like it’s from this other period?’ Just so much work goes into it that’s just not respected, and it’s so integral to what you see on screen,” Romvari said. “ So I think I’m just speaking up for costume designers. It’s a really important element that I think is undersung for its value.”

#3496. The 7 Best Opening Shots in Marvel Movies, Ranked

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Marvel movies are often known for their massive third-act battles. Every Avengers movie has one. Civil War had the airport battle. No Way Home united 3 generations of Spider-Men against their rogues' gallery. Those finales are what people remember and talk about for years afterward.

But the openings fly under the radar, when in reality, Marvel has delivered some of the greatest openings of all time. They just get overshadowed by the big finale fights. So today, we're going over the Marvel movies that have some of the greatest opening shots.

The movie opens in a dark, dystopian future where mutants and their human allies are hunted to near extinction by the Sentinels. Years of war have turned every mutant here into a master of their abilities, and it leads to the most inventive power usage in the entire franchise. Blink (Fan Bingbing) is the standout here. She links her portals with other X-Men's powers to chain attacks together in mind-bending ways, and it's top-tier X-Men stuff.

It also did a phenomenal job of establishing the Sentinels as truly menacing villains. The scene is a harrowing bloodbath, where fans watch their favorite characters get massacred by giant robots that are using the mutants' own powers against them. The scene left such a mark on fans that the Russo Brothers had no choice but to bring the Sentinels back for round two in Avengers: Doomsday.

Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 opens in the most James Gunn way it possibly could. A huge battle rages against a multi-dimensional, eight-limbed space monster, set to Electric Light Orchestra’s "Mr. Blue Sky." But the camera isn't on the fight at all. It stays on Baby Groot, panning around him as he dances to the song while the rest of the team fights in the background, just slightly out of focus. The most dangerous thing in the galaxy is trying to eat the team, but the movie couldn’t care less, and neither could the audience. All eyes are on a tiny tree bopping along to the music, having the best time of his life.

Mid-fight, Gamora (Zoe Saldaña) yells, “Groot, get out of the way, you’re going to get hurt!” and he turns around and just waves at her, with absolutely nothing going on in that little head of his except vibes. Then he fixates on a space bug flying around and tries to eat it. Rocket Raccoon rushes over, yells at him, and makes him spit it out in disgust. This entire sequence was pure, unadulterated joy, and did a phenomenal job of reintroducing the family dynamic of this team.

Infinity War opens inside the decimated Asgardian refugee ship, which holds whatever was left of the Asgardians. Ebony Maw (Tom Vaughan-Lawlor) walks among the dead bodies and delivers a speech about salvation. Thor (Chris Hemsworth), the strongest Avenger, lies defeated. Thanos (Josh Brolin) asks Loki (Tom Hiddleston) for the Tesseract in exchange for Thor's life. Loki tries an illusion to stab Thanos in one last heroic act, but Thanos sees right through it and snaps his neck.

Then the Hulk (Mark Ruffalo), the wildcard we all expected to be the best match for Thanos, bursts out and gets a few hits in. But Thanos easily overpowers him in hand-to-hand combat and beats him so badly that Hulk is scared to come out for the rest of the movie. Then, Thanos takes the Space Stone, kills Heimdall (Idris Elba), and teleports away while the ship gets obliterated. Those first few minutes paid off years of build-up and established Thanos as the strongest villain the MCU had ever seen. And it also set the grim tone for the rest of the movie, where for the first time it felt like anyone could die.

Iron Man opens on a desolate desert landscape, followed by a US military Humvee convoy kicking up dust while AC/DC's "Back in Black" plays. Tony (Robert Downey Jr.) sits in the back seat with a drink, cracking jokes with the soldiers escorting him. He brags about his lifestyle, takes pictures with them, and is completely unfazed by the war zone around him.

Then the convoy is ambushed. The vehicles around them begin exploding, and their Humvee gets riddled with bullets and taken down. Tony tries to hide behind a rock, only for a Stark Industries missile to land right next to him and detonate. In mere minutes, Iron Man introduces the brash genius billionaire playboy fans knew from the comics and sets up the origin story.

Four people, four completely different ideas of what it means to have somebody in your corner. Here is who picked up, what they would ask of you, and what you would get back.

You want the friend who does not leave. Steve is the one who turns up at the door without being asked, who remembers what you said you were worried about, and who has never once made you audition for his attention.

You want the friend who is genuinely exhausting and completely worth it. Tony will forget your birthday, then build you something at four in the morning that you did not know you needed, and hand it over as though it were nothing.

You want the friend who replies in four seconds and apologises for it. Peter is earnest in a way that is almost unfashionable, and he will take on far more than he can carry rather than admit that he is struggling.

You want the friend who insults your shoes, fixes your phone and then quietly rearranges your entire life for the better. Shuri does not do soft reassurance, and that is the reason you would believe her when she says you are fine.

Over two decades later, the opening of X2 remains one of the best action sequences in superhero movies. It starts with a recitation of Abraham Lincoln's first inaugural address from 1861: "We are not enemies, but friends. We must not be enemies." From there, we see a mysterious man stalking his way through the halls of the White House, walking past portraits of former Presidents who all survived or fell to assassination attempts. The camera follows him through the POVs of security guards and security cameras.

Then a guard asks what he's doing, and a forked tail rises from behind the man's back, and we find out it was Nightcrawler (Alan Cumming) all along. He pounces on the guard, Mozart's "Requiem in D Minor" kicks in, and we're off on a wild ride. Nightcrawler teleports through the hallways of the West Wing like a demonic jackrabbit and takes out Secret Service agents one after another. He gets all the way to the President, but gets shot before he can finish the job and is forced to teleport away. He leaves behind a dagger that reads "Mutant Freedom Now."

Blade begins with a guy who is led into a secret underground nightclub hidden inside a meatpacking plant. It's a gothic party vibe, with strobe lights making it hard to see and a heavy techno track blasting in the background. While dancing, he feels a mysterious drop of liquid hit his hand, and it turns out to be blood.

As the techno builds to its peak drop, the ceiling sprinklers go off and start spraying blood everywhere. The crowd erupts in ecstasy, and everyone shows off their fangs, revealing that everyone in the room is a vampire. It was an insane reveal that caught everyone off guard. And right after, Blade (Wesley Snipes) makes the coolest entrance ever, dressed in all black, and starts slicing vampires apart with razor-sharp precision.

Into the Spider-Verse had a phenomenal comic book-style opening that recapped decades of Spidey history, from radioactive spiders to emo dance moves and so-so popsicles. That left Across the Spider-Verse with a tough act to follow, but it not only matched it, some might say it even surpassed it. The film begins with a hyper-stylized, colorful narration from Gwen, made to look like her thoughts while she drums. On visual quality alone, it tops the first movie.

Then the words start landing. Miles was bitten by a radioactive spider, and he's not the only one. Now he's on his own, and he's not the only one. She didn't want to hurt him, but she did. If you're watching for the first time, you think she's talking about the end of Into the Spider-Verse, where they all leave him behind. Only after you've seen the full movie do you realize it wasn't a recap at all. It's actually from the end of this film, when she recruits her own Spider team, so the movie basically starts at the end. The sequence even shows off major plot points. You see Miguel explaining the Spider-Verse to Miles, Miles and Gwen upside down on the clock tower, and Miles cutting Gwen's web. You even see the fully powered-up Spot and all of the Captain deaths. All of it is right there in the opening sequence!

#3495. Sydney Sweeney’s R-Rated Thriller Officially Sets New Adaptation 3 Months Before Sequel Release

As Sydney Sweeney gets to work on its sequel, The Housemaid is about to get another adaptation.

Having already been a bestselling hit upon its 2022 publication, Freida McFadden's thriller novel further exploded in popularity with Sweeney's 2025 film, in which she starred as the eponymous Millie as her new job working for a wealthy couple immediately becomes a tangled web of passion and danger. Thanks to its record-breaking box office run and solid reception, plans for The Housemaid's Secret kicked off shortly thereafter, with Sweeney, Michele Morrone, director Paul Feig and scribe Rebecca Sonnenshine all returning.

Now, Deadline has brought word that Lionsgate is officially adapting The Housemaid into a stage production. The studio is teaming with Tony nominee Bekah Brunstetter to pen the script for the new adaptation of Freida McFadden's hit thriller novel, with fellow Tony nominee Matthew Dunster set to direct, and Simon Friend and Hanna Osmolska attached to produce via their Melting Pot banner. Additionally, The Housemaid play is set to begin at London's Richmond Theatre on September 14, 2027, three months ahead of Sweeney's sequel.

In addition to the announcement, Friend offered a brief tease of their plans for the Housemaid stage adaptation, describing the production as a "fresh and uniquely theatrical take" on both McFadden's novel and Sweeney's film, while also aiming to "bring a thrilling new dimension" to the proceedings.

While staying generally true to its source material, Sweeney's Housemaid did notably come with a few changes from the novel that the stage adaptation could better lean into or expand upon. From Morrone's Enzo being a much more active character in the Winchester family's lives and Millie's interactions with them to the fate and resolution behind the story's central villain, there are plenty of ways that the stage play can set itself apart from the blockbuster hit.

News of the new Housemaid adaptation also comes on the heels of production kicking off on Sweeney's Secret, which is slated for a December 17, 2027 release, sticking with the first movie's Holiday 2025 window that led to a $400 million worldwide box office haul. Joining Sweeney and Morone for the sequel are Kirsten Dunst, Paul Anthony Kelly, Brittany Snow and Stephen Kalyn, with filming currently underway in New York City.

Interestingly, The Housemaid continues both Lionsgate and other studios' trend of bringing some of their biggest film franchises to the stage with new adaptations. While having already adapted it for the stage, Dirty Dancing is set to get its first-ever Broadway debut in February, while the musical iteration of Now You See Me kicks off its Broadway run beginning this month. Furthermore, Stranger Things memorably expanded with the canonical prequel, The First Shadow, and Paramount's Paranormal Activity became a smash hit, all of which bodes well for Lionsgate's new production.

The Housemaid follows Millie, who takes a job as a housemaid for a wealthy couple, Nina and Andrew. While initially offering a fresh start, her position reveals the family's perilous secrets that far surpass her own challenges.

#3494. This Is the Robot Vacuum I Use Every Day, and It's 50% Off Right Now

I live in a 1,600-square-foot home, and vacuuming and mopping it by hand takes a considerable chunk of time. Passing that labor off to a robot vacuum was a great decision. I decided to go with the Roborock Qrevo CurvX since it seemed like a great fit for my circumstances. If you also have a dog, a mix of different floor types, and a gym with a workout mat, this robot vacuum might work for you, too. Amazon currently has it for $749.99 (originally $1,499.99), a 50% discount, and the lowest price it has ever been, according to price-tracking tools.

One of the main things I was looking for in a robot vacuum was suction power. The Qrevo CurvX has 22,000 Pa, which is stronger than most options at its price and is powerful enough to pick up anything that needs vacuuming in my house. I like that it has a self-lifting chassis so it can climb over my workout mat, rugs, obstacles like cables, or anything else that might be in the way, so I don't have to babysit it while it's doing its job. I also like the extendable mop pads and side brushes that allow it to reach corners and crevices it might not be slim enough to fit into. (Speaking of which, it's only 3.14 inches tall, so it can fit under most couches and beds without issue.)

My experience with the Roborock app has been great. It's easy to use and gives me enough control to clean my house how I want without a hassle. "No Go Zones" are easy to set up, as is the schedule. The main issue I've had is the size of the internal dust bin: It's small, so it needs to be cleaned after basically every scheduled use (though that shouldn't be as bad if you don't have a pet that sheds a lot).

Take it from me: If you're looking for a reliable hybrid robot vacuum that can clean multiple types of floors, mop, and comes with a great app, the Qrevo CurvX makes a compelling case at the current $750 discount.

#3493. Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself in Leg at Los Angeles Gun Range

Michael Mann, the director of “Heat” and “The Insider,” shot himself in the leg at a Los Angeles gun range on Saturday.

A spokesperson for the filmmaker said that “a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered resulting in a superficial injury.” Mann was treated at a local hospital for a wound that was subcutaneous and minor. He is being released. The event took place during target practice. Mann is an experienced shooter who has been practicing on ranges for decades.

A spokesperson for the Los Angeles said that officers had responded to a “shots fired” incident at The Range LA at roughly 4 p.m. An investigation determined that the shooting was “accidental.” TMZ broke the news of the shooting.

The 83-year-old Mann is known for directing gritty crime stories, many of which look at cops and criminals and are set in urban landscapes. He was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Director for his work on the 1999 journalism thriller “The Insider” and the film was nominated for Best Picture. Mann’s other credits include “Thief “(1981), “Manhunter” (1986), “The Last of the Mohicans” (1992), “Ali” (2001), “Collateral” (2004), and “Public Enemies” (2009). As a producer, Mann received an Oscar nomination for Martin Scorsese’s 2004 drama “The Aviator.”

Mann’s most recent credit was 2023’s “Ferrari” and he is about to shoot a sequel to “Heat” that is based on a novel he co-wrote with Meg Gardiner. That film will star Christian Bale, Leonardo DiCaprio, and Stephen Graham. Mann also helped create the ’80s TV hit “Miami Vice” and later directed a film version of the show.

Free up your iPhone's storage without deleting all your stuff

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Why is it that you seem to run out of iPhone storage at the worst possible moment? The knee-jerk reaction is to start frantically trashing holiday pictures or deleting apps you actually use. But you do not need to butcher your camera roll or pay for more just to claw back a few precious gigabytes.

A couple of clever, built-in settings reclaim space without touching the things you care about. To keep things simple, here are the two best ways to clear that storage warning for good.

High-definition clips and photos are almost always the secret culprits swallowing up your storage. If you shoot video in 4K, just sixty seconds of footage can eat through nearly half a gigabyte of local space.

Instead of manually picking through your photo library to delete memories, you can let your phone handle the heavy lifting automatically. Head over to Settings, Apps, Photos, and make sure iCloud Photos is switched on, and tap Optimize iPhone Storage.

This feature keeps smaller previews on your phone and moves the full-resolution files to iCloud, downloading originals on demand when you view them.

Most of us have a digital graveyard of apps we only open once in a blue moon — think airline boarding passes, occasional parking apps, or mobile games you haven't touched in weeks.

Offloading gives you the perfect middle ground. Navigate to Settings, General, and iPhone Storage, where your device neatly lists your apps from biggest to smallest. Tap on any culprits you don't need and hit Offload App.

This removes the app to free up storage while keeping your personal data, settings, and logins untouched. When you need it again, tap the grey cloud icon on your home screen to instantly reinstall it.

#3491. The Garmin Cirqa Finally Got a Much-Needed Feature

This week Garmin's screenless Cirqa smart band received a firmware update that fixes one of its most obvious gaps: the lack of alerts from your phone. With Version 4.20, you can now set up your smart band to buzz your wrist for texts, calls, and other smart notifications from your phone. The addition is listed on Garmin's forums as "Support vibration for smart notifications/incoming calls." Reaction has been upbeat, too—users on the Garmin subreddit have been glad to see the feature arrive.

Amusingly, Garmin's own FAQ still states that the Cirqa does not vibrate for text messages, phone calls, or other smartphone notifications. Clearly that page is now out of date, so Garmin will want to correct it. Since Garmin doesn't yet have step-by-step instructions, I tested the text-message vibrations myself. Here's how you can set up your Cirqa smart band to vibrate for calls and texts, in addition to a number of other promising updates to check out.

To receive these alerts, your band must be running firmware 4.20 or later. Here is how to get everything configured.

Update the firmware. Open your Garmin Connect app and sync your Cirqa, so the app can check for and install version 4.20 or newer.

Grant the necessary phone permissions. In your phone's settings, make sure Garmin Connect has permission to access SMS, Contacts, and Phone.

Configure notifications in Garmin Connect. Back in Garmin Connect, tap the Menu (or More) tab. Select Garmin Devices, then choose your Cirqa Smart Band. Go to Notifications & Alerts (or Smart Notifications) and turn on text and call alerts.

Troubleshooting tip: If alerts aren't coming through, check that Do Not Disturb, Sleep Mode, and any aggressive Battery Saver settings are turned off on both your phone and the band.

For most a lot of Cirqa fans, the phone alerts are the headline, but the 4.20 update carries a solid list of other improvements and bug fixes:

Trail Run: Run/Walk detection is now available for Trail Run activities.

Timestamp fix: Resolved a problem where an activity's recorded time didn't match the time on your phone.

Distance calibration: You can now calibrate distance for Treadmill Run, Indoor Rowing, and Indoor Cycling before saving the activity on the device.

Duration alerts: Duration time alerts for speaking out now accumulate.

Stress alerts: Stress alerts are now blocked while Auto Activity Detection is recording.

Bedtime reminders: Fixed an issue where the bedtime approaching notification sometimes failed to trigger.

Live Activity: Heart rate now appears on the Live Activity screen before recording begins.

Pinned activity bug: Fixed an issue where the pinned activity reverted to Timed Activity after changing the phone's language.

Workout editing: Fixed a problem that prevented editing reps during a workout.

Stability: General system stability improvements.

#3490. Producer Titles Can Be Bought, but Real Creative Producers Take Them for Themselves

As part of the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking team presents “Behind Their Lens,” a series of panel discussions with some of the most exciting artisans, directors, and producers of 2026.

On the producers panel, “Tangles” producer Lauren Miller Rogen, “Ghosts” and “Harlots” producer Alison Owen, and “Devil Wears Prada” producer Carla Hacken spoke to students and guests about everything from how they approach giving good, productive notes on a story to how they’re looking at the current, rapidly consolidating media landscape for actually getting projects off the ground.

But the thing that unites all their work, across all phases of production, is a persistence to muscle it past whatever obstacles and challenges lie in its path. And that’s something that’s been true for them since they got into the actual work of the producing business. Owen spoke about how her “degree” in producing is something she earned with a bunch of university students, but not by actually attending university. It just started with a conversation with someone who was attending the UK’s National Film School at the time. Related Stories Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself in Leg at Los Angeles Gun Range

“This was the early ‘80s, when things were a lot looser, but they said, ‘There are no producers there. But if you want to learn about producing, go to Notting Hill, where the bus stops outside the Coronet in the morning and just stand there and get on the bus,” Owen said. “You would get out to the film school, and the students who were making their graduation films would want someone to come out and produce for them. And they didn’t care that you hadn’t done anything. I didn’t know what a call sheet was or what PAs were or anything. But they were happy to have a pair of hands.”

Being a willing pair of hands led Owen to a small village in the middle of Wales, working on a senior graduation project, and that on-the-ground, very-on-location work has stood her in good stead since. “Not only are you learning stuff, but you’re meeting your peers. So they were all people who wound up directing major studio movies, editors, cinematographers, people that I work with now, like John Mathieson, who — you know, we all slept on a mattress above a pub, and he now lights for Joe Wright,” Owen said. I always say to students, ‘Network with your peers. They’re the people of the future that you’re going to want to get jobs from or hire.”

Being tuned into what your peers are up to can also show you what’s possible. Miller Rogen had written the script for her first feature, “For A Good Time, Call…” years before, but it was seeing Lena Dunham’s work in “Tiny Furniture” that made her realize it was something she could make happen herself.

“I saw ‘Tiny Furniture,’ and I thought, ‘Well, I could do that.’ And so I took the movie from the big producer, and I emailed my team and my writing partner, and I said, ‘We’re gonna make this on our own, and I’m gonna star in it.’ And they were like, ‘Whoa.’ And I was like, ‘No, that’s what we’re doing,’” Miller Rogen said.

That conviction — and the key connections to some independent backers care of Miller Rogen’s brother who worked in finance — led to a $750,000 raise for the film’s budget. “We shot in 16 days. And then we went to Sundance, which is, of course, lucky to get into. But we got into Sundance and Focus Features bought it and released it, and it was in movie theaters, which would never happen now. But it was extraordinary, and I felt shock and pride and fear because it was gonna be big and out there,” Rogen Miller said. “But it was incredible, and I think these days, there are so many ways to get your project seen.”

“ I think you just said the most important thing for all of them is there’s so many ways for you guys to get your work out there now,” Hacken added. “The success of ‘Backrooms’ and all these YouTube horror shows should give you hope that, you know, write something good, produce something good, find a great story, and there are other ways to get it made than the way it used to be.”

#3488. Landman Season 3 Could Undo Everything Tommy Achieved In Season 2

Landman season 3 has been delayed to 2027, so we have plenty of time to speculate on where Tommy Norris’ story will go next. The fact that Landman’s filming schedule has been pushed back, so we won’t be getting new episodes on the regular schedule, is especially frustrating because of how tantalizing Landman’s season 2 finale was. The last season ended with a major shakeup to the status quo, as Tommy went out on his own and started a new company to compete with his former colleagues. He’s filled out the staff with all his friends and loved ones, so Landman season 3 will be a family affair, and it’ll feel more like a true ensemble show with everyone under the same roof, working toward the same goal.

There are a few possible directions that Taylor Sheridan could take Landman’s story in season 3. It’s the perfect opportunity to finally push Ainsley outside her comfort zone. When she goes off to college, she won’t be as spoiled or coddled or sheltered as she is at home with her parents (we already saw a hint of that at cheerleading camp), so it’ll force her to grow up and develop into a more mature, independent person.

If CTT Oil Exploration & Cattle is as big of a success as Tommy hopes it’ll be, then Landman season 3 could be a corporate revenge story. If Cami fails now that she doesn’t have Tommy as her reliable middleman, CTT might be able to buy M-Tex for cents on the dollar, allowing Tommy to get the ultimate poetic justice against his old business rival. Alternatively, if CTT isn’t a success and it starts bleeding money (which, frankly, seems like the more likely outcome), then Tommy could be in a lot of trouble with Gallino and the cartel.

When Tommy first announced this new business venture in Landman’s season 2 finale, he was full of hopes and dreams. This new company would be different; it was a chance for Tommy to cut his own corporate puppet-strings and go out on his own. Now that he’s not a middleman at M-Tex, and he’s running his own company, he can do things the way he thinks they should be done, and he can reap all the rewards for himself, completely independently.

It all sounds great, but it’s not quite practical. As dreamy as a fully independent, family-run business sounds, that’s not really what CTT is. Tommy left M-Tex to start his own company so he could be free from his money-grubbing overlords, but he’s funding his new company through Gallino, so he’ll still have a money-grubbing overlord to answer to. The season 2 finale felt like a fresh start, but Tommy could be right back where he started in season 3.

Tommy’s new company probably won’t turn a profit, but that’s okay; that’s not why he’s doing it. Tommy founding a family-run company feels like a direct response to his conversation with T.L. about how Tommy needs to overcome his fear of failure and focus on what really matters, his family. This new company likely won’t be very financially lucrative, but it’s an opportunity for Tommy to keep the people he loves closer, and connect with them by doing what he loves.

But, at the end of the day, it is a business, and the people putting up money will want to see some return on their investment. Tommy’s intentions are good, but he’s courting disaster in Landman season 3. If CTT doesn’t work, then Tommy could end up in massive debt with the cartel, and the more he owes them, the more horrific the punishment is likely to be.

One of my favorite streaming traditions is checking out what each platform has added at the start of a new month. The very first day of the month is when the majority of the best streaming services refresh their libraries with major movie drops, and Prime Video is no exception.

In fact, Prime Video typically drops more movies on the first day of a new month than any of its streaming rivals, and on Sunday, November 1, 2026, Prime’s back catalog is getting a major boost with 103 movies arriving.

That’s an overwhelming amount of choice, which is why I’ve combed through the list to pick out the gems you should stream first. Because it’s now November, Prime Video’s latest movie drop is heavy on holidays, and I’ve picked a couple of Christmas classics to get you in the festive mood nice and early. However, I’ve also found some exciting thrillers for those who don’t start celebrating the holidays until December.

So, let’s get into my top picks; these are the five movies just added to Prime Video that should be at the top of your November 2026 watchlist.

Some of my fondest childhood memories of the festive season involve rewatching “Elf” so many times that the DVD was in danger of getting worn out. This 2000s holiday classic has it all: seasonal spirit, charming comedy, lovable characters and a message about the importance of family. Even now as a grown-up on the wrong side of 30, it’s still a holiday movie I watch every single year, and I’ve no plans to stop in 2026.

Will Ferrell plays Buddy, a human raised by Santa’s elves. Due to his human proportions and inability to make toys, he doesn’t quite fit in at the North Pole. So when Santa reveals to him that his father (James Caan), a New York City bigwig, is on the naughty list, Buddy travels to the Big Apple to meet his biological father and find his place in the world. Once in NYC, he discovers that humans are sorely lacking in holiday cheer.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The perfect movie doesn’t exist. Absolute perfection is an impossible goal. Even my favorite films of all time have some minor flaws. However, when it comes to a movie nailing exactly what it's trying to achieve, it’s hard to argue that “Mean Girls” doesn’t get pretty darn close to perfection. This movie is the quintessential teen comedy, packed with quotable lines, iconic outfits and legendary scenes. And yes, we’re talking about the original here, not the musical remake. Though for the record, I’m a defender of that movie; I think it’s very underrated.

Cady Heron (Lindsay Lohan) is a 16-year-old whose family has recently returned to the U.S. after spending 12 years in Africa. Now attending North Shore High School, Cady is introduced to a complex web of unspoken teenage rules and a strict social hierarchy. At the top of the food chain are The Plastics, a trio of ultra-cool mean girls led by queen bee, Regina George (Rachel McAdams). When Cady is invited into their inner circle, she hatches a plan to sabotage them from within.

This year will see the release of yet another big-screen spin on Charles Dickens’ enduring classic, “A Christmas Carol,” in the form of Ti West’s “Ebenezer.” But why trek out to your local theater when you can already enjoy the best movie adaptation of the timeless tale on Prime Video? Okay, so “Scrooged” is the best adaptation of “A Christmas Carol” that doesn’t feature The Muppets. It's still a great watch even if it doesn't include Kermit, Miss Piggy, and the gang. Plus, it stars Bill Murray at his sarcastic best.

You probably know the basic setup, but if you’re somehow unfamiliar with Dickens’ fable, it follows a cynical and selfish TV executive (named Frank Cross here rather than Ebenezer Scrooge), who is visited by three ghosts on Christmas Eve in an effort to convince him to change his self-centered ways. There’s a pleasant meta twist in “Scrooged.” Cross lives in a world where the “A Christmas Carol” story also exists, so when he starts living the tale for real, he’s not too happy about it.

Moving away from holiday classics and teenage comedies, another movie that’s just arrived as part of Prime Video’s huge November 1 drop is “The Manchurian Candidate.” This 1962 political thriller is one that fans of classic cinema definitely shouldn’t skip. It stars Frank Sinatra, Laurence Harvey, and Janet Leigh, alongside Angela Lansbury, Henry Silva, and James Gregory. And it is perhaps one of the sharpest American movies of the Cold War era.

Raymond Shaw (Harvey) is a U.S. soldier fighting in the Korean War, captured by the enemy, but then released three days later. Returned home, he receives the Medal of Honor, and on the surface it looks like a feel-good homecoming story. But Shaw is hiding a dark secret, a shocking memory that even he can’t recall. “The Manchurian Candidate” is a thriller that hasn’t lost its edge over the last 60+ years and has even inspired modern media like Showtime's “Homeland.”

Watch "The Manchurian Candidate" on Prime Video now

Staying on the theme of political thrillers, “WarGames” is an ‘80s techno ride that does feel a little outdated when watched in the 21st century. However, at the time of its release, it was a real cautionary tale about the dangers of technology and its potential uses in global conflict. Heavily influenced by the Cold War period in which it was released, it marked one of the first movie roles for Matthew Broderick, Ferris Bueller himself.

David Lightman (Broderick) is a smart but unmotivated high school slacker in Seattle. A computer whiz, he uses his aptitude for computers for teenage hijinks. But things get serious when he unknowingly accesses a military central computer with the ability to simulate and even launch a devastating nuclear attack against the USSR. He thinks he’s playing a game, but he might have just started World War III…

Amazon has dropped the price of the 65-inch Toshiba Z670R to $549.97 from $748.99, taking nearly $200 off and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. The deal also includes free delivery to a room of your choice, which normally costs $19.99, though it does not cover unpacking, setup, packaging removal, or haul-away services. You also get a 90-day free trial of Amazon Music with your purchase.

Beyond the discounts, the Z670R has quite a bit going for it, starting with a 4K Mini-LED panel that combines QLED color with local dimming to help bright highlights stand out without washing out darker scenes. It also supports Dolby Vision IQ and HDR10+, so you can enjoy compatible HDR content across a wide range of movies, shows, and streaming services.

Gaming is another area where this TV makes a strong case for itself—its panel can run at up to 144Hz, while Variable Refresh Rate, Auto Low Latency Mode, and AMD FreeSync Premium are there to keep fast movement looking smoother and cut down on screen tearing with a compatible console or gaming PC, making it well-suited for racing games, shooters, and sports titles. You also get four HDMI inputs, with support for 4K at 144Hz, so there is room for a console, PC, soundbar, and another device without constantly swapping cables.

Fire TV is built in as well, which means Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, and other major streaming apps are available without adding a separate streaming stick, while Alexa handles voice searches and basic controls. The built-in audio is also more substantial than what you get from many slim TVs, with a dedicated bass woofer and Dolby Atmos support, so you may be able to live without a soundbar at first if you are setting up a bedroom or smaller living room. One potential downside is that Mini-LED does not give you the perfect blacks of OLED, so movie fans who watch mostly in a dark room may still prefer to pay more for one. For someone who splits time between movies, sports, and gaming, though, the Z670R gives you a lot of flexibility for about $550 without immediately requiring extra equipment.

#3485. Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place

“You Can See Everything,” A24’s buzzy documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has narrowly defeated Warner Bros. and DC Studios’ “Clayface” at the domestic box office. It added $10.6 million to bring its haul to $63.9 million. That was good enough for a first-place finish, something that “You Can See Everything” pulled off for the first time in its third weekend of release.

“Clayface,” a body horror “Batman” spinoff, earned $10.4 million, bringing its North American gross to $44.1 million. The superhero adventure has earned $83 million globally. #3484. Ruth Madeley Never Thought Acting Was an Option — Now, She’s Playing a Disability Rights Legend in ‘Being Heumann’

Ruth Madeley originally thought she’d become a screenwriter, attending Thornleigh Salesian College where she studied English and creative writing with an emphasis on scriptwriting. “I wanted to be a storyteller,” “Being Heumann” star Madeley told IndieWire. “It’s not that I didn’t want to be an actor, or I didn’t pursue it. I didn’t even think it was an option.” And it’s easy to understand why. Born with spina bifida and growing up as a wheelchair user, Madeley was aware that disabled actors, and roles written for them, weren’t exactly plentiful. “I never saw anyone who looked like me,” she said. “So to even know that that was potentially an option was madness to me.” Related Stories Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place Producer Titles Can Be Bought, but Real Creative Producers Take Them for Themselves

When Madeley thinks back on some of the earliest disabled representation she saw in popular culture, her answer is similar to countless other disabled film and TV lovers: it was an abled actor playing a disabled part. “There’s a soap back at home where there was a wheelchair user, and I was like, ‘Oh, his wheelchair looks like mine.’ And then I found out the actor wasn’t a wheelchair user.” With that type of representation being the norm, it’s unsurprising that Madeley saw acting as something she was barred from. That is until 2009, when “Half Moon Investigations,” a children’s crime/comedy show, needed a wheelchair user for an episode. “I auditioned purely to be nosy and extend my network, and I got the role. I remember being terrified in the audition, thinking: ‘Why do people do this? This is awful,” she said in an interview with The Guardian earlier this year.

That role kickstarted a film and television career that has flourished over the last decade. Now, Madeley is the star of “Being Heumann,” which details the life of disabled activist Judy Heumann and the 504 sit-ins in 1977. It’s a performance that could not only make history if she and the movie are Oscar-nominated, but also finally give young disabled girls someone who looks like them onscreen. Something Madeley didn’t have growing up. “As a disabled person, being aware that you might make history, that’s huge for me,” she said. “It’s huge for the community. That’s a really heavy and exciting thing to have.”

But Madeley doesn’t want that history, or getting caught up in the discussion of representation, to overshadow the film’s content. “I’m not just a random wheelchair user they pulled off the street,” Madeley said. “This is my job, so talking about the actual craft is really exciting for me.”

And that craft was multifaceted. Not only was Madeley portraying an actual person, a legend in the disabled community. She also had to do accent work, ASL work, and appear in nearly every frame of the movie. The accent was particularly important to get right, as Heumann’s Brooklyn upbringing was a huge part of her life, and indicative of her prickly personality. “I don’t find [accents] easy,” she said. “I have to work at them, and learn the science of it, and the tongue placement. All of those interesting fun things that I get to play with. She was such a proud Brooklyn woman, I wanted to be able to sound so specifically like her.”

That specificity was imperative to Madeley in every aspect of playing Heumann. “Siân [Heder, director] and I spoke so much about movement, because we’ve been so starved of seeing disabled people on screen that you don’t always see how a disabled person moves through the world.”

Both Heder and Madeley were intrigued by the juxtaposition of Heumann’s desire for movement with her paralysis forcing her to be still. “Siân and I both were fascinated by Judy’s speed and freedom when she was in her chair; she was never still,” said Madeley. “Versus when she’s out of her chair, and she is in such a different state of vulnerability.”

The sequence in the trailer, where Judy is forced to wait for her in-home health attendant to show up so she can use the restroom, makes this painfully apparent. “Once she was in bed, she had all of these pillows, and she knew that she had to be comfortable when her attendant left because the second that attendant left she couldn’t move herself for the whole night.”

It was seeing the authentic lived experience of a disabled person, activist aside, that was so compelling to Madeley. “The worst thing I can watch on screen is if something looks too easy,” said Madeley. Too often movies made after the passage of the Americans With Disabilities Act present a rose-colored view of accessibility, or at least do so by never discussing it. Here, the movie authentically details what being a wheelchair user, a blind person, or a deaf person was like in 1977. The landscape is riddled with different access barriers, both individually and societally. But Heder and the production team made a point of showing all of those, not just the stairs crafted to enter buildings, but putting the wheelchair-using cast in actual wheelchairs from the 1970s.

“The 1970s chairs helped [with authenticity] because nothing is easy in those things for anyone,” said Madeley. “There were so many people on hand to help, which was so invaluable because even if the place was fully accessible, being in those chairs makes things so much harder. They weighed so much. Why did people keep them? That’s what I don’t get.”

Because the wheelchairs were so unwieldy, the actors needed to get out of them to relax their bodies. It was also a chance for Madeley to realize her own limitations as a disabled person, and remember that no two disabled people have the same experience. “I recognize my privilege. I’m an ambulatory wheelchair user. I can stand up and stretch if I need to. There were other people that couldn’t… So that was a learning curve as well throughout the process of filming. People need to get out of these every few hours.”

On the page, Heumann isn’t sanded down, and Madeley is happy with that. “I’m all for a messy queen!” Her Judy is impatient, stubborn, downright rude at times. But Madeley wanted to make sure that was placed alongside Heumann’s joy, warmth, humor, and vulnerability. Without that delicate balance, the character could have come off as too bitter, on one end of the spectrum, or too tragic.

“That feeling of having to be easy, or grateful, or nice, so that people — all of those things that society expects of a disabled woman–I’m not those things all the time, and no one is,” she said. “I love the fact that I got to play somebody who didn’t have her edges rounded off. I love the fact that she was able to be prickly.”

In the end, Madeley wants to keep showcasing flawed humans, not necessarily flawed disabled humans. “I’m just driven by character,” she said. Too often, disabled actors are only hired for disabled roles, and that’s something Madeley wants to subvert. “I don’t only have to play disabled. I can play the messy mom of two who’s got knocked up again, and who is completely inept.” Madeley continues to show that the different sides of disability will no doubt finally turn the tide on what disabled actors can do. It’s a far cry from the type of representation she, and many other disabled people, had growing up.

“Being Heumann” opens from Apple TV in select theaters starting Friday, November 6. The film streams on Apple TV starting Friday, November 13.

!!! WARNING: THIS ARTICLE CONTAINS SPOILERS FOR DUNGEON CRAWLER CARL BOOK 9 !!!Donut's newest class for Book 9 will officially be Vibe Coder, an unusual upgrade revealed in the opening chapters of The Beautiful Place. It continues a tradition stretching back to Carl's Doomsday Scenario, when Donut chose the Former Child Actor class. That class's Character Actor ability lets her select a new specialty on each subsequent floor, giving her an ever-changing set of abilities. That puts her full class list across the series as follows:

Deathbed Hellcat; Oak Fell (additional class)

Assassin of Sekhmet; Elite Gurkha Warrior

More importantly, it includes Backdoor Access, which Mordecai says allows her to tweak her existing spells to produce slightly different effects. She gets three slots for modified spells, opening the possibility of surprising combinations using powers she's accumulated throughout the series.

There's also a mysterious personal assistant included with the class, although the preview chapters don't explain much about this just yet. Mordecai recommends Vibe Coder over the hilarious alternative Nepo Baby, a competing class with a credit card that costs Charisma to use. Donut takes his advice and makes her choice.

The full potential of Opposite Day, Backdoor Access, and the assistant remains unknown. Considering how often Donut has turned ridiculous upgrades into essential survival tools, Vibe Coder could be one of her most interesting choices yet, especially with the Ascendency Games only just beginning. It's just one of the new updates readers have to be excited for when Book 9 of Dungeon Crawler Carl releases.

#3479. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Is 'Ballhog'?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's zeitgeist snapshot explains what ballhog means, how a video of someone wrapping a burger led to a new meme format, and the dangers of Benny tripping. So strap in, and let's go.

Ballhog or ball hog is a streetwear fashion style growing in popularity among younger people. The cool ones, anyway. The idea is to wear vintage clothes that look normal, even drab, to most, but that people in the know can recognize as interesting or unique. Like the best youth trends, it's an insider vs. outsider thing that takes connoisseurship to understand. Some examples: If you're wearing a late 1990s Helmut Lang denim jacket, most people will think "thrifted," but a ballhog-enjoyer would recognize it as a seminal piece of streetwear history. If you want to be ballhog, rocking a pair of skinny jeans isn't going to cut it unless they're from Dior Homme or at least Cheap Monday.

The style is named after the Ball Hog Collective, a group of rappers, Twitch streamers, and content creators founded by the Atlanta-based indie record label Ballhog. It was popularized by streamer Brady Goodwin, seen below looking quite ballhog:

The #ballhog hashtag is blowing up (as people used to say) lately with a growing collection of kids posting videos to show off their ballhog fits, like so:

The popularity of the style comes down to, I think, how difficult it is to commodify. Most truly organic trends are recognized quickly by culture vulture types, and in a few months, there's a line of clothes at Target, but you can't do that with ballhog. There's no way to make "new" ballhog gear, as that would mark it as inauthentic immediately. Gotta hand it to the kids for adopting a style that is at once exclusionary and impossible to rip off.

On the opposite edge of the spectrum from ballhog fashion is the "while they're out partying btw" meme, videos made to show off the strange, specific, and usually useless talent one develops while others are out wearing cool clothes and socializing. The phrase has been kicking around since last year, when TikToker @tacobella posted this video

but it's taken off more recently, thanks to the huge number of views on this video showing off some truly mind-blowing burger wrapping skills:

This led to an influx of videos of people showing off what they were doing instead of partying. Like this mechanic:

This is the second youth trend I support wholeheartedly. We can't all be cool ballhoggers and we don't all have talent, but we can all learn to do a thing really well through brute force and repetition.

The past tense of "cringe," "crunged" is often used to describe extreme cringe, like "I cringed so hard I crunged."

As for "scuba," it now describes something that is very smelly, which might be because the word conjures the dead air of unventilated, underwater spaces. But it's often accompanied by a pinch-your-nose gesture, which looks like the gesture in the Scuba Dance that was popular on TikTok a few months ago, so that's a more likely origin for the term.

There has been a steady stream of news stories about kids overdosing on Benadryl over the last few years. They call it "Benny tripping," and it's achieved by taking too much of the allergy medicine, like 10 times the amount recommended. Among the active ingredients in Benadryl is Diphenhydramine, and it's a particularly nasty drug. Unlike most recreational substances, tripping on Benadryl is not fun. It's a deliriant, and taking too much results in hallucinations that are usually described as terrifying—swarms of spiders, shadow people, whispering voices, etc. Benadryl overdoses can result in loss of short term memory, displacement from time and space, and panic attacks that last for hours or even days. Or you die from tachycardia. Here's how Reddit user Reasonable-County971 described their experience,

I lost access to my memories. I couldn’t recognize my mom—I mistook her for a 'pretty nurse'. Early in the trip, before you lose yourself, you develop tremendous anxiety, far far beyond anything else I can compare it to. Also, you have motor skills affected, including losing access to your bladder.

So yeah, it's a bad drug. And it's easy to get—just pop down to CVS. On the plus side, despite sometimes overly hysterical reporting on Benadryl as an "online trend" or challenge, tripping on Benadryl is such a harrowing, not-at-all-fun experience, its use isn't particularly popular among young people. But if you want to scare yourself, read some trip reports, watch this YouTube video, and imagine someone you love going through this.

This week's viral video is very meta, and it's hilarious to anyone who follows the trajectory of viral internet sensations. Brought to us by the great @ariisaysso, this video lays out the history of the fictional Cheezit Girl as she becomes an internet sensation, quits her job, sells merch, releases a rap single, releases a remix, reheats the nachos, and falls into obscurity, all in about two and a half minutes. We've seen this story before with the Hawk Tuah Girl, Dah Bih Gah Kid, and many more future members of the "remember that thing" club, and we'll no doubt see it all again soon. Such is the circle of life.

#3478. ‘Earthlings in Love’ Review: A Sentimental Sci-fi Journey Makes the Leap from TikTok to the Tokyo International Film Festival

It’s a queasy proposition for cinephiles: Take a TikTok series, retrofit it into a feature film, and premiere it at a major international film festival. But that’s exactly what happened with “Earthlings in Love,” the latest project from Japanese director Shinichiro Ueda. It’s the first so-called “microdrama” (also known as a “vertical drama”) to premiere at the Tokyo International Film Festival, an unusual choice given that in Japan, as abroad, these short-form videos are designed for casual viewing on smartphones, not the formal atmosphere of a film festival. “Earthlings in Love” was originally released in 30 parts on social media, then recut for its TIFF debut; this version is significantly longer, going from a 76-minute runtime to an 102-minute one. It’s also — and this is crucial — much better than anyone might expect, given its provenance. Related Stories Ruth Madeley Never Thought Acting Was an Option — Now, She’s Playing a Disability Rights Legend in ‘Being Heumann’ Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place

It’s not terribly surprising that Ueda in particular would be open-minded about working in a new media format: His “One Cut of the Dead” broke out internationally in large part because of its ingenious approach to low-budget storytelling. “Earthlings in Love” is similar in that it takes its limitations and turns them into strengths, thoughtfully incorporating the vertical-video format both into the film’s mise en scene and its structure. It would be disingenuous to say that you forget about the vertical framing after a while — I certainly didn’t — but Ueda makes the most of the tight 9:16 aspect ratio, shooting dialogue scenes from the waist up and composing shots so that they move the eye upwards rather than across the frame.

Even more clever is the way that Ueda, who also wrote the script, incorporates the feeling of claustrophobic disconnection into the story itself. This is a movie about selective memory, centered on a fortysomething film director named Shinpei (Kato Shinsuke) whose career has been prematurely halted by early-onset dementia. Returning to his hometown for the funeral of a former classmate, Shinpei tries to recall why he and his friends never finished their zero-budget high-school sci-fi opus, “Earthlings in Love.” Shinpei remembers a dramatic classmate quitting the shoot because he felt the movie was beneath him, and his secret crush encouraging him to keep going. But is that what really happened?

That’s what we see in the first 20 minutes or so of the movie, as Ueda blends “Rashomon” with “Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind” by having Shinpei consult a service that offers to recover his fading memories by feeding photos and diary entries into an AI-generated recreation of his own past. As we find out, the AI is reflecting Shinpei’s own faulty recollections back to him; Ueda insists that this isn’t a commentary on AI per se, but it does bring to mind the way that LLMs create feedback loops that have led to the pop-psychological phenomenon of AI psychosis. Luckily for him, Shinpei has Nagisa (Kiyose Yaeko), another former classmate with whom he reconnected on his trip back home, to keep him grounded in the present. Her role in Shinpei’s life is unclear at first, not least because he keeps forgetting where he knows her from. Over time, however, she becomes the story’s most tragic figure.

As with “One Cut,” the plot structure of “Earthlings in Love” is built on a series of dramatic twists. This is where Ueda puts the “microdrama” format to its most ingenious use, revisiting moments we’ve already seen from new perspectives that reveal important pieces of information previously left out of the frame. Simply by panning a few feet left or right, Ueda can completely change the narrative and emotional stakes of the film. And the way he applies this technique feels fresh and genuinely innovative, not to mention organic to a potentially offputting new style of storytelling.

The story itself is not as fresh, leaning on themes of high-school nostalgia and missed connections that are common in Japanese popular cinema. However, they’re given an earnest, if sometimes overly sentimental, airing here thanks to Ueda’s personal connection to the material. The director has not been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s, but he was a prolific amateur filmmaker beginning in junior high, and the flashback scenes of “Earthlings in Love” are set in the year 2000, when Ueda was a sophomore in high school. The fact that this ‘00s nostalgia piece was made via a very 2020s model of filmmaking is just further evidence of Udea’s casual formal brilliance.

These scenes are not the only ones that ring true, however, as Kato and Kyose successfully carry the plot through outrageous coincidence and into three-hanky tearjerking. “Earthlings in Love” aches for a lot of things, chief among them the simple joy of creating something with your friends just for the fun of it. Its core message is ironic, given the disposable nature of its initial release: Human memories fade, but movies are forever. Now that it’s a proper film, its lifespan has a better chance of being extended.

“Earthlings in Love” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

Wet weather and warm homes are a recipe for mattress mold

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mattress mold is a problem that sneaks up on you. A slightly whiffy bed and small stains can quickly turn to itching, sneezing and watery eyes. And right now is primetime for moldy conditions.

A combination of cold, wet weather outside and warm heating inside increases moisture in the air. Your mattress soaks it up like a sponge and, trapped inside your warm bed, that damp helps mold spores to multiply.

Mattress mold doesn't have to spell the end of your bed, but you need to catch it early. We spoke to Dr Gareth Nye, Biomedical Sciences lecturer at the University of Salford working exclusively with M&S, about how to identify early signs of mold — and get rid of it.

Mold can completely ruin a mattress, but before you rush off to browse our best mattress guide for a replacement bed, look out for these early indicators of mold.

You won't necessarily see early signs of mold in your mattress, but you might be able to smell the problem has taken hold.

Dr. Nye describes the smell of mold as "a persistent musty, damp, or earthy odor" and notes that it can linger "even after the bedding has been washed."

If this new smell is accompanied by an uptick in allergy symptoms when you go to bed (itching, sneezing or watery eyes, for example) mold is the likely culprit. Noticed a sweeter musty smell? It might be bed bugs.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Big, dark stains are often a sign that your mattress is past saving. But before you get to that point, Dr. Nye recommends looking for "tiny, clustered pinpoint stains."

These small marks are the signs of an early mold infestation and they can be treated (we'll explore how below). And don't just look on the top surface of the mattress for stains. The underside of the bed as well as the sides can house mold as well.

Signs of mold aren't always visible on the mattress itself. Look in the surrounding area for indicators your bedroom is growing mold.

Dr. Nye describes "spaces up against a wall or behind units" as 'mold magnets' because they prevent airflow. So if your bed frame is pushed against the wall, move it forward when you clean and check for mold.

He also advices looking in any common sites for condensation, including anything pressed to the "external environment" (like radiators against a window).

"The space under the bed is also a prime spot for mold," says Dr. Nye. And if the mold is under the bed, it might not take long for it to move into the bed.

Mold is more than just an unwanted stain. Left to grow, mold in your mattress can have serious negative repercussions on your health.

"Mold reproduces by releasing microscopic spores and mycotoxins into the air, which are easily inhaled during the 7 to 8 hours you spend asleep," explains Dr. Nye. "This triggers an immune response, leading to allergic rhinitis (sneezing, congestion, runny nose, and itchy eyes) and significantly exacerbating symptoms for those with asthma."

And the longer the problem is allowed to grow, the worse the impact it can have on your health.

"Prolonged exposure can result in chronic illnesses," says Dr. Nye. "Mold spores can also severely worsen conditions like eczema and trigger contact dermatitis."

We previously asked the experts how to get rid of mattress mold. They advised spot treating any stains with ingredients you probably have in your kitchen: white vinegar and baking soda.

Begin by mixing equal parts white vinegar and water. Spray the solution lightly on the stain and leave for 20 minutes. Blot dry, then apply a thin layer of baking soda. Leave to sit for several hours and then vacuum thoroughly.
