#3476. The Fitbit Edge Is Everything the Charge 6 Should Have Been

I’ve been using the new Fitbit Edge for a little over a week, and am happy to report that it’s quite good at its job. It shipped with more features than I expected (Google Maps directions were there from the jump) and corrects the missteps that Google made with the Fitbit Charge 6. After running the Fitbit Edge through its paces, here’s my breakdown of what works well, what doesn’t, and what I think of the device overall.

When I reviewed it in May 2025, I liked a lot about the Charge 6, but found it had a few serious flaws. Tightening the strap messed up its GPS readings (weird but true), and some of its features required a subscription (like the music controls that only worked with YouTube Music). Its promised side button wasn’t really a button, and didn’t even always work.

I’m happy to report that all of my biggest gripes have been fixed in the Fitbit Edge. Or to put it another way: the Edge is what the Charge should have been in the first place.

Accuracy tests are always one of my top priorities in testing, but honestly I wasn’t expecting much from this device. A Fitbit can still be successful in my eyes even if its heart rate sensor is only “good enough.” Nobody should expect lab-level precision from a Fitbit.

But I was pleasantly surprised by just how capable the Edge is in this regard. It sometimes takes a few minutes to lock on to a heart rate signal (as most optical devices do), but after it does, it is spot-on—I think it might be in the running alongside the Apple Watch and high-end Garmins as one of the better heart rate wearables on the market. The Edge’s accuracy is notably better than the Fitbit Air's, even though they seem to share the same sensor hardware.

Location accuracy is also quite good, only deviating slightly from a Garmin I tested alongside the Edge. It may not be the best out there, but it’s miles ahead of what the Charge 6 was able to do.

The Fitbit Edge has real music controls, unlike the Charge 6. I can play something in Spotify or in Castro (my favorite podcast app) on my phone, and then control the audio from my wrist—and you no longer need to use YouTube Music or have a subscription to get this feature.

When the Fitbit Air and the Google Health app first launched, it was possible to pair both a Fitbit and a Pixel Watch to the same phone, but not two Fitbits. That has finally changed: I was able to connect the Edge to my phone without losing my connection to the Air. It also works to swap seamlessly between the two Fitbits. For example, one night the Edge was low on battery, so I slept with the Air on, and then swapped back in the morning once the Edge was charged. The app happily showed my sleep data from the Air and my activity data from the Edge without my having to do mess around in the app.

As a nice bonus, the charger for the Fitbit Edge is the same as for the Fitbit Air. (The chargers for the Pixel Watch and for the Fitbit Charge 6 are not compatible with the Edge.)

The Fitbit Edge is a similar size as the old Charge 6, but with noticeably more screen real estate. The strap fits pretty much the same way as a Pixel watch band—that is to say, normally, not with the strange hang-off-the-wrist stiffness of the Charge 6.

The Fitbit Edge also has a physical button—not a haptic nub like the Charge 6, but an actual, physical button. And it even works (to return you to the home screen) nearly every time I press it. The Charge 6’s nub was not as reliable.

Overall, I’m quite happy with the Fitbit Edge. It’s much better than the Charge 6, and adds accuracy and a screen to the things I already liked about the Fitbit Air. But there are a few things I don’t totally love.

One is that there is no NFC chipset, which means no option to use Google Pay. I don’t mind using my phone or card at checkouts (and I always carry my phone), so this isn’t a big deal for me, but I know a lot of folks love a wrist-based payment, and that’s missing from the Fitbit Edge. (Google reportedly said most Fitbit users didn’t actually use Google Pay, so they removed the functionality—presumably to fit in the other components while keeping the device small.)

The other downside is, I hate to say it, the Google Health app. It’s OK, but I still find myself arguing with the AI when it assigns me workouts I never asked for, and I have to agree with the redditors who are commiserating about the lack of a “yesterday” view. (On the bright side, Google recently added a feature that lets you turn off the AI insights, which helps a lot.)

Overall, the Fitbit Edge is a great fitness tracker. It measures heart rate and running/walking mileage accurately; it can control music in a sensible way; and it looks good, feels good to wear, and works smoothly. The price also tracks: It’s definitely worth the $20 premium over the Charge 6, and it’s not quite double the price of the Air, which I think is fair. For anyone who doesn’t want a smartwatch or a running watch and will be satisfied with just “a Fitbit,” this one is pretty much perfect.

#3475. ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Season 2 Is a Perfect '30 Rock' Replacement | Review

At some point in his football career, Tracy Morgan’s loveably clueless character Reggie Dinkins filmed a public service announcement warning Americans about Y2K. His advice? Hide your money in the woods. It’s this kind of terrible guidance that should have ended his career long before his actual downfall as an NFL champion, but it’s also exactly the kind of joke that makes The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins so damn funny. The returning NBC comedy has never been interested in making any sense, and it’s all the better for it.

Returning for its sophomore season on Monday night on NBC, the half-hour sitcom continues to find humor in the most absurd situations alongside a cast that treats every outrageous line as perfectly normal. Created by Robert Carlock and Sam Means, The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins was already one of TV’s funniest new comedies of the year when it premiered this past winter, but if the first season established its odd, screwball humor, Season 2 shows how much more mileage it can get out of these characters.

With the first two episodes provided for review, the new season is seemingly packed with wonderfully stupid jokes, surprising sweetness, and the kind of laugh-a-minute comedy that made its spiritual sibling 30 Rock such a delight in the first place. Within the show’s initial few minutes in the premiere, “We Keep the Kisses,” it’s clear the single-camera sitcom has only elevated its brilliant humor and wit.

With his reputation slowly recovering after a gambling scandal ended his football career, Reggie is looking for ways to return to the spotlight. His ex-wife and manager, Monica (Erika Alexander), does her best to capitalize on revitalized visibility, while documentary filmmaker Arthur Tobin (Daniel Radcliffe) continues recording what he hopes will become an Oscar-worthy comeback story. But the problem is that everyone has their own idea of what success looks like, and Reggie’s ambitions aren’t necessarily at the top of anyone’s list. With his Saturday Night Live appearance finally available to stream and new opportunities coming his way, Reggie believes his comeback might actually be working. Of course, keeping that momentum going is another matter entirely.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

Season 2 uses that tension without making things too serious. Monica tries to modernize her business, Arthur becomes concerned with his credibility as a filmmaker, and Reggie’s best friend Rusty (Bobby Moynihan) faces questions over the value he brings to the household. Meanwhile, Reggie and Monica’s son Carmelo (Jalyn Hall) begins navigating a Romeo and Juliet-type romance complicated by his dad’s rivalry with Jerry Basmati (Craig Robinson), and Reggie’s fiancée, Brina (Precious Way), has her own frustrations with the household. Everyone tries to move forward, but they are also not too sure how to handle what comes next.

What makes the season opener and second episode so enjoyable is how the show finds fresh complications without needing to reinvent its premise. Reggie’s comeback remains the focal point, and the reason everyone sticks together, but the show is interested in what people around him want for themselves. Whether it’s professional independence or financial stability, their ambitions rarely line up, and that results in a season that gives everyone something to pursue without losing sight of the dysfunction that brought them together.

Much like 30 Rock, The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins has a fondness for ridiculous cutaways, unexpected punchlines, and jokes that get funnier the less you think about them. There’s also barely any time to recover from one laugh before another arrives, and that’s the show’s greatest strength. With writers who have a knack for turning the most ordinary situations into complete nonsense, Season 2 opens the door to some downright LOL moments, like a pizza order that sounds good in theory but absolutely isn’t, or Reggie proudly recalling that he used to eat cereal with a fork so he could save the milk for the next person. Add in a stress-relieving chair that gives Arthur considerably more pleasure than he expected, and the result is wonderfully ridiculous humor that works because the show commits to every bit.

Season 2 also finds plenty to laugh about in the increasingly strange world of celebrity and social media. Saturday Night Live’s Jeremy Culhane is a particularly hilarious addition as Max, a prospective publicity hire whose understanding of the digital landscape is considerably different from Monica’s. Between Reggie’s attempts to stay relevant through online content and Max’s inexplicable appearance in Britney Spears’ iconic red catsuit from the “Oops!... I Did It Again” music video, the series has lots of fun with all the strange ways people chase attention these days. Best of all, the explanations are often even more ridiculous than the situations themselves.

The cast breaks down Episode 4 and shares what they learned from working so closely with Tracy Morgan.

What’s especially impressive is how consistently the jokes land in Season 2. The writing moves at a relentless pace without ever feeling exhausting or overdone. The humor also isn’t always dependent on something outrageous happening on screen or through a sight gag. Sometimes, a character’s reaction to something the audience never sees is also enough to deliver the biggest laughs, as seen in Episode 2’s “The Spaghetti Loop,” which finds Arthur watching playback of Monica battling a single noodle. Yes, you read that right. The show knows exactly how much to pile on with its absurdity and when to let a single moment (or in this case, expression) do the work.

No doubt about it, but Morgan remains the heart of the series. Even with misguided observations that sound like perfectly reasonable advice, there’s something genuinely endearing about a character this clueless who believes he’s in the right. Alexander is equally wonderful, bringing a sharp, no-nonsense energy to Monica that makes her weariness over taking care of the family endlessly entertaining. Morgan’s on-screen fiancée Way gives Brina a fiery personality this season, showcasing more of her comedic chops, while Hall lends Carmelo a sincerity that makes his family’s behavior seem even more ridiculous.

Moynihan is another standout as Rusty, whose complete lack of ambition should make him an exhausting presence but somehow makes him one of the most lovable characters. There’s also a childlike innocence to his performance that gives the series some of its sweetest moments, particularly as the second episode explores just how much he means to the family, and the lengths he would go to be taken seriously.

But among the hilarious ensemble, Radcliffe might be having the most fun. His Arthur has become an exaggerated portrait of the self-serious documentary filmmaker, someone who approaches even the smallest developments with the gravity of an Oscar-winning director. Radcliffe commits completely to his character’s artistic pretensions, whether through a stunned expression or his increasingly dramatic reactions to the Dinkins family. It’s a performance that could easily become a caricature, but Radcliffe knows exactly how to make it work.

With the cast so comfortably settled into their roles, The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins feels more assured than ever and remains one of 2026’s funniest new shows. The affection and storylines between these characters give the comedy a genuine warmth without sacrificing any of its silliness. Reggie’s comeback might still be a work in progress, but the NBC sitcom certainly isn’t.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins Season 2 premieres at 8:30 p.m. EST on NBC and streams the next day on Peacock.

#3474. R-Rated Action Horror Movie With 0% RT Score Debuts With Record Box Office Low

Christmas at the Kringles did not have a holly jolly Halloween.

The new action horror comedy movie, which debuted on October 30, follows a suburban family that moves into a new home and finds that their neighbors are dangerously obsessed with Christmas. While the movie boasts a star-studded cast that includes comedy icons such as Thomas Lennon, Donald Faison, Rob Riggle, David Wain, and Beverly D'Angelo, critics' Christmas at the Kringles reviews were overwhelmingly negative, earning it a rare 0% score on Rotten Tomatoes at the time of writing. Verified audience members have given it a better, though still underwhelming, score of 40% on the same platform's Popcornmeter.

Per Box Office Mojo, Christmas at the Kringles earned a 3-day total of $675,000 in 1,825 at the domestic box office over the course of its opening weekend. This sees the movie earning a per-screen average of $369, which marks the 132nd lowest debut per-screen average of all time at the domestic box office. On top of that, it breaks the record for a 2026 horror movie that opened on more than 1,000 screens.

The only 2026 horror movies below it on Box Office Mojo's chart of the Top 200 worst debut per-screen averages of all time are the Justin Long movie Night Patrol (which earned an average of $312 in 800 theaters) and the Dot-Marie Jones movie Breeder (which opened the same weekend as Christmas at the Kringles and earned an average of $271 in 777 theaters). In fact, among all 2026 new releases so far, Christmas at the Kringles earned the eighth-lowest debut per-screen average.

Below, see a breakdown of the 10 worst debut per-screen averages for 2026 new releases and where they currently stand on the Top 200 chart:

Mystery Science Theater 3000: The RiffTrax Experiments: Sting of Death

There are likely several reasons why both Christmas at the Kringles and Breeder closed out the 2026 October horror movie slate with a whimper. First of all, Halloween took place on a Saturday, which means that many potential ticket buyers were kept away from theaters by trick or treating and holiday parties. Meanwhile, the ones who did go were more drawn in by the DC Studios body horror movie Clayface (which hit No. 2 during its sophomore weekend) and the record-breaking Zach Cregger video game adaptation Resident Evil (which rose from No. 11 to No. 9 during its seventh weekend).

Additionally, horror movies typically have steep drops in the immediate aftermath of Halloween. While they do tend to pick up again by December, the end of the horror-inflected holiday typically coincides with a brief drop in interest in horror, which likely means that Sunday did not help either new release gain traction.

While that 0% Rotten Tomatoes score may have also damaged the prospects of Christmas at the Kringles (which debuted at No. 17 above Breeder at No. 23), Breeder has significantly better reviews that earned it an 87% score on Rotten Tomatoes that nevertheless did not prevent it from similarly underperforming. The budget for neither movie has been announced, but it seems likely that both will have to rely on video on demand and streaming revenue rather than box office grosses if they hope to break even.

#3473. If You Loved 'Crystal Lake,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Peacock’s Crystal Lake is an unexpected treat in a lot of ways, taking one of horror’s most iconic figures—Jason Voorhees of the Friday the 13th franchise—and digging into the universe’s background by focusing on his mother, Pamela. Famously the actual serial killer in the original film, Pamela’s development into a psychotic killer who inspired her son to become the psychotic killer of all time is the engine that drives Crystal Lake, finding the damaged humanity behind the terror. If you’ve burned through all eight episodes of Crystal Lake’s first season, and you’ve worked through the streamalike series with similar DNA, it’s time to check out some movies—starting with the perfect companion film, 2022’s Pearl.

The second film in Ti West’s X trilogy (starting with X and concluding with 2024’s MaXXXine) is the ideal film to watch after Crystal Lake. Like the series, it explores a female serial killer’s backstory and recontextualizes your understanding of their motives and psychology. It also requires that you be familiar with the original story—while you can certainly watch Crystal Lake or Pearl without having seen the Friday the 13th films or X, you’ll be missing out on a lot if you do.

In X, a group of young people descends on a dilapidated old farm to film an adult movie in Texas in 1979, and by the end of the film most of them are dead, killed by the farm’s elderly couple Howard (Stephen Ure) and Pearl (Mia Goth), with Pearl presented as the most deranged and dangerous of the two. It’s a riveting update to the classic splatter movie template, and Goth nails her dual role as the Final Girl Maxine and the psychotic, murderous Pearl. The prequel, Pearl, jumps back to 1918, when Pearl (Goth again) was a young woman living with her strict mother and paralyzed father. Pearl has big dreams of being an entertainer, but her mother tries to trap her to ensure she’s there to care for her parents and work the farm. Pearl’s lonely unhappiness and frustration (both mental and, er, physical) inspire a slow boil of tension as her grip on sanity frays, and her anger toward her parents curdles into something frightening.

Like Crystal Lake, Pearl takes a killer who seems fairly one-dimensional in their original presentation and gives them a deeper back story and psychological framing. Pamela Voorhees wasn’t just crazy—she was driven to madness by the horrible things that happened to her and her son, and the awful way she’s treated by her fellow humans. Similarly, Pearl is a hopeful and innocent young woman who is slowly molded into a killer by the events of her life. Both the series and the film serve as reminders that monsters are rarely born—they’re made. And it’s usually the casual cruelty of the people around them that does the making. If you loved Crystal Lake’s fresh take on Pamela, Pearl is the perfect choice for a movie night. Stream Pearl on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Need more serial killer movies that hit the Crystal Lake vibe? Never fear—here are some other excellent choices to pair with the series.

If you’ve never actually seen the original Friday the 13th (or if it’s been a while), this is a must-watch for fans of Crystal Lake. Although the series takes some liberties to update the timeline, it’s still intended as a glimpse into the events that shaped both Pamela and Jason Voorhees into inhuman (and somewhat supernatural) monsters. Initially given savagely bad reviews, the film was a surprise blockbuster and is now regarded as a classic of a genre it helped to create in the first place; rewatching it today not only helps contextualize Crystal Lake, it puts the entire slasher genre into perspective. Stream Friday the 13th on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

The success of Friday the 13th led to a rush of copycat films, of course. Most of those weren’t particularly good or even interesting, but Sleepaway Camp is an exception (although it was similarly savaged by critics at the time). Now a cult classic, Sleepaway Camp has two things that recommend it to fans of Crystal Lake and Friday the 13th: a weird sensibility that gives it an otherworldly atmosphere that enhances the sense of dread, and what is probably the most unexpected twist ending in the history of slasher films (and it’s probably a Top 10 twist in general). Stream Sleepaway Camp on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

One reason Crystal Lake exists is the enduring power and influence of slasher films in general and Friday the 13th specifically. Few recent films have tapped into that dreamy nightmare feel like Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. As with most of Schoenbrun’s work, the film delves into themes of identity, subverting queer tropes, and the malleable nature of reality itself. If you’re looking for a slasher story that’s less straightforward than Crystal Lake while dealing with some similar themes of transformation and destiny, this is it. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

If you’ve seen all the Friday the 13th movies and want more slasher horror with a bit more edge, check out The Burning. Is it a great film? Not really. Combining the straightforward slasher thrills of Friday with some of the villain motivations of fellow classic franchise A Nightmare on Elm Street, The Burning dials the blood and guts up to 11 (and beyond) and remains notoriously gory even by today’s standards. But if your fave part of Crystal Lake is the frequently over-the-top gore and violence, this is an ideal movie choice. Stream The Burning on The Roku Channel or Kanopy.

Want a slasher film that explores the psyche of a female killer the way Crystal Lake deconstructs Pamela Voorhees? Check out May. A fragile young woman, May struggles to find connection with the people around her, and slowly descends into a fantasy world that inspires her to literally make her own ideal friend. What makes May so interesting is the depth of the exploration of May’s personality that’s similar to how Pamela is handled in Crystal Lake, tracing each step of her stumble into a bloody hell. Stream May on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

Recent news urges us all to prepare for sudden power cuts. I assumed I was fine, until an honest look around my house revealed I was woefully unequipped

Every time an emergency agency pops up on the news suggesting households keep a 72-hour emergency kit on hand, I do the same thing: nod knowingly, assume they’re talking to someone far less organized than me, and scroll on.

In my head, I’m a reasonably capable adult. The fridge is full, there are batteries rattling around in a drawer somewhere, and I have a phone flashlight. Surely that counts as disaster preparedness.

Curiosity finally won out, so I decided to run an honest, room-by-room audit of what would actually happen if our power lines went dark for three straight days. The verdict was... humbling.

It turns out my master survival plan was heavily reliant on an active Wi-Fi connection, an electric stovetop, and blind optimism. Here's five glaring blind spots I completely overlooked, and what you should do so you don't make the same mistakes.

Opening my junk drawer during the audit revealed two decorative candles, a lighter that took six clicks to spark, and I didn't have a flashlight. My entire plan, it seemed, was an iPhone and an ancient power bank that refused to charge past 12%. Using a phone flashlight burns through battery, leaving you without light, or a lifeline.

Retire your phone as a light source and stash dedicated LED lights or magnetic lanterns where you can grab them in pitch black, like a bedside drawer. Pair them with an inexpensive hand-crank AM/FM emergency radio: it pulls in vital civil broadcasts with zero Wi-Fi, and the built-in dynamo handle doubles as a manual charger as a last resort if your devices die.

I went looking for medical supplies and found a dusty tin with three sports bandages, one pack of ibuprofen, and a pair of blunt tweezers. That was the entirety of my home trauma unit. Navigating in the dark makes minor injuries inevitable, and local clinics won't be running at full capacity during a power cut.

Ditch the half-empty tin and get a proper, sealed multi-day medical kit stocked with sterile dressings, burn gel, antiseptic wash, and heavy-duty elastic wraps. Crucially, audit your prescription medications right now and set a reminder to refill them at least a week before they run dry.

When a storm knocks out power, pharmacies can't access electronic dispensary records, and nobody is handing out prescription pills over a dark counter.

A packed fridge gives you an immediate, unearned hit of confidence. But an unopened fridge only holds safe temperatures for about four hours, and my pantry was full of dry pasta, lentils, and rice — meals that require boiling water and an electric stove. Unless I fancied crunching raw fettuccine in the dark, I had zero edible food past day one.

Do a pantry check for foods that require zero heat and zero added water. Build a reserve of ready-to-eat staples: crackers, canned fish, pull-tab soups, peanut butter, spam, nuts. It won't win culinary awards, but it keeps you fed without burning precious cooking fuel or risking food poisoning on day three.

Municipal water relies on electric booster pumps. If the grid fails, pipe pressure drops fast, or contamination triggers boil-water alerts you can't comply with on a dead stove. My total water reserve was half a fridge filter carafe and a gym bottle on my desk.

Store the emergency baseline: four litres (one gallon) of water per person, per day, split between drinking and basic hygiene. For a 72-hour blackout, keep a minimum of 12 litres per person tucked into a dark cupboard or wardrobe, plus extra if you have pets. It's worth noting that your water heater has around 150-300 liters stored inside it too in case of an emergency.

Digital payments die the instant the power cut hits. Point-of-sale card readers, phone taps, and bank networks go dark, turning plastic and smartwatches into useless props. Checking my own bags, pockets and drawers produced exactly zero physical money.

If you're able, withdraw an emergency cash reserve and stash it. The guidance states between $100 and $500 depending on your family's size, covering essentials if card systems remain offline for several days. If you're like me and withdrawing in one go isn't feasible, simply start tucking away leftover change. Every little helps, and it adds up quickly.

If it plugs into a wall, sits on a vanity, or refuses to work when you need it most, she’s probably written a guide on it. Beyond troubleshooting everyday life, Kaycee is an award-winning poet, a quintessential Aries, and perpetually replaying the same four RPGs on repeat.

#3470. ‘Loser Core,’ ‘EBK,’ and Other Gen Z and Gen Alpha Slang You Might Need Help Decoding

If constantly being mogged by sigmas has you feeling like a fuhuhluhtoogan, and you have no idea what any of that means, you've come to the right place. This glossary aims to define and explain popular slang words and phrases of Generation Z (usually defined as people born between 1997 and 2012) and Generation A (anyone born between 2012 and now) so you'll know what the hell people are talking about.

A word of warning: If you aren't of those generations, and/or you need an online list to know what slang words mean, you should not say them aloud unless you're trying to be embarrassing.

Ballhog: A fashion trend among Gen Z and Gen A characterized by wearing vintage clothes that look normal, even drab, to most, but that people in the know can recognize as interesting or unique retro clothing.

Benny tripping: Intentionally overdosing on Benadryl to experience an (almost always unpleasant) "trip."

Crunged: The past tense of "cringe," "crunged" is often used to describe extreme cringe, like "I cringed so hard I crunged."

EBK: stands for "Extreme Baller Knowledge." It goes beyond the sports reference to apply to to anyone who has deep knowledge of a subject. It's usually used ironically.

GiGis: Good game. Pronounced like the name Gigi. The post game pleasantry "good game" has been a staple in sports since forever. Gamers adopted it and shortened it to "GG" in text. So GiGis is a way of saying "good game."

Glass skin: Describes skin that is so smooth, luminous, and clear, it seems to shine.

Loser core: A youth sub-culture/musical sub-genre categorized by listening to depressing, alternative-inspired music and dressing in drab, oversize clothing.

304: Hoe. (Type "304" on a calculator and turn it upside down.)

4+4: Ate. Four plus four is eight, or "ate." (See "ate.")

6-7 (or 67): This piece of Generation Alpha brainrot slang doesn't mean anything. It's just funny to some people to say "6-7," especially in answer to any question involving numbers. Ex: "Q: What time is it? A: six-seveeen."

6-7 weekend: A weekend in which Saturday falls on the 6th day of the month and Sunday on the 7th.

7x7=49: Often refers to a man who is attractive in a self-evident way. Based on the belief that the equation 7x7=49 makes intuitive sense in a way other equations do not.

80/20 rule: An axiom in online incel spaces, the 80/20 is the idea that 80% of women only date the "top" 20% of men.

Algo speak: Coded language used to bypass online content moderation. Examples: "regarded" used instead of "retarded" and "unalive" instead of "kill."

Alpha male: Taken from animal ethology, an alpha male is the dominant member of a group of males, or just a male who is in charge. (See "beta male" and "sigma male.")

Alpine divorce: An alpine divorce is when a man takes his wife or girlfriend on a hike, usually in the mountains, and then just leaves her there to fend for herself.

ASAP (or A$AP): When a rapper has ASAP or A$AP in front of their name, it indicates affiliation with the ASAP Mob, a New York hip-hop collective.

Ate/eat: Done very well, often regarding clothing. e.g.: "You ate that outfit." See also: "serving."

Aura: Someone who is mysterious and cool is said to "have aura."

Aura battle: Aura is coolness or charisma ("rizz" if you prefer). An "aura battle" is a public contest in which the person with the most aura, as determined by the crowd and/or comment section reaction, wins. (See "Aura")

Aura farming: Depending on the context, “aura farming” can refer to a person who does something cool without trying or someone who is trying too hard to appear cool.

Baby Boo syndrome: A joking reference to people who are very into the Baby Boo memes popular on TikTok.

Baddie: A bad/wild girl. Meant as a compliment.

Baka: Japanese word meaning “crazy" or “foolish.” Used mainly in the anime community.

Bed-rotting: Staying in bed all day. You may know it as “lazing around.” (See "Hurkle-durkle.")

Beez: Popularized in Nicki Minaj's 2012 track "Beez in the Trap," beez means something like "I am always." So "beez in the trap" means "I am always in the trap." (See "Trap.")

Beta male: A beta male, or just "beta," is a weaker, subservient male. (See "alpha male" and "sigma male.")

Boombayah: A euphemism for having sex. It’s used mostly online, often to defeat censorship algorithms.

Bop: A girl who sleeps around. Also: a great song.

Boy aquarium: TikTok slang that describes hockey games.

Boy kibble: The male response to "girl dinner," boy kibble is food boys eat. It usually consists of rice and ground beef, often served without spices or vegetables.

Boysober: Someone who has sworn off sex, relationships, and/or dating.

Brain-rot: A description of the overuse of stupid slang. See also: “Skibidi.” Also used to describe the effects of being overly online.

Brat: The contemporary meaning of "brat" is an adjective describing a person who is edgy, imperfect, and confident. It was coined by pop star Charli XCX who defined it as "that girl who is a little messy and likes to party and maybe says some dumb things sometimes. Who feels herself but maybe also has a breakdown."

Bruzz: Bros. Part of the -uzz family of slang words. See "Huzz" and "-uzz."

Bubba truck: A lifted or otherwise modified pick-up truck.

Catch a fade: To have a fight. (See "fade.")

Chad: An attractive man; an “alpha male.” See "Giga-Chad."

Chat: A reference to streamers addressing their chat windows aloud. Saying “chat” in real life is an ironic joke.

Cheesin': The slang word "cheesin'" refers to smiling, particularly a big, goofy smile. It comes from the common exhortation to "say cheese!" before a photo is taken. The word "cheesing," with a "g" at the end, often means the same thing, but it can also refer to the trend of throwing slices of cheese at cars and/or people.

Chopped: Ugly. Chopped is often applied to someone's face or outfit, but anything that isn't aesthetically pleasing could be called "chopped," as could anything that is generally not good, like an awkward situation.

Choppelganger: A portmanteau of "chopped" and "doppelgänger," a choppelganger is someone who looks like another person, but worse. (See "chopped.")

Chud: A physically unappealing person. Sometimes used for a man who holds right-wing views.

Clanker: A slur aimed at robots and AI agents pretending to be human.

Clock that: "I understand and agree." Not to be confused with older slang, where "clock" meant to see, or even older slang where "clock" meant "to hit or punch."

Corn: “Corn” is algo-speak that means “porn.” Used in online spaces where the word might cause your account to be flagged or banned.

Cortisol-coded: Describes something that's meant to be relaxing but is actually stressful, like watching a video of the 5 a.m. yoga routine of an influencer surrounded by $400 candles.

Coworker-core: A catch-all description for things that are unfunny or uninteresting in a way that appeals to older people.

Cracked: This slang term has two meanings: to have sex, as in "I got cracked last night," and to be really good at something, like "he’s cracked at Fortnite."

Crashout: To have an intense emotional outburst, usually accompanied by impulsive behavior. Crashing out is often due to being overwhelmed or overly frustrated.

D1 Crashout: An epic, elite level, extreme crashout. (See "crashout.)

Dah Bih Gah: "That bitch good," ie: "I like that thing." Usually used to describe food.

Dah Bih Tah: "That bitch tough," ie: "I like that thing." Usually used to describe food.

Dead: Past tense of having died laughing. If someone responds to a joke with "dead" or a skull emoji, they find it funny.

Deadass: Seriously. Used like, "I am deadass not lying."

Deriod: A combination of "dick" and "period," deriod refers to men seeming to experience the mood swings commonly associated with women's menstrual cycles.

Dih: Algo speak for “dick.” (See "Algo speak.")

Doi doi doi: This piece of brain-rot slang doesn't mean anything. It's correctly pronounced by putting your hand up to your mouth and saying "doi doi doi" in a way that sounds funny.

Doomer: A person who is overly negative and/or cynical.

Dwerking: A male-centric variation of twerking. A sexually suggestive dancing characterized by rapid, repeated hip thrusts and shaking of the dick. Other variants include "pwerking" and "bwerking" where the "p" and "b" stand for pussy and boobs.

Edgar: A variation of the Caesar haircut worn especially among Hispanic males. Also refers to the kind of person who wears the haircut.

Fambushing: A combination of "family" and "ambushing," fambushing refers to young people checking where their parents are on location-sharing apps so they can get free food—if you see mom at Chipotle, you ask for a burrito.

Fanum tax: The theft of food between friends. Named for streamer Fanum, known for “taxing” his friends by taking bites of their meals or stealing fries.

Fax, no printer: Telling the truth. Since "fax" and "facts" are pronounced the same, this is a colorful way of saying "facts, no cap."

Fent-fold: A description of the bent-over posture of people nodding on heavy drugs.

Fuhuhluhtoogan: Supposedly from Baltimore slang, this is a nonsense word used so people will ask what it means but never receive an answer. Often paired with "Jittleyang."

Fujoshing: The verb form of the Japanese slang term "fujoshi," fujoshing describes women/girls enjoying media that depicts romantic relationships between men. This word is used almost exclusively in online fandom communities.

Gamer dent: The temporary indentation left on someone’s hair or skin after wearing headphones for too long.

Glaze: To overly praise someone, often insincerely, or with the hope of getting something in return.

Gleek: An older slang term that is gaining prominence lately, gleeking describes squirting saliva from under the tongue.

Glizzy: Hot dog. "Glizzy" was originally slang for Glock or gun, but came to mean hot dog based on the hot dog shape of a Glock's magazine.

Green fn: An interjection one might used when someone does something cool or impressive. Often used ironically.

Goonbait: (See "gooning") Goonbait is, essentially, media that exists to inspiring gooning.

Gooner: A man who goons. (See "gooning.")

Goonette: A woman who goons. (See "gooning.")

Gooning: Extended masturbation without orgasm done for the purpose of entering an altered state of consciousness. (See "gooner," "goonette.")

Gyatt or Gyat: Once an interjection used when seeing someone sexy, like “god-DAMN,” “gyatt” has come to mean “attractive booty.”

Heavy soda: Pop with extra syrup. Some gas station soda machines have settings that control the ratio of syrup to carbonated water. A heavy soda is a soda with the syrup level set very high.

Hewwo: An overly cute way of saying "hello." Usually used online, and often ironically.

HGS: Abbreviation for "home girls" used in comment sections.

Hiplet: Derogatory slang for a woman who has "hip dips," i.e. inward curves on their outer thighs just below the hip bone.

Hozier yell: Named for singer/songwriter Andrew Hozier, a "Hozier yell" refers to the sound one makes when experiencing a peak, climactic, and/or awe-inspiring moment.

HTN: This acronym comes from the online incel community, where fairly good-looking men are described as "high-tier normies" or "HTN." (See "normie.")

Hurkle-durkle: Based on an archaic Scottish word, “hurkle-durkle” means to lounge in bed after it is time to get up. See also: “bed-rotting."

Huzz: -uzz slang for "hoes." See "bruzz" and "-uzz."

"It's giving": Used to convey that something has a specific vibe. Example: "That dude texts you every 10 minutes; it's giving desperate."

"It's so over": The situation is hopeless. The opposite of "we're so back." See also: "Doomer."

IWEL: This comment-section acronym is short for "I wouldn't even lie." Sometimes written as "IWL."

Jelqing: The use of stretching or weights in an attempt to increase penis size.

Jittleyang: Supposedly from Baltimore slang, this is a nonsense word used so people will ask what it means but never receive an answer. See also: "Fuhuhluhtoogan."

JOMO: A play on FOMO (fear of missing out) JOMO is an acronym that stands for “joy of missing out.”

"Learn Chinese": Sports slang directed at failing players. They are in danger of being sent to play in China, so they should "learn Chinese."

Loaded water: Water enhanced with something—a flavor boost, fruit juice, electrolytes, carbonation, and even vitamins or prebiotics. The idea is to increase hydration by making water more palatable.

Looksmaxxing: Maximizing one’s physical attractiveness through personal grooming, working out, and dressing stylishly. See also: “-maxxing.”

🪫 (low battery emoji): The low battery emoji means "I am experiencing emotional depletion, heartbreak, or a general feeling of 'I can't anymore.'"

Lowkenuinely: This mash-up of "low key" and "genuinely" expresses sincerity but in a way that says "let's not make a big deal about it."

Lucky Scoops: Lucky Scoops are a kind of TikTok or Instagram video where buyers purchase a scoop that represents a chance to win merchandise. These videos are very popular with children; critics feel like they are a form of gambling.

Mason (or Mason 6-7 kid): A "Mason 6-7 Kid" or "Mason" is a stereotypical male member of Generation Alpha. Mason kids are known for their love of baseball-inspired fashion (caps and shorts), their "ice cream" haircut, and for repeating brainrot slang like "6-7."

-maxxing: A suffix used with any word to indicate trying to improve. Seeing your friends could be called "friendmaxxing," working out could be called "gymmaxxing," making jokes could be called "jestermaxxing," etc.

Mewing: A facial exercise meant to strengthen the jawline.

Mirror sex: Using a mirror to watch yourself have sex.

Misery girl: A young woman with piercings, a penchant for the darkly dramatic, and highly stylized makeup that makes them appear to have a skinny, pointy nose and huge eyes and lips.

Mog: To be more attractive than someone, usually in an intentional or aggressive way. Example: "I was rizzing up this girl, but he walked in and totally mogged me."

"My 90 in a 30": A song played while driving that inspires speeding.

"My steak is too juicy": The phrase "my steak is too juicy" and other variants like "my lobster is too buttery," are online insults that suggest someone is complaining about something they should be grateful for.

Neurospicy: A different way of saying “neuro-divergent.”

Normie: A person who is considered normal or average. It's sometimes an insult suggesting someone is boring and witless. (see also, "mid.")

NPC: Non-player character. Originally describing video game characters, NPC is now used on the internet to mean people who don't think for themselves.

Opp: Short for "opposition." Someone who is out to get you. An enemy.

Performative male: An insult for young men whose tastes, hobbies, and lifestyle are seen as a performance aimed at obtaining societal approval, especially the approval of young women.

Pheromone maxxing: Trying to influence the behaviors of others through your stink. Supposedly, young men in the "looksmaxxing" community are skipping showers and not washing their clothing in an attempt to make young women like them more. (See "-maxxing").

Phonk: The word phonk can refer to one of two musical sub-genres. It originally referred to throwback '90s hip-hop categorized by slow-tempo "chopped and screwed" production and vintage Memphis rap vocals. It now more commonly describes the heavily distorted, up-tempo EDM used in brainrot videos.

Pink cocaine: Also known as "pink snow," pink cocaine is slang for a powdered drug mixture that usually contains some combination of ketamine, MDMA, meth, opioids, and other substances.

"Press F for respect:" In 2014 video game Call of Duty: Advanced Warfighter, the player attends a funeral and a prompt is given that reads "Press F to pay respects." Now, a singular "F" in a chat window indicates respect. It's usually ironic.

Quiet on the creek: A fishing-inspired way to say "keep it on the down low" or "be cool."

Rawdogging boredom: Rawdogging is "doing something with no safeguards or support," so "rawdogging boredom" is consciously doing nothing.

Regarded: “Regarded” is algo-speak for “retarded."

RegencyCore: A fashion and design aesthetic that springs from the popularity of the fantasy-regency era look of the Netflix show Bridgerton, RegencyCore combines the opulent style of the British Regency era of the early 1800s with fantasy elements like pastel colors and gold accents.

"Reheating your own nachos:" This slang phrase comes from cultural critics in online fandom communities. It refers to performers and/or artists whose new works are seen as trying to recapture what was good about their previous artistic output. It's not always negative; it's possible to successfully reheat your own nachos.

Rizz: As a noun, "rizz" means charisma. As a verb, "rizz" or "rizz up" means attracting someone with your charisma.

Scientology speedrun: Young people running into a Scientology building and acting foolish until they are ejected.

Scorigami: A slang term among football fans for when the final score of an NFL game has never happened before in the league's history. The most recent scorigami was on September 28, 2025, when the Green Bay Packers and Dallas Cowboys tied 40 to 40.

SDIYBT: An acronym for "start digging in your butt, twin," this brainrot phrase doesn't mean anything. Some people just think it's funny to say.

Sendy and “Let’s get sendy": Sendy is an adjective based on the older rock-climbing and extreme sports slang phrase "send it." A shortened version of "ascend it," "send it" is said right before one is about to do something challenging. "Sendy" describes a person who is prone to doing bold things. "Let's get sendy" means something like "Let's get wild." It's been adopted by brainrot fans, so it's often repeated with no meaning meant to be attached.

Serve: Wearing a particularly stylish outfit. See also: "ate."

Serve cunt: To act in a powerfully and unapologetically feminine way; to slay.

Sharking: Looking for people to hook up with.

Side quest: A side quest in a video game is a quest that is not necessary to complete the game's main objective. In slang, a side quest is anything you do in life just for the experience of doing it.

Sigma male: An internet-created male classification, a "sigma male" is as dominant as an alpha male, but is outside the male hierarchy, i.e.: a lone wolf. Originally used seriously, the concept was so widely derided it's now almost always used ironically. (See "Alpha male" and "Beta male.")

Skibidi: Named after “Skibidi Toilet,” a popular series of YouTube videos, “skibidi” itself has no specific meaning, beyond ridiculing the overuse of slang itself. See “brain-rot.”

Skrt: Onomatopoetic word for the sound of tires squealing upon acceleration.

Slopcore: This term describes the countless 100s of millions of cheesy-looking, unsettling, AI-generated images, videos, and songs that have hit the internet since AI was given to the masses a couple of years ago.

Slopper: Insult directed at people who use AI programs too much, people who takes conversations with LLMs too seriously, and people who have basically offloaded their thinking to an algorithm.

Snatched: Very attractive and/or flawlessly styled.

Spawn point: Mother. Based on the spot you start in a video game.

Surf Dracula: A hyper-specific phrase that describes "prestige" television series. The joke is that if there were an older TV show called "Surf Dracula," Dracula would be surfing in every episode, but modern shows would make the whole first season about how Dracula got his surfboard.

Sweat: A person who tries too hard, usually used in reference to video games. The adjective form is "sweaty."

SYBAU: An online acronym that stands for “shut your bitch ass up.”

That's AI: "I don't believe you" or "I doubt it," even when not connected to artificial intelligence.

TLPUR: This supposed acronym section has no meaning. The joke is to tell people it means something like "True Love Pills Until Rope" or "Too Late for Puberty."

Tradwife: Believer in traditional married gender roles.

Trap: Once used to refer to a house where drugs are sold, trap has come to describe both a form of music and any place where one works or hustles.

Treatler (and Treatlerite): "Treatler" and "Treatlerite" are online insults that combine "treat" and "Hitler" to refer to entitled users of services like Doordash or Uber Eats who regard luxury delivery services as a human right, and don't consider the hardships of the people who do the work that makes "private taxis for burritos" possible.

TS: TS originally was AAVE shorthand for "this shit," but it is often used to just mean "this."

Turnt: Excited or intoxicated, or excitedly intoxicated.

Tweaking: In older slang, "tweaking" referred to the nervous and erratic actions of someone on drugs, specifically, speed. Generations A and Z have expanded the definition to refer to any actions that are erratic, or even just mildly energetic, not necessarily related to drug use.

Tylenol baby: After President Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a scientifically dubious link between the active ingredient in Tylenol and autism, kids have been calling each other "Tylenol babies."

Unc: Short for "uncle," used to describe slightly older people. Example: "The class of 2024 are unc-status to the class of 2028." See "yunc."

-uzz: -uzz slang words use "uzz" at the end of any word, so "bros" becomes "bruzz," "hoes" becomes "huzz," "granny" becomes "gruzz," etc.

"We're so back": Opposite of "it's so over."

Venus tummy: When a woman's belly is a little fat, but not too fat, she is said to have a Venus tummy. Named for ancient Greek statues of Venus and Aphrodite who were a little fleshy.

Viking rap: A musical sub-genre consisting of AI-generated Vikings rapping about longboats, raiding, and other Viking things.

Wojack: The name of a style of internet drawings used to quickly stereotype someone. See this post for a full explanation of the Wojak universe.

Yapping: Describes a presentational style often seen on online streams of talking a lot and/or quickly while not saying anything worthwhile.

You the birthday: A phrase that means "you're awesome" or "you're great" in the way a birthday is great: fun, exciting, extra, etc.

Young ho: "Young ho" is both a reclamation of the word "ho" and an expression of youth-based solidarity. Young women are posting videos of themselves defining what makes them "young hos," noting things like "Getting up at 7:50 to be at work at 8," and air-frying chicken nuggets.

Yunc: Yunc is a variation of "unc." In AAVE, a "yn" is a "young n-word." So "yunc" means something like "young uncle," or a person who may be young but has uncle vibes or unc status.

Zoomer Perm: A curly on top, short on the sides haircut popular among young people.

#3469. ‘The Gilded Age’ season 4 review: HBO’s addictive period drama gets darker, juicier and even more watchable

There are few things I enjoy more than settling in for a good soapy period drama, preferably one involving extravagant gowns, vicious social maneuvering, forbidden romances and people getting spectacularly worked up over who gets invited to dinner. So of course, I'm a big fan of “The Gilded Age.” Four seasons in, I'm still thoroughly invested. I've been looking forward to this new chapter for months, and I'm happy to report that HBO's lavish historical drama has delivered another delicious helping of everything I love about it.

Verdict: “The Gilded Age” season 4 is another lavish, deliciously soapy treat, with juicy new conflicts and a terrific ensemble that makes even the smallest social squabbles entertaining. A few storylines stumble, but I'm still more than happy to spend another season among New York's most extravagantly dressed troublemakers.

Release schedule: Episode 1 on Sunday, Nov. 1 at 9 p.m. ET

The new season picks up several months after the events of season 3, with the usual assortment of New York's elite navigating romance, family squabbles, and the delicate business of maintaining their social standing. Bertha Russell (Carrie Coon) and George (Morgan Spector) are facing serious marital difficulties, while their daughter Gladys (Taissa Farmiga) is preparing for motherhood in England.

Across the street, Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) is adjusting to a household where she no longer calls all the shots; Peggy Scott (Denée Benton) is balancing her writing ambitions with her relationship with Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica); and Marian (Louisa Jacobson) and Larry Russell (Harry Richardson) remain frustratingly complicated.

There's plenty happening across these interconnected households, and while some storylines are more compelling than others, season 4 finds the show giving its best characters fresh reasons to scheme, spar, and occasionally make me want to yell at the television. I've seen all eight episodes, but I promise not to reveal too much, as this is a show's plot turns are best enjoyed weekly.

Warning: Light spoilers ahead (not much beyond the trailer)

Kelly most recently reviewed "Nobody Wants This" season 3 and "The Diplomat" season 4."

One of the things I've always loved about “The Gilded Age” is its ability to make seemingly trivial matters feel enormously consequential. A dinner invitation can become a declaration of war.

Season 4 also introduces some genuinely compelling stakes, particularly for the Russell family. I've always enjoyed watching Bertha and George operate as an unstoppable power couple, with her social ambition and his business acumen making them practically invincible. So, seeing them at odds is painful. At the same time, I have to admit that their relationship was in danger of becoming a little too perfect. Now, with their marriage under strain, both have to reckon with what happens when their greatest ally becomes their biggest obstacle.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Coon remains an absolute force as Bertha, who is accustomed to getting what she wants and isn't particularly good at taking no for an answer. Spector gets some terrific material, too, as George grapples with the consequences of getting shot and mounting professional pressures. Their chemistry remains one of the show's biggest assets, and I desperately want these two crazy kids to work things out. But I'm also enjoying the fact that the show isn't making it easy for them.

Meanwhile, Agnes has her own ambitions to pursue, setting up a delicious clash of wills as she and Bertha vie for the opportunity to host President Grover Cleveland (guest star Jim Gaffigan). Baranski is always a treat, particularly when Agnes has a reason to be indignant and mouth off. Seeing these two formidable women competing for the same prize is exactly the sort of society skirmish I break out the popcorn for.

One of the best facets of “The Gilded Age” is its exploration of the world of upper-class Black Americans, and season 4 blessedly gives us more of that. Peggy's growing success as a writer brings new complications as she navigates her upcoming marriage to William and the expectations of his family, particularly his mother, Elizabeth Kirkland Phylicia Rashad), who would make everyone in the r/JustNoMIL subreddit quake. Rashad is simply divine in the role, and I relish seeing her face off against both Peggy and Peggy's mother, Dorothy (Audra McDonald).

Then there's Oscar van Rhijn (Blake Ritson) and Enid Winterton (Kelley Curran), whose unconventional partnership is quickly becoming a favorite storyline. The two make a formidable team, and I love watching them scheme their way toward greater influence in New York society. They're a bona fide power couple in the making; long may their unholy alliance reign.

The show also continues to get plenty of mileage out of the household dynamics between Agnes and Ada (Cynthia Nixon). Baranski and Nixon are such a wonderfully entertaining pairing that I could watch them bicker over curtains for an entire episode. Even the lighter storylines involving the servants and their increasingly complicated lives add to the show's rich ensemble feel. Not every subplot lands with equal force, but there's rarely a dull moment.

My biggest frustration remains Marian and Larry, whose romantic entanglement continues to test my patience. I understand that a TV romance needs obstacles, but at some point, the writers have to give these two a break. Their continued complications seem so contrived. Come on, already!

Still, I have few complaints about "The Gilded Age" season 4. The production design and costumes are a feast for the eyes. This is the kind of show where I want to pause every few minutes just to admire someone's dress or the sheer extravagance of a dinner table. The performances are equally strong, with Coon, Baranski, Benton and Rashad among the standouts.

What I appreciate most is that “The Gilded Age” knows exactly what it is. It can explore serious subjects like race and women's independence while also giving us extravagant parties, romantic scandals and enough high-society backstabbing to fill several lifetimes. Sometimes I want challenging prestige television; other times, I just want to watch Christine Baranski deliver a devastating put-down in a spectacular hat. There's room for both. So, take a glass of champagne and enjoy.

Kelly is the managing editor of streaming for Tom’s Guide, so basically, she watches TV for a living. Previously, she was a freelance entertainment writer for Yahoo, Vulture, TV Guide and other outlets. When she’s not watching TV and movies for work, she’s watching them for fun, seeing live music, writing songs, knitting and gardening.

#3468. iOS 27.2 has two CarPlay improvements, here’s what’s new

iOS 27.2 arrived this week with new features for Messages, Apple TV, and more, plus two improvements for CarPlay. Here’s what’s new for CarPlay users.

Apple Podcasts in iOS 27.2 adds two new sections to the Home tab: ‘New Episodes’ and ‘Continue Playing.’

Essentially, Apple has rethought how the core ‘Up Next’ queue of its Podcasts app works.

Like you would expect, ‘New Episodes’ contains only the latest episodes from your favorite shows. But after you’ve started an episode, you’ll find it in the ‘Continue Playing’ row just below.

This overhaul to podcast management makes it easier to find the latest episodes of your shows and also pick up where you previously left off. I’m a big fan of the change.

Siri AI introduces a variety of upgrades in iOS 27.2, including two that carry over to CarPlay as well.

It can take some adjustment to remember that Siri AI is available in the car just like on iPhone. But CarPlay is an especially useful platform for Apple’s more powerful assistant.

I'm less interested in the "new" look of an app's icon and more interested in an app's actual performance.

It’s arguable whether this qualifies as an “improvement,” but it is a change worth mentioning. iOS 27.2 includes a new app icon for Apple Music, plus some minor design tweaks in the app.

These changes are related to the total rebrand Apple Music unveiled just last week.

For more new features in CarPlay that recently arrived in iOS 27, see our coverage here.

#3467. Final Fantasy 14: Evercold Has A New Release Date After Delay Announced

Final Fantasy 14 has set a new release date for the Evercold expansion after Square Enix officially revealed that the DLC will be delayed. The next big expansion for the critically acclaimed MMORPG is expected to set the game back on its tracks following the mild reception of the Dawntrail expansion. Even though Dawntrail’s post-MSQ content was beloved, its base content was heavily criticized, especially considering how strong the Endwalker expansion was. Final Fantasy 14: Evercold will embrace change, according to game director Yoshi-P. However, it seems we’ll have to wait a while longer before seeing that change.

Over the course of the weekend, Square Enix held the third and final version of this year’s FFXIV Fan Fest, this time around in Japan. These events are not only an opportunity for fans of the game to unite, but also for the company to bring new announcements to the table. According to a new report by IGN, one of the big announcements to come out of the FFXIV Fan Fest in Japan was the reveal that the Evercold expansion is getting delayed. The DLC was originally expected to be released in January 2027.

As seen in the new report, the release date for Final Fantasy 14: Evercold is now February 23, 2027. Those with early access to the content will be able to start playing on February 19, 2027. Based on the report, it doesn’t seem there is an explanation for the delay, so it’s likely only a matter of giving the team more time to polish the content. After all, players can expect a ton of new content in the upcoming expansion. The new DLC will add a brand-new storyline for players to follow.

The expansion will take players to the Fourth, one of the thirteen Reflections created by Hydaelyn during the Sundering. As was previously announced, the DLC will start The Godless Realms Saga for the MMORPG. There are also two new Jobs with Final Fantasy 14: Evercold. Revealed earlier this year, Bastion will be a new role for Tanks. During the FFXIV Fan Fest in Japan, Yoshi-P also revealed the upcoming Zephyr Job, which will be a ranged DPS that uses a crossbow and has a bird companion.

In addition to all of that, Square Enix has also announced that it is getting a massive crossover in the form of Evangelion raids for Final Fantasy 14, as part of the Evercold content. Of course, we’re all hoping that the main story being told in the new expansion is just as great as the ones in the Light and Dark saga – and there’s potential for that, as it will explore what made expansions like Shadowbringers and Endwalker so great.

The pre-orders for the Evercold expansion will open on November 4, and those who acquire it during this period will get a Wind-up Kottr Minion, as well as Halone’s Earring, which will give you an EXP boost for Jobs under level 100 (also, it’s based on the coolest of the Twelve). There’s a lot to look forward to with the new Final Fantasy 14 expansion, and even though it was delayed, we’re only a few months away from it.

#3466. ‘Ghosts’ Is About to Officially “Change the World” With 1 Episode

If you tuned in last week for the return of Ghosts on CBS, you may have noticed that Season 6 looks a little different. After five years, series lead Rose McIver is taking a well-deserved break following the birth of her new baby. The show has conveniently sent her character, Sam, to Australia to film her holiday rom-com “Polar Opposites. In her stead, Ben Feldman’s Kyle has moved into the mansion full-time to look after the ghosts and help Jay (Utkarsh Ambudkar) run the B&B. While we’ll have to wait another month for the next holiday special, I recently sat down with Rebecca Wisocky and Asher Grodman, who play Hetty and Trevor respectively, for an episode of Collider Set Stories, and from the sound of it, Ghosts fans have plenty to look forward to in Season 6.

When asked how the ghosts and the cast are dealing with having Kyle/Ben around full-time, Wisocky laughed, “Oh, we're ruthless with Kyle, even more than Sam, I think. And I love the way Hetty objectifies him so shamelessly as well.” Despite the ghosts' unabashed, bratty behavior with their new living butler, Wisocky was quick to explain that Feldman and his character are “a wonderful addition to the family.” While no one can replace the rom-com dynamic between Sam and Jay, Wisocky has enjoyed watching Feldman and Ambudkar find their own rhythm together in Season 6. “It's really cool to have the two dads attempt to be in charge while we're running ragged all over both of them. It's been a lot of fun,” said Wisocky. “We miss Rose so much, but Ben is a great guy and so good at his job. It's been kind of seamless.”

Answering the same question, Grodman joked that “Ben's a lot to handle. He's a bit of a monster,” before confirming that in reality “he's lovely.” While Feldman has big shoes to fill after five years of McIver setting the tone and leading the cast​​​​​​, Grodman says he “does it beautifully, and he's so funny, and just such a great teammate. And he's smart; he has a great sense of humor. He brings in this fresh energy. It’s like having a new kid at school. It's just fun.” Having Feldman around has also renewed the energy on set, as Grodman explained, “We’re also all so used to the rhythms of this, it's exciting to have a new perspective in the kitchen with us.”

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

While Feldman’s presence has certainly spiced things up for Ghosts, he’s joining an ensemble that knows it takes a village to make a television show truly come to life. Beyond the wonderfully talented cast, Ghosts is created by a massive team of artists and craftspeople. When asked about the people we never see on screen who make her job 100 times easier, Wisocky had plenty to say about the show’s fantastic crew in Montréal. “Carmen Alie and her entire team in the costume department, most especially my dresser, Sophie Godard, are superheroes. […] Zoë Sakellaropoulo is one of the finest production designers working in the business, and if nothing else, she should have received an Emmy nomination by now,” Wisocky told Collider. She continued, shouting out the show’s Director of Photography Michel St-Martin, calling him “a genius, [who makes] our show look like a movie.”

Wisocky also noted that while we’ve heard the Ghosts cast talk about being one big happy family, they really do love each other that much, and that love extends to the crew. “It extends beyond another 250 people that surround us that we work with every day, largely led also by the AD department, the assistant directors who keep our shit together and deal with sometimes impossible circumstances with schedule changes and sometimes late scripts and people becoming unavailable or people being sick. What they manage to do is an art form in and of itself,” she told Collider. She went on to name some of the most essential team members bringing Ghosts to life, saying:

“Our head of the AD department is a woman named Laurence Mercier, and we would be sunk without her. And our 1st AD is Matt Jemus; we would be sunk without him. We have a script supervisor named Jess Lee who gets to direct this season; we just finished the episode that she directed, and it's so wonderful that she's been promoted from within. She's our first Canadian director on the show as well! She did an excellent job. There's a woman named Gloria Cool, who takes care of all the ghost babies, all the ghost muppets, gets us coffee, and makes sure that we know where we're going, and she's invaluable. Saying [she gets] us coffee makes it sound like such a small job, but it's not; she completely holds all of us together in so many ways. She's invaluable.

There are so many people. We love them all: the camera department, the sound department. I mean, it's a very intimate relationship doing this together with 250 people, and it requires that everyone really give a damn and be really good at their job, both individually and together as an ensemble. And they really are; we are very lucky. Every single one of them deserves a shout-out, and they know that. They know how much we love them and value them too.”

Earlier this year at Ghosts' San Diego Comic-Con panel — hosted by Collider’s Perri Nemiroff — co-showrunner Joe Wiseman confirmed that the upcoming annual Christmas special would be a riff on Die Hard after referencing It’s a Wonderful Life and A Christmas Carol last season. Speaking about what to expect from the next two episodes ahead of the show’s weekly return in 2027, Wisocky said, “Utkarsh looks really buff; [he] managed to turn it into a tank top moment that’s for sure.” Both Wisocky and Grodman confirmed that the episode is “very high stakes,” with Wisocky saying, “lots of people are in peril. The stakes are perhaps the highest that they have ever been. And I don't say that lightly.”

Grodman told Collider, “When I heard we were doing Die Hard, I was like, ‘Well, that sounds like Trevor's gonna be involved in that.’ And he is, and he is both an agent of solutions and absolute chaos.” What kind of chaos ensues remains to be seen, but Wisocky teased that “there will be something that happens that completely changes the world. That sounds like something general. I can't get more specific, but it's true.” Continuing, she hinted that “there's an opportunity for one of the ghosts to go to town with a special skill that is really enjoyable and was very enjoyable to all of us. There's a claustrophobic aspect to some of it. It's very action-packed.”

Shouting out the show’s incredibly talented crew once more, Wisocky had high praise for Alie and Sakellaropoulo’s work on the special, and especially St-Martin’s work as the DP. “I think our show looks like a film. And that is largely because of his photography. He and his whole team are really remarkable artists, but he's one of the best DPs I've ever worked with. So big, big shout out to him, and there's a lot more fun stuff that he gets to do as a DP, given the fact that this is kind of an action-packed episode,” said Wisocky. Grodman meanwhile, also had some lovely things to say about his co-stars, saying, “It's a very talented cast, and some people in this cast really get to flex some muscles in that episode and get to do a lot of transforming.” While both stars remained tight-lipped on the impending ghost-on-ghost possession that Wiseman also revealed at SDCC, Grodman did confirm that having Kyle around may finally give Trevor someone to celebrate Hanukkah with. “There is a little bit of Hanukkah in the episode. And yes, there is a Trevor/Kyle connection, and it's a fun one. I'll leave it at that.”

While we’ll only have the two holiday specials to get fans through the end of 2026, Ghosts will return full-time in early 2027 and, with Season 6, Episode 6, will mark the 100th episode of the show’s tenure on CBS. At New York Comic-Con, Wiseman and the cast revealed that not only would the episode see the ghosts’ favorite reality show, “It’s Getting Hot in Here,” coming to film at the mansion, but that the episode would include appearances from Survivor alum Parvati Shallow as the host, and returning favorite Matt Walsh as Hetty’s demonic ex-husband, Elias. When Wisocky found out Shallow would be part of the episode, she was overjoyed as a Survivor fan. “I'm a big Survivor head, as you know. I was so thrilled to do those Survivor promos [in 2024]. And so when I heard that Parvati was coming, I was so excited. She had a lot of fun, and she was very indulgent with my bajillion questions that I asked about Survivor and how it works.”

Teasing the return of Elias, who typically shows up at least once a season to throw a wrench in the world of Woodstone and sow havoc amongst the living and the dead, Wisocky said, “The fact that, of course, horrible, horrible Elias is going to be there to rain on our parade. He throws a stick in the works, of course, but it was fun.” Continuing, she told Collider: “I think it's very cool. It's very meta that it's a show about TV, and it's our 100th episode, and it just highlights that our [the ghosts] favorite show is just so very lowbrow, but we treat it like such high art. I mean, the stakes for us with that show are very high, for Thor, especially. Devan Chandler Long has a very, very funny episode for the 100th with his relationship to the making of this reality show. It was a lot of fun.”

Ghosts will return for a 1-hour Christmas special on December 10, followed by a mid-season premiere for the rest of Season 6 in 2027. Stay tuned at Collider for more, and check out our full episode of Set Stories with Grodman and Wisocky below.
