Episode 1: Tropical Seas | Sunday, November 1

The warm, sunlit waters of the tropics support the greatest diversity of life in the ocean. Yet even in these seemingly familiar seas, astonishing new behaviours are still being discovered.

Episode 2: Open Ocean | Sunday, November 8

The Open Ocean is Earth’s largest wilderness. Covering more than half the planet, it appears to be an endless blue desert. Yet beneath its vast surface lies a world of extraordinary life, where survival depends on endurance, tenacity and teamwork.

Episode 3: Seasonal Seas | Sunday, November 15

Sitting between the tropical and polar oceans, the Seasonal Seas are among the most changeable waters on Earth. Here, life must endure fierce winters, violent storms and scorching summers, pushing animals to be resourceful, adaptable and adventurous.

Episode 4: Polar Waters | Sunday, November 22

Though they lie at the ends of the Earth, the polar seas help drive a global network of ocean currents that shape life across the planet. From Antarctica and the Arctic come powerful flows of water which transport oxygen and nutrients around the world, creating extraordinary opportunities beneath the ice and supporting wildlife far beyond it.

Episode 5: The Deep | Sunday, November 29

A journey into the last great frontier on Earth. Hidden beneath the ocean's surface lies a vast and largely unexplored world of deep coral reefs, underwater mountains, volcanoes and hydrothermal vents, home to some of the most extraordinary discoveries of our time. As new technology takes us deeper than ever before, astonishing creatures and entire ecosystems are revealed in spectacular detail.

Episode 6: Future Seas | Sunday, December 6

Our ocean is facing immense challenges, but for the first time, we have the knowledge and tools to help it recover. Future Seas follows the scientists, conservationists and communities working to secure a healthier future for the world's oceans.

The team behind "Blue Planet III" shot across the globe over a four year period, filming on every continent and in every ocean, including Japanese rock pools, Antarctic research stations, the seas around Australia and the open oceans.

There is no dedicated spin-off showing how the team captured the stunning aquatic footage, however, the final 10-15 minutes of each installment usually go behind the scenes, charting the production of the preceding episode.

Recently having celebrated his 100th birthday, Sir David Attenborough returns to provide the narration for "Blue Planet III", completing the trilogy, following his work on the "Planet Earth" series.

#3439. Firefox’s AI-powered Smart Window gets form autofill and website monitoring

Mozilla today announced two new features for Smart Window, its opt-in AI-powered browsing experience in Firefox. Here are the details.

Nearly one year ago, Mozilla announced plans to introduce AI Window, an opt-in experience that would let Firefox users interact with an AI assistant while browsing, with features like summarizing content, comparing information across tabs, and answering questions without leaving the browser.

Since then, the feature has been renamed Smart Window, and it has gradually gained new capabilities.

A few months ago, for instance, Mozilla introduced AI-powered web search to Smart Window, alongside automatic tab grouping, duplicate tab detection, and the ability to search browsing history using natural language.

Today, the company announced two additional features rolling out to Smart Window beta users: AI-powered form filling and website monitoring.

As Mozilla explains, the AI-powered form-filling feature can draw context from other open tabs to suggest answers for web forms. This means it goes beyond traditional autofill, which typically handles basic information like names, addresses, and contact details, by generating responses based on information found on other currently open pages.

For example, Smart Window could use information from your online portfolio or professional profile to fill in your work history, or draw on those details to draft an answer to a question like “Tell me about a time when…” Firefox’s regular autofill still handles saved information such as your name and address, which can be entered directly into forms without relying on AI models.

Mozilla notes that the feature relies on Google’s Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite model to analyze form fields and extract relevant information from selected tabs, meaning that information from those pages is shared with the AI model for processing.

The second feature rolling out today is website monitoring, which works similarly to Safari’s new “Notify Me” feature introduced with iOS 27 and macOS 27.

It lets users type /watch in the Smart Window chat to tell Firefox to monitor webpages for specific changes, such as price drops, product availability, or new job listings. Firefox then notifies users when those changes are detected.

Users can choose between daily and weekly checks, with up to 5 webpages per task, though monitoring runs only while Firefox is open.

When there’s a match, you’ll see an update through the Tasks button in the toolbar. With desktop notifications enabled, Firefox can also notify you directly; click the notification to open the watched pages. You can have up to 15 active tasks at a time, and you can edit, pause or delete tasks. Smart Window will automatically pause tasks after 60 days without a matching change. If 90 days pass without a change, it will stop checking altogether.

As with AI-powered form filling, the feature relies on an AI model to process information, although in this case Mozilla uses Qwen to identify changes that match what users are looking for.

Both new features are now available in the Smart Window beta for Firefox desktop, though they’re currently limited to English-language users in the US and Canada. Mozilla says they will “roll out to additional markets in the coming months.”

To learn more about these features and how to use them, follow this link.

In a roundup of what to expect from tomorrow’s “Pro and Tell” event, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman shared new details about the upcoming OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro models. Here’s what to expect.

Tomorrow, Apple is expected to announce its first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro models, featuring OLED displays, Dynamic Island, and a thinner, lighter design.

While previous reports have suggested that the new models will come with significantly higher prices, Bloomberg now offers more specific figures, along with additional details about their redesign.

According to Gurman’s sources, “Apple has discussed charging $2,899 for the new 14-inch model with an M5 Pro chip,” which, if Apple applies at least the same $400 premium to the 16-inch model, would mean “the new version will cost at least $3,399.”

Compared to the $2,199 and $2,699 starting prices of the 14-inch and 16-inch M5 Pro MacBook Pro models before Apple’s June price hikes, that would represent an increase of at least $700 in just four months.

Gurman added that “Apple plans to continue selling the non-touch versions alongside the new machines,” and further commented on that in a post on X:

I do not expect the current non-touch MacBook Pros (14 inch at $2499 and 16-inch at $2999) to go anywhere tomorrow. Retail stores are fully stocked up on those as well still. https://t.co/UTs2NJ1N3A

In other words, he expects the new OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro models to sit at the top of Apple’s current laptop lineup, rather than replacing the existing M5 Pro and M5 Max models.

However, users looking to get the redesigned hardware will likely have to pay the premium, regardless of whether they actually want a touchscreen.

At $2,899, the 14-inch model would mark the highest starting price for a new MacBook Pro model, surpassing the $2,799 Apple charged for a 17-inch version introduced in 2006. The pricing would also put Apple among the most expensive makers of touch-screen laptops, alongside premium offerings from Dell Technologies Inc. that also feature OLED displays.

Beyond the OLED touchscreen, Gurman reaffirmed that the new MacBook Pro models will feature a slightly thinner design, thinner bezels, a noticeably lighter body, and a redesigned hinge to prevent the screen from moving when touched, all of which we covered earlier today here.

The report also adds a new detail: Apple has reworked the cooling system to improve airflow through the hinge while helping reduce the computers’ weight.

I was holding off replacing my 2021 MBP in hops of getting a new touchscreen model. However, I can't pay a $3k starting price for one!

Apple has been pricing me out of multiple products this year because I can't justify the big price increases the put in place.

Finally, Gurman’s report offers some behind-the-scenes details about how Apple decided to bring touchscreens to the Mac. According to his sources, Tim Cook greenlit the touchscreen MacBook Pro project roughly four years ago, in part because the feature had become one of the most requested by Apple customers.

“He said we should just do it,” according to a person with knowledge of the decision.

Gurman added that Ternus oversaw development of the new MacBook Pro models. According to the report, Ternus believed “Apple had fallen behind in the area and indicated internally that touch screens had become table stakes for laptops, making it time for the company to embrace the technology.”

According to the report, Apple plans to open preorders for the new touchscreen MacBook Pro models tomorrow, October 28, with availability potentially beginning as early as November 6, alongside the new M6-powered Macs announced today.

#3434. How to Export Your Arc Data to a New Browser

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you've been a dedicated Arc browser user, the time has finally come to say goodbye. The Browser Company paused development of Arc in 2025, continuing only with security updates. As announced late last week, Arc will officially sunset on Dec. 22, 2026, giving users two months to transition their data to an alternative.

One option is to move to the company's new AI-focused Dia browser, though there are other (potentially better) choices depending on what you're looking for. Most data from Arc—including Spaces, Favorites, pinned tabs, and folders as well as passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history—will transition automatically over to Dia, but if you're switching to a different platform entirely, you'll need to take what you can with you before Dec. 22.

Officially, Arc supports exporting Spaces and tabs only, and the resulting Export.md plain-text file is simply a list of links that you can open and bookmark in your new browser. MacOS users can initiate this process via Arc > Settings > Advanced > Export Data and saving the file to a preferred location. On Windows, open the Arc menu, select Settings, and go to Export Spaces and tabs > Export Data.

To simply copy and paste every link from one folder, right-click the folder, select Copy All Links, and paste them wherever you'd like (select Copy All Links as Markdown to keep link titles on macOS). You can also save Easels as images by tapping the share icon > Share Via... and selecting PNG.

There's no formal process to export other Arc data. If you saved logins in Arc, now is a good time to start moving credentials over to a different platform. (Our top picks for password managers aren't tied to a single browser.)

There are a few alternatives to Arc's official export process, which is highly manual and doesn't keep your folder structure intact. There are several third-party scripts available (for free) that can facilitate the transition as well as a paid extension called ArcEscape that can export folders and pinned tabs and import into another browser. The extension is available for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Firefox. According to Arc's FAQ, all user accounts will be deactivated on Dec. 22, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days of deactivation.

In a crowded market of over-ear noise-canceling headphones, it can be tricky to find a pair with a distinctive style that stands out from the rest. Enter the retro-futuristic line of statement-making Nothing headphones. One of the brand’s popular pairs, the Nothing Headphone (1), is 33% off and down to $199 (originally $299), marking a record-low price.

The Nothing Headphone (1) pairs spatial head tracking audio with adaptive ANC, providing up to 80 hours of playback with ANC off and 35 hours with ANC on. The headphones support Bluetooth multipoint, high-resolution LDAC, AAC, and SBC, but can also be played through a 3.5mm or USB-C cable. If you still want to remain aware of your surroundings, you can turn on transparency mode. #3428. Apple wins expanded access to evidence in OpenAI trade secrets lawsuit

Apple has scored another win in its trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees, OpenAI, and io Products. Here are the details.

Earlier this month, Judge Edward Davila granted some of Apple’s requests for expedited discovery in the lawsuit where the company accuses two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), as well as OpenAI and io Products, of trade secret misappropriation.

As we’ve been covering since July, Apple filed this lawsuit accusing the defendants of improperly accessing or using confidential information about its products and technologies to help advance OpenAI’s consumer hardware development efforts.

As part of the lawsuit, Apple asked Judge Davila to issue a preliminary injunction (aimed at preventing the defendants from further using its alleged trade secrets), as well as expedited discovery to obtain early access to internal documents, forensic evidence, and employee testimony.

In his decision partially granting Apple’s request for expedited discovery, Judge Davila gave the company early access to select internal documents, forensic evidence, and employee testimony.

However, he postponed ruling on several other requests, finding Apple’s definition of “Apple Originated Information” too broad.

Following the decision, Apple and the defendants agreed on a narrower definition of the term, which Judge Davila has now adopted (with modifications), allowing Apple to pursue additional discovery.

In his new decision, Judge Davila granted several of Apple’s previously deferred requests, expanding the company’s access to records concerning its former employees’ handling of confidential information, their use of AI tools, and OpenAI’s recruitment and hardware development practices.

That said, he also denied Apple’s requests for details about OpenAI’s own devices and accounts, its internal investigations, and any potential deletion of confidential Apple information.

He also denied two additional requests for corporate testimony, finding that they were “too broad at this stage and better suited for merits discovery,” meaning Apple can pursue them through the regular discovery process.

Under the new order, the defendants have up to 14 days to produce the requested records and respond to Apple’s questions.

Why you should watch it: Though inspired by real events, the MGM+ series takes the story further, turning it into a gripping, character-focused thriller that delves into the complex dynamic between Heckman and Kiritsis as their increasingly tense conversations play out. In the show's tense and poignant conclusion, Fred must do everything he can to keep Tony alive (and keep his dead-man's switch from triggering) when they’re thrust into the spotlight.

#3425. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

#3424. New M6 Macs buck Apple’s second wave of price hikes

In addition to the spec bumps, today’s M6-powered iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro announcements came with an extra piece of good news: prices remained unchanged from the previous generations, unlike several other recent Apple product launches that brought another round of increases. Here are the details.

Earlier today, Apple announced two new M6-powered Macs, which start at the same prices as their predecessors.

And while both models benefit from the faster M6 chip, iMac buyers are also getting more CPU and GPU cores for the same price, as the base model now comes with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, up from the 8-core CPU and 8-core GPU in the previous generation’s M4 chip.

As 9to5Mac readers probably remember, Apple raised prices across much of its product lineup in June, including the iMac, which went from $1,299 to $1,499, and the 14-inch MacBook Pro, which went from $1,699 to $1,999.

At the time, the company also hiked prices for the HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K, and iPad mini, all of which saw new versions announced recently with yet another price bump.

The HomePod mini, which went from $99 to $129 in June, now costs $149 with the second-generation model. The Apple TV 4K, which previously started at $129, jumped to $199 in June, while the new generation starts at $299 (albeit with twice the storage). And the iPad mini, which went from $499 to $599 in June, now starts at $699 with the OLED model announced earlier this week.

And while iPhone prices were left untouched during the June increases, that changed in September with the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which now start at $1,199 and $1,299, respectively, up $100 from their predecessors.

Apple also raised prices by $100 for the older iPhone models still in its lineup, including the iPhone 17, iPhone Air, and iPhone 17e.

In Europe, the MacBook Pro did get a price hike of € 100 (on top of the previous price hike).

With that in mind, although the new M6-powered Macs are far from cheap, it’s still good news that they didn’t come with another price hike on top of the June increases.

Things are looking way less promising for those waiting for tomorrow’s expected OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro models, however, with Bloomberg reporting that Apple has discussed a $2,899 starting price for the 14-inch model. If Apple applies the same rumored $400 premium to the current 16-inch model, which starts at $2,999, the new version could cost $3,399 or more.

That, in turn, makes Apple’s decision to keep prices unchanged for today’s M6-powered Macs all the more welcome, especially for buyers who were already dreading the possibility of having to shell out even more after waiting for the new models. Whether that will hold remains to be seen.

What’s your take on Apple’s pricing strategy for the M6 Macs announced earlier today? Let us know in the comments.
